00_about/category-specification.title: Category Specification
00_about/category-specification.content:
Category Specification
Reader sections and primary subjects
A page’s subject determines its category. Progress, historical era, complexity and narrative importance do not.



































SectionPrincipal subjectMain questionMaterialsNatural, prepared or manufactured physical stockWhat properties and usable stock does this supply?SkillsPractised physical, perceptual, cognitive or social abilityWhat must a person learn to control or judge?Tools and EquipmentFunctional objects, components, carriers, clothing and machineryWhat object supplies the function?Technologies — Processes and SystemsA production workflow or coordinated continuing operationHow do inputs, controls and maintenance deliver the outcome?Structures and PlacesConstructed site frameworks/infrastructure, plus named locations in a separate atlasWhat is built here, or what does this location permit and constrain?
Reflections is a narrative/strategic section, alongside Survival. About, eras, mission routes and reference notes are other document roles.
Design families rather than use-by-use pages
Use Page Scope and Organisation. One authoritative page covers a design family and its meaningful variants. Construction, operation, inspection, repairs and failure modes belong on that page. A variation is a section unless it has a substantially different mechanism, dependency set or independent use across families.
Atlatl Dart covers blunt practice, fletched and pointed configurations. The recorded green unfletched specimen is one variant, not an invention requiring separate practice-dart and hunting-dart pages. Atlatl includes its simple assembly routes. Plant-Fibre Mats covers a small bedding pad and prospective larger or wearable variants without claiming that all have been made.
Keep Dart Shafts as intermediate stock: straightness, stiffness, defects and moisture concern the material before a dart exists. Keep Atlatl Throwing and Projectile Testing as reusable practitioner abilities. A use label does not create another physical object.
Measurement and other boundary cases
Measuring and recording are skills. Measurement and Records teaches reference comparison, counting, observation and reliable notation. Marked Reference Staff is equipment. A later shared calibration or standards service would be a technology/system when its reproducible references, procedures, responsibilities and checks need a separate page. It is not acquired by making one staff.
Twining is a skill; Plant-Fibre Mats is equipment. Bast Fibre and Bark Cordage are stocks, with Simple Cordage supplying the practised technique. Nettle Retting is a distinct changing batch process with readiness checks, not merely a motor action.
Clay Vessel describes equipment; Clay Vessel Making describes forming and drying; Pottery describes the larger verified ceramic-production chain. Those stages retain separate pages because their controls and acceptance differ. The failed vessel does not demonstrate the whole chain. Pit Firing is a firing operation; Kiln is a constructed firing enclosure.
Structures versus equipment
A structure chiefly arranges a site, creates a usable enclosure or supports a fixed working/resting area: shelter, camp drying framework, kiln enclosure and later built storage, bridges or waterworks. Its page includes location requirements, construction, loads, access, operation, inspection and maintenance.
A tool chiefly performs an object function: knife, vessel, spindle, spear thrower, mat, heating stone, machine or component. Portability alone is not the test. A stationary machine remains equipment; the building and foundations that house it are structures. A fixed camp drying frame belongs with structures; a small removable drying accessory can be equipment.
The three existing constructed-space pages—Basic Lean-to, Drying Rack and Kiln—now live under Structures and Places. Classification does not build a planned kiln.
Places are location records, not capability unlocks
A place records a particular location’s terrain, approaches, water, use, dangers, occupants and dated changes. Projectile Practice Ground is the named trial site in this valley. Selecting and checking a practice site is explained in Projectile Testing, so the local place page need not pretend to be a universal technology.
Traveller’s Camp, Neanderthal Clearing, Meeting Ground and Fallback Bench are atlas entries linked to Valley Map. A visited place does not prove ownership, safety, a supplied refuge or a manufactured asset.
Structures participate in the capability dependency graph. Local places do not: record their use or observation in daily location fields and describe necessary operating conditions in the relevant handbook page. Physical markers already accounted for remain accounted for; relocating a page changes no inventory.
Metadata and browsing
Capability types are material, skill, tool, technology and structure. Place uses type: place and is an atlas role, not a sixth invention category. Each capability has one matching primary tag, valid subtype and one or more domains. Place entries also have domains for cross-topic browsing.
Material subtypes: natural-resource, prepared-material, intermediate-stock, food, fuel. Skill subtypes: technique, judgement, identification, communication. Tool subtypes: implement, container, carrier, clothing, apparatus, component, toolkit, weapon, trap. Technology subtypes: process, system. Structure subtypes: shelter, framework, enclosure, infrastructure. Place subtypes: camp, clearing, working-area, candidate-site.
Folders are 03_Materials, 04_Skills, 05_Tools and Equipment, 07_Technologies and 06_Structures and Places. The last section has distinct Structures and Places subfolders. Function/design-family subfolders organise equipment, including Projectiles. 02_Reflections contains the lunar reviews. Reader order is now 00 About, 01 Survival, 02 Reflections, 03 Materials, 04 Skills, 05 Tools and Equipment, 06 Structures and Places, 07 Technologies, 08 Eras, 09 Reference and 10 Mission. Stable page IDs and aliases preserve identity when sections move.
Stable IDs survive moves and renaming; a historical ID prefix is not the current category. Merged pages retain one canonical ID and old names/path aliases, with removed IDs recorded in the migration manifest. Dependencies link direct requirements for the specified route; no self-dependency is created by an object absorbing its own assembly page.
Topic Index browses the five capability categories together and links relevant atlas places separately. Page Templates, Style Guide and Vault Maintenance define authoring and regeneration. Acquisitions are derived from events, not from folder location or a new name.

00_about/introduction.title: The Mission and the Handbook
00_about/introduction.content:
The Mission and the Handbook
In your departure civilisation, an asteroid threatens Earth. The available knowledge and industrial capacity do not provide a functioning way to avert the impact in time. A one-way time machine offers a speculative alternative: send one prepared person far enough into the past to give civilisation a longer technological runway.
You volunteer. Your cells are modified so that you do not age. You can still be injured, become ill and die. Only your living body can make the journey. You arrive without clothing, tools, cargo or implants.
Before departure, humanity’s accumulated technical knowledge is embedded in your long-term memory. You also practise essential primitive techniques. You can remember a machine’s design; you cannot make it without its materials, tools, energy, tolerances and supporting workforce.
The task
You arrive in northern Iberia around 40,000 calibrated years BP. Your first work is shelter, food, water and fire. Soon you meet people whose field skills exceed your own. Progress will depend on exchange and cooperation as well as invention.
The handbook follows dependencies from natural materials to an industrial society capable of spaceflight and, ultimately, planetary defence. It asks which steps are unavoidable, which have alternatives, and which historical delays could be shortened by knowledge and suitable conditions.
A discovery date is not a physical prerequisite. You do not have to repeat all of archaeological history. You do have to establish every capability on which your chosen route depends.
Reading the vault

Survival: the traveller’s particular experience, currently continuous Days 1–50, titled by Moon and Day. Outcomes here are contingent.
Reflections: the arrival appraisal and state-of-play reviews at new/full moon milestones; begin with Reflections.
Materials: natural and manufactured stocks, described by their properties, condition and uses.
Skills: abilities developed through practice, including physical techniques, observation, judgement and communication.
Tools and Equipment: design families of functional objects, including containers, carriers, clothing, components and machinery.
Structures and Places: reusable construction pages and a separate atlas of named sites; begin with Structures and Places.
Technologies — Processes and Systems: arrangements of resources, equipment, skills and operating conditions that deliver an outcome or continuing service.
Eras: historical orientation, not gates controlling availability.
Reference: dependencies, evidence, continuity and project roadmap.
Mission: a reading route through cooperation, knowledge transmission and the systems needed to sustain production.

The full definitions and boundary cases are in Category Specification. A bark vessel and a clay vessel are both equipment; their manufacturing and water-treatment routes are processes. An object page can include construction instructions. Topic Index groups related pages across the five capability categories, with atlas places separately linked, including containers.
Begin with Setting Specification, Valley Map, Survival Ledger, Capability Dependency Map and Civilisation Roadmap. The map establishes the first valley’s terrain, camp layout and travel assumptions. Mission Coordination introduces the social capabilities. Authoring conventions are in Style Guide, Page Scope and Organisation and Page Templates; rebuilding views and exports is explained in Vault Maintenance.
The knowledge in your memory supplies possible routes. The handbook explains what is needed to make those routes work.

00_about/page-scope-and-organisation.title: Page Scope and Organisation
00_about/page-scope-and-organisation.content:
Page Scope and Organisation
The page unit
Write a page for a reusable subject that a handbook reader can find and apply. The daily narrative may first encounter a narrow specimen; its state is a case study inside the broader subject.
Use a design family for equipment and structures. Describe the common function and mechanism, then give variants and their different inputs, tests and limits. Add folders for related families rather than spawning a page for every intended use.
For example, Projectiles contains Atlatl Dart. Its blunt practice, feathered and pointed variants share a shaft and rear engagement. The Day 30 specimen is identified in a current-narrative-state section. It does not warrant a separate hunting-dart page later. Arrows and other substantially different projectile families can receive their own pages when needed; no empty acquisition pages are pre-created.
When to combine
Combine pages when they repeat the same object-specific construction, operating checks and inputs. Atlatl now includes the former assembly page; Atlatl Dart includes the former dart-making route. Plant-Fibre Mats includes the first small bedding-pad trial rather than restricting the handbook to that specimen. Split Wood Strips describes the intermediate stock with willow as the current route.
Keep an object’s simple recipe on its equipment page. A heading can explain a variant, repair, material option or intended use. A variant being described does not mean it has been built, tested or acquired.
When to split
A separate page earns its place by answering a distinct reusable question:

Material: stock condition and properties before allocation; for example Dart Shafts.
Skill: a person’s practised control or judgement across specimens; for example Atlatl Throwing, Projectile Testing or Twining.
Process/system: a distinct workflow, changing batch, multi-output production, coordinated service or acceptance stage; for example Nettle Retting, Pottery or Food Reserve Management.
Structure: a built site framework or enclosure; for example Basic Lean-to or Kiln.
Place: the particular site and its dated access/state; for example Projectile Practice Ground.

A production stage such as Clay Vessel Making can retain its own page when it explains greenware and drying controls used for several later ceramic outputs. Naming three steps does not by itself justify three pages.
A scalable equipment page
Use: function and common design; base construction and inputs; variants; operating and acceptance tests; maintenance/failures; current narrative instance; evidence and alternatives. Give the YAML prerequisites for one explicit base route. Optional stone points or feathers do not become requirements for a blunt unfletched route.
Dates refer to the first documented limited instance, not to every variant on the broadened page. Record later specimen and variant states in the daily ledger. One material allocation cannot furnish several designs.
Navigation and preservation
Projectiles groups projectile families. Structures and Places separates reusable construction knowledge from the valley atlas. Reflections appraises the situation at moon milestones without manufacturing capabilities.
Preserve old names as aliases when moving or combining pages and rebase local images. Keep approved art and historical prompts; a moved note does not require a regenerated image. Update dependencies, topic views and galleries. Historical source archives remain historical, while live links use the canonical page.
Do not create parallel pages solely to fill each category, distinguish practice from hunting, or give each captured animal’s product another name. A different mechanism or independently useful production route is a stronger reason to split than a different scene.

00_about/page-templates.title: Page Templates
00_about/page-templates.content:
Page Templates
Reference page
Choose the primary subject using Category Specification, then copy the shared metadata and the appropriate category outline. Replace the example values. Required subtype and domains describe the page; unknown dates and dependency lists remain null or empty rather than speculative.
---
id: tool-example
title: Example Tool
type: tool
tags: [tool]
subtype: implement
domains: [woodworking]
aliases: []
status: draft
evidence: [physical-reasoning, research-needed]
sources: []
prerequisites: []
alternatives: []
improvements: []
demonstrated_day: null
reviewed_on: 2026-10-01
---

The stable type codes are material, skill, tool, technology and structure; tool displays as Tools and Equipment, technology as Technologies — Processes and Systems, and structure as Structures. Use exactly one primary type tag. Keep the stable ID when reclassifying a page. Subtype values and available topic domains are defined in Category Specification and tools/category_model.py.
Materials
Use type: material and a subtype such as natural-resource, prepared-material, intermediate-stock, food or fuel.
# Example Material
## Stock, composition and condition
## Identification, sourcing and preparation
## Properties and intended uses
## Batch checks and failure signs
## Allocation, storage and losses
## Alternatives and evidence

Describe input versus finished stock, useful quantity, condition and allocation. Link to production methods without treating the finished output as their raw input. Manufacturing does not turn a stock page into an equipment page.
Skills
Use type: skill and subtype: technique, judgement, identification or communication.
# Example Skill
## Ability and scope
## Equipment, materials and prior abilities
## Practice and control
## Feedback, diagnosis and failure signs
## Demonstration, operating limits and further practice
## Alternatives and evidence

Explain what the person must perceive, control and learn. An ordered technique can remain a skill. Give an observable demonstration while keeping practice, mastery and performance in unfamiliar conditions distinct.
Tools and Equipment
Use type: tool and a subtype such as implement, container, carrier, clothing, apparatus, component, toolkit, weapon or trap.
# Example Equipment
## Object, function and scope
## Form, materials and construction
## Assembly or manufacturing routes
## Operation and handling
## Construction and performance tests
## Maintenance, repair and limits
## Alternatives and evidence

Include useful construction instructions on the object page. Link a separate manufacturing process only when it adds a distinct route or substantial workflow. Specify actual capacity and coverage rather than assuming that construction proves performance. Selected natural tools, fixed structures, machines and experimental specimens all fit this category.
Technologies — Processes and Systems
Use type: technology and subtype: process or system.
# Example Process or System
## Outcome or continuing service
## Inputs, equipment, skills and operating conditions
## Stages and controls
## Outputs, completion and acceptance tests
## Time, labour, throughput and ongoing supply
## Failures, maintenance and fallback routes
## Alternatives, scaling and evidence

Explain the organised operation. A batch process has an output and completion criteria; a continuing system also needs replenishment, responsibilities and maintenance. Separate producing a specimen, passing an operating test and establishing reliable supply.
Requirements in prose should explain the YAML links. Alternative methods need their own stated requirements. Dependencies can cross categories in any direction consistent with the actual route. Use only headings that serve the page; do not fill a template with empty boilerplate.
Structures
Use type: structure, subtype: shelter, framework, enclosure or infrastructure. Store under 06_Structures and Places/Structures. Include site requirements, construction/materials, access and loads, operating conditions, inspection, repair and limits. One structure page covers a family and its meaningful variants; constructing it does not demonstrate every operation within it.
Places
Places are atlas records outside the capability graph, stored under 06_Structures and Places/Places.
---
id: place-example
title: Example Place
type: place
tags: [place]
subtype: working-area
domains: [environment]
aliases: []
status: draft
evidence: [setting-choice]
sources: []
first_observed_day: null
reviewed_on: 2026-10-04
---

Use camp, clearing, working-area or candidate-site subtypes. Describe terrain and bearings, approach/return, water, observed use, occupants/rights, hazards and dated state. Link general methods rather than duplicating them. Omit demonstrated_day and manufacturing prerequisites. A site has no invented inventory.
Daily narrative
---
id: survival-day-029
title: Moon 1 Day 29 - Working Title
type: survival
tags: [survival]
status: draft
day: 29
demonstrates: []
community_demonstrates: []
locations_used: []
locations_observed: []
location_events: []
evidence: [setting-choice, physical-reasoning]
sources: []
fuel_collected_kg: 0
fuel_used_kg: 0
water_treated_l: 0
water_untreated_l: 0
work_budget: {}
asset_events: []
food_events: []
work_hours: 0
sleep_hours: 0
ongoing_processes: []
illustration: null
illustration_scene: null
illustration_checked_on: null
---
# Moon 1 Day 29 - Working Title
## Today's constraint
## Work and observations
## End of day
## Next decision

A demonstration is a wiki-link to the capability actually used. An asset event has asset, change, unit, state and reason. Use stable asset keys such as pot-a or needle-a. Construction, disposal, repair and gifting are separate events. The validator replays quantities. For example: {asset: bark-cord, change: -0.5, unit: m, state: allocated to ties, reason: clothing}. A zero change updates the state of an existing object; it cannot create one.
A food event has lot, change_kg, disposition and reason. Disposition is collected, consumed, processed or lost; calorie accounting uses this explicit field rather than interpreting prose. Weight is edible mass, after shelling or dressing. Separate fresh game by catch so it cannot reappear after consumption. For example: {lot: rabbit-day29, change_kg: 0.3, disposition: collected, reason: dressed catch}, followed by the matching negative cooked-and-eaten event. Add work tasks and their hours to work_budget; work_hours must equal their sum. ongoing_processes holds the latest snapshot of unfinished batches, specimens and unsupplied plans; it grants no assets or outputs. Use Survival Ledger for current stocks and First Month Ledger for the fixed Day 28 starting state. Estimated quantities and patch assumptions belong in the ledger.
Evidence note
---
id: research-example
title: Research Question
type: research
tags: [research]
status: draft
---
# Research Question
## Claim under consideration
## Sources and their scope
## What the evidence supports
## What remains uncertain
## Consequence for the handbook

Lunar reflection
Use type: reflection in 02_Reflections. Set as_of_day and knowledge_cutoff_day to the same completed lunar milestone day (or Day 1 for the arrival review, half_cycle: 0); moon_phase is full-moon or new-moon, with half_cycle from tools/lunar_calendar.py. Include the common metadata, authored reflective prose and one snapshot block:
<!-- ledger-snapshot:start -->
<!-- ledger-snapshot:end -->

The generator fills ledger_snapshot and the author-quantity table at that cutoff. No asset_events, food_events or demonstrates are introduced. Appraise current capabilities/unfinished work, supply, dangers, bottlenecks, intentions and reasons to reconsider. Future entries are scheduled in the index rather than written with invented outcomes.
Daily moon model fields, including moon_day, are derived by the generator. Survival titles/filenames use Moon N Day M; continuous day remains the inventory and chronology key. The rounded new-moon boundary starts the next labelled moon, as specified in Lunar Calendar. These fields are not nightly observation claims. Link the matching reflection from its Survival day. See Lunar Calendar.
Later narrative
Use project entries with start and end dates or seasons, inputs, workforce, outputs and verification. Do not continue daily reporting by habit once the important dependencies operate on longer timescales.
When a Survival illustration is ready, embed it at the beginning of the body and follow Illustration Continuity. The illustration metadata points to the asset from the vault root; the Markdown image path resolves from the note folder. Leave these fields null until an image is selected.
Compact daily prose from Day 51
Daily frontmatter remains the continuity source, but the visible page follows the day’s technical question: intent, mechanism and construction, observed test, then its next useful consequence. Food/fuel/water routines can be one brief sentence when nothing changes the choice. A full end-of-day stock list, repeated inventory of missing items and exhaustive description of the gathering circuit are no longer required. See Style Guide.

00_about/setting-specification.title: Setting Specification
00_about/setting-specification.content:
Setting Specification
Purpose and canonical constraints
The project explores the physical and organisational dependencies of civilisation through a remembered technical handbook and one traveller’s experience. The narrative records one contingent path. The handbook compares paths, including inventions that could become useful earlier under different conditions.
The traveller arrives alone and naked in a fictional low-elevation valley of northern Iberia, approximately 40,000 calibrated years before 1950. The date is deliberately approximate. Regional human coexistence is plausible but does not prove a particular local encounter; this valley and its inhabitants are setting choices. See World and Research Register.
Arrival is in early autumn, during nut harvest. Sheltered woodland patches alternate with open slopes. The first month contains cool nights, wet weather and one light local frost, rather than sustained winter freezing. These conditions are authored for this sequence, not a reconstructed daily weather record.
The traveller
He does not age, but he can suffer exposure, disease, injury, exhaustion and death. Healing is ordinary unless a later explicit setting decision changes it. Long life does not guarantee psychological endurance or uninterrupted leadership.
Uploaded memory contains the technical and scientific knowledge available in his departure civilisation. It does not provide contemporary observations of this valley, unrecorded languages, guaranteed experimental outcomes, or solutions his civilisation never achieved.
Before departure he receives practical training in flaking, friction fire, basic fibre work, shelter and species identification. He has rehearsed primitive methods under controlled conditions. He has less field experience than local people and lacks their environmental knowledge. Training supports competence, not instant mastery.
Transit rule
Only the traveller’s living body, with its normal incorporated tissues and physiological contents, can pass. Clothing, loose seeds, concealed cargo, tools, implants and deliberately packaged supplies cannot pass, irrespective of whether they are organic or inorganic. This is a fictional transit constraint; it replaces the earlier shorthand about inorganic matter. It is not a claim about real biology or physics.
First-month resource assumptions
The landing valley has a productive, accessible hazel patch and further patches identified over the month. This is the principal food assumption supporting the opening. Harvest returns must still be recorded, patches can be depleted, and weather and territorial access can interrupt collection.
Willow, nettle, pine, oak and some birch occur in suitable local patches as setting assumptions. A gravel bar provides knappable stone, and a small bank exposure provides clay for trials. Finding a plant or clay deposit does not establish that it works for every proposed use.
Rabbit and small rodent captures are intermittent supplements. Freshwater crayfish occurrence is unresolved and is not used to support the revised food budget. Freshwater mussels are observed but not relied upon for meals. Dangerous carnivores may be present; fire and weapons do not guarantee deterrence.
The first month’s detailed food, fuel, water and object changes are in First Month Ledger. Measured-looking quantities are author estimates, not measurements by a naked traveller without a balance.
Local people
The first encountered group is Neanderthal. Eleven people are seen on one visit; this is not necessarily the group’s total population. Their language, kinship, leadership, resource rights and wider contacts are initially unknown.
They are skilled makers and users of local tools. This fictional group knows plant cordage, hide work, fire management and hafting, including stone-pointed spears. Day 25 shows a knapped stone point bound into a wooden shaft; the traveller still carries his simpler wooden-pointed spear. Both designs are compatible with Neanderthal weapon evidence (R21). Choosing a composite weapon here does not make every wooden spear inferior or establish this design at a real northern Iberian site. These choices are compatible with evidence for Neanderthal technological sophistication, without asserting that every group shared one uniform toolkit.
The traveller may contribute unfamiliar methods or a useful comparison. The group may teach him materials, technique and local judgement. Interest is not agreement, a gift is not a contract, and no garment or device guarantees respect.
Decisions intentionally left open

Timeline mechanics: whether intervention changes the departure timeline or produces another branch. Do not claim either as established fact in daily entries.
Asteroid engineering: exact object, warning interval and why available deflection capacity is inadequate. The premise currently retains centuries of warning; the scale and institutional constraints require later specification.
Regional chronology: a real archaeological location and narrower arrival date would require another evidence pass.
Later travel and biological change: no domesticated crops, animals or imported resources appear until their acquisition, selection or movement has been described.

These open decisions do not prevent revising the first month. Changes to them must be recorded here and in Revision Record.
First contact and the proposed thrower
Smoke and distant firelight are noticed on Day 19; observation follows on Day 21, route planning on Day 24, and the first approach is rebuffed on Day 25. One warning incident belongs to these individuals and circumstances, not a claim that Neanderthals were uniformly hostile. The traveller stays away on Day 26; no gifts, communal food or shared instruction are secured in the first month.
This group has competent spear users as well as cordage and hafting expertise. An atlatl is chosen as a possible useful comparison on Day 26. Its presence in their toolkit is unknown, and the traveller’s own assembled example is untested at Day 28. Much later direct European evidence (R16) supports the choice of a potentially unfamiliar device without proving ancient absence. Effective hand throwing (R17) prevents automatic technological superiority. Future contact requires successful practical tests and a willing audience.
Day 20’s unidentified movement near camp and Day 22’s single wolf sighting are modest danger events, with retreat and maintenance costs. They introduce no injuries, predator kills or new resources. Agelessness gives no immunity to a bite, spear thrust, infection or exposure.
Moon rhythm and reflection cutoffs — 4 October 2026
Arrival is near a new moon. Lunar Calendar uses a fictional Day 0 new-moon epoch and a mean 29.53-day cycle for author bookkeeping. New/full moon reviews occur roughly fifteen days apart, beginning with Days 15 and 30, then Days 44 and 59. This is a setting choice and approximate rhythm, not a historical ephemeris.
Reflections reviews only the completed milestone day’s knowledge and inventory. Continuous days and the existing four-week planning blocks remain; no Survival event or work budget is moved to make a rounded month length. New moon supplies no bright lunar disk; actual sky visibility still depends on weather and terrain.

00_about/style-guide.title: Vault Style Guide
00_about/style-guide.content:
Vault Style Guide
Purpose
Keep the manual technically useful and the narrative engaging. Explain real dependencies, alternatives and bottlenecks without forcing the traveller through historical eras. This guide supersedes the earlier category-purity and closed-reference rules.
Voice
Write daily entries in restrained second-person present tense. Describe what you do, observe, attempt and infer. Use a different emphasis each day; maintenance need not become an identical trap-line scene. Include failure when it changes a decision or cost, not as a ritual gesture before guaranteed success.
Reference pages use direct instructional prose. State mechanisms plainly. Avoid motivational endings, game statistics, invented productivity percentages, unearned spectacle and absolute claims about what ancient people must think.
The protagonist is modern and knowledgeable. His reasoning may use modern concepts, but speech requires an established shared language. Keep observation separate from interpretation: an observer sees a sample taken, not a contract accepted.
Categories
Follow Category Specification. Classify stock as Materials, practised control/judgement as Skills, object design families as Tools and Equipment, distinct operations as Technologies — Processes and Systems, and constructed site frameworks as Structures. Named Places form a separate atlas under Structures and Places. Use one capability type/tag and a valid subtype/domain list; folders follow the subject rather than complexity, portability or narrative success.
Use one primary type, an appropriate subtype and one or more domains per capability. The primary type tag must match the type; other categories belong in links, rather than extra primary tags. Topic Index uses domains to browse across categories. Store equipment by function in 05_Tools and Equipment, including mixed-material designs.
An equipment page may describe its construction and operation. A skill page may give ordered practice instructions. Keep a separate process page when it explains a distinct production route, batch control, several outputs or a coordinated system. Complexity, portability, historical era and the presence of a recipe do not determine type. Categories are independent of draft status, acquisition, mastery and reliability.
Distinguish raw or prepared input from manufactured output. Bast Fibre supplies strips or fibres to Simple Cordage; Bark Cordage is the resulting line. A produced material must not become its own manufacturing prerequisite. Describe outputs explicitly without adding them to the input list. Do not duplicate a recipe solely to satisfy folder boundaries.
Historical eras and lithic modes provide context. They are not universal sophistication levels. Do not label a spindle, trap or institution Mode 4 merely because it appears alongside blade technology.
Page scope and narrative pauses
Use Page Scope and Organisation. Keep use variants and simple assembly on their design-family page; split when the mechanism, production controls or independently useful question warrants it. A narrow first specimen does not force a narrow canonical title. Atlatl Dart covers practice and hunting variants; each retains its own current state.
Measurement and Records is a skill at this stage. Projectile Practice Ground is a local place; reusable site-selection guidance belongs in Projectile Testing. Structures participate in the capability graph; places do not.
Use Lunar Calendar and Reflections for new/full-moon reviews. Write at the end of the milestone day without future knowledge or extra acquisitions. Appraise resources, reliability, bottlenecks, threats and intended choices. Snapshot tables derive from that day; narrative prose is authored. Moon model fields constrain future night images, not weather visibility.
Common metadata
Use the fields in Page Templates. YAML must parse, type must match the primary content, and lists must remain lists even with one member.

id: stable identifier independent of title and folder.
title, type, tags: basic identity; include the primary type tag.
status: draft, reviewed or planned. Reviewed means reviewed for a specified scope; never imply experimental validation.
evidence: a list drawn from historical-attestation, experimental-replication, modern-guidance, physical-reasoning, setting-choice and research-needed. Generated continuity views also use author-model.
sources: Research Register identifiers supporting specific claims.
prerequisites: only direct requirements for the base method described.
alternatives: substitute routes, with the affected requirements explained in prose.
improvements: optional developments that improve performance or scale.
demonstrated_day: first narrative demonstration of the stated capability, otherwise null.
reviewed_on: editorial review date, with remaining limits in the body.

Knowledge is available from arrival, but skill and productive capacity are not automatically demonstrated. Acquisition is derived from daily events. Do not maintain a second manual acquisition date that can drift.
Dependencies and alternatives
A prerequisite is necessary for the method actually described. Distinguish a requirement from a convenience and a performance improvement. Separate the base method’s requirements from route-specific alternatives.
Examples: a suitable percussor is required for percussion knapping; an antler billet is one refinement, not a universal requirement for every biface. Pottery is useful for boiling but a tested bark vessel and heated stones provide another route. A wooden spindle whorl can avoid a ceramic-firing dependency.
Physical manufacture dependencies should form a directed acyclic graph. Operational feedback and institutional cycles belong in explicit discussions, rather than being hidden in circular recipe prerequisites.
Evidence and technical completeness
Attach sources in Research Register and link to them from the relevant notes. Evidence for a technology elsewhere does not establish its presence in this fictional valley.
Separate historical attestation from physical feasibility, experimental performance and narrative choice. Record uncertainties where they affect a decision. Avoid universal yield, strength, mastery or adoption claims without a matching experiment.
Use SI measurements when they matter; add field approximations where useful. Never equate steam with boiling, hardness with strength, smell with absence of pathogens, or medicinal tradition with proven treatment.
A process page states inputs, sequence, tests, failure signs, time and labour assumptions, outputs, maintenance and limits. Unvalidated hazardous processes remain explicitly draft. Describe a sensible fallback when a measurement or material cannot yet be supplied.
Narrative continuity
Every day has a numbered day, work budget, demonstration events, asset events, food lots and ongoing processes. Daily frontmatter is the continuity source; Survival Ledger is its continuing generated view; First Month Ledger preserves Days 1–28. Quantities are modelling estimates, not measurements made with modern equipment.
Maintain conservation: produced or collected minus consumed, lost and gifted equals remaining. A hide cannot become both a complete sling and a complete garment. Tools need repair; the traveller needs sleep; collecting fuel takes labour. Small animals supplement, rather than automatically establish, food security.
Days 1–28 remain daily because survival and first contact need detail. Later narrative can use weeks, seasons and projects as the practical questions change.
People and teaching
Local people have expertise, priorities and agency. Never infer species-wide incapacity from a device they have not used. The traveller learns local methods and asks, demonstrates, exchanges and observes. Record what has actually been reproduced independently before declaring knowledge transfer successful.
Illustrations
Follow Illustration Continuity. Use the approved Day 1 image to preserve the protagonist and watercolour-and-ink style. Select an actual moment in the day and check the objects, clothing, resource quantities and unfinished processes against the narrative before generating. Images belong at the beginning of Survival pages, with local files and a saved prompt record. A visual detail must not introduce a future technology or promote a failed trial to a success.
Authoring workflow

Check Setting Specification and the latest ledger state.
Select a problem and identify direct physical and social requirements.
Check available methods, sources and unresolved questions.
Draft the reference method and the contingent narrative outcome.
Update events, quantities and ongoing processes.
Regenerate views with python tools/update_views.py, run python tools/validate_vault.py, then rebuild the context export.
Inspect links and Dataview in Obsidian before publication.

Publication readiness requires a separate check of consequential instructions. This revision is an editorial and continuity pass, not a certification of every field recipe.
Intentions, risk and earned outcomes
Before a new project, state the problem it is meant to solve, why this route is chosen, what the traveller expects to demonstrate, and what would change the plan. Explain inputs and the intended test before showing construction. Memory supplies options; present observations select between them.
Build encounters from noticed signs, uncertain interpretations and chosen actions. Show trepidation through distance, an exit, hesitation, a neglected task or a vulnerable body rather than declaring constant terror. Small threatening events should affect work, location or equipment; count any losses and extra labour. Fire, weapons and shelter reduce particular risks, not danger in general.
Technical novelty, social acceptance and demonstrated usefulness are separate outcomes. A neighbour may be unimpressed, refuse access or warn a stranger without being portrayed as intellectually inferior. A successful catch can remain useful despite a flawed mechanism. Reject food for an observable reason or a stated risk decision, not invented contamination.
Technology-led continuation — 7 October 2026
From Day 51, give each daily page a practical technical question and a clear connection to the protagonist’s mission. Explain the next useful tool or process, why it is chosen, the mechanism, a credible test and what its result enables. Survival provides the constraints and setting; routine supply rounds should not become the principal continuing plot.
Compress food collection, trap checks, water, fuel and ordinary repairs unless an unusual result changes the technical decision. Omit repeated exact-stock and time-budget summaries from the narrative. Use measurements where geometry, capacity, fit or a comparison needs them, rather than as compulsory inventory recitation. Keep modest author estimates in frontmatter and the generated ledger for continuity; they are not protagonist measurements or an obligation to describe each food run. Record consequential material allocations, losses and new working results without duplicating the entire inventory in prose.
Introduce realistic progress without forcing a failure before every useful result. Distinguish a working specimen, repeatable production and independent learning by another person. New capabilities should create options and expose the next dependency. As the project grows, move towards project-based passages rather than stretching daily survival scenes indefinitely. This direction supersedes any earlier stylistic expectation of exhaustive daily routine narration.

00_about/world.title: Northern Iberia around 40,000 BP
00_about/world.content:
Northern Iberia around 40,000 BP
Regional frame
Northern Iberia provides a plausible broad setting for an encounter between late Neanderthals and incoming Homo sapiens. Dating and the extent of local coexistence remain uncertain. Research modelling France and northern Spain suggests a period of overlap, but does not demonstrate direct interaction in every valley. See Research Register.
BP uses 1950 as its reference year. The working date is approximately 40,000 calibrated years BP; do not mix it with an uncalibrated radiocarbon determination.
The fictional valley
The first camp lies on a sheltered, well-drained terrace near a small stream and a larger river. Its debris shelter is above flood level. Hazel and some oak occupy protected patches; pine and birch occur elsewhere; willow and nettle grow in selected river margins. Open slopes and rocky ground separate woodland patches.
This deliberately suitable landing site is a narrative assumption. It does not imply continuous woodland, uniformly abundant flint, or modern species distributions across Ice Age Iberia.
The initial water source is an upstream seep. It appears less exposed to runoff than the river but cannot be certified safe by appearance. The hearth is outside the debris shelter. A separate waste area and animal-processing surface reduce contamination.
Resource geography








































LocationObserved resourcesLimitsSheltered nut patchesHazel kernels; later oak acornsSeasonal, finite, labour to collect and shell; possible human resource rightsGravel barCobbles and selected knappable stoneMany cobbles fracture poorly; transporting weight costs timeStream marginsWillow shoots and nettle standsRetting water must be kept downstream of collection water; harvesting is seasonalPine patchDry fuel and small resin depositsResin is flammable; fuel reserve must be maintainedBank exposurePlastic clay-rich sedimentSuitability requires drying and firing trialsRidge and river bendsTracks, smoke, feathers, wider routesObservation does not establish ownership, species identity or safety
The narrative records encounters with squirrel, rabbit, vole, mouse and fox. Day 22 adds one grey wolf sighting at the river margin as an explicit author choice for this fictional habitat; it establishes neither regional abundance nor a pack, attack or reliable deterrence. The unidentified rustling on Day 20 is not retroactively identified as that wolf. Other regional animals may be introduced only with appropriate habitat and evidence or an explicit setting assumption. No fixed local abundance is asserted for reindeer, mammoth or large predators.
Freshwater crayfish biogeography requires research before their presence becomes canonical. Existing identification pages remain draft reference entries.
People and movement
Local people know routes, stone sources, weather signs and seasonal food. The traveller cannot infer their entire society from one distant observation.
A maintained hearth is evidence of people, not proof of their species. A stone-tool style does not by itself identify its maker. Group identification remains a working interpretation until close observation supports it.
Contact is governed by their choices. Distance, visible hands and predictable visits can reduce surprise; they do not establish a universal prehistoric diplomatic protocol.
Spatial reference
Valley Map fixes the fictional valley’s orientation and landmark relationships from Day 28 onward. The larger river flows generally north to south; the small stream approaches from the west. The traveller’s terrace lies north of that tributary and west of the larger river, with the shelter entrance facing broadly southeast. The Neanderthal clearing lies northwest beyond a rocky spur, on the same western side of the larger river. The established contact route skirts the spur’s western flank and requires no main-river crossing. These bearings and provisional travel allowances are author choices added on 3 October 2026, not geographical measurements from earlier entries.

01_survival/moon-1-day-1---immediate-pri.title: Moon 1 Day 1 - Immediate Priorities
01_survival/moon-1-day-1---immediate-pri.content:
Moon 1 Day 1 - Immediate Priorities
A place to stop
You arrive on a sheltered slope with no equipment. You recognise the broad terrain, not the particular valley. The first useful decision is where to stop moving.
You make a short circuit, keeping the arrival point in sight. A small seep runs above the river terrace. You choose drained ground away from the waterline and examine the fallen branches overhead. Nothing about clear water proves it safe, but you have no treatment system yet. You drink from the seep and record that exposure as a necessary tradeoff.
Shelter and an edge
You select a sound cobble through Stone Selection and use the flaking motion practised before departure. Several strikes crush an edge. One produces a useful Oldowan Knife Flake. You retain it and mark a place for sharp waste away from your feet.
A fallen limb supports a low debris frame. You spend most of the afternoon collecting small branches and dry litter. The bed has depth beneath your hips and shoulders; the covering reduces wind. This is Basic Lean-to in its simplest debris form, without a lashed structure. You inspect it by lying inside before dark.
A nearby hazel patch supplies a small amount of positively identified food. Shelling reveals less edible material than the apparent pile of nuts. You eat the kernels and leave unknown shoots alone.
Limited coverage
You separate a few flexible bark strips as Bast Fibre and twist short ties using Simple Cordage. Small overlapping panels cover the waist and reduce some abrasion. They leave most of your skin exposed and are no substitute for the shelter.
You gather dry fuel and tinder while light remains. A fire attempt is possible in principle, but the unfinished shelter and lack of a prepared kit make it a poor use of the remaining light today.
Dependency exposed: knowledge supplies a method; a useful edge still requires a suitable specimen, controlled movement and a safe place to work.
End of day
The shelter is provisional and the food reserve is empty. You have no fire or water treatment. Your feet and skin need protection, and the first night is interrupted by cold.
The night is pitch black - you notice that you have arrived during a new moon.
Estimated active work: survey and water: 1.5 h; shelter: 4 h; food: 1.5 h; flaking and ties: 2 h; fuel and bedding: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 5 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Lunar reflection
Pause for Reflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 1 after the first day’s work. This arrival review weighs the difference between remembered knowledge and the few things which can sustain tonight.
Next decision
Improve the usable tool set and food reserve while preparing a complete ignition kit.

01_survival/moon-1-day-10---a-carrying-s.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 10 - A Carrying Sling with a Tested Limit.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-10---a-carrying-s.title: Moon 1 Day 10 - A Carrying Sling with a Tested Limit
01_survival/moon-1-day-10---a-carrying-s.content:
Moon 1 Day 10 - A Carrying Sling with a Tested Limit
Restore the working route
You remake the strained bark fastening with more support around the edge. Cold water holds at the marked level. The next Hot-Rock Boiling batch reaches a rolling boil without opening the seam.
The repair restores a particular tested route. It does not establish that bark containers are permanently reliable.
Finish and load gradually
You assemble Rawhide Carrying Sling from yesterday’s rabbit panel. The awl makes holes with generous margins, and a separate bark cord forms the shoulder strap.
A small blunt load holds. You increase cautiously, inspect the holes and stop below a kilogram. This object frees a hand for light trips, but it is not the carrier for several kilograms of acorns. Bulk collection still uses repeated trips and the bark container for dry loads between water batches.
More materials, not automatic security
The traps provide a squirrel and a vole. You prepare and eat their small edible portions today. Their pelts are cleaned and set aside separately: the squirrel panel may contribute to warmth; the vole provides a patch.
Your hands ache after the repeated scraping. Rest, adjusted grip and shorter sessions address the immediate strain.
Dependency exposed: capacity is a tested property of an object. Knowing how to make a bag does not establish the strength of a thin panel, its holes or the cord bearing its load.
End of day
The sling is useful for small loads, and the water route is restored. The second squirrel panel and a vole patch are reserved for clothing. Most of the body remains exposed.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; vessel repair and sling: 2.5 h; butchery: 1 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Compare clay test pieces while retaining the established non-ceramic water route.

01_survival/moon-1-day-11---clay-samples.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 11 - Clay Samples and Another Pelt.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-11---clay-samples.title: Moon 1 Day 11 - Clay Samples and Another Pelt
01_survival/moon-1-day-11---clay-samples.content:
Moon 1 Day 11 - Clay Samples and Another Pelt
Compare before committing
You take a little damp clay from the protected batch and make test strips at comparable thickness. One mixture crumbles when worked; adding more grit does not solve it. You adjust moisture and compare a less heavily tempered sample.
You form a small pinch vessel through Clay Vessel Making, keeping walls approximately even and smoothing the base transition. It rests in shelter with airflow. The remaining scraps become comparison pieces, drying beside the vessel.
A second rabbit
The trapping trial supplies another rabbit, somewhat larger than the first. You cook and consume its dressed meat today. You reserve this pelt for clothing rather than making a second sling from the same material.
Selected bone and tendon form separately labelled lots. A wider bone blank may offer another needle attempt, but it needs cleaning and inspection first.
Observe the river without assuming a meal
You survey the shallows and see bivalves. Their identification and source safety are not established, so they do not enter the day’s food. You also leave freshwater crayfish out of the local resource map until there is reason to assert their presence.
The day has a complete staple meal without either aquatic addition. That makes the decision to leave uncertain food possible.
Dependency exposed: a clay shape, a stable fired object and a heat-resistant food vessel are distinct outputs. Work can begin on ceramics without making water treatment depend on their success.
End of day
The pot is greenware, not cookware. Rabbit pelt B is allocated to warmth; pelt A has already become the sling. The nettle batch is on its seventh elapsed soaking day and still needs a physical test.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; clay trials: 2 h; butchery: 1 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Work the better bone blank and compare a scrap seam while the clay dries.

01_survival/moon-1-day-12---a-usable-eye.title: Moon 1 Day 12 - A Usable Eye
01_survival/moon-1-day-12---a-usable-eye.content:
Moon 1 Day 12 - A Usable Eye
Work a better blank
The second rabbit’s selected bone has enough width for another eye trial. You score, scrape and abrade gradually, preserving material around the blunt end. The process uses several short sessions instead of one uninterrupted strain.
This time the eye remains intact. You polish its edges and pass a fine test thread through it. A pre-pierced scrap seam works without cutting the line. You have a usable Bone Needle, not proof that it can punch through every stiff hide unaided.
Prepare the limited thread supply
You separate dried tendon from the rabbit into a small further Sinew Thread lot. The strands are joined conservatively. You retain the awl for holes that would otherwise put sideways force on the needle.
The cleaned pelt is beginning to stiffen. You flex a test area and compare it with the supported drying panel. Rehydrating and working untanned skin can help temporarily; it is not equivalent to a durable tanning process.
Pay for quiet work
No new game is recorded. Nut collection and shelling still take several hours. The empty traps make the time spent at the nut patches worthwhile.
Water batches and fuel collection continue, and you inspect the clay base for dampness before turning it. The test strips remain beside the drying pot for comparison.
Dependency exposed: selecting a suitable blank can matter more than knowing the final shape. A finer tool also has operating limits, so it works alongside the earlier awl rather than replacing it entirely.
End of day
One eyed needle is available. It is stored in the small case with its point protected. The pot remains drying; the nettle fibres do not yet separate usefully.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; needle and thread: 3 h; pelt and clay checks: 0.75 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 7.5 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Test a small clothing seam and improve rain protection before extending the daily range.

01_survival/moon-1-day-13---cold-ground-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 13 - Cold Ground and Limited Coverage.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-13---cold-ground-.title: Moon 1 Day 13 - Cold Ground and Limited Coverage
01_survival/moon-1-day-13---cold-ground-.content:
Moon 1 Day 13 - Cold Ground and Limited Coverage
Respond to the weather
The upper slope shows a light frost; the sheltered camp is damp rather than deeply frozen. Your interrupted night points to a bedding problem as much as a garment problem.
You add dry interior litter and repair the windward roof. Moisture has reached a small nut portion. You discard it and rearrange the dry reserve rather than assigning all stored kernels an indefinite life.
Make a panel, not an imagined coat
You begin Fur-On Pelt Clothing with rabbit pelt B, the second squirrel panel and a small vole patch. You preserve useful area and compare seam placement before piercing.
The needle works in holes made by the awl. One edge starts tearing when pulled tight. You move the seam farther in, losing a little coverage. The result is a small pelvic pad with extensions, not a full encircling garment or insulation over the torso.
A short fishing trial
After the necessary food and camp work you make a brief Basic Spear Fishing trial from stable shallow ground. You correct below the apparent position, but the fish move and the point strikes nothing useful. You stop before cold and repetition consume the afternoon.
The trapping trials provide a mouse and a vole. Their tiny portions are cooked and eaten today; the cleaned skins become patch materials.
Dependency exposed: knowing how to sew does not supply garment area, moisture resistance or thermal performance. A small panel is useful only within the protection actually supplied by the rest of the camp.
End of day
The limited pad is unfinished and the rest of the body still needs shelter in cold wind. The damp-food loss and higher fuel use reduce margins. No fish was caught.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; shelter and clothing: 3 h; short fishing and small catches: 1 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 6.5 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Finish adjustable ties and dry bedding; postpone any work that requires a long exposed excursion.

01_survival/moon-1-day-14---fit-and-bedd.title: Moon 1 Day 14 - Fit and Bedding
01_survival/moon-1-day-14---fit-and-bedd.content:
Moon 1 Day 14 - Fit and Bedding
Finish what helps now
You fit the small fur panel and add adjustable ties. It reduces abrasion and supplies warmth over a limited area of the pelvis. You can crouch and walk without pulling directly on the fragile seam.
A rough bark shoulder screen remains part of the equipment. Your arms, lower legs and much of your torso still lack good protection. The clothing does not make you winter-ready.
The quieter improvement
You move dry bedding into the shelter’s interior, replace compressed patches and inspect the repaired cover after the damp night. This work gives a clearer benefit than making another named tool.
Extra fuel collection restores some margin after yesterday’s higher use. The traps are empty today; nuts supply the meals.
Prepare the experiment
The pot’s surface is pale and firm, but the base needs continued checking. You inspect the sacrificial strips rather than declaring it dry because a certain number of days has passed.
You choose a separate outside firing place and put aside enough dry fuel for a supervised trial tomorrow. The drinking-water route remains independent. If the pot fails, the failure will cost clay, work and fuel rather than end hydration.
Dependency exposed: reserves turn an optional experiment into an affordable experiment. The important advance today is the capacity to absorb a failure without losing the established survival route.
End of day
The bed and fuel reserve are improved. One small pad is wearable, with clear coverage limits. The firing load remains experimental greenware.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; fit and bedding: 1.5 h; extra fuel and water: 2.5 h; clay and hearth preparation: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Run a small supervised firing, leaving ordinary food and water supply intact.

01_survival/moon-1-day-15---a-firing-tri.title: Moon 1 Day 15 - A Firing Trial
01_survival/moon-1-day-15---a-firing-tri.content:
Moon 1 Day 15 - A Firing Trial
Use the planned fuel
You prepare a small Pit Fire with the dry test strips and the pot. Preheating is gradual, and supports keep larger fuel from collapsing directly onto the thin load.
The fire develops unevenly. You change the fuel arrangement to improve air access without smothering the base. Bright coals and a darkened surface show heating, but do not reveal a precise peak temperature or prove vitrification.
Supervision has a cost
The firing takes most of the craft allowance. You collect and shell food before the main trial and make drinking-water batches at the established hearth.
You eat from the nut supply at the ordinary hearth. The experimental pot stays in the firing bed, hot and uninspected.
You record substantial fuel use rather than allowing the firing to run on an invisible wood supply. Enough remains for ordinary camp work, but tomorrow must include replenishment.
Leave the load alone
As fuel burns down, you keep the load in place. You do not lift a warm pot for a dusk test or quench it to accelerate inspection. Cooling continues overnight.
A small sound-looking object would still need a test. A crack may not announce itself loudly in the fire; absence of a noise is not evidence of success.
Dependency exposed: controlled heating consumes preparation, supervision and fuel. A surviving shape cannot be promoted to a useful vessel until after cooling and operating tests.
End of day
The load is cooling overnight. No cooking-pot capability has been established. The dry-fuel reserve is lower after the trial.
Estimated active work: food: 3.5 h; firing supervision: 4 h; fuel water and camp: 2.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Lunar reflection
While the firing load cools, pause for Reflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 15. This full-moon review takes stock before the cold vessel is inspected tomorrow.
Next decision
Inspect and test the cooled pieces before deciding their role; check the nettle batch independently.

01_survival/moon-1-day-16---fibre-and-a-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 16 - Fibre and a Rejected Pot.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-16---fibre-and-a-.title: Moon 1 Day 16 - Fibre and a Rejected Pot
01_survival/moon-1-day-16---fibre-and-a-.content:
Moon 1 Day 16 - Fibre and a Rejected Pot
Test the result
The cooled pot has a fine crack. When you place water inside on dry ground, a line of moisture appears along it. You reject it for drinking-water storage and cooking instead of treating a slow leak as sufficient success.
The surviving specimen can hold dry non-food samples and supply evidence for another clay trial. It has not established reliable Pottery. You leave hot stones out of it.
Check the ret
The nettle batch has been submerged since Day 4. A test stem now releases a fibre ribbon while retaining useful strength. You remove part of the batch for Nettle Fibre Processing, leaving the remaining material clearly identified.
Rinsing occurs downstream of water collection. You drain and break the woody cores carefully, then scrape off debris without cutting every ribbon into short fragments.
Removing woody material leaves a small heap of fibre. You spread it to dry; the volume of the wet stems had concealed how little useful material this portion would provide.
Retain the alternatives
Food and fuel work still take several hours. You do not have a free full day merely because the camp is more familiar.
Water continues through the bark vessel. The rejected pot changes the next ceramic experiment, not the availability of drinking water or the fibre work.
Dependency exposed: tests decide an object’s role. A failed cooking-pot trial can still provide useful information, while an alternative process prevents the failure from blocking unrelated developments.
End of day
A usable fibre portion is drying. The remaining retted stems need prompt assessment to avoid over-retting. The pot is kept as a failed non-food specimen, not counted as cooking equipment.
Estimated active work: food: 3.5 h; pot tests and fibre: 3 h; fuel water and camp: 2.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Turn a measured portion of fibre into line and start a small acorn batch rather than processing an assumed bulk harvest in a single afternoon.

01_survival/moon-1-day-17---line-and-a-s.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 17 - Line and a Small Leaching Batch.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-17---line-and-a-s.title: Moon 1 Day 17 - Line and a Small Leaching Batch
01_survival/moon-1-day-17---line-and-a-s.content:
Moon 1 Day 17 - Line and a Small Leaching Batch
Spend part of the fibre
You prepare a limited portion of Nettle Fibre for Simple Cordage. Long overlaps and staggered joins matter more than the fibres’ colour. Several short samples break at uneven splices before you obtain a useful lot.
You lay the finished line back and forth to estimate its length. About eight metres of mixed light cord is useful for bindings, though the weak joins rule out treating it as heavy rope. You keep the remaining fibre separate.
A modest acorn trial
You collect and shell a small quantity of identified acorns. Some kernels are rejected. About 400 grams of sound shelled input enters the Acorn Leaching trial.
You use the tested bark vessel and heated stones in small batches. Water replacement, containment and cleaning take time. The first comparison remains astringent, so the process continues tomorrow.
The vessel allows only a small quantity at once. You set aside another session for the remaining water changes, leaving ordinary food preparation at the established hearth.
Protect the excursion margin
You inspect the spear, small sling and water vessel and select dry nuts for a limited excursion. The prepared food reserve makes an unsuccessful search affordable.
The remaining nettle batch is checked. Fibre work can proceed alongside leaching, but wet stems cannot be left indefinitely without deterioration.
Dependency exposed: small-container volume and preparation labour limit throughput. Scaling a recipe requires a larger or repeated process, not simply increasing the stated harvest.
End of day
The nettle line is available for modest bindings. Acorn input is still processing and is not counted as a finished ration. Dry nuts, not a hypothetical preserved cake, supply the excursion.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; cord work: 2.5 h; leaching trial: 1.5 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Complete and assess the small leaching batch, then search within a safe return budget for useful old material.

01_survival/moon-1-day-18---an-old-antle.title: Moon 1 Day 18 - An Old Antler
01_survival/moon-1-day-18---an-old-antle.content:
Moon 1 Day 18 - An Old Antler
Finish a small food process
You complete more water changes on the acorn trial and compare the result. The batch produces wet Acorn Meal for prompt use, not a durable brick. Water retained in it increases wet weight without creating calories.
You eat part before departure and keep the remaining small portion for tomorrow. Its short retention and clean handling are explicit; no months-long shelf life is inferred.
Search without approaching a kill
You follow a limited route upstream, using Scavenging and Tracking to choose ground worth inspecting. Fresh carnivore sign at one bend makes you turn away rather than treat predators as convenient suppliers.
Later you find an old red-deer antler fragment apart from any active feeding site. Weathering limits part of it, but one sound section is suitable to trial. The weathered find is quiet evidence of an earlier animal, with no fresh carcass to investigate.
Use its existing shape
At camp you scrape and abrade the damaged end and grip the useful section. It becomes Soft Hammer Billet with little cutting. A small flint trial suggests a different removal behaviour from the hard hammer, while several strikes still fail.
The whole sound section serves as the billet. Reshaping it for another task would give up this working surface.
Dependency exposed: a material find opens an option. It does not supply a new skill automatically, and a different route can be chosen when finding it would require excessive risk.
End of day
The dry-nut and fuel reserves cover a day without collection. The small wet-meal remainder is intended for tomorrow. The billet is an option for further practice, not a universal technology gate.
Estimated active work: meal and water: 1.5 h; excursion: 4 h; billet trial: 1.5 h; camp maintenance: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Compare a rough biface with the existing flakes, and begin a container using the most workable local material.

01_survival/moon-1-day-19---a-rough-bifa.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 19 - A Rough Biface and a Basket Start.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-19---a-rough-bifa.title: Moon 1 Day 19 - A Rough Biface and a Basket Start
01_survival/moon-1-day-19---a-rough-bifa.content:
Moon 1 Day 19 - A Rough Biface and a Basket Start
Compare methods
You choose a suitable blank and begin Bifacial Knapping with controlled hard-hammer removals. The edge becomes useful before the object becomes symmetrical.
You try the billet for selected removals, but a prepared platform matters more than simply changing the percussor. One trial blank breaks. The retained Acheulean Hand Axe is a rough usable biface, and you compare it with a flake on a modest cutting task. Neither wins every job.
Select a container route
You bend fresh willow samples before deciding to soak or steam them. Thin suitable shoots already accept the required radius; thicker ones do not.
A small coiled foundation trial uses Simple Basketry (Coiling). It consumes fine line slowly and does not justify forcing a needle through rigid rods. You then start a willow stake basket through Simple Coiling and Weaving, which suits the available material better for this job.
A distant sign
During the return from fuel collection you see a thin smoke column beyond the ridge. It suggests a maintained fire, but it does not establish the makers’ species or number.
Your first impulse is to move towards it. You stop. Whoever maintains that fire may already use the nut patches and river crossings you have been treating as unoccupied. They could offer local knowledge and company; they could also kill you before you find a shared word. Remembering human history does not tell you who is beyond this ridge.
You mark a possible observation route rather than crossing today. From the near side at dusk, a small steady orange glow appears in the gap where the smoke rose. You leave before darkness hides your footing. The present base and reserve stay in place. You eat the remaining wet acorn meal today and wash its handling implements.
Dependency exposed: competing methods expose different costs. Historical names do not decide whether a rough biface or a basket technique is worthwhile for the present materials and task.
End of day
One rough biface and an unfinished basket exist. Smoke is recorded as evidence of a possible occupied camp, not a confirmed Neanderthal group. No acorn meal remains.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; knapping comparison: 2 h; container trials: 1.5 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Finish the small basket and begin an aquatic trial without making its yield part of the assumed food supply.

01_survival/moon-1-day-2---consolidation.title: Moon 1 Day 2 - Consolidation and Fire Preparation
01_survival/moon-1-day-2---consolidation.content:
Moon 1 Day 2 - Consolidation and Fire Preparation
Work within a return route
The night leaves you tired rather than refreshed. You remain close to camp. More exploration would add distance without solving the immediate problems.
You return to the gravel bar and make a small working set through Oldowan Toolkit. You select a scraping edge and a heavier robust core for rough shaping. You do not impose a quota of perfect tools. Fresh flakes remain available for jobs where they work better.
Build the reserve first
The hazel patch is productive enough to justify a longer collection session. You bring nuts back in small bark packets, then shell them on a clean stone. The edible yield is enough for today’s meals and a small dry reserve. You inspect kernels and keep them off damp ground.
Collection and shelling take much of the usable day. That labour is what permits a fire experiment tomorrow; it does not disappear from the budget because it is no longer novel.
Prepare friction fire
You choose dry willow pieces from sheltered dead material and inspect them for softness and cracks. A thick piece becomes the Fireboard. You make a socket and notch with the flake and select a spindle of compatible material, rather than automatically choosing the hardest available wood.
You twist more bark line and trial it around the spindle. One splice slips under repeated movement. You cut out that section and join again. The result is adequate for short trials, not proven durable for dozens of ignitions.
A curved stick supplies the bow. A natural socketed stone supplies the upper bearing. You assemble the parts without running an exhausting ignition attempt in the fading light.
Dependency exposed: the bow drill depends on a complete compatible kit. Having a sharp stone and a remembered recipe is insufficient when the cord slips or the bearing absorbs the effort.
End of day
A small nut reserve exists. The kit is prepared, but neither the board nor the cord has produced an ember. Dry material is protected inside the shelter; water remains untreated.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; tool work: 2 h; cord and fire kit: 2.5 h; shelter fuel and water: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 6 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Trial the fire kit in short sessions while retaining enough time to gather food and maintain shelter.

01_survival/moon-1-day-20---pitch-and-wo.title: Moon 1 Day 20 - Pitch and Woven Work
01_survival/moon-1-day-20---pitch-and-wo.content:
Moon 1 Day 20 - Pitch and Woven Work
Finish a useful carrier
You weave the basket walls, secure the rim and test a modest blunt load. Woven Foraging Basket can now carry more dry material than the little sling, though its practical capacity remains limited.
The line used at the rim is counted. Fine cord is not a free input simply because a retted batch exists.
Begin a fishing cage
You use the remaining selected willow to form a small cage and a separate inward funnel for Woven Fishing Trap. An access closure and anchoring remain unfinished. You leave the prototype on land rather than declaring passive calorie production has begun.
A defined adhesive trial
A short resin collection yields a small batch for Pine Pitch Manufacture. You heat it indirectly, compare cooled samples and add a conservative amount of crushed charcoal to one.
The better small-joint sample becomes Pine Pitch Adhesive. It is reserved for non-food tool work, not used to seal the cracked pot or the drinking vessel.
You also finish extracting the remaining nettle portion. This occupies time that a claimed mass-production device would not remove. The usable fibre allowance is entered separately.
Keeping a way out
While tending the ordinary outside hearth at dusk, you hear something moving in the brush on the dirty-material side. It stops when you rise. You cannot identify it, and you do not follow it into cover. You bring the plain wooden spear within reach and clear loose branches from the short path out of the shelter. The hearth remains outside: bringing flame beside the dry bedding would create a different danger.
The sound may belong to a small scavenger. The practical lesson is larger. Your shelter protects you from some weather, not an attack; a sharp stick is limited defence, and a broken ankle would end most of your plans. You keep animal scraps away from the sleeping place and leave enough daylight for tomorrow’s return from observing the distant fire. These checks take part of the existing camp allowance, not a second uncounted day’s work.
Dependency exposed: an adhesive is a formulation for a particular joint, while a fishing cage is a system that needs closure, placement and retrieval. Material conversion does not guarantee either function.
End of day
The basket is usable and the cage remains a prototype. The pot is still rejected. The fibre store is larger because another portion was processed, not because an earlier material regenerated.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; basket and cage: 3 h; resin and fibre: 2 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Complete the cage, trial a simple wooden whorl and make a limited observation visit.

01_survival/moon-1-day-21---a-wooden-who.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 21 - A Wooden Whorl and Distant Neighbours.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-21---a-wooden-who.title: Moon 1 Day 21 - A Wooden Whorl and Distant Neighbours
01_survival/moon-1-day-21---a-wooden-who.content:
Moon 1 Day 21 - A Wooden Whorl and Distant Neighbours
Work that can be repeated
A small dry wooden disk provides a route around the failed pot. You trim it with a sharp flake and slowly open its centre with the awl, supporting the wood rather than forcing the point. On a fitted shaft, the Spindle Whorl turns unevenly but prolongs rotation. Eight grams of prepared nettle fibre yield about twelve metres of uneven single yarn. That is a spinning trial, not twelve metres of load-bearing rope: strength, joins and plying still need tests.
You use five grams of the pitch batch and a short cord binding for Simple Hafting. The resulting Hafted Knife keeps your fingers farther from its edge. Once cool, it survives light cutting; a loose socket or softened adhesive would still require repair. You complete and anchor the Woven Fishing Trap in shallow water where you can retrieve it without wading into a strong current.
People across the valley
The smoke and last evening’s firelight give you a direction, not an invitation. You follow the near slope slowly, carrying the plain wooden spear low. At each change of cover you check the way back. A stranger appearing above a camp with a weapon might look like a threat; approaching unarmed would not make you safe either. You stop short of the open ground and watch.
