Observation consumes much of the remaining afternoon. You count eleven people at one gathering place; you cannot yet know whether that is a whole group. Their movements around fire, hide work and stone tools look practised. Someone examines and adjusts a bound tool handle. You see cord, but cannot identify its plant or construction at this distance.
Their compact builds and, when a face turns sideways, low foreheads and projecting midfaces suggest Neanderthals. Distance leaves that identification tentative. That does not tell you their language, motives or range of knowledge. Your uploaded knowledge cannot translate a language never recorded. Smoke and a cleared working area tell you people live here; they do not establish a stock of food available to a stranger.
A person turns towards your slope. You lower yourself behind the rock and wait, heart beating hard, without knowing whether you were seen. You withdraw by the same route. What frightens you is not their species: there are several skilled adults here, and you are alone, poorly clothed and ignorant of their intentions.
The spindle now has a possible second purpose. You hope a visible comparison in a familiar task could give someone a reason to tolerate your presence. You have seen cord in their hands; you cannot assume that spinning will impress them, or that usefulness will overcome suspicion.
Dependency exposed: a wooden spindle bypasses successful ceramics, while useful communication requires observation, permission and shared reference points.
End of day
The trap is deployed. The pot remains a rejected sample. Your new knife has only a light-work test; the spindle has produced yarn, not demonstrated a production rate.
Estimated active work: food and water: 2.5 h; craft and trap: 3 h; observation: 3 h; camp maintenance: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Check the trap and reserves before allocating another afternoon to the neighbouring camp.

01_survival/moon-1-day-22---a-fish-and-a.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 22 - A Fish and an Experimental Spring Snare.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-22---a-fish-and-a.title: Moon 1 Day 22 - A Fish and an Experimental Spring Snare
01_survival/moon-1-day-22---a-fish-and-a.content:
Moon 1 Day 22 - A Fish and an Experimental Spring Snare
A small return
The cage holds one small fish. You lift it onto the safe bank, untie the rear access closure and draw the fish out through that opening; the inward entrance funnel stays in place. You close and retether the cage before leaving. The catch is approximately eighty grams after dressing, and you cook and eat it today. You record the catch and the empty checks separately: a single success establishes that this placement can catch something, not that it will provide dependable daily food. Stream access and fluctuating catches must remain part of the food budget.
Most calories still come from hazelnuts. Their edible kernel mass matters more than the apparent volume of shells. You add to the reserve before attempting another mechanism.
Watched at the water
On the return from checking the cage, a grey wolf appears on the opposite gravel margin. It stops with its head towards you. The distance is enough to leave, not a reason to test whether it fears people. You take up the wooden spear, keep the animal in view and back towards the open terrace path. It does not follow while you can see it. You cannot infer that it will never return, or that there was only one nearby.
The fish offers little reward for a confrontation. You process it at the separate dirty-material surface, clean the working tools and keep remains away from the shelter. You bring the spear within reach during bank work from now on. Fire, a low shelter and one pointed stick still leave gaps in your defence.
Testing a spring
A bent sapling can store energy, but the trigger, anchor, loop and animal’s path must work together. Your Snare Trap uses two and a half metres of nettle cord, including anchorage. You repeatedly set it off with a stick while standing outside the returning branch’s sweep. The loop sometimes slips before tightening; you adjust the anchor and record the flaw rather than treating a working trigger as a proven hunting system.
You place the trial on an observed small-animal run and plan an early inspection. Cord is a finite asset. The newly spun single yarn is not substituted for a strong loop simply because you can make more of it.
Dependency exposed: mechanism construction, capture, humane dispatch and dependable food yield are different milestones. Passive equipment still demands checking, repair and opportunity cost.
End of day
One small fish has been consumed. The cage remains in place, and the spring snare requires a morning check.
Estimated active work: food and water: 3 h; snare trial: 2.5 h; trap checks: 1 h; camp and equipment: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Inspect the spring snare before treating the capture mechanism as useful food technology.

01_survival/moon-1-day-23---a-difficult-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 23 - A Difficult Catch and a Repair.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-23---a-difficult-.title: Moon 1 Day 23 - A Difficult Catch and a Repair
01_survival/moon-1-day-23---a-difficult-.content:
Moon 1 Day 23 - A Difficult Catch and a Repair
A gain with a cost
The snare has caught a fox awkwardly. The line is damaged, the ground disturbed and the animal still alive. A capture is not the same as a clean kill. You keep clear of its teeth while completing dispatch, shaken by the struggle and by how close your hands must come. The mechanism has delivered food, but it has not performed as intended.
There is no observed reason to reject the whole carcass as contaminated. You recover a limited portion of meat while keeping gut contents, dirty fur and the clean working surface apart. You retain roughly nine hundred grams of dressed meat for today’s meals; that is the portion actually kept, not the fox’s whole edible yield. Damaged and soiled trimming and other remains are kept out of the food lot.
You know foxes can carry parasites. You cut the retained meat into small pieces, cook it promptly and thoroughly, keep raw handling separate from cooked food, and eat it over the day. You do not store it as dried rations. Without a thermometer you cannot certify a safe internal temperature from colour or texture: this is a field decision with residual risk, not a handbook claim that predator meat is either automatically poisonous or automatically safe. See Research Register.
The catch lets you eat fewer nuts today and retain more of that reserve. Skinning, cooking and cleaning cost an extra hour and additional fuel. You clean and stretch the damaged skin at the dirty-material side. Enough may remain for a narrow shoulder panel, not a full garment. The broken snare leaves service; damaged cord is not silently returned as new line.
Keeping small things
The edge of the squirrel-hide pouch has split. A dry mouse skin from Day 13 supplies a patch, stitched with fifteen centimetres of reserved sinew thread. You inspect the needle eye and awl afterwards. The pouch holds a few small implements; it is not a container for the entire toolkit.
You replenish nuts, treat water and check the fishing cage. There is no fish today. Before dusk you clear the sleeping approach again and put the spear where you can reach it without searching in the dark. Yesterday’s wolf and today’s struggling catch make defence an immediate constraint, even though neither has injured you.
Dependency exposed: a partly failed mechanism can still yield useful food and skin. Its benefit has to be weighed against dispatch, parasite risk, cleaning, repair and time; success is not an all-or-nothing label.
End of day
The retained fox meat has been consumed and the damaged skin is drying. The snare is out of service; the fishing cage remains experimental. The food gain is real, the capture method still unreliable.
Estimated active work: food and water: 3 h; capture, skin work and cooking: 4 h; pouch repair: 1 h; camp and checks: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Assess how much usable skin remains, and finish clothing before spending more cord on traps.

01_survival/moon-1-day-24---a-small-pane.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 24 - A Small Panel and a Contact Plan.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-24---a-small-pane.title: Moon 1 Day 24 - A Small Panel and a Contact Plan
01_survival/moon-1-day-24---a-small-pane.content:
Moon 1 Day 24 - A Small Panel and a Contact Plan
Coverage, not a coat
The fox skin has dried enough for further working, though a stiff raw skin needs repeated softening and will suffer if it is wetted. You cut around damaged areas and make a narrow panel that can hang over one shoulder or lie beneath a hip at night. Four tenths of a metre of sinew thread joins its pieces; bark-cord ties keep it in position.
It does not cover your torso like a tailored winter garment. The pelvic pad, bark panels, bedding and shelter still do different jobs. You check for abrasion and adjust the ties during movement. A skin that exists is not necessarily clothing that fits, insulates or remains flexible.
A predictable approach
Another distant observation gives you a safer place for an initial approach: open ground within sight of the camp, with room for both sides to withdraw. You prepare a small cord sample and plan to show the spindle only if someone chooses to remain nearby. Neither a fox skin nor a sharp stone establishes social rank.
The purpose is limited: earn a few minutes of attention by showing something useful, not announce yourself as their teacher. You leave the spear concealed well away from the meeting ground so your approach does not begin with a raised weapon; that also leaves you more exposed. You trace a return route with firm footing and decide not to let curiosity carry you into their living area.
You cannot rehearse their response. You can keep your hands visible, move slowly, avoid blocking anyone’s path and stop when gestures suggest distance. The knife stays secured for transport. You have no reliable greeting to offer.
Dependency exposed: a physical demonstration needs an audience who understands the task and is willing to participate. Social access is a dependency with its own uncertainty, not a reward unlocked by inventory.
End of day
The panel is usable with limited coverage. Food, water and retreat remain your own responsibility during contact.
Estimated active work: food and water: 3 h; skin work: 2.5 h; observation and route: 1.5 h; camp: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Approach only while there is adequate daylight to return to your own camp.

01_survival/moon-1-day-25---an-unwelcome.title: Moon 1 Day 25 - An Unwelcome Demonstration
01_survival/moon-1-day-25---an-unwelcome.content:
Moon 1 Day 25 - An Unwelcome Demonstration
A reason to be tolerated
Before leaving, you spin another short uneven trial from eight grams of prepared fibre. You take eight metres of yarn, half a metre of cord and the wooden spindle. Your hope is specific: if the weighted shaft holds twist visibly longer than hand rolling, someone may see a useful comparison and allow another meeting. You have not measured a better rate, and their existing cord may be stronger than yours.
You leave the spear at the concealed stopping place chosen yesterday, well short of the open meeting ground. You step into view with your hands clear. Two people come partway towards you; others remain back. At this distance the heavy brows, low foreheads and projecting midfaces support the Neanderthal identification. Their speech is articulate but unintelligible to you. Their expressions are no more a translation than yours would be to them.
Nothing they need yet
You lay the cord on a stone and step back. One person lifts it, pulls at a join and puts it down. Another holds up a length of their own line, rolls a short section between palm and thigh and points at your weak join. That is observable skill, not evidence of people waiting to discover string.
You lift the spindle and turn it. The whorl rotates, but the fine yarn parts at a join when you try to extend it. Neither person reaches to take the device. One turns away. You cannot tell whether they already know a comparable technique, dislike this example or simply want you gone. What you have shown gives no obvious advantage over the cord in their hands.
The distance closes
You mistake a brief look back for permission to try once more and take a step forward. The person nearest you speaks sharply and brings a stone-pointed spear across your path. A knapped point sits in a fitted wooden shaft, held by close bindings. Your own spear is only shaped wood; this composite weapon represents stoneworking and hafting practice you have not yet reproduced in a spear. A stone strikes the ground nearby. You stop. Whether this is a territorial warning, fear of your movement or something else, the safe response is the same.
You back away with empty hands visible. When the spear carrier advances another pace, you turn and run to the rise. The spindle drops beside the sample stone; the yarn and cord stay there. You do not turn back for them. You recover your own spear only after reaching the concealed stopping place and waiting to see whether anyone follows. None appears before you withdraw along the route you know.
At your camp the failed meeting keeps replaying while you tend water and the hearth. You have lost an object you can replace. An injury would have been harder to repair. No food, shelter access, accepted gift or agreement enters the ledger.
Dependency exposed: a clever mechanism earns nothing unless its useful result is visible and the audience is willing. Technical knowledge cannot supply consent, translate a warning or make a lone stranger secure.
End of day
The first spindle and samples are abandoned, not recorded as accepted gifts. Local cordage skill has been observed at close range. You have learned a boundary through a frightening mistake; no shared lesson or alliance exists.
Estimated active work: food and water: 3 h; sample preparation: 0.75 h; approach and retreat: 3.25 h; camp: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Stay away tomorrow. Repair your own equipment and decide what, if anything, could justify a later approach.

01_survival/moon-1-day-26---retreat-and-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 26 - Retreat and a Better Question.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-26---retreat-and-.title: Moon 1 Day 26 - Retreat and a Better Question
01_survival/moon-1-day-26---retreat-and-.content:
Moon 1 Day 26 - Retreat and a Better Question
Your camp is still your responsibility
You do not return to recover the spindle. You inspect the route near your own terrace before settling to work, then tighten the knife’s loosened binding with its existing cord. You keep the plain wooden spear within reach, clear the shelter’s exit and check the separate waste area. These are modest precautions, not fortifications. Your own smoke can reveal you just as theirs revealed them.
The food and water routine continues. You are not among people who have agreed to defend or feed you, and yesterday’s warning may affect which gathering routes remain available. For now you stay on your side of the ridge. You allow time for looking and listening instead of starting another long excursion.
What might actually help them?
The fitted stone point on the spear is another correction to your assumptions. They already join wood, stone and binding into a working weapon while yours remains a plain wooden point. You have made a light-work hafted knife, not an equivalent hunting spear.
The failed pitch was built around your invention, not their need. They already make good cord and handle local materials better than you. The broken yarn gave them no reason to stop their own work. Even a sound spindle would need a longer comparison before you could claim that it saved labour.
You recall the spears at the meeting and the repeated journeys out of camp. A device that might let a hunter deliver a useful projectile from farther away could address a task they recognise. An atlatl, or spear thrower, seats at a dart’s rear and extends the throwing motion. It needs a matched, flexible projectile and practised release; it is not a handle you can attach to any heavy spear and instantly double its effectiveness.
This is a candidate, not a discovery of Neanderthal incapacity. Remembered archaeology gives you much later direct European examples, but perishable objects leave gaps and you have not inventoried these people’s equipment. They may know a thrower; their hand-thrown spears may already perform well. You also lack their hunting practice. The useful claim must therefore be something you can demonstrate repeatedly yourself, not a story about how advanced you are. See Research Register and Research Register.
Two purposes, two limits
You choose the wooden thrower route because it can be attempted with your flakes, a sound forked branch and light binding. You must restore the spindle, select shaft candidates, assess drying and flex, fit the rear engagement, and practise on a target in clear ground. A failed cast is less costly there than in front of a wary audience.
A working projectile could eventually help hunting and defence, but an untested one cannot protect you today. The plain spear and a clear retreat remain your immediate provisions. If the comparison succeeds, any later visit must begin outside their camp with a lowered weapon and an invitation to watch a cast away from people. You will not arrive pointing an unfamiliar projectile at them. A useful demonstration still cannot cancel their refusal.
Dependency exposed: intention must precede construction. A proposed advantage leads to a test, that test needs inputs and practice, and a social approach remains conditional on willingness.
End of day
The knife binding is retightened by your own work. No spindle, fibre or cord is given away today, and no community teaching has taken place. The atlatl is a plan with a purpose and a test, not another acquired weapon.
Estimated active work: food and water: 3 h; equipment and camp defence: 2 h; observation and route checks: 1 h; projectile planning: 1 h; camp: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Replace the lost spindle and collect the inputs for a controlled thrower trial while keeping the daily food routine intact.

01_survival/moon-1-day-27---replacement-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 27 - Replacement Work and Green Shafts.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-27---replacement-.title: Moon 1 Day 27 - Replacement Work and Green Shafts
01_survival/moon-1-day-27---replacement-.content:
Moon 1 Day 27 - Replacement Work and Green Shafts
Replacing what was lost
A second wooden whorl takes much of the morning. The previous dimensions guide you, but the dry blank, central opening and balance still need work. You fit it to another shaft and compare its turning with what you remember. The first model helps you choose the shape, but aligning the opening and balancing the rim still take patient work.
Gathering remains a daily task. Your reserve allows a failed experiment, but it does not release you from treating water, maintaining fire and collecting fuel.
Parts for a useful comparison
Yesterday’s plan sets the task: build a thrower-and-dart pair that you can control well enough to test against hand throwing. Only after that would a demonstration to the neighbours make sense. First you need projectiles that fit the device; remembered dimensions cannot tell you how these local shoots will flex or dry.
You select two straight shoots as candidate Dart Shafts. They are green, with uneven stiffness. You strip and trim them and put them under cover where you can inspect their drying and distortion. Two days will not automatically make them seasoned shafts.
Several long feathers lie near the remains of a bird. The bird cannot be reliably identified from their colour alone. You take a small usable set, clean it and store it dry. Flight Feathers provide a possible stabilising route; their presence does not establish that you have a completed dart.
For a thrower body you choose an older fallen branch with a suitable projecting fork. You remove decayed wood and start shaping it while preserving the fork as a possible integral hook. This is a test blank, not a ready hunting weapon.
Dependency exposed: a design can bypass an antler hook, but it cannot bypass material condition, fit or trials. Green wood and gathered feathers remain inputs awaiting successful processing.
End of day
The replacement spindle is available. Neither dart shaft is a finished projectile; the feather lot and thrower blank remain separate assets.
Estimated active work: food and water: 3 h; replacement spindle: 2.5 h; projectile materials: 2 h; camp: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Finish a conservative wooden thrower and specify a trial before committing scarce materials to its projectiles.

01_survival/moon-1-day-28---a-thrower-be.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 28 - A Thrower Before a Weapon.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-28---a-thrower-be.title: Moon 1 Day 28 - A Thrower Before a Weapon
01_survival/moon-1-day-28---a-thrower-be.content:
Moon 1 Day 28 - A Thrower Before a Weapon
A route without an antler fitting
You shape the old branch into a short thrower, preserving a low integral wooden hook and rounding the grip. The base route on Atlatl uses that integral hook without a separate antler spur or adhesive joint. A short bark-cord grip binding improves handling but does not compensate for a weak hook.
You inspect the grain around the fork and press a blunt wooden test piece against the hook. It seats, but a static fit does not demonstrate a safe or effective launch. The finished object is recorded as an assembled, untested Atlatl. The green dart candidates remain under cover.
What to test next
The purpose remains a useful comparison for hunting, and eventually a possible reason for the neighbours to tolerate another meeting. It has not become a promise that a weapon will win them over.
The next launch trial should use open ground with a clear backstop and nobody within reach of the arm or projectile path. You need a compatible projectile, an intact nock, adequate shaft straightness and a record of failures. You plan to compare repeated short casts with the performance of a hand-thrown practice shaft, rather than claiming more power from the mere existence of a lever.
You will compare what you can actually do, without pretending to match an experienced local spear user. Range alone would not establish better hunting: repeatable accuracy and reliable release matter. If the candidates are still unsuitable, preparation continues; the calendar does not force a launch tomorrow.
A hunting system would also require tracking, approach, useful accuracy, recovery and the ability to deal with a wounded animal. None of those follows automatically from construction.
After twenty-eight days you have a modest camp, intermittent small catches, a nut-based reserve, several working tools and one rebuffed approach to the neighbours. Your most valuable gain may be a better account of the work between knowing a process and relying on it.
Dependency exposed: the next step is validation, not an automatic leap to large-game hunting. The handbook advances when a repeatable capability is established, including the limits under which it works.
End of day
The atlatl is an untested object. Projectile testing, completed darts and reliable hunting remain planned capabilities, not acquired successes.
Estimated active work: food and water: 3 h; thrower shaping and inspection: 2.5 h; trial planning: 1 h; camp: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Day 29: inspect the shaft candidates. Prepare a compatible practice projectile and run limited trials only if its condition and fit permit; otherwise continue preparation. Continue food, water and fuel work regardless of the outcome.

01_survival/moon-1-day-29---a-margin-bef.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 29 - A Margin Before an Experiment.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-29---a-margin-bef.title: Moon 1 Day 29 - A Margin Before an Experiment
01_survival/moon-1-day-29---a-margin-bef.content:
Moon 1 Day 29 - A Margin Before an Experiment
Count what makes tomorrow possible
The thrower waits at the uphill craft spot. You want to use it, partly because it promises an answer to the humiliating approach at the neighbouring clearing. That is a poor reason to spend the whole day on it.
You set out the loose fibre, bindings and food before choosing the work. The fox panel covers one shoulder, the rabbit pad protects only a small part of the waist, and the nights are cooling. An empty fuel stack would matter sooner than a better projectile.
The nuts are harder to collect from the nearer patch. More shells are empty or damaged, and the ground you have already searched does not refill. You shell and inspect today’s modest gathering, then divide the working food into roughly comparable portions. The portions are not precise weights; they give you a repeatable way to see whether experiments are using up tomorrow’s meals. Food Reserve Management begins with that decision, rather than a larger imaginary store.
Give comparison a fixed object
A sound dry stick becomes a Marked Reference Staff. You choose its usable length, distinguish one end and transfer several divisions by repeated comparison. The marks are imperfect, but keeping this stick will be better than changing the unit whenever you spread your fingers.
On a separate bark slip you scratch grouped marks for food portions and leave a different area for trial results. Your memory could retain every observation. A physical register also makes you define what an observation means before remembering it.
This is a first personal instance of Measurement and Records, not a standard that someone else has agreed to use. It supplies neither kilograms nor a reliable modern metre.
Inspect before launching
The two shaft candidates have changed differently. The second has a more obvious bow. You keep it as a blank, instead of forcing it into tomorrow’s comparison. The first remains green but shows no opening split under the gentle checks you make; it is worth preparing cautiously. Neither has become seasoned because two nights have passed.
You inspect open ground west/southwest of camp, above the tributary and short of the trap circuit. A local earth bank offers a possible west-facing backstop. The river and contact route lie outside the intended flight line. You check the sides and the ground behind the bank as far as you can see. This is a candidate Projectile Practice Ground, not yet a working range.
Back at camp, you place the ordinary wooden spear where you can reach it without stepping into the hearth. You will not bring the atlatl to another meeting until its purpose has survived some tests of your own.
End of day
The author model records 2.54 kg of edible kernels and 19 kg of dry fuel. The staff and scratch register exist; both darts remain unfinished, and the selected practice site needs preparation. No material has come from the neighbours.
Active work is estimated at 8.5 hours, with an eight-hour sleep allowance. Survival Ledger carries the quantities; Valley Map governs the locations.
Next decision
Prepare one blunt expendable projectile if its inspection still permits. Give the first trials a short, repeatable line and a stop condition. Keep the second candidate out of the comparison.

01_survival/moon-1-day-3---first-fire.title: Moon 1 Day 3 - First Fire
01_survival/moon-1-day-3---first-fire.content:
Moon 1 Day 3 - First Fire
A controlled attempt
You eat from the nut reserve before working. Bow Drill Fire is familiar from training, but the local wood and cord are new.
The first session produces dust and smoke. When you stop, neither persists as an ember. You inspect the socket and find that too much effort is heating the upper bearing. You adjust contact, lubricate that upper surface with an appropriate small plant sample, and keep it separate from the lower friction point.
The next session abrades the cord. You replace the worn section and pause before fatigue distorts the stroke. Materials are finite; repeated full-force attempts are not costless.
Ember to flame
A later attempt leaves a compact hot dust pile that continues glowing after rotation stops. You let it consolidate, transfer it gently into the prepared Tinder Bundle and feed the resulting flame into the small dry fuel bed.
You establish Camp Fire outside the debris shelter. It lets you warm briefly and cook, but it cannot be enclosed beside the bedding. You clear the space and inspect the wind before adding larger pieces.
Keep the day viable
Food collection continues in a shorter session. Today’s yield falls below what you eat, so the reserve decreases. You do not spend every remaining hour celebrating or rebuilding camp.
You inspect the bed and arrange a modest ember reserve where the hearth can safely hold one. If it dies, the kit remains available for another start. You plan to sleep in the insulated shelter rather than waking every hour to sustain a large exposed fire.
Dependency exposed: an ember is only one stage. Tinder structure, graded dry fuel and a safe hearth are also required to turn friction into useful sustained heat.
End of day
You have achieved ignition once. A few charcoal pieces remain in the hearth, but there is no industrial stockpile. Drinking water is still untreated because no usable water vessel exists.
Estimated active work: food: 2.5 h; ignition trials: 3 h; fuel water and shelter: 2 h; cooking and kit repair: 1 h. Sleep allowance: 7 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Make and test a small bark vessel so heat can be applied to water.

01_survival/moon-1-day-4---a-point-and-a.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 4 - A Point and a Vessel.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-4---a-point-and-a.title: Moon 1 Day 4 - A Point and a Vessel
01_survival/moon-1-day-4---a-point-and-a.content:
Moon 1 Day 4 - A Point and a Vessel
Shape what the wood allows
Fire has given you warmth, but not a safe perimeter. Before a longer collecting trip you want a point you can keep between yourself and an approaching animal, and a way to probe cover without reaching in bare-handed. It will not make you a competent big-game hunter. You select a sound fallen shaft and shape a gradual point using the cutting flake and scraper. You scrape the wooden spear smooth and let the point dry without charring it.
A low-load plant-target test shows that the point can survive modest pressure. This is a shaped implement, not proof that you can hunt large animals or stop a predator.
A small container
You find a sound birch bark sheet on fallen material and work a folded Bark Container. The first corner splits as you tighten it. You trim to a smaller usable area and distribute the fastening load.
Cold water sits in it at a modest level. It holds only a few large drinks. Several small batches would be needed for a day’s water.
You attempt the next step immediately. With screened Heating Stones and handling sticks you begin Hot-Rock Boiling, but the warmed seam opens before a rolling boil is reached. You stop and empty the vessel. Steam and heat have not proved treatment.
Start a parallel process
After food and fuel work, you cut a modest batch of mature nettle stems. You begin Nettle Retting in a secured downstream pool, away from drinking-water collection. You keep a few unretted stems for comparison.
The shelter receives new supports and a better layered covering. The rough bark panels are repaired; a small shoulder screen gives limited wind protection.
Dependency exposed: storing cold water and tolerating repeated heating are separate requirements. A vessel’s failure can block treatment even though fire is available.
End of day
The vessel needs repair before heat treatment. The nettle batch has begun; readiness will be checked physically, not promised for a calendar date. Clothing remains inadequate for prolonged cold exposure.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; point and vessel: 3 h; nettle preparation: 0.75 h; fuel water and shelter: 2 h. Sleep allowance: 7.5 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Repair the heating vessel first, then undertake only the extra craft work the food and fuel budget permits.

01_survival/moon-1-day-5---water-and-a-d.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 5 - Water and a Digging Stick.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-5---water-and-a-d.title: Moon 1 Day 5 - Water and a Digging Stick
01_survival/moon-1-day-5---water-and-a-d.content:
Moon 1 Day 5 - Water and a Digging Stick
Repair before expansion
You reinforce the bark corner with a supported fastening and reduce the fill level during the next trial. You test it cold again, then transfer heated stones carefully.
This time the whole water surface reaches an observable rolling boil. You maintain it for the ordinary low-elevation time described in Hot-Rock Boiling, then leave it to cool away from dirty tools. The method uses several small batches. Remembering a temperature has not supplied a thermometer; observable boiling supplies a practical endpoint instead.
A lever, not a new era
You shape a broad bevel on a sturdy fallen branch to make Digging Stick. Loose-soil trials show where it works and where the wood begins to flex. You leave hard stony ground alone.
On a short survey you expose a small plastic clay-rich patch. A modest sample becomes Clay for later tests. You do not carry a large load home merely because the sediment is sticky.
One trapping trial
You inspect rodent sign through Tracking, then make a trial Figure-4 Deadfall Trap. The initial arrangement collapses during a low-load test. You adjust the bearing surfaces and use a remote release before setting it.
Only one trial is installed today. Food, fuel and water still require labour, and a first mechanism is not enough to justify spending the whole afternoon on three more.
Dependency exposed: water treatment can precede pottery. A tested alternative vessel and a heat-transfer method remove a ceramic bottleneck, while introducing handling and maintenance costs of their own.
You also make one metre of replacement bark cord, checking its joins before using it for repairs.
End of day
The first successful water-treatment route exists, with limited volume. The trap may fail or catch nothing. The clay remains damp stock, distinct from a drying object.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; vessel repair and treatment: 1.5 h; stick clay and trap: 3 h; fuel and shelter: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Inspect the trap without presuming a meal; prepare to handle any catch separately from clean water and food.

01_survival/moon-1-day-6---a-small-catch.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 6 - A Small Catch and a Drying Frame.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-6---a-small-catch.title: Moon 1 Day 6 - A Small Catch and a Drying Frame
01_survival/moon-1-day-6---a-small-catch.content:
Moon 1 Day 6 - A Small Catch and a Drying Frame
The trap supplies material
The trial has caught a squirrel. You assess the catch and condition before carrying it back. Dressing leaves a small meal, far less than the animal’s whole weight.
You use Small Game Butchery on a supported surface apart from drinking equipment. The first skinning cuts damage an edge, but leave a useful panel. Meat and organs are cooked with the meal. You keep raw offcuts apart from the cooked meal. The smell makes you look towards the brush more often. You keep the wooden spear beside the working place and clear scraps from the sleeping approach before dark; a small meal is not worth drawing a scavenger to your bedding. The separate processing surface matters for defence as well as cleanliness.
Preserve useful state
You separate a limited tendon lot and retain suitable bones. These are not yet sewing thread or needles.
A small frame made with Tripod Lashing provides the first Smoking Rack. Its task today is supporting the pelt and tendon for drying, with separate clean surfaces. The squirrel meal is consumed today; no smoked meat enters a travel reserve.
You flesh the pelt promptly and spread it under moderate tension. Thin skin tears at one fastening, so you move the support rather than pulling harder.
Keep the ordinary supply
Nut collection remains the principal food source. The catch adds variety and materials, but it has not replaced the daily staple labour. You inspect the heated-water vessel for seam movement after use and retain the same conservative fill level.
Dependency exposed: an animal supplies several possible inputs, but each remains perishable or unfinished. Food handling, cleaning, drying and suitable tool blanks are separate operations with separate losses.
End of day
One pelt, a small bone lot and tendon are processing. Their existence supports trial objects, not unlimited garment material. All squirrel food has been consumed.
Estimated active work: food: 2.5 h; butchery and drying work: 2.5 h; frame: 1 h; fuel water and camp: 2 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Compare an awl with an eyed needle rather than forcing the more difficult design before a usable point exists.

01_survival/moon-1-day-7---the-awl-befor.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 7 - The Awl Before the Needle.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-7---the-awl-befor.title: Moon 1 Day 7 - The Awl Before the Needle
01_survival/moon-1-day-7---the-awl-befor.content:
Moon 1 Day 7 - The Awl Before the Needle
Choose the easier useful object
You inspect the cleaned squirrel bone blanks. Their dimensions are small, and hammering destroys one potential strip. You score and abrade another gradually to make a Bone Awl.
A scrap hide test shows that it can open small supported holes. That capability is already useful. You do not need an eye in the same object to guide a line through a pre-made hole.
A failed eye
You attempt an eyed Bone Needle on a second slender blank. The shaft becomes smooth, but the eye cracks before it can support thread. You retain the failed sample for comparison and stop rather than claiming a needle because the overall shape looks right.
The tendon has dried enough to separate. You prepare a short Sinew Thread lot and test it in a hole made with the awl. Its available length is limited.
A small supplement
The trap yields a vole. Its food contribution is tiny and is cooked and consumed today. You clean a small skin for possible patch work; its bones are not automatically useful precision stock.
The staple collection continues, and you add a second deadfall after testing its release. This is gradual expansion, not a permanently productive trap line.
Dependency exposed: an eyed needle is one route to sewing. An awl and hand-guided line can support simple seams earlier, avoiding a difficult manufacture step without eliminating the need for sound thread and skin.
End of day
The awl is usable; the eyed needle is not. The squirrel pelt has dried toward rawhide. No vole meat remains for another day.
Estimated active work: food: 3 h; bone and thread trials: 3 h; trap and pelt: 0.75 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Make a small tool case and organise the work surface before trying another delicate blank.

01_survival/moon-1-day-8---an-organised-.title: Moon 1 Day 8 - An Organised Working Place
01_survival/moon-1-day-8---an-organised-.content:
Moon 1 Day 8 - An Organised Working Place
Organisation changes the work
You choose a supported work area uphill from the hearth. A manageable flat stone becomes an abrasion surface. You do not drag a heavy slab merely to give the camp a table.
A protected cache holds sharp flakes apart from fine tools. The drying frame stays on its dirty-material side of camp. Drinking-water handling and cooked food have separate places.
A modest case
The sound area of the squirrel rawhide is enough for a small Rawhide Pouch. You fold it, make supported holes with Bone Awl and hand-guide a fine line through them using Stitching.
The first seam puckers. You loosen it and increase spacing before tightening evenly. The case can protect the awl tip and thread; it is not a sack large enough for firewood or a day’s food.
The whole squirrel panel is now allocated to this object. It cannot reappear intact as a collar later.
A reserve day
You give extra time to nut collection and shelling. There is no new game, and none is needed to justify a meal: the earlier squirrel and vole have already been eaten.
You add a third trapping trial only after the routine work is complete. The extra mechanism increases inspection and repair labour as well as possible return.
Dependency exposed: reliable handling and protected storage can matter before more sophisticated tools. Organisation reduces losses, but making a case still consumes a specific panel and line.
You also make one metre of replacement bark cord, checking its joins before using it for repairs.
End of day
The case protects small equipment. The eyed needle remains a future trial. The food reserve has grown through collection, not through unexplained preserved meat.
Estimated active work: food: 3.5 h; case and work area: 2 h; trap: 0.75 h; fuel water and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Inspect equipment wear and use any next catch according to a specific material allocation.

01_survival/moon-1-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 1 Day 9 - A Rabbit and a Leaking Seam.md
01_survival/moon-1-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.title: Moon 1 Day 9 - A Rabbit and a Leaking Seam
01_survival/moon-1-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.content:
Moon 1 Day 9 - A Rabbit and a Leaking Seam
A useful pelt, a limited meal
One deadfall has caught a juvenile rabbit. Small Game Butchery leaves a modest meal and useful material, with offcuts kept apart. You cook and consume it today alongside nuts.
The pelt is larger than the squirrel panel, but still small. You assign it to carrying equipment. Tendon and selected bone are cleaned separately. This choice leaves the panel unavailable for the first garment.
Water equipment wears
During the day’s first heating batch, a bark seam begins opening. You stop before further damage. Water already brought to a rolling boil remains treated, but today’s later needs cannot all be supplied through the damaged vessel.
You use the better upstream source for the remaining water and record the unresolved risk. A past successful boil has not permanently made all future drinking water safe.
Begin the sling
You clean and support the rabbit panel, retaining maximum usable area. The shoulder strap will have to be a separate cord. You do not cut both a wide cradle and long straps from the same small hide.
You identify weak edges and prepare to reinforce them with distributed fastening points. The panel dries in a shallow supported shape, away from scorching heat.
Dependency exposed: maintenance belongs in the technology chain. When a container fails, the useful heat source remains, but the water-treatment capability is temporarily reduced.
End of day
The rabbit panel is drying for the sling. The bark vessel needs repair and part of the day’s water was untreated. No smoked-rabbit reserve exists.
Estimated active work: food: 2.5 h; butchery and sling preparation: 2.5 h; water assessment: 1 h; fuel and camp: 1.5 h. Sleep allowance: 8 h. These are author continuity estimates; see First Month Ledger for quantities and reserves.
Next decision
Restore boiling first, then test the sling with a small load.

01_survival/moon-2-day-1---six-attempts-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 1 - Six Attempts and No Advantage.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-1---six-attempts-.title: Moon 2 Day 1 - Six Attempts and No Advantage
01_survival/moon-2-day-1---six-attempts-.content:
Moon 2 Day 1 - Six Attempts and No Advantage
Make a projectile for a question
At the craft spot you finish the less distorted shaft into a blunt atlatl dart. Its front is rounded; its rear receives a conservative seat for the actual wooden hook. You leave the feathers in their dry lot. Adding them now would introduce another alignment and attachment problem before you know whether the bare pair releases.
The base route on Atlatl Dart has produced an experimental object. It is not ready for hunting, and the wood is still green. You accept it only for modest attempts after rechecking its grain, gentle flex and slow engagement. A changing specimen will need checking again tomorrow.
A place to stop a miss
At the selected ground you remove a few loose obstructions and mark a short launch line with collected sticks. You lay the reference staff repeatedly along the same accessible line to the broad earth bank. The count is a local comparison; the slope and imperfect placements make an exact distance claim pointless.
The flight area is clear, but it will not stay clear by virtue of a name. You look towards the contact route, check the bank’s sides, and set the ordinary spear outside the casting swing where you can reach it. There is no target hide or cord stretched across a path.
The first comparison
You make three modest hand casts with the same blunt dart, retrieving and inspecting it between attempts. They reach different places. Familiarity with a wooden spear does not make this thinner projectile feel identical.
The three thrower attempts are less reassuring. On the first, the rear leaves the hook before the useful part of the movement and the dart drops short. The second releases but lands well to one side of your intended patch. The third reaches the bank crookedly. You inspect the end after each attempt and find no spreading split, but that is a reason to retain the experiment, not to increase effort.
Projectile Testing keeps these events separate. You scratch six attempt marks and distinguish the hand-cast group from the thrower group. You do not turn the best landing into a claimed range or velocity. There is too little evidence, and your movement is too inconsistent, to judge an advantage.
Atlatl Throwing asks you to coordinate something your remembered explanation can describe more easily than your body can repeat. You stop before fatigue makes every subsequent result less useful. The unused feather lot and second shaft stay at camp.
End of day
The model records 2.34 kg of kernels and 20 kg of dry fuel. One green blunt dart has replaced candidate A; candidate B remains a blank. The atlatl has been launched, but no useful hunting performance or stable grouping is established.
Estimated active work is 8.5 hours; sleep allowance is eight hours. Survival Ledger records the conversion rather than counting both shaft and finished dart.
Lunar reflection
After the first erratic casts, pause for Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1. This new-moon review weighs supply, exposure and intentions before another week of work.
Next decision
The first failures do not justify another public pitch. Start the fibre supply that bedding and clothing will require, and return to short practice when essential work permits.

01_survival/moon-2-day-10---the-price-of.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 10 - The Price of a Clear Route.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-10---the-price-of.title: Moon 2 Day 10 - The Price of a Clear Route
01_survival/moon-2-day-10---the-price-of.content:
Moon 2 Day 10 - The Price of a Clear Route
A warning at a useful patch
The nearer hazel patches are giving less for the time spent beneath them. You try the western edge of the familiar gathering area, intending to extend the circuit rather than take another day’s deficit for granted. It lies short of the route around the rocky spur; you have not entered the neighbouring clearing.
Someone is already gathering there. This adult is not the spear thrower you watched two days ago. A second figure stands farther back among the trees. When you stop, the nearer person straightens and extends an arm towards the way you came, repeating the gesture as you shift your basket. There is no greeting you understand.
You could interpret the gestures as a demand to leave. You cannot infer the boundary of a whole territory from them, or assume the curious observer would speak for these people. You lower the basket, keep your wooden spear low and withdraw along the visible route. You take no nuts from their collected material and search no discarded equipment after leaving.
The detour costs time and supplies a smaller own harvest. You remember the occupied patch and choose to avoid it for now. It may be productive ground; that does not make it available to you.
Make the exit usable
At camp you put the essential carrying order into practice. The existing pouch holds the small working edges and ignition provision; the bark vessel and basket remain separate. You lift what you could take quickly and walk through the southeast entrance gap, then return the objects to their ordinary places.
You would leave the pot specimen, drying frame and most bulky stores behind. That decision is painful enough without pretending you could carry the whole workshop. You clear a fallen twig that catches the basket on the approach. No perimeter barrier has been built, and nothing has been moved to the Fallback Bench. It would still expose you to weather and a water trip if you had to stay there.
You shorten the planned clothing work to protect a later food round. That is what the encounter changes today: access, timing and a clearer abandonment decision. It does not need to become an attack to matter.
Test the line on the task it must do
At the craft spot you use a small portion of the reserved long grass to make a flexible top-edge sample. The bedding pad used stiff willow foundations and light cord. A shoulder panel must move differently. You arrange soft hanging grass bundles and work paired portions of the old single nettle yarn across them with Twining.
Single yarn is too uncertain for a stressed shoulder tie. In this sample it carries only the light rows retaining the grass; a separate tested nettle cord would take the suspension. You check the joins and lift the little section. One crossing creeps, so you rework the spacing. The retained sample bends without immediately shedding its bundles under gentle handling.
You do not wear it, rate its strength or spend the remaining yarn on a full panel today. The sample consumes its own grass and yarn. It cannot also reappear as loose insulation or line.
Inspect work that is waiting
The fresh rabbit pelt has no observed hair slip, but dampness remains near a fold. You adjust its support, continue cautious edge working and keep it apart from food. The old fox piece remains a narrow left-shoulder panel; the new rabbit does not enlarge it yet.
The clay pair looks drier outside, but the thicker section still feels cooler on comparison. That is a reason to wait, not a measurement of internal moisture or proof that the thinner piece is ready. You have not broken either sample. The nettle sample releases a few outer bundles more readily, while much remains attached to the woody core. You leave the batch secured and record the change instead of assigning an output.
End of day and next choice
The reduced harvest leaves 1.29 kg of kernels; dry fuel reaches 23 kg. The small grass sample uses 0.05 kg of the garment lot and 2 m of single yarn, leaving 0.75 kg and 14 m respectively. Loose nettle cord remains 1.8 m. The reserve is now only about two and a half recent kernel rations.
Eight estimated active hours include the interrupted gathering, withdrawal, ordinary supplies, sample work, pelt care and exit check, with eight hours for sleep. Tomorrow’s panel attempt must stay small enough to leave time for a fuller gathering round. If the bindings or grass fail the handling check, warmth and food will not be improved by forcing a finished garment into the record.

01_survival/moon-2-day-11---a-covering-t.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 11 - A Covering That Can Be Worn.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-11---a-covering-t.title: Moon 2 Day 11 - A Covering That Can Be Worn
01_survival/moon-2-day-11---a-covering-t.content:
Moon 2 Day 11 - A Covering That Can Be Worn
Choose a smaller garment than the one you need
You wake aware of how little the narrow fox panel protects when air moves across the rest of your back. The rabbit skin is still in preparation. A full core covering remains the aim, but waiting for enough pelts would make warmth depend on a sequence of catches you cannot command.
The little grass sample retains its bundles after another lift and bend. You choose a modest hanging back panel: broad enough to screen part of the shoulder blades and reach towards the waist, with the arms free and the front mostly open. Soft grass will serve as the hanging foundations. There is no rigid willow grid, woven fine cloth or claim that this will shed rain.
Before starting, you leave the sample separate and check the remaining yarn. Weak joins are reworked within the available lengths. The paired yarn rows will retain light grass bundles; tested nettle cord will carry the top edge and shoulder attachment. The last arrangement must be removable without a tight neck loop.
Make, lift, then wear
At the uphill clean craft spot you lay the grass in overlapping narrow bundles. Twining retains them across two spaced rows; working across the width gradually lets you correct migrating bundles before securing the margins. You allocate fresh portions from the recorded garment lot, not from the bed. A short upper cord supports the edge, and loose shoulder fastenings keep the load off the throat and clear of the arms.
The result is roughly half a metre across and a little over half a metre down the back, with irregular fringes. It is a first instance of Plant-Fibre Clothing, not a completed winter mantle. The grass is coarse, the rows visible, and the front of the chest and abdomen remain largely exposed. The bark waist panels and pelvic pad stay in use. The fox panel remains its own small left-shoulder piece; it has not been sewn into the new garment.
You first lift the panel from its supports, then wear it for a short walking, crouching and arm-raising trial near camp. A stiff end rubs beside one shoulder. You shorten that projection and adjust the fastening. The panel stays on during the repeated movements, and moving air feels less direct on the covered part of your back. You do not have an insulation measurement, a wet-weather result or evidence that the yarn will survive prolonged wear.
You take it off for wet bank work and keep it away from the hearth. It has not been tested during a cast; dangling material might snag the thrower or interfere with release. Covering the back is useful precisely because it is a limited improvement you can inspect and repair.
A repaired cage can still give only a small meal
The cage holds one small fish. From stable bank footing you retrieve it, release the rear cap and remove the catch through the repaired opening. The inward entrance funnel is untouched. The cap seats again without the earlier side lift, and you inspect the anchor before resetting.
That confirms the closure remains serviceable in another actual handling cycle. It does not show that the repair caused the catch or predict tomorrow’s return. The small dressed fish lot is cooked and eaten today; no fish store is made.
You spend the fuller gathering allowance on accessible patches rather than returning to yesterday’s occupied ground. The return almost balances today’s kernel meals. You keep the evening’s decisions short because a useful garment has not replaced the need to find food.
Preserve the distinctions for tomorrow
The nettle bundle is improving unevenly. A small sample separates more readily, but the whole bundle has not passed a useful extraction check. It stays secured downstream. The rabbit pelt also remains in process, with a worked edge more flexible than its drying centre. Neither is counted as ready material or a new garment.
The clay pair remains unfired under cover. The next ceramic question is still drying and a modest sample test, not a bigger vessel. You make no atlatl casts today and add no point or feathers. The second shaft is still a blank.
End of day and the next part of the plan
The author model records 1.31 kg of kernels and 24 kg of dry fuel. The back panel uses 0.55 kg of dry grass, 12 m of single yarn in paired retaining rows and 1.2 m of nettle cord for the supported top and fastenings. Remaining loose stock is 0.2 kg dry grass, 2 m single yarn, 0.6 m nettle cord, 24 g prepared nettle fibre and 0.7 m sinew thread. The earlier sample, pad and pelt remain separate objects.
Estimated active work is 9.5 hours, including supplies, cooking, panel construction and fit checks, with eight hours for sleep. Survival Ledger keeps the supplies and experimental states distinct.
Days 41–42 should restore attention to accessible food, complete the fibre check when its condition permits and make another short, private projectile trial. The early comparison in Month Two Outline has happened; the gap remains large. Hunting approaches belong to the next phase and will need a food margin as well as better throws. The unsupplied fallback bench remains the most obvious hole in the defence plan.

01_survival/moon-2-day-12---a-roof-is-no.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 12 - A Roof Is Not Yet a Winter Home.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-12---a-roof-is-no.title: Moon 2 Day 12 - A Roof Is Not Yet a Winter Home
01_survival/moon-2-day-12---a-roof-is-no.content:
Moon 2 Day 12 - A Roof Is Not Yet a Winter Home
Choose the work before the weather chooses it
You wake with cold air moving through the southeast opening. The bed is dry, but the grass panel protects only part of your back when you get up. You can remember heated houses, fitted coats and the calculation of heat loss. None of that supplies another dry layer this morning.
The next substantial project must be the sleeping shelter. You want less moving air around the whole resting body, a roof that keeps the bed dry, and enough loose bedding to separate you from the ground. A higher roof or a larger room would need more material and expose more space. A small chamber is the more manageable aim.
Before dismantling anything, you examine the retained fallen limb and the pieces that bear against it. One loose cover twig crumbles when pressed; it is not a useful structural member. The heavy limb’s existing seats show no movement during a cautious inspection from outside. That is reason to investigate a light return frame beside it, not permission to stand under it while cutting a support or adding a heavy load.
You follow runoff marks below the roof and check the north/east margin of the resting space. The terrace still offers a way to add a second sloping side without moving the camp or closing the southeast exit. You plan to retain the existing covered side until the new work can shelter you. The hearth stays outside, downhill and separate. Bringing it inside a small combustible chamber would introduce smoke, exhaust and spark problems you have not solved.
A second food route has a processing bill
The accessible hazel patches give less for the same searching. You do not return to the occupied patch from Day 39. Instead, you extend the familiar oak part of the western circuit, staying clear of the route towards the neighbouring clearing. Sound acorns lie among damaged and partly eaten ones. You reject the poor portions and keep a modest lot from the already recognised oak resource.
Gathering and shelling occupy the larger share of the day. The author model records 0.8 kg of sound shelled acorn input, divided into two rough portions and held dry on a clean bark surface under the existing cover. This is untreated food input, not an edible reserve to be counted with the kernels. You intend to repeat Acorn Leaching in small charges through the one bark vessel. Its capacity, fresh water and heated stones limit the pace.
The grass back panel is worn only on the dry part of the circuit. A projecting stem catches briefly on brush; you free it rather than pulling against the retaining rows. You take the panel off for bank work and construction inspection. No wider garment is made.
Small maintenance protects the proposed build
You collect a separate 0.4 kg of clean dry bedding material, air the little pad and renew the compressed foot end. The unallocated long grass remains separate. You check the rabbit pelt’s centre and gently work its edges; the centre is stiffening. You have not made it into soft leather or assigned it to clothing.
A sample of the second nettle batch now releases in longer strips, but some stems still cling to woody material. Tomorrow you will compare several positions in the bundle and decide whether to stop immersion. Waiting indefinitely could lose useful fibre as easily as lifting too early.
The cage and three deadfalls are checked without a retained catch. You collect dry dead wood and keep tinder under cover. The spear stays reachable when your attention is on the roof; concealment and a low opening do not make you secure from people who know the terrace.
End of day and next decision
The model retains 1.16 kg of edible kernels, 0.8 kg of untreated shelled acorns and 25 kg of dry fuel. The newly collected bedding lot is entirely allocated. Eight estimated active hours include supplies, inspection, bedding and unfinished-batch care; eight hours remain for sleep.
Tomorrow’s first new food work is a limited acorn portion. Shelter stock must then be selected and carried, not conjured from the branches already holding up the roof. Month Two Outline now has a practical order: food, sound support, weather cover, insulation, then further experiments.

01_survival/moon-2-day-13---the-cost-of-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 13 - The Cost of Another Meal.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-13---the-cost-of-.title: Moon 2 Day 13 - The Cost of Another Meal
01_survival/moon-2-day-13---the-cost-of-.content:
Moon 2 Day 13 - The Cost of Another Meal
Work with the vessel you actually have
The shelled acorns can spare some hazelnuts only after processing. You choose half the new lot, leaving the other half dry. The bark vessel holds about 0.6 litres; filling it with the whole portion and then adding water and stones would exceed its working space.
You crush the selected kernels between clean stones and divide them into four small charges, each about a quarter of the chosen portion. The author model’s 0.4 kg input is spread across those charges. You leave space for liquid and a heated stone in each. Hot-Rock Boiling and the familiar bark-vessel handling come before changing water over the acorn material; clean food work stays away from the pelt frame and retting pool.
Repeated fresh-water changes and reheating take much longer than lifting a handful of hazelnuts from the store. You compare the cooked material with the strongly astringent starting sample. The reduced astringency is a process observation, not a laboratory tannin result or a rule for every oak. Today’s accepted small portions are an authored repeat of the earlier local trial. You cook and eat the wet output today; nothing becomes a dried travel cake.
The model allows roughly 6 litres of processing water and 2 kg of extra fuel beyond the colder ordinary routine. Those are planning estimates, separately identified from the 2.5 litres of treated drinking water. About 0.65 kg of wet meal results after draining and cooking; absorbed water increases the mass. It does not create extra dry food.
Stop the ret at a condition, not an anniversary
At the downstream pool you examine samples from several parts of nettle batch B. Long outer strips separate from the woody cores, and a few rinsed bundles withstand gentle bending and pulling. The poorest ends break readily. There is enough promising material to stop leaving the whole bundle in water.
You lift the secured batch, rinse it downstream of drinking collection and drain it. At camp you separate a small selected portion and spread the strips under the existing ventilated cover, apart from food and the dirty pelt frame. The remaining coarse material stays part of the same batch. The old retaining tie is not credited as fresh loose line; its condition is poor after immersion.
The material is wet and uneven. You have ended the immersion stage of Nettle Retting, not produced an equal heap of dry Nettle Fibre. Cleaning, drying and strength checks still stand between these strips and a useful cord.
Keep a short experiment short
Once ordinary supplies and the acorn work are finished, you allow four modest private casts at the inspected Projectile Practice Ground. You remove the grass panel so it cannot catch the thrower. The two earliest releases reach the broad bank patch; the other two do not. Your later movements feel less deliberate as your arms tire.
You stop. Another dozen attempts would make it harder to tell fatigue from a fit problem and would take time from the wet strips. The seat survives inspection without a spreading split. You record all four landings rather than keeping only the reassuring pair. No watchers appear and there is no new comparison, point or second dart.
End of day and next decision
All 0.65 kg of wet acorn meal is eaten. The model now retains 1.21 kg of kernels, 0.4 kg of untreated acorn input and 23 kg of usable dry fuel. The acorns have protected a little kernel stock at the cost of three estimated hours and extra heating.
Work totals 9.5 estimated active hours, with eight hours for sleep. The rabbit pelt and clay pair remain unfinished. Tomorrow, assess the drying fibre and select the shelter members. A better food route is useful, but the vessel’s small charges show why increasing throughput eventually needs containers as well as remembered recipes.

01_survival/moon-2-day-14---wood-that-ca.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 14 - Wood That Can Bear a Roof.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-14---wood-that-ca.title: Moon 2 Day 14 - Wood That Can Bear a Roof
01_survival/moon-2-day-14---wood-that-ca.content:
Moon 2 Day 14 - Wood That Can Bear a Roof
A hunt would spend today’s building time
You see red-deer tracks on the outer part of the familiar gathering circuit. They continue towards open ground where you would be easier to see. For a moment you consider following. A hide would alter the clothing problem, and you can picture the remembered approach diagrams.
You do not go after the animal. The tracks do not supply its present position, a safe cast or help with recovery. The reserve is short, and a half-day pursuit would postpone the shelter stock you have decided to collect. You note the direction and turn back to the known route. This is scouting judgement within the supply round, not a completed hunt or a promised deer encounter.
Another quarter of the acorn input is processed in two small charges. You repeat the vessel and water controls rather than doubling the load. The roughly 0.35 kg wet output is cooked and eaten today; 0.2 kg of dry input remains. The estimate includes about 3 litres of processing water and 1 kg of extra heating fuel.
Select pieces by their job
Near the western woodland edge you look for manageable sound fallen members. Fuel tolerates defects that a support cannot. You reject a fork with a soft crotch and a long piece whose split opens when flexed. A tree is not felled to create today’s convenient beam.
Over several short carries you bring back ten selected light members: two forked braces, one slender longitudinal rail and seven prospective return ribs. They are not heavy house timbers. The rail is intended to sit on the two fork seats beside the retained limb, giving the ribs a consistent bearing; it will not jack up or replace the heavy fallen support.
You take off the grass back panel before handling the timber. At the craft spot you remove projecting ends with the existing robust chopper edge and compare the pieces against the intended small resting space. Gentle fit checks show which ends will need further trimming. You leave them as stock, not an assembled frame. The southeast approach stays clear. Your spear is put down within reach during trimming and carried on the supply circuit; choosing manageable loads matters because you cannot carry everything and keep both hands ready.
You also sort a separate 2 kg author-estimated lot of dry brush, sound loose bark and coarse leaf/grass material for roof cover. Plant Covering Stock will fill and overlap a roof layer; it is distinct from clean bedding and the long garment grass. You put it under existing cover. No waterproof sheet or roof has been manufactured merely by selecting it.
Only the accepted fibre becomes stock
The selected nettle strips have dried sufficiently to clean and align a small portion. You remove woody fragments, reject weak sections and compare several bundles under light bending and pulling. The author model credits 18 g of usable dry fibre from this portion. It is a modest output after losses, not a measured extraction efficiency for the unweighed stem bundle.
The coarse remainder of batch B still needs work. You keep it separate from the accepted fibre. With the old 24 g, the loose ready stock reaches 42 g. You do not turn it into yarn or line in the same interval, and the replacement spindle does not remove the preparation labour.
The rabbit skin remains stiff through its centre. Brief working preserves a useful question about its edges, but it is not ready to become a wide chest covering. The clay pair stays protected and unfired. Neither project gets a fictitious completion while you carry wood.
End of day and next decision
The model retains 1.11 kg of edible kernels, 0.2 kg untreated acorn input and 23 kg dry fuel. The ten shelter members and 2 kg cover lot are unallocated; loose prepared fibre is 42 g. Work totals 9.5 estimated active hours, with eight hours for sleep.
Tomorrow you can begin Shelter Construction with actual pieces. First seat and test the forked braces and rail from outside the fall space. If they rock or the rib feet creep, cover material must wait. A roof assembled on unstable supports would spend the reserve without buying a reliable night’s rest.

01_survival/moon-2-day-15---a-frame-befo.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 15 - A Frame Before a Promise.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-15---a-frame-befo.title: Moon 2 Day 15 - A Frame Before a Promise
01_survival/moon-2-day-15---a-frame-befo.content:
Moon 2 Day 15 - A Frame Before a Promise
Keep somewhere to sleep while you build
The original covered side is still your resting space. You will add a low return frame along its north/east side rather than stripping the whole roof at once. The intended sleeping chamber remains in the northwest camp footprint and opens southeast. The craft spot, outside hearth, dirty frame and separate firing patch stay where they are.
The grass back panel is put aside so its fringe cannot catch during the fit work. You scrape loose litter from two small brace seats with the digging stick, keeping the bed itself apart. The forked pieces must stand on stable ground and bear the light rail without rolling. You fit them from outside, lower the rail into their forks and press modestly in several directions. One foot shifts. You take the load off, alter its seat and repeat the check. You do not hide the movement beneath a roof and call it settled.
The rail runs beside the sound retained fallen limb; neither brace is used to raise that heavy wood. Two short portions of the remaining nettle cord, about 0.4 m altogether, restrain a tendency to roll at the fork seats. Wood geometry carries the main load. Those small ties are not proof of a structural rope rating.
Three of the prepared ribs seat against the rail and slope outward to the north/east ground margin. You adjust the feet before putting weight over them. The new work creates the outline of a lower return side, not a finished enclosure. Four ribs remain stock. The existing leaf/bark side is left intact, so you still have the old roof tonight.
A framework is a separate result
This first stage of Framed Debris Shelter uses six selected members: two braces, the rail and three ribs. Shelter Construction includes site, fit, support and staged occupation; it cannot be reduced to remembering a hut shape. A framework which stands under light pressure has answered less than a roof loaded with damp cover in wind.
You leave the new side bare for inspection. Collecting more cover today is useful, but closing it before the remaining ribs are set would hide the feet and make adjustment harder. A modest 4 kg new lot joins yesterday’s 2 kg under protected cover. The dry coarse material is not added to the fuel pile or counted as clean bedding.
Separately, another 0.6 kg of clean dry material is gathered and allocated to the resting layer. You lift the little pad, remove damp or compressed refuse and extend the loose dry layer towards the feet. The improvement comes from that separate collection; the pad has not expanded into a whole mattress.
Food still owns part of the day
The last 0.2 kg acorn input goes through two small controlled charges, with the same extra water and heating allowance as yesterday. The roughly 0.35 kg wet output is cooked and eaten. There is no remaining dry acorn lot and no retained wet meal. Further use of the route needs another independent harvest and the labour to process it.
The cage and deadfalls are checked empty. Hazel gathering stays on accessible ground. No local person appears at the build, and no helper steadies the rail while you fit it. You pause to look up the western approach before returning both hands to the work. The partly framed opening could slow your own escape if you left members across it; you stack the remaining pieces to one side.
End of day and the full-moon review
The model retains 1.06 kg of kernels, 23 kg dry fuel, four unallocated shelter members and 6 kg of separate cover stock. Loose nettle line has fallen to 0.2 m; ready fibre remains 42 g. The new framework stands after limited fit and movement checks, but the added side has no weather covering. The pelt and coarse fibre remainder remain unfinished, and no vessel firing occurs.
Estimated active work is 9.5 hours, including a short evening appraisal, with eight hours for sleep. There are breaks in the cloud tonight; the nearly full moon gives glimpses of the open valley but no certainty about its occupants. Read Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15 after this day’s completed state.
Tomorrow, finish the light rib line and begin the covering. The test you owe the shelter is whether it keeps a resting person dry and protected in actual weather, not whether it resembles a remembered winter home.

01_survival/moon-2-day-16---the-roof-sti.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 16 - The Roof Still Owes You a Test.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-16---the-roof-sti.title: Moon 2 Day 16 - The Roof Still Owes You a Test
01_survival/moon-2-day-16---the-roof-sti.content:
Moon 2 Day 16 - The Roof Still Owes You a Test
Make line for a job, not for the stock table
The new framework is still exposed on its return side. Four ribs wait, but loose cord has nearly gone. You choose a little hand-made line for light cover retention, rather than trying to spin enough fine cloth or making every wooden contact depend on a lashing.
From the 42 g ready-fibre stock you allocate 10 g and work two-ply cord by hand, aligning overlaps and rejecting weak joins within that portion. The author model credits about 2 m of slender nettle line. You compare several lengths under gentle pull and use a short piece to restrain a light cover bundle. This is a limited handling trial; it assigns no breaking strength or universal fibre-to-length yield.
You reserve most of the new line loose. About 0.8 m goes to two light cover-retaining points, leaving 1.4 m loose when combined with the previous 0.2 m. These fastenings keep small outside pieces from shifting. They are not the main support for the rail or a dependable suspension for your body.
Close part of the space without closing the way out
From outside the fall space you recheck yesterday’s brace seats and rail. They have not visibly shifted overnight. You seat the four remaining ribs along the north/east return slope, preserving the southeast opening. The result remains a low chamber in the same camp footprint, not a second house.
Another 4 kg screened cover lot is collected. You begin from the lower part of the new slope, laying brush to retain the coarse material and overlapping sound bark pieces where they can direct water outward. You then work higher rather than pushing every loose layer under the top edge. Six kilograms from the combined ten-kilogram lot are allocated today. Four kilograms remain protected stock for repairs and the unfinished upper junction.
You do not call this a waterproof roof. The old covered side remains, the new return slope is partly covered, and the upper meeting line and southeast opening still need work. No hinged door or tightly sealed front appears. A clear exit and some ventilation remain necessary, and the hearth stays outside on its established bare ground.
Let the flaws change the next task
During an ordinary breeze the lower cover resists light movement. A loose upper corner lifts. You adjust the retaining brush and one small tie, then repeat the observation. The cover settles, but a breeze is not a storm or a rain test. Looking from the resting space, you can still see a gap at the upper junction.
You renew a further part of the bed with a separate 0.5 kg dry lot. A short resting trial feels less draughty on the newly covered side. You have no thermal measurement and no reason to declare a winter night solved. The plain framework check, the wind observation and the eventual rain test answer different questions.
The grass back panel is kept off while you handle the ribs, and put back on only for a short dry walk. It is still a back panel with an open front. The rabbit pelt is inspected at the dirty frame, its stiff centre still unassigned. No hide is moved into the roof, and no wall material is quietly reassigned as a coat.
A catch does not finance another long project
The fish cage holds one small fish. You retrieve it from stable footing, open the repaired rear cap and take out the catch without disturbing the inward funnel. The cap reseats before the cage is reset at the same anchor. The 0.08 kg dressed lot is cooked and eaten today.
