The routine circuit and accessible gathering provide less than today’s kernel use. You make no atlatl casts and do not follow deer tracks. Spending another half-day on the upper roof while ignoring the food decline would turn a shelter improvement into a different survival problem.
End of day and next decision
The model retains 0.93 kg of edible kernels and 24 kg of dry fuel. All ten selected shelter members are incorporated. Four kilograms of coarse cover remain loose; ready fibre is 32 g and loose nettle line 1.4 m. The unallocated 0.2 kg long grass, unused yarn and reserved sinew remain distinct from the new bed and roof allocations.
Estimated active work is ten hours, including cord making, fit checks, covering and supplies, with eight hours for sleep. The next day must prioritise another food collection and appraisal of the upper gap. A damp spell would make that gap urgent; a poor harvest would limit how much building you can afford. The Framed Debris Shelter has become a useful ongoing project, not a completed winter guarantee.

01_survival/moon-2-day-17---food-before-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 17 - Food Before the Last Roof Layer.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-17---food-before-.title: Moon 2 Day 17 - Food Before the Last Roof Layer
01_survival/moon-2-day-17---food-before-.content:
Moon 2 Day 17 - Food Before the Last Roof Layer
Give the day back to gathering
The little kernel reserve is too small to treat another building session as the whole day’s work. You take the basket and ordinary wooden-pointed spear along the accessible western circuit. The grass back panel goes on for the dry walking portions. You keep clear of the occupied patch where the warning came; a useful harvest is not worth pretending that encounter never happened.
You search longer in the nearer hazel and oak ground, turning leaves and rejecting damaged nuts. The basket fills slowly. Today’s larger collection comes from more work and a careful extension of the familiar patches, not a newly discovered inexhaustible grove. Gathering, shelling and the trap circuit occupy four estimated active hours. The cage and all three deadfalls are empty.
The author model records 0.75 kg shelled hazelnut kernels and 0.6 kg sound shelled acorn input. The acorns stay dry on a clean bark surface under protected cover. They are not an edible ration yet. You plan three small processing portions over the following days, using the one vessel rather than beginning a larger project without its water and fuel allowance.
Join the roof without stripping it
At camp you inspect the fork seats and rib feet from outside before adding more load. You remove the grass panel for this close work. The old covered side remains untouched. Three kilograms of the four-kilogram cover stock go onto the upper return slope and meeting line: retaining brush beneath, weather-facing bark overlapping the lower pieces so water has an outward route. The pieces meet beside the retained fallen limb; neither brace lifts that heavy wood.
You use another 0.2 m of nettle cord to hold one light outside overlap against lifting. Existing ties are inspected, not counted as fresh stock. The two slopes now have a connected covering, although the southeast mouth remains open. You can still see and reach the exit from the bed. The roof has yet to face rain, and adding cover changes the load which the light frame must carry.
A wider garment begins as yarn
You want a separate front panel to work with the existing grass back panel. The front and sides are still exposed whenever you leave the bed. Expanding coverage requires more retaining yarn; the two loose metres cannot make another full panel simply because you remember its construction.
From the prepared nettle stock you select 9 g, align the cleaner strands and use the replacement wooden spindle in a short, slow session at the clean craft spot. You turn, draft and wind in stages, stopping weak joins before they reach the stored length. The model credits about 7 m of uneven single yarn after waste within that allocation. It is light retaining material for twining, not a strong line. You wind it separately and stop before poor light makes inspection difficult.
A separate 0.4 kg of long, clean, flexible grass is gathered and screened for the garment. It joins the 0.2 kg already held loose. Roof cover does not become garment grass. Brief edge-working of the rabbit pelt improves a few bends, but its centre remains stiff and it stays unallocated.
End of day and next decision
The model retains 1.23 kg edible kernels, 0.6 kg untreated shelled acorns and 25 kg dry fuel. Loose cover is 1 kg, garment grass 0.6 kg, ready fibre 23 g, loose yarn 9 m and nettle line 1.2 m. Estimated active work is nine hours, with eight hours for sleep.
The better harvest buys a small amount of time. Tomorrow you will process one acorn portion and inspect the roof if the weather changes. Further yarn preparation, rather than another invention, is the next clothing dependency.

01_survival/moon-2-day-18---what-the-rai.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 18 - What the Rain and the Visitor Find.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-18---what-the-rai.title: Moon 2 Day 18 - What the Rain and the Visitor Find
01_survival/moon-2-day-18---what-the-rai.content:
Moon 2 Day 18 - What the Rain and the Visitor Find
Watch where the water goes
Rain begins before dawn and continues in short spells. You stay on the old resting side while watching the added return cover. A dark track appears at its upper meeting line; a small drip reaches the edge of the extended bedding. You lift that local wet material away. The little twined pad remains on its separate dry upper-body area.
The fault is in the overlap beside the retained limb. Water has found a narrow inward path beneath a curled piece. From outside, with the grass garment removed, you unload the small local cover patch and inspect the rail and fork contacts. There is no visible seat movement or new crack during this inspection. That observation permits a limited repair; it does not establish a general wet-load rating.
You adjust the curled bark, extend the weather-facing lap with 0.5 kg of protected cover stock and reuse the existing light retainer. Later showers leave no further visible drip at that location during the period you watch. The exposed mouth still admits gusts. You have found and changed one leak, not demonstrated a waterproof winter room.
A separate 0.4 kg clean dry bedding lot is collected from protected material and allocated to the wet edge. The removed bedding was already part of the occupied layer, not loose stock which can now be counted as fuel or clothing. The remaining 0.6 kg long garment grass stays dry and separate.
Something is using your dirty flank
Late in the morning, movement beyond the small drying frame stops your hands. A large grey-brown canid noses the ground at the southwest edge of the dirty-work flank. Its size and outline suggest a wolf. You cannot tell whether it is the animal once seen across the river, or whether other animals are out of sight.
You are on the clean side, with open ground between you and it. You stay upright, keep the spear low and ready, and speak sharply. You do not run after it or try to retrieve a frame-side object while it is there. It pauses, turns and passes back through the brush. You watch the approach for a while before resuming work. The ordinary outside fire has not kept it from investigating.
The visit changes the afternoon. The pelt is intact and no food store has been reached, but an old scrap caught beneath the processing surface is a plausible attractant. You remove loose animal scraps, clean the dirty surface, and keep the pelt protected during the interruption. Waste removal stays on the established dry southwest route, away from water collection; it does not become a fresh bait pile at the edge of camp. Existing separated waste is inspected and covered. These measures reduce accessible remnants without making the camp predator-proof.
You clear a narrow sight gap through loose brush on that approach so movement is easier to notice, keeping the retreat path open. It is an inspection gap, not a wall, a trap or an automatic alarm. Time spent waiting and cleaning replaces today’s planned yarn session.
Small charges still take their time
You process 0.2 kg of the new acorn input in two small charges, with about 3 litres additional processing water and 1 kg extra fuel beyond ordinary use. Fresh-water changes and reheating follow the already trialled route; the accepted wet output is about 0.35 kg, cooked and eaten today. No wet meal is saved.
Gathering provides 0.4 kg edible kernels. Routine checks retain no catch, and the rabbit pelt is inspected without a new allocation. The model ends at 1.15 kg kernels, 0.4 kg untreated acorns and 25 kg dry fuel. Loose roof cover is 0.5 kg; yarn, fibre and line remain at yesterday’s values.
Nine estimated active hours cover supplies, two acorn charges, roof and bed repair, vigilance and cleanup; eight hours remain for sleep. The planned hunting reconnaissance can wait for a clear morning and a firm stopping time. A visit by an animal is not a reason to make a hurried weapon upgrade.

01_survival/moon-2-day-19---the-deer-hav.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 19 - The Deer Have More Than One Way Out.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-19---the-deer-hav.title: Moon 2 Day 19 - The Deer Have More Than One Way Out
01_survival/moon-2-day-19---the-deer-hav.content:
Moon 2 Day 19 - The Deer Have More Than One Way Out
Set a limit before leaving camp
The showers have passed, and the changed overlap shows no fresh inward drip during the morning inspection. You decide on a short outing along the red-deer signs seen while collecting shelter wood. It is reconnaissance with the possibility of a careful ordinary-spear approach, not a promise to return with a hide. You allow two and a half active hours for the whole outing, including the return.
The test dart stays at camp. It is still blunt, green and unfletched; a practice landing does not make it a hunting projectile. You take the familiar wooden-pointed hand spear, a modest portion of today’s kernels and the essential pouch. The kernel portion comes from the day’s recorded consumption. No food or tool is left at the fallback bench.
You leave the grass panel under cover because wet undergrowth and hanging fringe would hinder this approach. The bark waist panels, pelvic pad and narrow left fox panel remain. Bare feet make you choose each step carefully on the stony ground. You follow the western gathering terrain, short of the occupied nut patch and contact route, without crossing the main river or entering the neighbours’ clearing.
Read a moving situation
Several prints cross softer ground beside a rocky shoulder. Their pattern and nearby browsing are more useful than a single crisp mark, but you cannot date the trail precisely. You pause where two paths separate, note a return route you can recognise, and watch grass tips to judge the local air movement.
Beyond the shoulder, two red-deer hinds feed across an open strip. You begin a slow approach from cover with the spear low, intending to get closer only while you retain footing, a clear cast and a recoverable line. The first path looks promising from your stopping point. A shallow stony dip lies between it and the animals, and brush screens the ground beyond them.
You move a few careful steps. One hind lifts its head while the other continues feeding. When you shift around the dip, gravel moves beneath your foot; the local breeze also turns along the slope. Both animals now attend to your side of the strip. You cannot tell which cue mattered first. They walk away, then bound through separate breaks in the cover before you have a close, controlled opportunity.
You do not throw after them. The moving line is partly screened, and following a doubtful injury alone would take you into ground you have not checked. The outing stops at its planned limit. You return with the spear, no meat, no pelt and a clearer view of the problem.
The lesson in Hunting Approach is larger than reaching another metre. No companion can hold the other opening, watch the second hind while you move, or help with a difficult recovery. An atlatl might eventually extend a useful cast; it would not remove those tasks. Today’s refusal to cast is part of the failed approach, not an unexplained absence of effort.
The cost returns to camp with you
The outing cuts into the gathering period. The model records only 0.25 kg new kernels, against 0.48 kg eaten. You process the next 0.2 kg acorn portion through two charges, using another 3 litres processing water and 1 kg extra fuel. All 0.35 kg wet meal is cooked and eaten. The routine cage and deadfall checks are empty; no craft workshop occurs while you are away.
At the clean craft spot you allocate a second 9 g of prepared fibre to a short spindle session, crediting another 7 m uneven single yarn after rejected joins within the portion. The reserve is now 16 m yarn and 14 g prepared fibre. The front-panel grass remains dry stock. The rabbit pelt receives a brief condition check but no further clothing claim.
Estimated active work is ten hours, including the short outing, supplies, acorn work, drafting and records; eight hours remain for sleep. The model retains 0.92 kg kernels, 0.2 kg untreated acorns and 25 kg dry fuel. Tomorrow’s larger job is fitting the front covering from earned stock. Further hunting needs a fresh budget, rather than extending today’s disappointment into an evening chase.

01_survival/moon-2-day-2---they-know-whe.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 2 - They Know Where to Look.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-2---they-know-whe.title: Moon 2 Day 2 - They Know Where to Look
01_survival/moon-2-day-2---they-know-whe.content:
Moon 2 Day 2 - They Know Where to Look
Begin the slow part early
The remaining prepared fibre is a small dry stock, and every prospective fastening seems to claim it. A mantle, another binding and a trap repair cannot all spend the same line. You decide to start another independently harvested batch before colder conditions make the wait more troublesome.
At the known nettle margin you find enough sound mature stems for a modest bundle, rejecting badly weathered pieces. Collection, stripping leaves and arranging the stems take time that could have gone into another throwing session.
You use a short portion of the remaining bark line as the bundle’s retaining tie, together with a weighted branch arrangement at the established downstream pool. Nettle Retting begins again there, below drinking-water collection. You check that the bundle can be reached without risky wading. No prepared fibre enters the stock today, and colder water gives you no reason to expect the first batch’s twelve-day sequence to repeat.
Two figures above the near slope
On the return you notice two people near the ridge lookout. One stands against the pale rock while the other moves lower along the near slope. They have come from the direction of the northern clearing. At this distance you cannot read their expressions or identify everything they carry.
You stop in open view with the wooden spear low. Neither approaches. One remains turned towards your part of the terrace long enough to make the location of your smoke feel obvious.
They might be curious, checking a route, or watching the stranger who ran from their warning. You have no reliable way to decide. You also have no reason to treat their present restraint as a promise.
You return by the known ground and spend a while watching the approach before resuming work. There is no threat you can repel by polishing the atlatl. If several determined adults came down together, the useful question would be where you could go and what you could take.
The work that changes
You abandon the planned practice interval. Instead, you inspect how the pouch, vessel and small food portion could be gathered without crossing between the hearth and an approaching person. The spear remains close while you work. You do not tie shut the shelter entrance or pile a barrier across your own exit.
Watching has a cost: the active-work account includes the pauses, withdrawal and resetting of the day’s tasks. It creates no theft, wound, gift or extra tool.
End of day
The model retains 2.24 kg of kernels and 20 kg of dry fuel. Nettle batch B is a separate wet stem batch, secured downstream. Loose bark cord has fallen to 0.4 m; the rest of the existing fibre, yarn and nettle cord remains available.
Active work is estimated at 8 hours, with eight hours for sleep. Contact consists of distance and observation, not cooperation. See Survival Ledger.
Next decision
Prepare a small bedding trial from independently collected plant material. Then inspect a fallback route that does not depend on swimming the main river or on the neighbours’ permission.

01_survival/moon-2-day-20---cover-the-fr.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 20 - Cover the Front Without Losing Your Hands.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-20---cover-the-fr.title: Moon 2 Day 20 - Cover the Front Without Losing Your Hands
01_survival/moon-2-day-20---cover-the-fr.content:
Moon 2 Day 20 - Cover the Front Without Losing Your Hands
Choose coverage that can be removed
You have enough prepared working material for the front panel planned three days ago. The aim is modest: less direct air movement over the chest and abdomen, with the arms free and the covering easily removable. A densely closed coat would need more material, different shaping and better moisture control. You will fit a separate flexible panel to work with the existing back screen.
At the clean craft spot, with the old back panel put aside, you sort the 0.6 kg long grass stock. You allocate 0.5 kg to the new piece; rejects are included in that portion. Small overlapping bundles hang from a supported top edge, about 0.45 m across and 0.6 m long in the author model. The grass is flexible foundation material, not stiff willow splints from the bedding pad.
Twelve metres of the uneven single yarn supply the paired retaining rows and their margins. You maintain the two-element crossing between bundles, stop to rework a creeping section, then lift and bend the sheet before fitting it. The retained stock is 4 m yarn. This is Twining applied to the same Plant-Fibre Clothing family, not a new technology acquired because the first specimen was narrow.
Make the fastenings before trusting them
You allocate 10 g of the remaining ready fibre to about 2 m slender hand-made two-ply cord, including rejected weak sections within that portion. Gentle pulls and a light bundle trial precede use. The line is for garment suspension, not a structural load or climbing system.
About 1.2 m goes into the front panel’s supported top edge and loose, accessible attachments. Its header lies below the collarbones. Shoulder attachments sit clear of the narrow fox strip on the left, and light side adjustment keeps the lower margin from swinging into your hands. There is no tight neck loop. You wear the two independent grass panels together, adjust a rubbing stem and repeat a short walk, crouch and reach.
The front and back of the core are now mostly screened, but the sides, upper chest, arms, legs, head and feet retain exposed areas. Air feels less direct across the covered abdomen in this short dry check. There is no measured insulation, rain result or projectile-clearance test. Both grass pieces come off for the hearth, bank work and wet processing, and hang under protected cover when removed.
Work at the mouth, not across the escape
The shower repair has held during the periods inspected, but gusts enter the southeast opening. You collect 2.5 kg separate coarse cover stock and allocate 2 kg as a light offset brush bundle beside one edge of the mouth. It bears on the outer rib margin and ground; no new post, hinge or animal hide is introduced.
You shift it by hand and check that you can leave the resting space without moving a loaded beam or squeezing behind the bundle. The open passage and ventilation remain. This first wind baffle reduces a direct gust during observation; it is not a barricade or a door that can hold off a visitor. One kilogram of loose cover remains after today’s collection and allocation.
End of day and next decision
Routine gathering supplies 0.45 kg kernels. The last 0.2 kg acorn input is processed in two charges, again allowing 3 litres extra water and 1 kg extra fuel. All 0.35 kg wet meal is cooked and eaten. The traps and cage retain no catch. There is no acorn input left, no stored meal and no firing or projectile session.
The model retains 0.89 kg edible kernels and 25 kg dry fuel, 4 g prepared fibre, 4 m single yarn, 2 m loose nettle line and 0.1 kg long garment grass. The new front panel is a distinct object, not an enlargement counted twice. Active work is 10.5 estimated hours, including supplies, two acorn charges, cord, panel construction and the entrance adjustment; eight hours remain for sleep.
The rabbit pelt is still a separate unfinished lot. Tomorrow you will assess whether its worked margins can support a limited crown covering, while assigning a longer period to gathering. Feet need their own material and movement trial. A quieter draught does not remove either need.

01_survival/moon-2-day-21---a-smaller-ga.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 21 - A Smaller Gap Between Work and Warmth.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-21---a-smaller-ga.title: Moon 2 Day 21 - A Smaller Gap Between Work and Warmth
01_survival/moon-2-day-21---a-smaller-ga.content:
Moon 2 Day 21 - A Smaller Gap Between Work and Warmth
Give the pelt one job
The rabbit skin from Day 38 has been fleshed, protected and worked while drying, yet its middle is still firmer than its edges. You examine it at the dirty-material flank before bringing it to the fitting task. Hair is holding on the inspected areas, no deteriorating fold is apparent, and the worked margins bend without a spreading tear under gentle handling. Those observations do not turn untreated skin into durable leather.
You choose a small crown covering rather than saving it for an imagined full coat. The new grass front panel addresses part of the body, while the exposed head remains uncomfortable in cold air. One rabbit pelt can pad the crown and part of the upper back of the head; it cannot also become footwear, a bag and extra shoulder coverage.
You allocate the entire pelt to this variant of Fur-On Pelt Clothing. The stiffer centre stays as a shallow crown pad, fur outward, with small folded side margins. You flex the margins over a smooth support without stretching them hard. After a little edge-hole comparison, about 0.2 m of reserved sinew thread secures the folds. The awl makes holes away from weak edges; the needle follows them without being forced through a stiff centre.
About 0.8 m of inspected nettle line supplies a loose adjustable band around the forehead and back of the head. It is not tied beneath the chin or around the throat. You lift it off readily, adjust a pressure point and repeat a short walk and head turn. The face, ears and much of the nape remain exposed. The pad is a dry-use head covering, not a fitted hood or wet-weather cap. The narrow fox strip remains on the left shoulder; it has not grown into it.
A longer gathering round is still necessary
The food reserve remains short even after the acorn meals. You spend a longer period on the accessible circuit, wearing the paired grass panels during the dry walk and taking them off before close water and fire work. The front header creeps slightly on one side during the return. You stop, re-seat the existing fastening and remove a rubbing stem without adding new material. This first longer walk exposes a maintenance task which the short fitting did not.
The own-work harvest provides 0.5 kg shelled kernels. The cage holds one small fish; stable footing, the removable rear cap and the unchanged inward funnel remain the retrieval route. The 0.12 kg dressed fish is cooked and eaten today. All three deadfalls are empty. No large hide, stored meat or guaranteed capture appears.
You gather a separate 0.5 kg clean dry bedding lot and allocate it to the resting layer, lifting the small pad to inspect beneath it. The repaired roof overlap shows no fresh inward drip at today’s inspection; there is no new storm test. The entrance bundle remains movable and clear of the passage. No canid is seen on the cleared sight gap. Absence during these checks is not proof that it has stopped visiting.
Find a baseline you can repeat
After ordinary supplies, you allow four modest private atlatl casts at the inspected practice ground. The head pad, both grass panels and fox strip are removed and kept dry there so nothing can catch the thrower’s sweep. You recover every item before leaving.
Three landings reach the broad bank patch and one misses. You record all four and stop; that small result is not enough to establish a narrowing gap against the local expert. The green dart’s rear seat is still intact on inspection, and no new point or fletching has been added. Nobody watches today. The more deliberate release is a setting to repeat when food work allows, not a reason to invite another comparison immediately.
End of day and the next allocation
The model retains 0.94 kg kernels and 26 kg dry fuel. Prepared fibre is 4 g, loose yarn 4 m, nettle line 1.2 m and reserved sinew 0.5 m. One kilogram coarse roof cover and 0.1 kg long garment grass remain distinct. Rabbit pelt D38 has left loose material stock and become one limited crown covering. The original back panel, new front panel, head piece and fox strip are separate maintained items.
Estimated active work is ten hours, including the longer supply round, head-piece fitting, bed renewal, repair and short practice, with eight hours for sleep. Feet remain bare. The next phase must put food yield, rudimentary foot protection, spare ignition, a second water route and the unsupplied retreat ahead of more decorative improvements. The later observer’s interest is still something the narrative must earn.

01_survival/moon-2-day-22---let-the-grai.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 22 - Let the Grain Do the Work.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-22---let-the-grai.title: Moon 2 Day 22 - Let the Grain Do the Work
01_survival/moon-2-day-22---let-the-grai.content:
Moon 2 Day 22 - Let the Grain Do the Work
Choose a tool that makes other tools
The shelter now leaves you a dry place to wake and a little space in which to think beyond the next repair. You lay the fireboard beside the flake and the rough chopper. Much of your woodwork has followed the shape of whichever branch you could find. A second fireboard, a flat support and eventually better joints would be easier if you could choose the shape of the stock.
You remember saws, adzes and benches. Each would bring another construction problem. For today’s short billet, the grain offers a simpler route: a Wooden Splitting Wedge, driven by a Wooden Mallet. These are tools for making useful pieces of wood with tools you already possess.
Your mission still ends far beyond this valley, with people able to build instruments and machines and act on the threat in the sky. The immediate link is reproducible work. A remembered machine cannot be assembled from an unlimited collection of fortunate branch shapes.
Open the wood instead of cutting it all away
During ordinary collection you choose a short sound hardwood piece with a natural thick end for a one-piece mallet, two smaller pieces for wedges, and a straight dry willow billet. All are your own collected material. You leave the larger timber where it lies; this is work you can brace and handle alone.
At the craft spot you reduce the mallet’s grip, smooth the striking face and scrape gradual tapers on the wedges. The sharp flake does small cuts. The robust chopper works on supported wood, clear of the holding hand. You put the crown pad aside with the flexible grass panels and sit on the bare ground rather than inventing a bench before you need one.
The willow has a small end check. You seat the first wedge there and strike gently. The opening moves ahead of the tip. A second wedge holds it farther along while you free the first. For a short distance the wood separates cleanly; then the split bends towards a small knot. You stop and turn the billet to inspect the changing line.
The narrow portion running out at the side will not make your intended board. The remaining piece gives you a rough flat blank with enough thickness to trim. You retain that piece and reject the damaged portion. Neither wedge has developed a spreading crack, though one tip is already bruised.
Give the blank its next job
You set it beside the existing fireboard. It is a candidate for a spare hearth board, still needing a flat bearing surface, a sound socket and a real ignition test. The matching spindle will have to come from its own suitable piece; a board alone cannot restart a dead fire.
Food, water and fuel take their usual part of the day. There is no extended hunt or firing to compete with the woodwork. Before putting the new tools under cover, you mark the chosen blank so it will remain separate from firewood.
Tomorrow you need flexible ties as well as rigid parts. Footwear offers a small useful test of the same principle: select a function, use available material, then find out what the finished object can actually do.

01_survival/moon-2-day-23---a-sole-befor.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 23 - A Sole Before a Boot.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-23---a-sole-befor.title: Moon 2 Day 23 - A Sole Before a Boot
01_survival/moon-2-day-23---a-sole-befor.content:
Moon 2 Day 23 - A Sole Before a Boot
Begin with the ground contact
On the last deer approach, loose stone moved beneath a bare foot before any weapon could be useful. A better projectile will leave that problem in place. You choose Plant-Fibre Footwear as today’s experiment: a sole that stays under the foot, with a little replaceable dry lining.
Your memory supplies many shoe designs, but the remembered leather is absent from the pile of materials. The rabbit skin is already on your head, and the fox piece already covers part of the left shoulder. You start with local willow bast and a short dry-ground trial. A successful sole could make some work more comfortable; a slipping sole could make it worse.
Make the flexible material do two jobs
At the nearer willow stand you inspect a small strip before taking more from sound recently fallen material. The weathered outer surface is unpromising in places. Beneath one sound section, selected inner strips separate and bend without breaking. You discard brittle sections rather than fastening them into a failure you will discover while walking.
Back at camp you prepare two grades. Broader supple strips will make the sole; narrower sound fibres become coarse Bark Cordage. Opposed twisting and staggered joins are familiar from Simple Cordage, but this fresh material earns its own pull and knot checks. You protect the remaining line for the spare fire kit and vessel work.
You interlace the broad strips into two small flat footbeds, turning the margins so cut ends will not press into the skin. The over-and-under structure is a flat application of Simple Coiling and Weaving, rather than a new claim to fine cloth. Coarse line closes the edges and supplies loose forefoot and heel retention. A thin layer of separately collected clean dry grass sits above each sole.
Test the shoe, then the ground
Beside a low natural support you stand, turn and crouch. One heel comes free on the first turn. You reposition its retaining tie and repeat, keeping the fastening loose enough to remove readily. On a short level dry circuit the soles stay beneath you, and the ground’s cold contact feels less direct. You stop to examine both feet and the underside, rather than treating the first comfortable steps as the whole test.
On a small dry incline one sole begins to creep sideways. You remove the pair and finish the return barefoot. A thicker sole has also changed how your foot feels the ground. The short result leaves you experimental footwear for dry level camp work, with an obvious retention problem to revisit. It supplies neither a wet-weather boot nor permission for a longer hunt.
The ordinary supply work continues in the background. You keep the pair dry, remove grit and leave the footbeds open to air. A second version can be judged against something you have actually worn. For now, the remaining coarse line has a more urgent job: helping you reproduce fire away from the one kit on which the whole camp depends.

01_survival/moon-2-day-24---fire-that-ca.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 24 - Fire That Can Be Started Again.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-24---fire-that-ca.title: Moon 2 Day 24 - Fire That Can Be Started Again
01_survival/moon-2-day-24---fire-that-ca.content:
Moon 2 Day 24 - Fire That Can Be Started Again
Replace a single point of failure
You take out the split willow blank. Its next job is already decided. The first fire kit has kept working through weeks of care, but damage or a hurried departure could separate you from it. Stored embers are useful only while something remains to tend them.
Today you will make a second complete bow-drill kit and try it on its own parts. This is the beginning of a reproducible service: suitable wood, a maintained mechanism and a practised action that can be repeated when needed. The same question will later apply to a furnace, a pump or a workshop’s power source.
Reproduce the mechanism, including the awkward parts
You flatten the blank with supported cuts and scraping. A socket goes near a sound edge; its dust notch will lead to a separate dry catcher. The original Fireboard remains available as a comparison, but you do not borrow its working socket for the new kit’s test.
A separate piece of dry willow supplies the spindle. New sound wood supplies a modest bow and bearing block. You use the old kit to judge the relation between the parts: room for the bow stroke, stable upper support, and a lower contact that turns without jumping out. Exact copying of a branch’s length matters less than those relationships.
Part of yesterday’s coarse bark line becomes the new bowstring. A small separate dry tinder bundle waits beside the catcher. You take off the grass panels and crown pad and clear the work of loose dry material beyond what the test needs. Your bare foot can brace the board without the experimental sole shifting underneath it.
Make a test that can fail clearly
You set the adjustable bowstring tension before the working run. Short slow strokes show steady rotation, and the upper bearing stays aligned against your supported arm. This time the familiar checks let you proceed without a repair interrupting the trial.
The controlled working run leaves a small glowing dust coal after the spindle stops. You let it hold, transfer it into the new tinder and work it into a small flame. Only then does the second kit earn an ignition result. You extinguish the little test fire on the cleared outdoor hearth area; the established camp fire was kept available throughout.
Bow Drill Fire has now succeeded with another set of local parts. It has still been tested dry, at camp, with time to diagnose a slipping string. A cold wet departure would be another problem.
Keep the second kit separate
You mark the new board and pack the kit’s dry components together. It goes under a different protected part of the existing shelter cover, clear of the opening where rain has entered before. This separates two bundles without pretending they are independent of the same shelter’s weather damage.
Ordinary supplies have allowed the workshop session, and the shelter still needs care. The fallback bench remains unsupplied. You have created something portable that could later help furnish it, rather than moving your only working ignition there and merely relocating the original risk. The next vulnerable service is water treatment, still resting on one much-repaired bark vessel.

01_survival/moon-2-day-25---make-the-sec.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 25 - Make the Second One Deliberately.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-25---make-the-sec.title: Moon 2 Day 25 - Make the Second One Deliberately
01_survival/moon-2-day-25---make-the-sec.content:
Moon 2 Day 25 - Make the Second One Deliberately
Copy what worked and examine what wore out
The bark vessel has supplied a practical alternative to pottery. It has also leaked, needed repair and remained small. You want a second vessel that can take over a real job, with its construction informed by the failures of the first.
You turn the empty original over at the clean craft spot. The corner fold and fastening tell you more than its outline: where a sharp bend has weakened the sheet, where a hole bears on the material, and how the support keeps its bottom from taking every movement of a heated stone. These are the details worth carrying into the next Bark Container.
A functioning pair could later separate stages of food processing or protect water treatment during repair. First, the second one must hold and tolerate the same limited heating route. A bigger outline would only increase the demands on bark and bindings.
Use a pattern without pretending the sheets are identical
You collect a small pliable birch-bark sheet from a sound accessible fallen piece, testing a corner before accepting it. A separate little scrap receives fold marks from the old vessel. You keep it as a rough pattern, then adjust the marks to avoid a weak place in the new sheet.
The vessel stays shallow. You support each fastening hole, keep it back from an edge likely to tear, and allocate fresh coarse bark line to the overlapping corners. The new split tools do not solve the bark work for you; their board-making lesson does suggest saving a reusable pattern instead of beginning every replacement from memory.
Test containment before heat
You fill it on a stable support over dry ground. A damp trace appears beside one corner. You empty it, ease the strained fold and re-seat the binding. On the repeat, a modest marked working level holds without a continuing leak. This is a cold containment result; it does not yet replace the boiling vessel.
At the outside hearth you use the established screened stones and handling sticks. You avoid striking the bark and watch the seams as the water heats. Steam appears before the water boils throughout. When the rolling boil is sustained, you follow the existing treatment interval, then leave the vessel supported while it cools.
After emptying, you inspect the corner and repeat with another small charge. The sheet and binding hold through both trials. You retain a second vessel with a conservative working mark. Its capacity is judged by comparison with the old charge, rather than an invented measuring jug. Its durability remains an open question.
Two routes into the next experiment
Food and ordinary camp care leave room for this focused work; there is no ceramic firing today. You keep clean treated-water handling separate from collection and dirty material work. Both bark vessels remain at the main camp.
The spare vessel opens useful choices. Small leaching charges may eventually be organised with less interference between stages. Pottery can be tested as a material route while drinking water still has another vessel available. Your next ceramic work should compare prepared samples, drying and firing deliberately. The objective is a repeatable heat-resistant container, with more to learn than whether one new cup happens to survive.

01_survival/moon-2-day-26---a-demonstrat.title: Moon 2 Day 26 - A Demonstration Worth Watching
01_survival/moon-2-day-26---a-demonstrat.content:
Moon 2 Day 26 - A Demonstration Worth Watching
Return to one question
The camp now has a few more ways to keep working when an object fails. None of them creates the skilled companions your mission will eventually require. The atlatl remains your clearest possible demonstration of a useful unfamiliar mechanism, but the first watched trial displayed the local spear user’s competence much more clearly than your own.
You return to Projectile Practice Ground with the same blunt unfletched dart. Its wood is still changing as it dries, and you inspect it rather than awarding it a seasoned status after counting days. The bowed second blank stays at camp. The crown pad and grass panels come off for the session; the experimental footwear is also put aside. A new outfit would add another variable to an already uncertain movement.
You choose a familiar broad bank patch and a modest starting position. Today’s question is whether you can repeat a controlled release there. Extending the distance can wait.
Preserve a setting you can compare
Slow engagement shows no new split or snag at the rear seat. You make the first casts without an extra backward cocking movement and keep the release in the same plane. The first goes low. The next three land in the chosen patch. You recover the dart, inspect it and mark every attempt on the bark record.
After a pause, you repeat from the same place. Four casts reach the patch. The landings are visibly closer together than the scattered opening trials, although the patch remains broad and you are working at modest reach. You have eight attempts, including the low first cast, and a better repeated result. Changes in the wood, familiarity with the place and technique may all contribute. You have neither a hunting test nor a controlled comparison against the local expert.
Let curiosity determine the distance
Before the second sequence ends, you notice two adults on the northern edge of the open ground, clear of the westward cast and retrieval line. You stop with the thrower lowered. They remain where they are. When the ground ahead is clear and their positions remain outside it, you complete the last modest cast. You do not increase force for the audience.
After retrieval, one gestures towards the short launcher and the rear of the dart. You hold them separately at your own position, then slowly seat the dart to show the engagement. The adult takes a few steps closer and stops. You lower both again and leave the intervening space open. No weapon is offered, no equipment changes hands, and nobody tries the device today.
They remain longer than on the earlier watched session. That is the observation you can keep. Their interest may concern the lever, your changed release or merely what the stranger will do next. You have no shared words with which to turn a gesture into agreement.
Choose a useful next lesson
Ordinary gathering has been shorter to allow the session, and the food buffer remains limited. You end with enough daylight for the return and camp care. There is no victory hunt after a promising target result.
The next technical task is still improving the system: an independently accepted second shaft would help distinguish a particular dart from a reproducible design; fletching could then be compared without disguising a release problem. The next social task is finding whether someone willingly wants to try a useful part of it. A future planetary-defence industry needs skills that pass between people. Today has earned a better example to show and the beginnings of a willing audience.

01_survival/moon-2-day-3---a-small-patte.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 3 - A Small Pattern for the Cold.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-3---a-small-patte.title: Moon 2 Day 3 - A Small Pattern for the Cold
01_survival/moon-2-day-3---a-small-patte.content:
Moon 2 Day 3 - A Small Pattern for the Cold
Warmth cannot wait for a large hide
The fox panel does useful work over one shoulder and leaves much of your body exposed. Nothing in the recent trap circuit suggests that a conveniently large hide is about to solve the problem.
You choose a smaller task: hold part of the bedding together so it can be lifted, aired and renewed without the whole layer migrating. A wearable covering will need different flexibility and movement tests. Today’s pad experiment can teach a construction pattern without claiming to be a coat.
From dry ground near the western gathering route you collect clean grass and sound leaves, shaking out grit and rejecting damp or fouled portions. Dry Plant Insulation is useful only in its observed condition. You refresh the shelter bed with part and keep the rest under ventilated cover, away from sparks.
Prepare coarse material before fine cloth
At the known willow margin you select a modest number of shoots and try narrow splits. Several wander with the grain or leave sharp sections and are rejected. You smooth the retained willow strips at the craft spot. They are coarse foundations, not extracted bark fibre or spun thread.
You convert part of the old prepared nettle stock into a light line lot, inspecting uneven joins before keeping it. The new retting bundle is still waiting downstream; it has produced nothing you can spend.
On a few willow foundations you practise Twining. Two working portions of cord cross between neighbouring strips and retain them. The first crossings slide when you lift the sample. Reworking the spacing gives you a small piece which holds under gentle handling. You stop at that scale rather than allocating the entire lot to an untested broad sheet.
The remaining single yarn stays separate. Its length does not make it interchangeable with the line you have just inspected.
A catch without a new supply system
The fish cage holds one small fish. You retrieve the cylinder from stable bank footing, untie the rear cap and remove the catch through that access, leaving the inward entrance funnel intact. You check the closure and anchor before resetting it.
The fish is cooked and eaten the same day. It is a useful contribution, but an intermittent cage catch does not establish a preserved fish store. The food account records the modest dressed lot, not an imagined regular yield.
You give the retting bundle a brief sample check during the downstream work. Its fibres do not yet separate usefully. It stays in process.
End of day
The model records 2.21 kg of kernels and 20 kg of dry fuel. Prepared nettle fibre is down to 24 g; loose nettle cord is 8 m after making the new lot and allocating the sample. Ten cumulative metres of willow strips and one kilogram of loose dry plant matter remain reserved. The small sample exists separately.
This is a busy day: 10 estimated active hours and an eight-hour sleep allowance. There is no atlatl practice or clothing construction on top of that work. Survival Ledger keeps the allocations distinct.
Next decision
Use tomorrow’s travel allowance to inspect a fallback place. Finish the bedding pad only after the sample and retained materials have been rechecked.

01_survival/moon-2-day-4---a-way-out-is-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 4 - A Way Out Is Not a Refuge.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-4---a-way-out-is-.title: Moon 2 Day 4 - A Way Out Is Not a Refuge
01_survival/moon-2-day-4---a-way-out-is-.content:
Moon 2 Day 4 - A Way Out Is Not a Refuge
Decide what you would leave
You cannot carry the whole terrace. The pottery specimen, drying frame, fuel pile and basket-making scraps would slow a hurried departure more than they would help the first hour away.
The ordinary spear, a cutting edge, maintained ignition provision, bark vessel and a little food are the priorities. You check where the existing pouch and carrier could hold the smaller items, but you do not pretend that listing them is a tested loaded escape pack. The vessel would need handling, and the little sling has only passed its original modest load.
Retreat Planning starts by admitting those limits. The task is to find a plausible exit and inspect its return, not acquire a second camp by thinking about it.
Follow a route that does not need a crossing
You leave by the western ground and follow the upstream side of the small-stream route. Above the seep’s head you can skirt the drainage without crossing the larger river or relying on a new bridge. You continue south along higher ground towards the pine patch, keeping sight of landmarks that would still help on the reverse journey.
Beyond the patch, a small higher bench southwest of it has a natural rock screen and reasonably drained ground. You examine the overhanging vegetation, resting surface and surrounding tracks. No fresh sign persuades you to enter an occupied animal resting place, but an empty inspection cannot prove future safety.
There is no dependable drinking source at the bench itself. The route back towards the known seep is therefore part of its cost. The rock screen reduces exposure from one direction; it does not make a shelter with a dry bed or weatherproof roof.
Check the return, count the cost
You deliberately retrace a difficult part while it is light, then return by the route you intend to recognise under pressure. Some sections would be slower when wet. You remember where the contour becomes less obvious and where you would have to stop rather than choose blindly.
You leave no food, fuel or tool at the bench. Supplying it later will mean subtracting something from the main camp, not duplicating the current inventory. Building even a small emergency shelter will take another visit and materials.
Today’s longer circuit leaves less time for shelling and gathering. The resulting food deficit belongs to the plan’s cost. It is preferable to learning about the drainage for the first time while someone follows you, but it does not make the reserve larger.
At camp you inspect the practice dart without launching it, check the nettle tie on the routine downstream round, and keep the spare shaft under cover. The small pad remains a sample and reserved inputs.
End of day
The model records 1.96 kg of kernels and 20 kg of dry fuel. No supplies have moved to the fallback bench. The only demonstrated advance is route judgement and a limited return check.
Estimated work is 8.5 active hours, with eight hours for sleep. Survival Ledger records the smaller harvest; Valley Map retains its Day 28 graphic and records this new site in the dated written additions.
Next decision
Patch the windward shelter before poorer weather turns a small gap into a bad night. Begin another modest clay comparison only within the remaining work allowance.

01_survival/moon-2-day-5---rain-finds-th.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 5 - Rain Finds the Weak Places.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-5---rain-finds-th.title: Moon 2 Day 5 - Rain Finds the Weak Places
01_survival/moon-2-day-5---rain-finds-th.content:
Moon 2 Day 5 - Rain Finds the Weak Places
Repair the shelter you actually have
Rain arrives with a west/northwest wind. A loose edge in the windward covering admits a fine spray, and the colder air makes you notice the difference between being out of the rain and being warmly covered.
You repair the same fallen-limb shelter. The entrance still faces southeast, the ordinary hearth stays outside, and the craft spot remains uphill of it. A damaged patch cannot justify moving the fire beside dry bedding.
You replace displaced covering with independently collected branches and overlapping material, weighting what can be held without line. One awkward edge needs the last short loose portion of bark cord. Basic Thatching supplies the arrangement and inspection; a tiny tie does not make the whole roof stormproof.
The refreshed resting material remains usable after you inspect and air the affected edge. You do not add wet grass to the dry insulation stock. Several pieces of gathered wood are too wet to count as usable dry fuel today. You burn more of the existing reserve to maintain the ordinary heat-and-water routine.
A smaller pottery question
The failed first pot is still a non-food specimen. Rather than make another larger vessel and hope, you want to distinguish drying problems before spending firing fuel.
During the same downstream circuit you take a small clay lot from the established bank. At the craft spot you form two modest comparison pieces from the same prepared body, giving one a thinner section and one a thicker section. You keep the shapes otherwise similar and mark them distinctly in the scratch register.
Clay Vessel Making allows this smaller trial. You use the retained reference staff and comparison marks to keep the intended distinction recognisable; you do not claim accurately realised millimetres. No new temper additive or new clay source confounds today’s pair.
Both pieces go under ventilated cover. Their surfaces and centres will dry differently, especially in this weather. No test can happen merely because a prescribed number of days has passed, and no ceramic water container has been produced.
Let the record alter the plan
The new nettle sample still resists useful separation. The material stays secured in the downstream pool. You have spent some old fibre, and the next batch cannot yet replace it.
The food portions have been shrinking during experiments and reconnaissance. This is why you made the record: a sequence of individually reasonable jobs is still drawing down the buffer. Tomorrow’s short practice must fit around gathering and the reserved bedding work.
End of day
The author model records 1.66 kg of kernels and 17 kg of dry fuel. Loose bark cord is exhausted. The old cracked pot remains separate from the two new damp greenware samples; none is cookware.
Active work is estimated at 8.5 hours, with eight hours for sleep. No injury, abandoned camp or successful firing is added to make the weather dramatic. Its effects are repair time, reduced collection and greater fuel use. See Survival Ledger.
Next decision
Finish a small bedding pad from the reserved materials, recheck the dart and keep the casting interval short. Food supply now needs more attention than a demonstration to the neighbours.

01_survival/moon-2-day-6---a-pad,-a-shor.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 6 - A Pad, a Short Trial, and a Smaller Reserve.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-6---a-pad,-a-shor.title: Moon 2 Day 6 - A Pad, a Short Trial, and a Smaller Reserve
01_survival/moon-2-day-6---a-pad,-a-shor.content:
Moon 2 Day 6 - A Pad, a Short Trial, and a Smaller Reserve
Put the sample to work at a modest scale
The little twining sample still retains its foundations after handling. You recheck the reserved willow strips for splitting and sharp ends, then make a small twined bedding pad large enough for only part of your upper-body contact area.
The light cord runs through spaced paired rows. You work across the width gradually, adjusting where foundations start to migrate. The pad is coarse, with no resemblance to a fine woven blanket. Its job is to retain some dry grass and leaves and let you lift that part of the layer for inspection.
You fit it on the existing bed and keep a loose dry layer between your body and the foundations. In a brief rest you find one pressure point and shift the filling. The pad lifts without immediately losing everything, but that test says little about a whole wet week or a freezing night.
The allocation exhausts the recorded willow-strip and loose insulation lots. The old sample remains separate, and a little nettle cord survives for necessary work. You cannot take a duplicate pad to the fallback bench or convert the same filling into a mantle.
Make room for another meal
You extend the gathering circuit instead of trusting yesterday’s nearest patch. The better return today requires more searching and shelling. It gives a small improvement in the reserve rather than erasing the week’s deficit.
The clothing problem remains visible while you work. The single fox shoulder panel and small waist pad do not become broader because the bed is better organised. A coarse wearable plant covering is the next related experiment, with flexibility and movement to test before relying on it.
Return to the same short line
At the practice ground you check the flight space and earth bank, retrieve the ground markers’ positions by the reference staff, and inspect the dart’s rear seat. It shows slight compression from use but no opening split. That condition permits only another short cautious session, with reinspection.
Six thrower attempts give six observations. Three reach the broad bank patch; the others fall short or to a side. The result is encouraging only in the narrow sense that you can sometimes maintain engagement through release. The group is too scattered for a useful hunting claim, and the changing green shaft prevents a clean equipment comparison.
You record all six, keep the effort modest and stop at the allotted interval. You have not attached the feathers or a point, prepared the second shaft as ammunition, or compared yourself with the neighbours. The remembered lever still needs a practised body and a stable projectile.
Take stock before the next week
The nettle bundle has not passed its separation check. The clay pieces are drying at the surface but are not accepted as dry throughout. Both remain processes awaiting observations, not capabilities completed by elapsed days.
The model ends the week with 1.71 kg of kernels and 19 kg of dry fuel: roughly three and a half days of kernels at the recent ration, less than you had on Day 28. Twenty-four grams of prepared nettle fibre, 2.6 m of loose nettle cord and 16 m of single yarn remain. Loose bark cord is gone.
Estimated active work is nine hours, with eight hours for sleep. Survival Ledger records every allocation. The alternative bench remains unsupplied, and the neighbours remain independent people who can choose to watch or warn.
Next decision
Day 36 should begin with supply and repair priorities, then examine the dart’s changing fit before another trial. Improve the fish cage only after inspecting a specific weakness. Do not make the next encounter depend on a technology already being impressive.

01_survival/moon-2-day-7---a-better-clos.title: Moon 2 Day 7 - A Better Closure
01_survival/moon-2-day-7---a-better-clos.content:
Moon 2 Day 7 - A Better Closure
Fix a fault you can actually see
The fish cage is empty. When you lift it from the sheltered western river margin, the rear cap shifts against one side of the body. A worn tie lets the cap lift farther than you intend. That is an observable escape opening; it is not proof that fish have been entering and leaving overnight.
You want to make retrieval dependable before changing the entrance or moving the cage. A smaller funnel might exclude the fish you hope to catch. A larger cage would need more material and another installation trial. Repairing the closure offers a limited question you can answer today.
From the known downstream willow stand you select flexible withes, rejecting ends that split when bent. At the bank you take out the damaged tie and fit a light collar around the rear opening. You leave the inward funnel and the main woven cylinder alone. A short new portion of nettle line holds the removable cap against its seat; the old worn tie is discarded, not returned to the loose stock.
You work the closure open and shut, then lower the cage into the shallow margin and retrieve it again from stable footing. The cap stays in place in that handling trial. You check the existing anchor and reset at the same location below the tributary confluence. An empty check after repair will still be possible. Better retention cannot create fish.
Collect tomorrow’s covering today
On the western gathering circuit you look for long, clean dry grass rather than another armful of mixed leaf litter. The bedding pad showed that a retained plant layer is possible. A wearable version must bend with the shoulders and should not put hard willow foundations against the back.
You sort a small grass lot, shaking out grit and removing sharp stalks. A few handfuls survive bending and light pulling without immediately breaking apart. Those portions go under ventilated cover, away from sparks, for a possible hanging back panel. They remain loose stock. The bed is not stripped to furnish a garment, and no mantle has been made.
The longer gathering round provides about the same edible nut portion as you eat. This holds the reserve rather than rebuilding it. Food work still occupies more of the day than either repair.
Check the fit before asking for another flight
At the clean craft spot you inspect the compressed rear seat of the trial dart. There is no spreading split, but a raised rough edge catches during slow disengagement. You remove only the loose projection and repeat the fit check against the actual thrower’s hook. You do not deepen the hollow or reshape the hook at the same time.
The movement is freer in your hands. A launch will impose a different load, so you leave that question for a short session tomorrow. The second shaft still bows noticeably and remains a blank. The feathers stay dry and unused.
Before settling, you gather usable dead wood and protect the ignition kit from ground damp. You check the shelter’s southeast exit before putting small equipment away. You can make a closure harder for a fish to open; you have no comparable way to keep determined people out of camp.
End of day and next choice
The author account ends with 1.71 kg of edible kernels and 21 kg of dry fuel. The cage consumes 0.8 m of loose nettle cord and four cumulative metres of newly gathered willow withes; 1.8 m of nettle cord remains. The separately collected dry grass lot is 0.8 kg. These are model estimates, not readings from a balance.
Eight estimated active hours include gathering, water treatment, fuel, the cage repair, grass selection and a brief fit inspection; eight hours remain for sleep. The clay comparison pieces and nettle bundle have produced no new usable output. Survival Ledger records the allocations.
Tomorrow you can test the small fit correction at the same modest effort. If the dart still disengages badly, the next step is diagnosis, not a point, stronger throw or another visit to the neighbours.

01_survival/moon-2-day-8---a-lever-and-a.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 8 - A Lever and a Practised Arm.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-8---a-lever-and-a.title: Moon 2 Day 8 - A Lever and a Practised Arm
01_survival/moon-2-day-8---a-lever-and-a.content:
Moon 2 Day 8 - A Lever and a Practised Arm
The audience you did not invite
You finish the morning’s water and supply work before taking the thrower west/southwest to the Projectile Practice Ground. The ordinary wooden-pointed spear rests within reach behind the start position, clear of your movement. You inspect the bank, footing and both approaches. The little rear-seat correction is today’s equipment change; you intend to keep the effort and short line familiar.
Two modest casts release without the loose edge catching. One reaches the broad bank patch and one lands short to its left. While retrieving the dart you notice movement on the open ground north of the line. Two people have stopped there. Their position is off the flight path, but you lower the equipment and stay on your side of the open ground.
The broader adult carries a well-kept stone-pointed spear. Low brow, projecting face and compact, heavily built limbs distinguish him from you even at this distance. The other watches your hand and then the short wooden lever. You cannot tell whether either was among the people who rebuffed you. Their attention does not tell you their intentions.
You leave a clear way back towards camp. When they remain still and the flight space is empty, you make two more modest casts. The observer’s head follows the movement from lever to dart. That looks like curiosity about what the device does. One flight reaches the patch; the other veers wide. There is little in the landings to recommend you as an instructor.
The spear does not need your lever
The spear carrier points towards a bare part of the same bank and moves onto open ground, keeping away from your equipment. You step back with the dart lowered. He waits until the space ahead is clear, then throws his own spear by hand.
The movement is economical: a planted step, a coordinated turn and a release without your last-moment correction. The spear crosses the open space with a decisiveness your casts lack and strikes near the ground he indicated. He retrieves it himself, checks its stone head and binding, and makes another controlled cast from a position farther from the bank. Again it reaches the chosen area. His companion remains behind him during each throw.
There is no fair numerical experiment here. His spear has a different mass and point, and penetration cannot be compared with your blunt wooden front. You have no speed measurement. What you can see is that his chosen casts cover more ground, land much closer together and arrive with useful force, while your lighter projectile wanders. His strong, practised body and well-made weapon are part of the system. The lever’s mechanical promise has not compensated for your unstable release.
He looks towards the thrower once more, then holds his own spear upright. You do not read a precise message into the gesture. Neither person offers equipment or comes to examine yours. They leave along the northern side of the opening. You wait until they are out of sight before collecting your things and leaving in the other direction.
Choose what the comparison is for
At camp the disappointment arrives after the relief. You had hoped an obvious useful result might make another approach less dangerous. Instead, they have seen an odd device and a poor thrower. You still do not know whether that will encourage watching, ridicule or another warning.
The result gives you a better work question. Preserve the repaired fit and practise a repeatable movement before adding another variable. A stone head cannot fix a release that sends the dart to the wrong side. A second dart will eventually help distinguish specimen behaviour from technique, but the bowed candidate has not earned that role.
You record your four attempts, including the two before the observers arrived: two reach the broad patch, two miss it. The neighbours’ two casts occupy a separate hand-spear comparison entry. Their equipment leaves with them; nothing is borrowed, traded, recovered or taught.
End of day and next choice
Shortened gathering leaves 1.56 kg of kernels; dry fuel reaches 22 kg. The dart survives with no new opening split, but remains green, blunt and unfletched. Eight estimated active hours include the cautious session and waiting, ordinary supplies, inspections and dry-stock care, with eight hours for sleep.
The cage and three deadfalls are checked without a retained catch. Tomorrow’s priority is the supply circuit and cold-weather material. The observed difference justifies continued practice, not spending the remaining buffer on an immediate second demonstration. Atlatl Throwing and Projectile Testing separate that decision from a claim of technological superiority.

01_survival/moon-2-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 9 - A Rabbit and the Work It Brings.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.title: Moon 2 Day 9 - A Rabbit and the Work It Brings
01_survival/moon-2-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.content:
Moon 2 Day 9 - A Rabbit and the Work It Brings
A catch changes the order of work
At the western trap circuit one deadfall has fallen. A rabbit lies beneath it, with no obvious scavenger damage. You approach with the spear ready, inspect the surrounding ground and collect the animal rather than remaining bent over an occupied feeding place. The other two trials are empty.
Back at the southern processing flank you assess the catch before counting it as food. The protected meat has no obvious deterioration, although appearance alone cannot establish safety. You retain a small dressed lot and discard damaged tissue. Small Game Butchery takes place apart from the clean craft and food-storage areas. Hands, edge and handling surface need cleaning before you return to those jobs.
You divide the retained meat for prompt cooking at the ordinary outside hearth. There is no preserved rabbit ration at the end of the day. The useful catch lets you eat slightly fewer kernels; it does not let you skip gathering or claim several days of meals.
A pelt is an urgent job, not a finished jacket
You wanted broader core protection before the colder nights. The rabbit supplies some new skin, but the usable area is still small, and thin edges tear more easily than the remembered garment drawings suggest. You flesh it promptly and support it on the existing dirty-material drying frame under moderate tension. No new large tanning frame appears.
The pelt is intended for a later small clothing addition, if it remains usable. You have not chosen its final coverage. It cannot become both a carrying bag and a chest panel, and today’s damp skin is neither sewn clothing nor durable leather.
On one small edge you compare careful flexing with a neighbouring area left undisturbed as moisture begins to leave. The worked area bends more readily for now. That is an observation about handling this skin at this stage, not a tanning result. You stop when the thin edge starts to stretch. Neither the catch nor the old fox panel provides an unrecorded supply of dressing fat, brains or preservative.
You retain no separate bone, tendon or fat stock from this catch. The meat and the one pelt are its recorded outputs. Further extraction would add work, and you choose prompt food and skin care over accumulating every possible material.
Reset one mechanism before trusting it again
The catch-bearing deadfall’s bearing notch has polished and shifted. Before returning it to service, you brace the weight, keep out of the fall path and recheck the wooden members. You clean the seating surface without making the lock tighter merely to make it look secure.
A modest non-animal test, released remotely with a long locally selected branch while you stay clear, confirms that the assembled weight drops when the trigger is displaced. You then reset the existing trial. A successful catch and a successful release check answer different questions. Neither makes this a dependable food system.
Let warmth take the spare interval
During gathering you collect another small portion of clean dry plant material. This lot refreshes a compacted section of the bed and is allocated there immediately. The longer grass reserved for clothing stays separate under cover. The small bedding pad is lifted, aired and returned, rather than counted as a second object.
The wet pelt requires repeated brief attention through the day. You do not fit an atlatl session into those pauses. Looking up from scraping also reminds you how little warning the dirty flank offers: the spear stays on the accessible side of the frame and the route to the shelter remains open. Today’s benefit has created exposed work and attractive waste as well as food.
End of day and next choice
The model records 0.32 kg of cooked-and-eaten rabbit meat, one freshly cleaned pelt in process, 1.59 kg of remaining kernels and 21 kg of dry fuel. The new 0.3 kg bedding refresh is fully allocated; the 0.8 kg garment grass lot is untouched. Work is estimated at 9.5 active hours, including capture inspection, butchery, cooking, skin care, resetting and supplies; sleep retains an eight-hour allowance.
Tomorrow, inspect the pelt rather than assuming it is dry or supple because a night has passed. The plant covering remains the route you can expand without requiring another catch.

02_reflections/reflection-01---arrival--.title: Reflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 1
02_reflections/reflection-01---arrival--.content:
Reflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 1
End of Moon 1 Day 1 · Arrival near new moon · Continuous Day 1 · Read after Moon 1 Day 1 - Immediate Priorities.
Everything remembered, almost nothing held
You lie inside the low debris frame and listen to the valley disappear into darkness. The work of the afternoon still aches in your hands. There is no fire to watch and no food left for tomorrow. Bark covers a little skin; dry litter separates you from some of the ground. Every sound beyond the entrance reaches you without a visible source.
The departure is already beyond recovery. People who could explain this valley with instruments are somewhere behind you in time, facing an approaching catastrophe. You cannot send a question back or return for one forgotten object. Their knowledge is present in your memory, but their workshops, shelter and company are absent.
You expected the difference. You are only beginning to feel it. A useful stone edge has cost failed strikes. A bed has taken hours of carrying. The future you came to change has narrowed tonight to whether this covering stays in place and whether the ground takes too much heat from your body.
What is real tonight
You have a chosen terrace, a provisional shelter, a useful flake and a sound hammer cobble. A short bark line can hold the rough waist panels. You have found a seep and positively identified a little food. Those observations give tomorrow a starting point; they do not establish the valley’s yearly supply, ownership or safety.
The nuts you collected have been eaten. The dry fuel is merely a pile: without a prepared ignition kit it supplies no warmth. The seep has relieved thirst, but the water is untreated. There is no vessel, no spear, no animal skin and no dependable protection for your feet.
Your altered lifespan does not make a fall, a wound or cold harmless. The gaps between what you can describe and what your hands can do matter immediately. They will matter again at every larger scale.
A home has not been granted
You have seen enough ground to choose a stopping place, not enough to understand its occupants. The absence of people on your short circuit proves little. Other humans might know the nearby resources far better than you; predators might use routes you have not noticed. Darkness removes the small advantage of seeing an approach.
You keep the cutting edge where it will not injure you when you reach for it, and leave the shelter entrance usable. These are small precautions, not a defence. Tomorrow’s observation must include tracks, unstable branches and a way to move away from trouble, alongside useful plants and stones.
Loneliness is part of the exposure. There is nobody to keep watch while you sleep, hold a branch while you bind it, or fetch water while your hands are occupied. The work plan must allow for one body.
The first intentions
Tomorrow begins with food, inspection of the bed and covering, and care of the edges already made. A complete ignition kit is the first major preparation. You need its parts to work together before an ember can become an ordinary service. An attempt at fire cannot spend the light required to keep the shelter usable or find another meal.
A container and water treatment will follow only when the materials and tools support them. Protection for skin and feet remains urgent. You cannot name those needs into completed equipment, and the same bark tie cannot hold two different things at once.
The long purpose remains rebuilding enough capability to change humanity’s eventual fate. The immediate test is smaller and exacting: make tomorrow possible without spending the conditions which made tonight possible. If the first shelter fails, repair outranks the ignition experiment. If food collection fails, the experiment shortens. Your memory must serve those decisions rather than distract you from them.

02_reflections/reflection-02---full-moon.title: Reflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 15
02_reflections/reflection-02---full-moon.content:
Reflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 15
End of Day 15 · First full moon · Read after Day 15 - Fire Holds Shape.
A place to return to
The brightening sky gives the valley a shape beyond the little circle of fire. You have spent half a moon here. A remembered civilisation still fills your mind, but what keeps you alive is smaller: one dry resting place, a maintained ignition set, a vessel which can sometimes tolerate repeated water treatment, useful cutting edges and the food you can carry back.
Those are real gains. Their maintenance is also real work. A bark seam has already interrupted the water routine. Clothing is still scraps of plant covering and small animal panels. The fact that you expect to live for centuries does not make tonight’s exposed skin less vulnerable.
The camp has begun to acquire an arrangement: clean work above the ordinary hearth, animal processing on another flank, firing on separate bare ground. That organisation matters as much as another small object. The bed and water source cannot follow the dirty work wherever convenience suggests.
A fired shape is still a question
The clay vessel remains in the firing bed, cooling. You want tomorrow to reveal something useful. That desire cannot decide the result.
You have formed, dried and heated a specimen. You have not inspected it cold, established that it holds water or shown that it survives repeated cooking. A useful outcome would ease part of the water problem. Failure would cost clay work and fuel, but it should also identify a more specific question for the next trial.
The nettle bundle has been waiting downstream for a different reason. It might supply fibre, but the stems must separate without becoming weak. Pottery and retting both expose the same mistaken temptation: treating elapsed time as completion because you know the name of the process.
What supplies the time to think
Nuts still carry most meals. Small-game returns add useful food and small material lots, but three mechanisms are not a dependable supply of animals. A needle and an awl help use what has already been caught; they do not enlarge the animals or bring the next catch.
The firing has drawn down the dry-fuel reserve. Your food buffer is short enough that another long experiment immediately competes with gathering. The cold will increase those costs, while the nearby patches can be exhausted.
You have no identified neighbours or agreement about this ground. That does not mean the valley is empty. The spear’s wooden point and your inexperience would offer little reassurance against several skilled people, and an animal can approach while your attention is on a seam. Work should keep an exit available rather than turn the shelter into a place where you are cornered.
Intentions before the next moon
First replenish usable fuel and inspect the cold clay load. Keep the bark treatment route working whether the vessel succeeds or fails. Check the nettle bundle by its material condition, then allocate any actual fibre between immediate repairs and future work.
Improve dry resting coverage and body protection with the modest materials you can obtain. Do not make clothing depend on finding a large hide. Maintain the small trap circuit, but keep gathering time until returns justify changing that balance.
Observation can extend the known ground in short affordable outings. You need routes, material sources and warning signs; you do not need an ambitious excursion that consumes the last food margin. A smaller experiment with a clear result is worth more than several unfinished objects competing for the same fuel and cord.
At the next review, ask whether the camp is less easily interrupted: another failed seam, a wet night or an empty trap circuit should not immediately consume tomorrow’s choices.
