02_reflections/reflection-03---new-moon-.title: Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1
02_reflections/reflection-03---new-moon-.content:
Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1
End of Day 30 · New moon · Read after Moon 2 Day 1 - Six Attempts and No Advantage.
The valley is inhabited
The night has no bright moon to broaden the view beyond camp. Since the last reflection, you have seen a maintained fire beyond the ridge, watched skilled people at their work, approached them and been made to leave.
The first pitch was based on a true possibility and a false expectation. New knowledge might be useful to them; possessing it did not make your awkward demonstration better than their familiar cordage and practised handling. They had no reason to give you the time or space you wanted.
Their warning belongs to that encounter. It neither proves that they mean to hunt you down nor assures you that another visit will be welcome. Your smoke makes concealment uncertain. You should plan for the possibility that this terrace is already known, without inventing an intention you have not observed.
A lever has not made a hunter
Today’s six attempts answer a modest question: the wooden thrower can launch the prepared trial dart on some attempts. It has not supplied stable release, accuracy or a demonstrated advantage.
Three hand casts and three thrower casts are not a fair contest between two perfected technologies. You are inexperienced with one and uncomfortable with this particular projectile in both. The shaft is green and changing. The rear engagement, your timing and the flight need work before you can isolate a useful improvement.
The second shaft is still a bowed blank. The feather lot is unused. No pointed or fletched hunting dart exists. The ordinary spear remains the immediate defensive object; the atlatl is an experiment which can occupy your hands while leaving you exposed.
Even a much better cast would not supply a companion to watch another exit, help recover a wounded animal or stand guard during processing. Hunting alone is an organisational limit as well as a technical one.
Improvements which still need supply
The first pot failed its operating test. A better-looking new shape would not remove the need to compare clay, drying, firing and leakage separately. The small bark vessel remains the water-treatment route, with repairs and handling costs.
The cage has supplied a fish, and the damaged snare still supplied useful fox meat and a narrow skin panel. Those gains were worth keeping; neither establishes a regular food source or a winter garment. The fox covers one shoulder, not the entire core.
Prepared fibre and usable line are small, finite lots. Spun yarn is not a substitute for every binding. Another trap, a dart fitting, a broader covering and an escape provision could all demand the same material. A new fibre batch must start with your own harvesting and pass its own checks before you can spend the output.
The measuring staff and scratches are useful because they make comparisons repeatable. They are not a balance, a calibrated metre or an agreement with the neighbours. Their value will be shown when a disappointing record changes tomorrow’s allocation.
Priorities before the next full moon
Keep supply ahead of pride. Gather, shell, treat water and collect genuinely usable dry wood. Protect and inspect the existing reserve; a long demonstration or reconnaissance draws on food even when it produces nothing.
Begin the additional fibre batch. Work towards better bedding and a coarse body covering using available plant material, adding independently acquired pelts where they help. Do not wait for a deer to provide an entire wardrobe.
Inspect an alternative route and resting site. A possibility on the landscape is not a supplied refuge: any cached food, fuel or spare kit must be made or transferred from the actual stock. Decide what you would carry and what you would leave before a hurried departure forces that decision.
Retain short, inspected casting sessions and change only a manageable part of the experiment. If curious neighbours watch, do not interpret attention as admiration, access or an alliance. Their own practised spear use deserves to be taken seriously.
Before the next review, look for a camp that is harder to interrupt and a projectile system whose limitations you can describe more precisely. There is no need to win a contest in order to learn something useful.

Author model at the end of Day 30; allocated stock is excluded.

02_reflections/reflection-04---full-moon.title: Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15
02_reflections/reflection-04---full-moon.content:
Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15
End of Day 44 · Full moon · Read after Moon 2 Day 15 - A Frame Before a Promise.
The gap between a design and a life
Through breaks in cloud, moonlight reaches the open valley. You can see more of the ground beyond camp than on the last new moon, but seeing ground is not knowing who moves through it. The people beyond the ridge remain independent of your plans.
Since the last reflection, they have watched your camp, watched your odd lever and shown you what a practised spear arm can do. The device interested an observer; your landings offered little advantage. Another adult warned you from an occupied nut patch. Curiosity did not grant access, and a quiet departure did not grant protection.
You are less certain that the first useful thing you show must be a weapon. A repeatable method could still matter later. For now, proving yourself to an audience has to compete with the need to get through a colder night. Their experience is not an obstacle invented for you to overcome. It is part of the world you have entered, and you have learned how much of it you cannot yet match.
Several improvements, very little margin
The repaired fish closure has remained usable, with a few small catches. The deadfalls have supplied a rabbit; its meat was useful immediately, while its skin created urgent work and is still unfinished. Neither route gives a dependable meal each day.
The bed has gained a small retaining pad and renewed loose material. Your grass back panel is wearable in a short dry trial, yet your front, head and feet remain poorly protected. You have used real fibre, yarn, cord and gathering time to reach those modest results. Remembering a coat is easier than obtaining a coat’s worth of material and making it survive use.
The second retting batch has left the pool. Only a selected 18 g portion has become accepted dry fibre; the coarse remainder is not stock simply because it lies under cover. The vessel samples remain unfired. They can wait. The one repaired bark container has supported water treatment and small acorn charges, at a pace that exposes its limited capacity.
The acorns have been another meal route, not a store. All the new input is now processed and eaten. You have about two recent kernel portions remaining, with no reserve of dried meat and no large hide waiting to rescue the clothing problem. The next gathering round matters more than the number of methods you can name.
A frame is an intention made visible
Today you have set a light rail and the first return ribs beside the old roof. One brace foot moved during the trial; you unloaded it and corrected the seat. That small failure changed the work before it was hidden beneath covering.
The open frame gives your decision a physical shape: a compact sleeping chamber, still in the same footprint, with the exit kept clear and the fire outside. It does not yet shelter the new side. Four ribs and the protected cover lot still need fitting. A claim about winter would be premature even after they are installed.
You can feel the attraction of finishing everything tomorrow. The food account prevents that wish becoming a plan. Construction consumes the daylight which produces meals and usable fuel. You need to build in stages without making an exhausted, hungry body the hidden price of a better-looking roof.
What must happen before the next review
Finish and inspect the return covering and its junction, protect and renew the whole resting layer, and work towards practical front, head and foot protection. Keep fuel and tinder dry. A second tested water vessel and a spare ignition provision remain worthwhile, but neither has been made. The fallback bench is still a route to an unsupplied place.
Continue short private projectile practice only when it fits the survival work. A second suitable dart and better release may eventually narrow the gap. A scouting outing can teach approach and retrieval limits without forcing a dangerous cast or requiring a deer kill. Contact can remain limited; there is no reason to assume that the next observer offers an alliance.
A wet spell, a poor harvest or a shifting support should change the allocation immediately. You are beginning to choose work by what it makes reliable, rather than by how far ahead its idea belongs. Before any distant industry can exist, you need a place where you can rest, wake and do useful work again.
Author continuity snapshot

Author model at the end of Day 44; allocated stock is excluded.

02_reflections/reflection-artwork-propos.title: Reflection Artwork Proposals
02_reflections/reflection-artwork-propos.content:
Reflection Artwork Proposals
The user approved these compositions and the recommended watercolour/gouache treatment. The three frontispieces are now generated and embedded; view the selected series. The proposals below retain the artistic intent. Each picture follows its own end-of-day knowledge cutoff, with the original Day 1 protagonist as the identity reference.
Recommended visual language
Give Reflections the feeling of a painted chapter frontispiece: translucent watercolour and matte gouache on lightly toned paper, with sparse graphite or fine brown ink. Keep the recognised traveller, valley and material scale, but use a more deliberate composition, deeper tonal range and stronger negative space than the daily action illustrations. Light should carry the emotional argument. Objects can work as a quiet still life rather than an inventory spread.
Use one shared wide format, paper tone and palette across the series. Let colour evolve from cold darkness at arrival, to an uncertain warm centre at the first full moon, to the divided warm/cold light of the second new moon. Avoid labelled diagrams, decorative collage, heroic portraits and literal magical visions of the future. A lunar phase may be suggested by light and composition; new-moon scenes have no bright disk.
Two alternatives worth considering: tonal charcoal with restrained watercolour, for a more austere psychological series; or matte egg-tempera/gouache landscape frontispieces, with simplified masses and meticulous small material details, for a timeless illustrated-book quality. The watercolour/gouache approach is the strongest bridge to the existing Survival art while giving this section its own weight.
Reflection 01 — Arrival: knowledge without sheltering power
At the end of Moon 1 Day 1, look from outside towards the mouth of the very low debris shelter. The traveller sits or curls just within its leaf-lined opening, keeping his eyes on the dark valley. He occupies a small part of a broad composition. A single flake and hammer cobble catch the last cool light; a few dry fuel sticks lie unused, while empty hazelnut shells mark the meal already eaten. Rough bark waist panels provide the only clothing. No fire, vessel, spear or animal products.
The shelter opening becomes a fragile oval of enclosure within a much larger dark landscape. The unfinished roof is held together visually by the fallen limb, echoing how precarious his new starting point is. Pale indigo and slate washes, a narrow remnant of dusk and warm leaf tones convey exhaustion, loneliness and irreversible departure. No moon is visible. The contrast between remembered civilisation and present vulnerability is conveyed by his expression and the emptiness around him, without showing imaginary cities or machines.
Reflection 02 — First full moon: a small island of working capability
At the end of Moon 1 Day 15, use an elevated, intimate view across the correctly arranged camp. The traveller sits at the uphill clean craft spot, watching the separate firing patch as its last heat subsides. The small open pinch cup remains untouched on its non-combustible support, cooling and untested. The ordinary hearth is separate and farther downhill. Within the foreground still life, select only the bark water vessel, tiny awl/needle and a modest nut portion; leave other earned equipment outside frame.
The low shelter and organised working patches suggest genuine gains without making an established homestead. His hands rest rather than work: hope for tomorrow’s vessel test competes with fatigue and the smallness of the reserve. The unprocessed nettle batch stays downstream and off-screen; no fibre, whorl, basket or known neighbours appear. Retain the modest rabbit pelvic pad and bark coverage, with no fox panel yet.
Use silver-blue moonlight if clouds allow, small amber accents from the distinct outside heat sources, and quiet breathing space around the untouched cup. An airy, broad sky and small warm camp communicate both possibility and exposure. The image must not pre-empt the next day’s crack or represent a completed pottery success.
Reflection 03 — Second new moon: being seen, learning limits
At the end of Moon 2 Day 1 (continuous Day 30), seat the traveller at the uphill craft spot with the day’s six attempt marks on the bark register. A single blunt unfletched green dart and the wooden-hook thrower lie apart, imperfect tools rather than triumphant weapons. A modest food portion, the old rejected cracked pot and unused feathers form a sparse secondary still life. The narrow fox shoulder panel provides a small new comfort and makes the continuing exposure of his body visible.
His gaze leaves the objects and follows the remembered western approach beyond the spur. A far, faint wisp from the neighbours’ known clearing may be seen only if the mapped view permits it; otherwise let the obscured ridge and the direction of his attention carry their presence. No visiting observers appear, since those belong to Day 31. No new retting batch, mat, clay comparison pair or inspected fallback refuge appears either.
The visual centre is a triangle between the six recorded attempts, the dwindling provisions and his outward gaze: technical ambition, subsistence and unease about the people who may locate him. Warm low hearth light gives way to deep blue-grey beyond the terrace, with no lunar disk. His mood is chastened and watchful, yet intentional. It should feel like a person revising a plan after costly lessons, not a conquered valley or despairing defeat.
Reflection 04 — Second full moon: ambition gives way to enclosure
At the end of continuous Day 44 (Moon 2 Day 15), the traveller appraises the bare first return frame beside the retained old roof. The new side has only three ribs and no covering. A small kernel basket and the set-aside blunt unfletched dart and wooden thrower carry the competing demands of food and ambition. A full moon appears through breaks in cloud; the valley remains large, cold and uncertain. The standing profile keeps the anatomy simple. The section’s watercolour, gouache and spare graphite language gives the moment quiet weight.
The selected artwork is embedded in Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15. It depicts no Day 45 covering, new cord or fish catch; the accompanying snapshot remains fixed at Day 44. The complete prompt and fresh replacement record are in the Days 41–45 commission.

02_reflections/reflections.title: Reflections
02_reflections/reflections.content:
Reflections
The moon offers a recurring pause to review what actually sustains you. At arrival, then at each new-moon or full-moon milestone, a reflection gathers the state of play: reliable capabilities, unfinished work, resources, dangers, intentions and choices worth postponing.
Read a reflection after its associated Survival day. It knows only events through that day’s end. It does not introduce a catch, acquisition, agreement or success which the daily entries have not earned.
Completed reflections

























MilestoneState-of-play entryMoon 1 Day 1 · arrival near new moonReflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 1Moon 1 Day 15 · first full moonReflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 15Moon 2 Day 1 · next new moon (continuous Day 30)Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1Moon 2 Day 15 · full moon (continuous Day 44)Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15
Rhythm and future milestones
Lunar Calendar anchors a fictional new moon around arrival, with reviews roughly fifteen days apart. The mean-cycle model places the next review on Day 59 (new moon) after the completed Day 44 full-moon review. These are scheduled milestones, not unwritten narrative outcomes. The real phase cycle is about 29.5 days, so exact repeating fifteen-day halves would slowly drift.
The existing “Month Two” outline names a four-week planning block, Days 29–56; it is not silently renamed a lunar month. Moon cycles are the story’s reflective rhythm, alongside continuous day numbering. Survival page titles use Moon/Day labels from the same model; continuous day metadata still governs stocks and chronology.
Shape of an entry
A reflection should identify what can actually be relied upon, what is only a specimen or trial, the current bottleneck, threats and uncertainties, the priorities before the next review, and what outcome would change the plan. It should also admit a mistaken expectation when observations justify it.
Write reflective second-person present-tense prose rather than reciting every daily task. Use the hero’s rough practical judgement in the narrative. A separate author-continuity table can show model quantities and is checked against the day’s ledger snapshot.
Reflection time sits within ordinary pauses/planning; the entry creates no additional workday or resource events. The reflection series uses painted frontispieces in the approved watercolour/gouache style. Browse the series; Reflection Artwork Proposals records the approved compositions and style choices.

03_materials/animal/animal-fat.title: Animal Fat
03_materials/animal/animal-fat.content:
Animal Fat
Properties and collection
Animal fat supplies concentrated energy, but a small lean animal may yield very little. Inspect each catch and record usable fat rather than assigning a fixed quantity. Fat, marrow and organ tissue are different materials.
Separate clean fatty tissue during Small Game Butchery. Avoid gut contamination. Cook the first month’s small quantities with the meal; they are not a recurring store.
Rendering and limits
Later rendering separates melted fat from wet tissue. It needs a suitable vessel, gentle heat, separation and clean storage. Removing tissue and moisture can improve keeping qualities, but does not establish an unlimited shelf life. No first-month preserved-fat reserve is assumed.
Fat can lubricate some bearings or change an adhesive mixture. Test the relevant formulation; grease alone does not turn rawhide or sinew into waterproof material. Food and tool-use portions must be recorded separately.
Evidence
Composition and process details require additional sources. Local people may already understand fat processing; the traveller should observe before offering instruction.

03_materials/animal/animal-pelt.title: Animal Pelt
03_materials/animal/animal-pelt.content:
Animal Pelt
Material and handling
A pelt is skin with its hair retained. Preserve useful area when skinning; holes, cuts and edges reduce the available panel. Record each animal’s pelt as a separate asset.
Remove adhering flesh and fat promptly on a clean surface. Use a supported, blunt scraping edge, applying enough pressure to lift tissue without cutting thin skin. Hair slip, decomposition and insect damage indicate deterioration; their absence does not establish freedom from pathogens.
Processing routes
Rawhide Processing produces dried untanned skin suited to rigid cases and bindings. Fur-On Pelt Clothing describes temporary clothing from carefully softened pelts. Durable leather requires a further preservation and softening process; drying alone is not tanning.
Keep wet and dry lots separate. Do not allocate one complete rabbit pelt simultaneously to a sling and a waist garment. In the narrative, the first rabbit pelt becomes the sling; the second becomes the garment panel.
Limits
Drying and handling depend on weather and skin thickness. A thin pelt can tear under stitching and can stiffen again when wet. Local makers’ knowledge of hide preparation is a resource to learn from, not a presumed gap.
The separate Day 38 lot
Rabbit-pelt-d38 is one newly caught skin, promptly fleshed and supported on the existing dirty-material frame. Days 38–40 compare cautious working at a small edge with the drying centre. Damp areas remain and no final clothing allocation is made. No bone, tendon, brain or dressing-fat stock is silently added from this catch. The meat is separately recorded and consumed on Day 38. Earlier rabbit and fox skin allocations stay unchanged.
Day 38 rabbit lot leaves loose stock on Day 50
After protected drying and brief mechanical margin work, the whole separate rabbit pelt is allocated to one limited crown covering. It is not durable leather and supplies no second object. The stiff centre and dry-use limit stay visible in Fur-On Pelt Clothing. The old fox shoulder piece remains separate.

03_materials/animal/antler.title: Antler
03_materials/animal/antler.content:
Antler
Identification and selection
Antler is a seasonally grown bony structure of deer, distinct from permanent horn. Mature antler includes compact outer tissue and a more porous core. Its utility depends on species, section and condition.
Find an old shed or a fragment left from an animal. In early autumn, the narrative finds an old red-deer antler, not a newly shed spring antler or a newly identified reindeer resource. Inspect for weathering, deep cracks and insect or microbial damage.
Uses and preparation
A sound section can make a Soft Hammer Billet, wedge or worked point. Grip and test a naturally useful section before undertaking extensive trimming. A tool requires suitable geometry and repeated inspection, not simply ownership of the material.
Antler can be shaped by scoring, scraping and abrasion. Avoid treating it as soft wood that a flake effortlessly whittles. It is replenished biologically but may be locally scarce.
Limits and alternatives
Wooden percussors and hard-hammer techniques offer alternatives for particular knapping tasks. Breaking one antler tool does not erase knowledge of bifacial manufacture.
Archaeological applications and exact performance specifications require further sources. The local find is a setting choice.

03_materials/animal/bone.title: Bone
03_materials/animal/bone.content:
Bone
Material
Bone is a composite of mineral and organic components, not a pure organic polymer. Dense cortical tissue can provide blanks for awls and needles; porous or weathered parts often fail.
Small Game Butchery supplies small bones. Larger suitable blanks may be acquired through Scavenging or exchange. Their dimensions limit the tool that can be made: a vole bone cannot be assumed to provide a strong full-sized needle.
Selection and working
Clean off tissue and inspect for cracks. Use scoring, controlled splitting, scraping and abrasion according to the blank. Reckless hammering can destroy the usable strip. Grinding against a suitable abrasive allows gradual shaping; bone can also be cut and scraped.
A Bone Awl can be useful before an eyed Bone Needle is successfully made. Neither object requires an entire new archaeological era.
Food and hygiene
Marrow from small bones is a minor contribution, not a meal-sized energy store. Cook edible tissue with the catch meal; the narrative no longer eats raw marrow from bones left overnight.
Keep manufacturing debris away from food. Bone tools used on raw carcasses need cleaning before other uses. Precise processing instructions remain an experimental-review task.

03_materials/animal/flight-feathers.title: Flight Feathers
03_materials/animal/flight-feathers.content:
Flight Feathers
Sound wing feathers can provide vane material for projectile experiments. Choose by condition and useful geometry; colour alone does not identify the bird. A feather found at a predator’s feeding site belongs to the prey, not automatically the predator.
Collect only a few intact pieces for trials, inspect rachis and vane, and clean appropriately. Weathered shafts, broken vanes and dirty tissue can make a sample unusable. The narrative’s Day 27 samples are from an unidentified large bird and are not assigned to raven or goose without evidence.
Atlatl Dart may use matched vane sections, but fletching is not the only route to stable flight. It introduces alignment, adhesive and attachment requirements. Do not discard useful insulating down as universally worthless; it simply serves another job.

03_materials/animal/raw-meat.title: Raw Meat
03_materials/animal/raw-meat.content:
Raw Meat
Perishable food input
Raw meat is edible animal tissue before adequate cooking. Record dressed edible mass, not whole-animal mass. A 700 g rabbit does not provide 700 g of meat.
Small Game Butchery must separate edible tissue from gut contents, dirty fur and damaged portions. Maintain separate clean and dirty work surfaces; wash hands and tools before handling ready-to-eat food.
First-month use
The revised sequence cooks and consumes each small catch on its acquisition day. No persistent smoked-rabbit reserve appears. Taste, colour, freshness or a lack of bad smell does not prove microbiological safety.
Cook portions thoroughly. The handbook’s future publication needs a validated method and a means of checking the relevant internal temperature. Remembering a target temperature does not supply a thermometer.
Preservation
Smoking Rack provides equipment for handling and drying trials. Cool smoke or visual dryness alone does not demonstrate a safe shelf-stable product. Later storage requires a validated combination of preparation, pathogen control, drying, packaging and storage conditions.
Evidence
R07 supplies modern safety constraints, not certification of an improvised rack. Carcass scavenging adds uncertainty about contamination and time since death; finding usable antler does not justify eating nearby remains.

03_materials/animal/rawhide.title: Rawhide
03_materials/animal/rawhide.content:
Rawhide
Rawhide is cleaned untanned skin dried into a usually stiff material. It may be used for light containers and bindings after its section and condition are tested. It is a different state from a fresh pelt and from soft durable leather.
Rawhide Processing describes preparation. Dried skin can soften and change size when wet, then stiffen again. It is not inherently waterproof. Small mammal skin can tear at holes and cannot be assumed to support a heavy load.
Record each panel’s source and allocation. The narrative’s squirrel panel becomes a small pouch, the first rabbit panel becomes a sling, and the second rabbit panel becomes temporary clothing. Once cut or sewn, those complete panels are no longer available for another object.

03_materials/animal/sinew-thread.title: Sinew Thread
03_materials/animal/sinew-thread.content:
Sinew Thread
Material and preparation
Tendons contain collagen fibres that can provide sewing thread or bindings after preparation. The output from a small animal is short and limited; record it instead of assigning enough thread for every later project.
Separate tendon without cutting through it unnecessarily. Remove adhering tissue, dry in a protected place, then gently pound or flex and separate fibres. Join or twist strands according to the intended use. Test a sample for breaks and uneven weak sections.
The first small sewing sample is completed on Day 7, after the Day 6 squirrel tendon dries. The second rabbit contributes a further small lot on Day 12.
Use and limits
Sinew can tighten as it dries, but moisture can soften it. An untanned sinew binding is not waterproof and fat is not a guaranteed waterproof adhesive. Wet-dry cycling requires inspection.
Use Stitching for hide work and Simple Hafting for joints. Keep cooking and fibre preparation separate. Do not treat saliva-moistened fibre as suitable sterile suture material.
Alternatives
Plant cordage or suitable rawhide strips can replace sinew in some applications. Strength depends on section, preparation and load; claims that it is universally strongest require comparative evidence.

03_materials/mineral/clay.title: Clay
03_materials/mineral/clay.content:
Clay
Natural input
Clay-rich sediment is a natural material. Fired ceramics are a manufactured output. Raw clay is not the first synthetic material in history.
Colour alone does not identify a usable clay body. Remove roots and coarse debris; work a damp sample and compare its plasticity, drying shrinkage and behaviour after firing.
Collection and screening
Take a small sample from a stable exposed bank without undermining it. Roll and bend a coil. Record cracking, stickiness and grittiness. A cracked coil does not identify one universal problem: moisture, particle mixture and plasticity can all matter.
Dry small test pieces before committing to a vessel. Temper selection is experimental. Adding sand to an already non-plastic mixture can make it worse. Charcoal, shell and grit are not interchangeable ingredients.
Storage and use
Keep the working batch damp and protected if it is intended for later forming. A drying pot and a stored clay batch are different states. Reworking damp clay is permissible; it is not a violation of primitive practice.
Clay Vessel Making and Pottery separate forming from firing and testing. A clay deposit does not establish refractory quality for a future kiln or furnace.

03_materials/mineral/stone/knapping-ston.title: Knapping Stone
03_materials/mineral/stone/knapping-ston.content:
Knapping Stone
Knapping stone is material that can provide useful sharp edges through controlled fracture. Flint and chert are common candidates; some quartzite and other rocks can also work. A geological name does not guarantee that the specific specimen is suitable.
Use Stone Selection to test a small sample before hauling a large core. Inspect weathering, internal flaws and fracture. A fresh continuous edge can serve an immediate cutting task even when the core is unsuitable for a thin finished biface.
The fictional gravel bar supplies a limited set of useful cobbles. Higher-quality sources must be found or obtained through exchange; no universal Iberian flint abundance is assumed.
Keep raw cores, usable flakes and waste distinct. The first-month tool count treats expendable flakes as a small working cache rather than tracking every removal. Fine technical performance remains a research and practice question.

03_materials/mineral/water.title: Water
03_materials/mineral/water.content:
Water
Choose a source with reduced visible contamination and upstream exposure, but do not certify it by clarity, temperature or movement. Avoid taking collection water downstream of waste, butchery or fibre retting.
Before a usable vessel and heating system exist, untreated water may be a survival tradeoff. The narrative records that unresolved exposure rather than declaring the choice safe.
Hot-Rock Boiling provides observable microbial treatment for suitable water and a tested vessel. Boiling does not remove chemical toxins. Keep treated water apart from dirty collection tools and vessels. Quantity needs vary with exertion and weather; the first-month ledger explicitly assumes relatively cool conditions.

03_materials/plant/acorn-meal.title: Acorn Meal
03_materials/plant/acorn-meal.content:
Acorn Meal
Manufactured food input
Acorn meal is shelled, cleaned and leached nutmeat, then processed to the intended particle size. It may be wet mash or dried meal; these states have different storage limits.
Use Acorn Leaching before counting a bitter batch as an available ration. Initial whole-nut mass includes shells and rejected kernels. The narrative records the edible output separately.
Properties and use
Meal supplies carbohydrate and fat in proportions that vary by oak species and batch. Wet meal is perishable. Cook it for immediate consumption or follow a separately verified drying and storage method.
A dense cake placed near a fire can remain damp at its centre. It is not automatically a durable travel ration after one afternoon. First-month meal is recorded as wet and consumed promptly; expedition food is dry hazelnut kernels.
Storage checks
Keep stored dry ingredients protected from damp, insects and rodents. Discard spoiled material, but do not infer a universal safe shelf life from appearance.
Evidence
Processing duration and edible yield need species-specific research. R13 is a nutrition-reference starting point, not a measurement of prehistoric acorns.
Days 42–44 allocation
The new independently gathered shelled input remains a separate untreated food lot until processed. Wet outputs of 0.65 kg, 0.35 kg and 0.35 kg are cooked and eaten on those days; none remains after Day 44. Water increases output mass. R33 supports the distinction between acorn storage and leached meal, not the authored yield or nutrient model.
A meal route, still no dry reserve — Days 47–49
The separate Day 46 untreated lot becomes about 0.35 kg wet cooked meal on each of Days 47, 48 and 49. All output is consumed that day. Water uptake is part of wet mass, not added dry food. The input lot is exhausted on Day 49. Further meals require a new own-work collection and its processing time.

03_materials/plant/bark-cordage.title: Bark Cordage
03_materials/plant/bark-cordage.content:
Bark Cordage
Manufactured line stock
Bark cordage is usable line made from prepared Bast Fibre, normally by twisting and joining with Simple Cordage. A simple sound strip can serve as a tested tie; raw strips and fibre bundles still belong to the input stock until prepared for that use. The cordage note describes the output, not its own raw material.
In this setting willow bast provides short coarse lengths. Record the successful batch without asserting that every willow or season gives the same result. No mulberry, banyan, banana or palm is supplied by the Iberian valley.
Performance
Use Simple Cordage for reverse-wrap manufacture and splices. Test samples with the expected load, including wet condition where relevant. Inspect fraying, weak joins and slipping knots.
A workable shelter tie need not be an adequate bow-drill string. A string may survive several short attempts but require replacement. Do not equate metres produced with metres of dependable heavy-duty line.
Storage and alternatives
Dry protected from rain, and preserve samples for comparison. Nettle Cordage offers another fibre source after extraction; it is not guaranteed stronger for every diameter or preparation.
The first month’s quantities are rough length allowances. Comparative tensile data and exact local bark preparation remain open research.

03_materials/plant/bast-fibre.title: Bast Fibre
03_materials/plant/bast-fibre.content:
Bast Fibre
Prepared input stock
Bast is the inner-bark material selected and separated for flexible strips or fibre bundles. This page describes the stock before it becomes twisted line. Bark Cordage describes the finished coarse ties or cord; Simple Cordage supplies twisting and joining skills.
Select an identified locally available tree and test a small strip for soundness, flexibility and skin irritation. Weathered bark can have degraded fibres. Preparation varies with material and condition; do not assign one soaking or beating schedule to every local bark source.
First-month route
The opening scene already separates flexible bark strips and twists short ties. That preparation is recorded on Day 1; no additional harvest, finished line or asset is introduced by this distinction. The setting uses local willow bast where suitable, without claiming every willow or season supplies dependable fibre. The broader Barkcloth Processing trials compare panels and strips rather than proving a full cloth-making capability.
Allocation and alternatives
Keep unworked strip or fibre stock separate from completed cord. Once incorporated into a tie, panel or seam, the same material is not still available for another product. Nettle Fibre offers a later alternative after its own extraction and cleaning.
Protect useful stock from damp and inspect brittle, rotten or weakened pieces before use. A sound-looking strip is only a candidate; intended knots, wet condition, abrasion and load need their own tests.
Exact local preparation, yield and performance remain research and replication questions.

03_materials/plant/charcoal.title: Charcoal
03_materials/plant/charcoal.content:
Charcoal
Material
Charcoal is carbon-rich residue from heating wood with limited oxygen. Some survives in an ordinary hearth. Recover fully cooled sound pieces and keep them dry, away from ash and soil.
Incidental pieces are suitable for a small adhesive filler trial. They are not a large industrial stockpile. Deliberate production requires a separate fuel and yield budget.
Uses and limits
Charcoal can fuel hot work and can be crushed for Pine Pitch Manufacture. Burning it requires ventilation; low visible smoke does not mean absence of carbon monoxide.
Ordinary camp charcoal is not pharmaceutical activated charcoal, and is not a reliable treatment for poisoning. A charcoal filter is not demonstrated drinking-water disinfection.
Scaling
A later charcoal-making process would need wood supply, controlled air admission, cooling without reignition, fire management and transport. Do not require charcoal for every ceramic trial: suitably managed dry wood can provide the heat.
Evidence
General material behaviour is a physical-reasoning draft. The revision removes unsourced medicinal claims and guaranteed smokeless-fire assumptions.

03_materials/plant/dart-shafts.title: Dart Shafts
03_materials/plant/dart-shafts.content:
Dart Shafts
Dart shafts here are intermediate blank stock: selected wood or another suitable stalk being prepared for a projectile system, before it qualifies as completed equipment. Length, mass, straightness, stiffness and moisture interact; a thin flexible sapling is not automatically an effective dart.
Select through Wood and trim with Oldowan Knife Flake or an appropriate alternative. The narrative collects two green hazel candidates on Day 27 and begins drying trials. They remain candidates, not finished ammunition ready after an assumed two-day seasoning period.
Support with air circulation and inspect warping. Straighten only by a separately tested treatment. Bundling can reduce movement but can also slow drying. Record each shaft independently.
Atlatl Dart and Projectile Testing establish whether a candidate works with the thrower. No animal hunt is justified by a shaft merely looking straight.

03_materials/plant/dry-fuel.title: Dry Fuel
03_materials/plant/dry-fuel.content:
Dry Fuel
Dry fuel includes prepared tinder, small kindling and larger wood of known condition. Keep their quantities and roles distinct. Collect modest dry dead branches, where available, before a night or industrial firing.
The ledger records estimated dry-equivalent mass. In wet weather, actual collected wood may contain substantial water, so a nominal armload is not immediately usable. Record shortfalls and allow drying time.
An outside hearth needs ventilation and separation from shelter material. A night-long open fire requires fuel and attention; the narrative uses insulated bedding and banked embers rather than assuming uninterrupted sleep beside an automatically fed fire.
Fuel demand depends on wood, moisture, hearth, weather and operation. Recorded quantities are a continuity model requiring physical validation.

03_materials/plant/dry-plant-insulation.title: Dry Plant Insulation
03_materials/plant/dry-plant-insulation.content:
Dry Plant Insulation
Stock and condition
Clean, dry, loose plant matter selected to retain a lofted layer between the body and colder surroundings. The opening shelter already uses leaf bedding. Day 32 is the first separately recorded and allocated lot, not the first discovery that leaves can be slept on.
Dry grass and sound leaves are the local route. Their exact species and availability are setting assumptions. Do not introduce reeds, sedges, wool or imported fibres without identifying and acquiring them.
Selection and preparation
Collect modest material from a dry patch rather than stripping a wet stream margin. Reject visibly moulding, fouled, sharp or insect-infested portions. Shake out grit and stiff fragments; examine the material while spreading it. These checks reduce obvious defects but do not sterilise it or certify freedom from allergens and pests.
Dry and air a suspect damp lot before counting it as dry usable stock. Keep it away from the hearth, hot stones and sparks. Do not allocate damp gathered mass as if it supplied the same bedding performance.
Properties and checks
Loft traps relatively still air. Compression, moisture and wind penetration can reduce the practical benefit. Compare an actual resting trial on the same ground; retained warmth is an observation, not a measured insulation rating.
A mat can hold the material in position but is not itself sufficient insulation. Keep the resting layer thick enough for the observed ground conditions, maintain ventilation and replace compressed or damp material.
Allocation and losses
Record loose stock separately from bedding or clothing to which it is allocated. Day 32 assigns part of the lot to renewed shelter bedding; Day 35 assigns the remainder to a small bedding pad and its loose top layer. It cannot then furnish a mantle or escape cache without new collection.
Inspect and air in daylight. Discard failed material away from clean food and bedding. R24 documents plant bedding elsewhere in the Palaeolithic; it does not establish these local plants, a woven form, a numerical thermal value or an insect-repellent recipe.
Days 36–40: garment and bedding lots
Day 36 separately records 0.8 kg of clean long dry grass after bend/pull screening, held under ventilated cover for a wearable trial. Day 38 collects and immediately allocates a different 0.3 kg to the existing bed. Day 39 assigns 0.05 kg of the long-grass lot to a small sample; Day 40 assigns another 0.55 kg to Plant-Fibre Clothing. The sample, garment and bedding allocations cannot be counted again as loose stock. The remaining 0.2 kg is only the unallocated long-grass portion, not all the plant matter in camp.
Days 41–45 bedding renewal
New clean dry lots of 0.4 kg on Day 41, 0.6 kg on Day 44 and 0.5 kg on Day 45 are fully allocated to the existing resting layer. The earlier partial pad remains one object. The 0.2 kg long-grass loose stock stays separate. Coarse Plant Covering Stock is counted in its own roof lot, not twice as clean bedding or garment material.
Distinct bed and garment lots, Days 46–50
Day 46 adds 0.4 kg long garment grass to the 0.2 kg already loose. Day 49 allocates 0.5 kg to the front panel, leaving 0.1 kg loose. Separately, new clean bedding collections of 0.4 kg on Day 47 and 0.5 kg on Day 50 are entirely allocated to the occupied layer. The removed wet bed edge was previously allocated, not a new loose stock or fresh dry fuel. No whole-body warmth rating is inferred from these mass estimates.

03_materials/plant/hazelnut-kernels.title: Hazelnut Kernels
03_materials/plant/hazelnut-kernels.content:
Hazelnut Kernels
Hazelnut kernels are the first month’s principal food lot. Collect only positively identified sound nuts, reject damaged or spoiled kernels, and record edible mass after shelling. Shells and collection debris are not calories.
The narrative assumes productive accessible patches, surveyed before prolonged craft work. These are finite seasonal resources. Gathering, carrying, shelling and keeping the food dry all consume time. Collection may also cross other people’s resource areas.
Keep dry kernels separate from wet foods and raw game. The ledger’s approximate 6 kcal/g is an author modelling assumption, not an extracted nutrient-database value or a measured wild-nut yield. See First Month Ledger and R13 in Research Register.
Food reserves allow small experiments; they do not constitute year-round security. The first month does not establish winter supplies or a sustainable harvest for a whole community.

03_materials/plant/nettle-cordage.title: Nettle Cordage
03_materials/plant/nettle-cordage.content:
Nettle Cordage
Manufactured material
Nettle cordage consists of prepared nettle fibre twisted and usually plied into a line. Simple Cordage supplies the first method; spindle spinning is an alternative for appropriate fibre preparation and line sizes.
For each batch note approximate length, diameter, splice density, condition and intended load. Fine single yarn is not automatically a durable two-ply snare line or bowstring.
Testing
Load a short sample progressively away from the face, then repeat wet if the line will be used near water. Reject visibly damaged or slipping sections. A simple test screens gross failure; it does not produce a certified breaking load.
Bottleneck
A Spindle Whorl changes twisting mechanics. It does not harvest stems, ret them, clean fibres, supply skill or remove plying and winding work. Compare total labour per usable length before claiming a productivity gain.
Storage and scaling
Protect from moisture and abrasion. Worn bindings consume the inventory. Community production requires several independently capable workers and agreements about food, harvest and output.
Exact strength and throughput remain research questions.
Day 45 light-cover line
Ten grams of prepared fibre are allocated to an authored approximately 2 m hand-twisted, two-ply line. Gentle sample pulling and a light-cover handling trial screen conspicuous weak joins without assigning a breaking strength. A 0.8 m portion is allocated to two light roof-cover retaining points, leaving 1.4 m loose line including the previous 0.2 m. Geometry carries the frame’s main load; these short ties do not certify structural lashings, a bowstring or a renewed snare.
Uses through Day 50
Day 46 allocates 0.2 m light line to the upper roof overlap. Day 49 adds 2 m hand-made two-ply line from a separately allocated 10 g fibre portion and uses 1.2 m for the front-panel header and fastenings. Day 50 uses 0.8 m for the loose crown-pad band. Loose nettle cord ends at 1.2 m. Gentle pull/light bundle checks support these limited uses, not structural suspension or a breaking-strength value.

03_materials/plant/nettle-fibre.title: Nettle Fibre
03_materials/plant/nettle-fibre.content:
Nettle Fibre
Input
Nettle bast fibre is extracted from suitable stems by Nettle Fibre Processing. Fibre ribbons are not finished cordage or uniformly prepared spinning stock.
Record batch, cleanliness, approximate dry quantity and remaining woody material. A few successfully peeled stems do not establish a net-sized supply.
Selection and use
Long, sound strands can be split and aligned for Simple Cordage or prepared for spindle work. Compare test sections before committing a large batch. Retting too far can weaken fibres; insufficient cleaning can obstruct drafting.
Keep fibre dry and ventilated. Do not store damp retted stems as if they were a clean, shelf-stable fibre stock.
Narrative and evidence
The first successful batch is extracted on Day 16 after checks over twelve days. This duration belongs to one authored batch. R11 supports the existence of multiple extraction methods, not a fixed prehistoric schedule or a claim of superiority over all bark.
Batch B, Days 42–45
Immersion ends on Day 42 after condition checks; selected strips are rinsed and dried. Day 43 accepts 18 g cleaned dry fibre after weak/woody sections are rejected, increasing the loose stock from 24 g to 42 g. The coarse remainder remains unfinished. Day 45 allocates 10 g to hand-made cord, leaving 32 g prepared fibre. There is no new yarn output or measured extraction efficiency.
Yarn and cord allocations, Days 46–50
Two separately recorded 9 g allocations on Days 46 and 48 produce about 7 m uneven single yarn each, including weak-section losses within the allocated portions. Day 49 allocates another 10 g to about 2 m slender hand cord. Ready fibre falls from 32 g at Day 45 to 4 g at Day 49; the coarse batch B remainder is still unfinished. These small authored outputs do not validate a general fibre-to-length yield.

03_materials/plant/pine-pitch-adhesive.title: Pine Pitch Adhesive
03_materials/plant/pine-pitch-adhesive.content:
Pine Pitch Adhesive
Composite adhesive
Here the name refers to a heat-softened pine-resin adhesive with a tested filler addition. It is not a claim that adding charcoal causes one defined chemical reaction or produces the first thermoplastic in history.
Pine Pitch Manufacture describes small comparison batches. Record composition by approximate parts, observed brittleness, softening and the joint tested.
Application
A well-fitting handle and appropriate binding carry important loads. Adhesive fills gaps or resists particular movement; it does not rescue an unsuitable joint. Use Simple Hafting and inspect after cooling, wetting and use.
Limits
Mixtures can be brittle, soften in heat or fail under shock. Charcoal is not guaranteed to improve every property, and adding more filler can make a mixture worse.
Avoid food-contact sealing and wound application without relevant evidence. A cracked cooking vessel remains cracked; glue is not proof it can be safely boiled.
Evidence
The narrative demonstrates only a small knife joint. Exact durability and formulation are provisional. Ancient adhesive evidence in R03 does not validate this recipe.

03_materials/plant/pine-resin.title: Pine Resin
03_materials/plant/pine-resin.content:
Pine Resin
Natural input
Pine resin is a tree exudate, distinct from manufactured birch tar and from a resin-filler adhesive. Collect a small quantity from existing wounds without assuming every tree carries an accessible deposit.
Use a scraping edge and a dedicated bark tray. Remove coarse bark and dirt where possible. Resin is sticky and flammable; work away from sparks and keep contaminated collection tools apart from food.
Uses and limits
A trial in Pine Pitch Manufacture can produce an adhesive for particular joints. Raw resin is not a universal requirement for composite tools: mechanical fit and binding may suffice.
Do not treat resin as candle wax or use an unspecified mixture to seal a drinking vessel. Suitability for food contact requires a separate assessment. Melting does not by itself establish chemical conversion or detoxification.
Evidence
R03 concerns manufactured ancient birch tar, not this pine-resin formulation. Local resin availability is an observed narrative resource. Formulation and mechanical properties remain experimental-review tasks.

03_materials/plant/plant-covering-stock.title: Plant Covering Stock
03_materials/plant/plant-covering-stock.content:
Plant Covering Stock
Stock and purpose
Selected brush, loose sound bark and coarse plant cover for a shelter’s weather-facing layer. This is a mixed working stock, not a woven waterproof sheet. It is recorded separately from structural Wood, Dry Fuel and clean Dry Plant Insulation. The same gathered portion cannot supply all four uses.
Selection, sorting and storage
Use already identified local material and inspect condition. Reject decayed structural-looking pieces, heavily fouled matter, sharp projections and visibly moulding cover. Bark recovered from fallen wood is acceptable only where its condition and shape suit the intended overlap; do not strip unidentified living trees indiscriminately.
Separate material by job: small brush to retain loose fill, coarse leaf/grass to build the covering, bark pieces to direct water where they lie soundly. Keep damp collections separate until suitably dried; wet mass is not interchangeable with dry stock. Protect with air circulation and keep clear of the hearth and hot stones.
Checks and allocation
Flex and handle small pieces, fit them against the actual roof slope and observe whether they shed, slide or break. Layering and retention belong to Basic Thatching and Shelter Construction; selecting material alone does not establish waterproofness or insulation. Wet loading and wind can expose faults absent in a dry handling trial.
The model begins a separate 2 kg lot on Day 43, adds 4 kg on Day 44 and 4 kg on Day 45. Six kilograms are allocated to the partial return-side covering on Day 45; four kilograms remain loose. These masses are author estimates for mixed stock, not a universal roof recipe, measured density or finished thickness.
Inspect protected stock and installed cover after weather. Record losses and replacement from new collection. Bedding, clothing and food-contact material need their own cleaner selection and allocation. Exact plants and local abundance remain setting assumptions.
Allocations through Day 50
The 4 kg loose Day 45 roof lot supplies 3 kg upper cover on Day 46 and 0.5 kg shower repair on Day 47. Day 49 adds 2.5 kg own screened cover and allocates 2 kg to the offset entrance bundle; 1 kg remains loose. The long grass intended for wearable twining is a separately screened lot under Dry Plant Insulation. Neither the bed replacement nor garment can reuse the already allocated roof material.

03_materials/plant/split-wood-strips.title: Split Wood Strips
03_materials/plant/split-wood-strips.content:
Split Wood Strips
Intermediate stock
Narrow split or shaved pieces of suitable wood, described by usable length, thickness, flexibility and surface condition. Willow supplies the current coarse-mat route; other wood needs its own grain and bend trials. A rod, a split strip and extracted bast fibre are different stocks. This route works the wood of selected shoots; it does not assume autumn bark will peel easily.
Day 32 produces a small lot after trial splits. Recorded length is cumulative usable strip length, not the dimensions of a finished sheet. Offcuts and rejected strips do not enter that useful total.
Preparation
Select modest straight Willow shoots and test a split on one before committing the bundle. Support the wood and work small portions with Oldowan Knife Flake or an appropriate existing edge. Follow the grain; a knot or wandering split can leave a sharp, unusable portion. Smooth projections before bringing strips into contact with bedding or skin.
Compare bending around the intended turn. Fresh material may work without soaking; condition each lot by observation rather than an automatic recipe. Too thick a strip resists the turn, while an over-thinned strip can fail at a weak section.
Batch checks and storage
Separate suitable foundations from thinner flexible material. Check thickness variation, sharp edges, end splits and brittle sections. Drying can change flex and dimensions, so a successful green trial needs later reinspection.
Hold unused pieces under ventilated cover, not in the cooking hearth or drinking vessel. Record strips allocated to a practice sample separately from those incorporated in a pad. The Day 32 trial and Day 35 pad exhaust this recorded lot.
Uses and alternatives
Twining can secure spaced foundations with paired flexible weavers. Day 35 uses light nettle cord as those weavers; the willow strips supply the foundation. The remaining single spun yarn has not been rated for this job.
Whole flexible stems or other locally tested strips are alternative inputs with their own sharpness, drying and flexibility checks. This is a material trial, not evidence that every wood species supplies flexible or clothing-quality stock.

03_materials/plant/tinder-bundle.title: Tinder Bundle
03_materials/plant/tinder-bundle.content:
Tinder Bundle
Prepared input
A tinder bundle combines a fine, dry interior that can receive an ember with progressively coarser fibres that support flame. Use positively identified non-irritating material from local dry grass or suitable bark.
Collect before ignition attempts. Keep a protected reserve, and distinguish surface dryness from damp interiors. Wet conditions may require sheltering and drying material before another attempt.
Preparation and test
Tease fibres apart without packing the centre tightly. Give the ember contact with fine material while leaving an air path. A bundle need not be enormous; its structure, dryness and the ember’s condition matter.
Handle a developing flame with space around the hands and move it promptly to a prepared fuel bed. Smoke inhalation and sparks are risks.
Limits
The bundle cannot compensate for an ember that never forms. Species and preparation affect ignition. Feather down, dung and unidentified fungal material are not default interchangeable substitutes.
The first successful batch is used on Day 3; reliable repeatability remains a separate skill milestone.

03_materials/plant/willow.title: Willow
03_materials/plant/willow.content:
Willow
Local material source
Willow provides shoots, branches and bast of different properties. Select the part needed for the task. A green branch, seasoned shoot and extracted bark fibre are different inputs.
The fictional valley has accessible willow stands. This is a resource assumption; botanical identification and local growth form still matter.
Harvest and test
Take modest quantities of suitable shoots, inspect knots and damage, and bend a sample around the intended radius. Fresh material may already be pliable. Do not assume all autumn willow is brittle or that every rod needs prolonged soaking.
Dry rods can require soaking or another preparation, depending on size and condition. Steaming needs a system large enough for the material; a tiny pot cannot conveniently steam a full-length bundle.
Uses
Simple Coiling and Weaving and Woven Fishing Trap use tested flexible material. Coiled basket foundations normally need bendable bundles or split material, not thick rigid rods pierced with a delicate needle.
Willow also supplies coarse first-month cordage. Medicinal use is a different claim; identify species and dose rather than using the material note as a treatment prescription.

03_materials/plant/wood.title: Wood
03_materials/plant/wood.content:
Wood
Select wood by species where identifiable, grain, dimensions, moisture and defects. A sound fallen branch can supply an immediate implement without sophisticated felling tools. Green, partially dried and seasoned pieces have different properties.
Inspect knots and cracks. For a handle, test splitting and grip. For a dart shaft, inspect straightness, flex and drying behaviour. Do not call wood seasoned because it has spent two days near a fire.
Dry protected with air circulation; aggressive heating can distort or crack it. Record a selected piece as a work-in-progress asset when later work depends on it.
Manufacture and maintenance use Oldowan Knife Flake, Oldowan Simple Chopper or Hafted Knife as appropriate. These are alternatives, not an automatic escalation in archaeological era.
Shelter members, Days 43–45
The new light frame lot contains two selected natural fork braces, one slender longitudinal rail and seven return ribs. Rejected split/soft pieces are not usable stock. Six members are incorporated on Day 44 and four on Day 45, leaving none from this lot loose. These manageable fallen pieces are distinct from collected fuel and coarse roof cover. The rail sits beside the old fallen limb; no light prop is credited with safely lifting that heavy support.
