04_skills/animal-processing/small-game-b.title: Small Game Butchery
04_skills/animal-processing/small-game-b.content:
Small Game Butchery
Goal
Recover usable food and materials without transferring dirt, gut contents or damaged tissue into the meal. A small catch provides limited quantities; do not assign the whole body weight as edible meat.
Work sequence

Confirm the animal is dead and assess condition and time since capture. Do not treat a sprung trap as proof of an immediate clean kill.
Prepare a supported work surface, separate clean food and dirty skin areas, and keep drinking equipment away.
Skin with shallow controlled cuts that preserve useful panel area. A damaged pelt can still provide small pieces.
Remove the gut without puncturing it. Set aside questionable or contaminated tissue rather than trying to rescue every gram.
Separate meat into portions that can be cooked thoroughly. Organs are cooked with the meal, not eaten raw as a strength boost.
Recover suitable tendon and bone separately. Flesh the pelt and protect it from insects before drying.
Clean hands, implements and the work area. Dispose of remains away from water collection and camp traffic.

Yield and food storage
Record dressed edible mass. The first month cooks and consumes each small catch on its catch day. Smoking Rack is equipment for drying work, not proof that meat is shelf-stable.
Limits and evidence
Wild animals can carry pathogens even when apparently fresh. R07 supports cooking and preservation constraints, but a field procedure still needs validation before publication. Craft capability cannot erase those limits.

04_skills/communication/communication-an.title: Communication and Exchange
04_skills/communication/communication-an.content:
Communication and Exchange
Purpose
Establish enough shared meaning to explore cooperation. A useful object can support contact but cannot guarantee trust or status.
Practice
Begin with visible, predictable actions and observe whether distance increases or decreases. Respect a refusal or a stopped approach. Demonstrate one process without expecting observers to infer the complete chain.
Introduce words or gestures through repeated reference to the same visible object or action. Check understanding by a response that could distinguish competing interpretations. Do not translate an unknown grunt into a precise intention.
Exchange and limits
A gift may be taken, ignored or redistributed for many reasons. Agreement about access, labour and output requires further communication. A shallow stream does not guarantee protection.
Day 25 records an attempted spinning comparison, visible local cordage expertise and a warning followed by retreat. The samples and spindle are abandoned; acceptance of a gift is not observed. A failed exchange can still demonstrate the need to read distance and stop an approach, but it does not establish trust, translated intentions or a willing learner.

04_skills/construction/basic-thatching.title: Basic Thatching
04_skills/construction/basic-thatching.content:
Basic Thatching
Goal
Build a rain-shedding covering on a sound framework. Loose leaf piles and layered thatch have different functions.
Procedure
Use identified material that can be bundled and laid in overlapping courses. Start low and work upward so each course covers the top of the one below. Support bundles on the frame and secure them without crushing the drainage structure.
Give the roof enough slope to shed water for the chosen material. Protect openings and prevent water entering through fastenings. Maintain a route for smoke and air if a separate fire is nearby; the opening shelter has no indoor hearth.
Test and repair
Inspect after rain. Find drips, wind gaps and compressed patches. Replace or add material where the covering fails. Ground insulation remains a separate requirement.
Limits
A few leafy branches are not a guaranteed waterproof roof. Availability, decay, wind, fuel collection and repeated repairs constrain performance.
Basic Lean-to combines the frame, covering and bedding. The narrative’s Day 4 upgrade reduces some rain penetration but still needs repair in later wet weather.
Day 45 partial return covering
The Framed Debris Shelter variant uses sorted brush to retain coarse plant material and overlapping bark pieces to direct water outward. Lower portions are fitted before higher ones. Six kilograms of mixed Plant Covering Stock are allocated to a partial slope, not a universal thatch recipe. The upper junction and southeast front remain unfinished. A loose upper corner lifts in an ordinary breeze and is adjusted; neither this observation nor the first resting trial supplies a rain result.

04_skills/construction/knots--and--lashi.title: Knots - Primitive Set
04_skills/construction/knots--and--lashi.content:
Knots - Primitive Set
Scope
Use a small set of appropriate knots with tested Simple Cordage. Knot names do not guarantee security in every fibre, diameter or load.
Working set

An overhand knot can stop an end pulling through a hole.
A clove hitch can start a lashing on a suitable pole, but can slip under changing loads.
A reef knot can join equal cords for low-consequence binding; it is not a dependable general load-bearing bend.
A fixed loop such as a bowline remains a fixed loop. A running noose requires the standing line to pass through an eye or a separately appropriate construction.

Practice and test
Form each knot with enough tail, dress it evenly and tighten before loading. Test using the actual material and direction of pull. Mark or observe the tail to detect creep. Leave a way to release tension without cutting every line.
Limits
A drawing or hands-on demonstration is needed for complete knot instruction; this is a selection and testing note. Reject knots that slip in wet fibre or put a sharp bend into brittle cord.
For a spring trap, the noose, trigger and spring connection are separate components. Simply naming a bowline does not supply the full mechanism.

04_skills/construction/knots--and--lashi.title: Tripod Lashing
04_skills/construction/knots--and--lashi.content:
Tripod Lashing
Purpose
Join three poles so they spread into a stable tripod. Use matched sound poles and suitable Simple Cordage. A three-legged object is stable only if its geometry and load are suitable.
Procedure
Lay the poles together with their top ends aligned. Start a secure attachment to one pole. Make several wraps around all three without crushing or splitting them. Pass frapping turns between the poles to gather the wraps. Finish with a tested fastening.
Spread the legs gradually. Orient them so the load lies inside their base footprint. Seat the feet on stable ground and inspect the top joint.
Test
Apply a small load first and check movement, cord creep and leg sinking. Increase only within a conservatively tested range. Repair a loosened joint rather than declaring the whole frame permanent.
Uses and limits
Smoking Rack can use this frame. Drying hides and holding food require different surface cleanliness and placement. Heat, sparks, weather and animal interference can damage the structure.
No tripod is required for every storage task; a simple supported drying bar can be a cheaper first route.

04_skills/construction/simple-hafting.title: Simple Hafting
04_skills/construction/simple-hafting.content:
Simple Hafting
Goal
Develop the reusable joint-making skill of fitting and binding an insert to a handle so intended loads pass through a supported seat. A mechanical joint can precede glue.
Base method
Select a handle from Wood and a suitable insert, such as Oldowan Knife Flake. Make a supported seat or controlled cleft with a cutting edge. Bind below any split to prevent uncontrolled extension.
Fit the insert so it cannot rotate or slide under the first light test. Wrap with Simple Cordage, leaving the working edge exposed and securing ends outside the cutting path.
Test
Apply modest forces in the expected direction, then inspect movement, wood cracks and binding abrasion. Start use on soft expendable material. Do not automatically pry with a thin blade or transfer full shoulder force into it.
Improvements and limits
A tested Pine Pitch Adhesive can fill gaps and resist particular movement. Sinew Thread or rawhide can provide other binding options with moisture limits.
Handles change grip and stress paths; they do not multiply every cutting force by a fixed factor. R03 shows that manufactured adhesives and hafted tools were not necessarily new to Neanderthal makers.

04_skills/craft/shelter-construction.title: Shelter Construction
04_skills/craft/shelter-construction.content:
Shelter Construction
Ability and scope
Turn a selected resting site and available natural material into a stable, maintainable shelter through controlled fit, staged assembly, inspection and repair. This skill covers judgement during work as well as the physical placement. A remembered plan and a structure which briefly stands are insufficient evidence of competence under changing weather.
Prior requirements and working control
Use Environmental Observation to assess runoff, overhead hazards, animal routes, weather exposure and access. Select Wood for the actual duty, considering defects, dimensions, moisture, grain and contact geometry. Sound manageable fallen pieces can avoid a felling requirement. They do not remove the need to check their condition.
Work from outside a potential fall space while seating supports and testing fit. Remove load before adjusting a moving seat; never cut a bearing member while occupying the space it supports. Light ties may restrain rolling or cover movement, but they cannot be assumed to carry structural loads without a suitable design and test. Simple Cordage is a useful route where lashings are selected; natural forks and bearings are another route with their own limits.
Stages and feedback
Retain a usable sleeping cover during rebuilding when feasible. Set the main bearing geometry, fit a few ribs and check seats before adding the rest. Apply cover in inspectable stages; stop if feet creep, a fork opens, the rail rolls, a member cracks or the added load changes the fit. A controlled light-pressure check cannot certify storm or snow loads.
Fit weather cover to slope, drainage and the opening. Keep the exit usable, prevent runoff entering the bed and retain appropriate ventilation. Maintain a distinct clean resting layer. Repeat inspections after wind, rain, ground wetting and bedding compression. Note both useful improvements and unresolved faults.
Narrative demonstration and limits
Day 44 demonstrates limited seating, fit and adjustment of a light return frame beside the retained shelter support. Day 45 adds ribs and partial cover, then checks ordinary wind and a short resting trial. The upper junction and southeast opening remain incomplete. No rain test, safe indoor combustion system, snow-load performance or winter survival is demonstrated.
Basic Lean-to and Framed Debris Shelter describe structures. This page describes the control and diagnosis used while building them. Later foundations, joinery and larger spans need their own methods and evidence; small-branch success does not qualify a maker to construct any building.
Evidence and continuing practice
R32 in Research Register supports attention to wet exposure, insulation and the hazards of enclosed combustion. It is not a load calculation or a validated natural-material building standard. The present geometry and labour estimates are authored physical trials requiring replication. Keep combustion outside the small combustible sleeping chamber.
Learn from the first occupied weather — Days 46–50
Connected cover on Day 46 is followed by a real shower observation on Day 47. An inward drip changes the overlap and bed allocation before a broader success is claimed. Inspect bearing seats when cover gains moisture; an unchanged seat during a limited check is not a general load rating. Stage local unloading and repair from outside. A later offset entrance bundle is accepted only after testing the occupant’s exit and ventilation. Framed Debris Shelter records the dated material and observation limits.

04_skills/fibre-work/simple-coiling-and-.title: Simple Coiling and Weaving
04_skills/fibre-work/simple-coiling-and-.content:
Simple Coiling and Weaving
Scope
Coiling and stake-and-strand weaving are distinct techniques. Learn the one needed for the chosen object, rather than treating them as one interchangeable motion.
Coiling
Use a flexible foundation bundle, such as suitable fine plant stems or split fibres. Start with a small loop, bind it securely, then add successive coils with stitches that join to the preceding coil. Lift coils gradually to form the wall.
Do not try to pierce a thick rigid willow rod with a thin bone needle. Use an awl in gaps or select a softer foundation. Maintain consistent tension and stagger joins.
Stake-and-strand work
Arrange sound uprights, then pass flexible strands alternately around them. Keep spacing and tension consistent. Turn around a rim or terminate ends without leaving an unstable wall.
The narrative makes a small willow stake basket; the coiled foundation trial is a comparison, not a compulsory prerequisite.
Test and limits
Load the base lightly and inspect joins, rim and carrying attachment. The finished capacity is a tested property, not a promised fivefold gain.
Nets need different knots, mesh control and line preparation. Basketry does not automatically establish net manufacture.
Flat strip work — Day 52
The same over-and-under relationship can interlace flexible strips into a small flat sheet without a stake basket’s upright wall. Day 52 uses broad selected willow bast for experimental footbeds, turns the margins and binds them separately. This does not introduce a loom, fine textile or a completed boot. Fit, abrasion, ground grip and retention belong to Plant-Fibre Footwear and its actual trials.

04_skills/fibre-work/simple-cordage.title: Simple Cordage
04_skills/fibre-work/simple-cordage.content:
Simple Cordage
Purpose and inputs
Make a line from tested fibres. Bast Fibre supplies the first prepared strip or fibre input; Nettle Fibre is a later alternative. Select equal fibre bundles and preserve long overlaps at joins.
The usable line produced by this technique is Bark Cordage or, with nettle inputs, Nettle Cordage. This page develops twisting, grip and joining control; it does not require finished cord as the raw input.
Reverse wrap

Hold the junction firmly between finger and thumb.
Twist one bundle consistently in one direction.
Cross it over the other bundle in the opposite direction.
Move the grip to hold the new junction and repeat.
Add new fibres before a bundle runs out, staggering joins so both strands do not weaken together.

Twist direction and crossing direction must oppose each other. Watch the actual movement rather than relying on ambiguous left/right instructions.
Tests
Pull a sample gently, inspect uneven thickness and check whether splices slide. Test the intended knot and load. A line adequate for a tie may fail under a bow drill’s abrasion.
Time and limits
Output depends on fibre preparation, diameter, joins and practice. The narrative provides a small useful lot, not immediate industrial capacity. Fatigue and skin injury limit continuous work.
A spindle is an alternative for some fine yarn production. It still requires drafting, winding, suitable fibre and often plying.

04_skills/fibre-work/stitching.title: Stitching
04_skills/fibre-work/stitching.content:
Stitching
Goal
Join prepared thin hide or other material with a thread that suits the load. Bone Awl can make holes and guide a blunt thread before an eyed needle is available.
Procedure
Support the panel on a clean surface. Place holes far enough from the edge to avoid tearing, and leave enough spacing that the row does not become a perforation line. Test on a scrap.
For an overlapped seam, pass thread repeatedly through both panels and around the edge. Tighten evenly rather than pulling each stitch to the material’s breaking point. Secure the ends with an appropriate tested fastening.
An eyed Bone Needle speeds some operations but may be fragile. Use the awl to make holes in tougher material instead of forcing the eye sideways through stiff rawhide.
Test and limits
Pull a scrap seam in the direction of its intended load. Look for tearing, thread abrasion and hole enlargement. Wet sinew can tighten on drying but can also cut fragile edges or soften in damp conditions.
Sewing a small pouch does not prove mastery of fitted cold-weather clothing. Fitting, panel area, preservation, weather resistance and maintenance remain separate constraints.

04_skills/fibre-work/twining.title: Twining
04_skills/fibre-work/twining.content:
Twining
Ability and scope
Control two flexible working elements as they cross between successive foundations, enclosing them rather than relying on a single over-and-under strand. Twining can stabilise a coarse sheet without fine yarn or a loom. It is distinct from coiling and from the stake-and-strand method already practised in Simple Coiling and Weaving.
R23 supplies museum descriptions of the structure. Their examples are not evidence that this exact technique or object existed in the fictional valley.
First practice route
Arrange a few tested Split Wood Strips on the ground. Use paired portions of light, tested Nettle Cordage as the working elements. Cross the pair between neighbouring foundations and retain the same working sequence along the row. Make a short sample before a broad sheet.
Keep enough space for the intended stuffing without leaving foundations free to slide. Equal-looking gaps do not guarantee equal tension. Work gradually across the width, checking that earlier crossings remain engaged.
Stagger joins and keep their ends where they can be inspected. A join which survives handling may still fail when damp or repeatedly rolled. Secure the margins without pulling a brittle foundation into a tight turn.
Feedback and diagnosis
Lift, bend and gently shake the sample. Look for migrating foundations, opening crossings, sharp protrusions and an edge that unravels. Compare dry and slightly damp handling when moisture is part of the intended use.
The Day 32 sample holds its few foundations under light handling. That demonstrates a limited movement pattern, not full garment manufacture. Day 35 adds practice at maintaining rows across a small bedding pad.
Limits and further practice
A coarse successful sheet does not establish spinning, a fine textile, a waterproof layer, net knots or comfortable clothing. A pad used on the ground needs different flexibility and edge checks from a wrap worn while walking.
Plant-Fibre Mats describes the design family and its first small bedding-pad variant; the skill can later support other objects if their materials, tension and use tests are earned. The technique’s low hardware requirements do not remove harvesting and line-making labour.
Flexible wearable foundations
A foundation need not be a hard splint. Days 39–40 use small hanging bundles of flexible grass, held by paired working elements of existing single nettle yarn. The rows retain light bundles; separate inspected cord carries suspension. Crossing two yarn lengths in a twined row is not the same as plying them into load-rated cord. Examine creeping rows, bundle escape and edge security before wearing a larger piece. Plant-Fibre Clothing contains the garment-specific construction and fit checks.
Another wearable panel — Day 49
A separate flexible front panel uses the same paired-yarn crossings between hanging grass bundles as the earlier back piece. Day 49 earns the added width with new fibre/yarn work, separate grass and inspected fastening line. Inspect migration before fitting, then inspect again after walking; Day 50’s header adjustment demonstrates that a dry first fit does not remove maintenance. Plant-Fibre Clothing carries the variant rather than a separate article for each panel.

04_skills/fire/bow-drill-fire.title: Bow Drill Fire
04_skills/fire/bow-drill-fire.content:
Bow Drill Fire
Purpose and prerequisites
Produce an ember through friction, then transfer it to prepared tinder. The first month’s traveller has practised this technique before departure. A successful Day 3 attempt does not establish mastery under all weather.
Use a dry board and spindle of a combination tested in training, then test the local samples. Wood labelled hardwood or softwood is not a sufficient recipe. The narrative uses suitable dry willow pieces for both; a dense oak spindle is not compulsory.
Kit and posture
Prepare a board socket with a notch to collect hot dust, a spindle, a bow with adjustable cord tension, a low-friction bearing block and a dry ember catcher. Lubricate only the upper bearing surface with an appropriate non-food sample; do not contaminate the lower friction contact.
Brace the board with a foot, keep the bearing arm stable against the shin, and maintain a clear bow path. Set tension so the spindle turns without the string slipping or jamming. Extra twists do not inherently increase revolutions per bow stroke.
Procedure
Run short controlled strokes to establish contact and a dust pile. Adjust pressure and speed while keeping the spindle stable. Stop if the cord abrades, contact glazes or exhaustion destroys posture. When a sustained ember remains in the dust after rotation stops, allow it to consolidate and transfer it gently into Tinder Bundle.
Failure and limits
Smoke without an ember is not success. Dry materials, geometry, upper-bearing friction and cord condition all matter. Make short sessions, protect hands and keep a fallback shelter and food plan. No fixed number of attempts or seconds guarantees ignition.
A new fire kit requires a fresh test. Preserving embers reduces daily ignition labour but does not remove the need to restart after loss.
Independent second kit — Day 53
Day 53 uses a newly made board, spindle, bow, bearing, catcher, coarse bark string and tinder. Tension and alignment are checked with slow strokes before a working run leaves a sustained ember and produces a small tinder flame. Original kit A remains complete. Kit B is a separate dry-tested bundle at the main camp, not an all-weather guarantee or provision already placed at the fallback bench.

04_skills/fire/hand-drill-fire.title: Hand Drill Fire
04_skills/fire/hand-drill-fire.content:
Hand Drill Fire
Purpose
Rotate a slender dry spindle by hand against a compatible dry hearth board. It avoids a bowstring requirement but can be physically demanding. It is not an automatic backup that succeeds when an exhausted traveller’s bow drill fails.
Material choice
Choose an identified dry stalk or wood combination that has been tested, with a straight spindle and suitable lower contact. The setting does not supply giant hogweed, and unidentified umbellifer stems are excluded. Even named mullein or elder candidates require the relevant material and preparation, not merely their presence.
Procedure
Prepare the socket, dust notch and ember catcher. Brace the board. Rotate between the palms while applying pressure and maintaining contact. Reset hand position without scattering the developing dust. Pause before blisters or fatigue make controlled work impossible.
Confirm a sustained ember before attempting tinder transfer. Smoke alone is insufficient.
Limits and evidence
Moisture, spindle geometry, friction, hand condition and practice govern outcomes. The old guarantee that the first twenty attempts fail, followed by a universal callus schedule, is removed.
R09 explains the hazard of the removed hogweed option; it does not validate every remaining plant. The revised narrative does not demonstrate hand-drill fire. It remains an alternative requiring practical trials.

04_skills/fishing/basic-spear-fishing.title: Basic Spear Fishing
04_skills/fishing/basic-spear-fishing.content:
Basic Spear Fishing
Scope
Attempt shallow-water fishing only when the expected return justifies exposure and effort. Failure to catch a fish is a valid result.
Method
Observe fish movement from stable ground. Select clear shallow water where a miss will not drive the point into an unseen rock. The apparent position is displaced by refraction; aim below the apparent fish and adjust through observed trials rather than a universal behind-the-fish rule.
Keep footing secure. Position the point near the surface when practical, and make a controlled thrust. Do not chase a missed fish into deeper or fast water.
Equipment and testing
A Fire-Hardened Spear can be trialled, but is not specialised fishing equipment. Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear is another design with different failure points.
Inspect the point after contact and keep catches separate from clean food. The opening’s short Day 13 trial produces no fish and does not establish reliable subsistence.
Limits
Glare, turbidity, water temperature, species behaviour and user practice affect results. No fixed success rate is assigned. Establish several repeatable catches before relying on this food source.

04_skills/fishing/crayfish-gathering.title: Crayfish Gathering
04_skills/fishing/crayfish-gathering.content:
Crayfish Gathering
Status
Freshwater crayfish presence in the fictional valley is unresolved. The revised Days 11–12 do not depend on crayfish catches, and this skill has no demonstrated date.
Required research
Identify the proposed species and evidence for its regional prehistoric occurrence. Modern introduced populations cannot establish ancient availability. Add identification, seasonal behaviour, edible yield and cooking requirements before adding a catch.
General handling considerations
Shallow-water collection still involves slippery footing, cold exposure, hand injury and disturbance of sediment. Avoid reaching blindly under stones or presenting a low catch as inherently calorie-positive.
A successful catch needs a clean container, appropriate dispatch and thorough cooking. No claim of safety is based on shell colour, brief roasting or the animal’s apparent cleanliness.
Comparison
Compare collecting time and edible output with established nut gathering and other local foods. A remembered technique without a confirmed organism is not an available subsistence method.
This page is retained for later research rather than supplying a fictional guarantee.

04_skills/fishing/mussel-harvesting.title: Mussel Harvesting
04_skills/fishing/mussel-harvesting.content:
Mussel Harvesting
Status and scope
The fictional river contains observed bivalves, but identification and food safety are not established. No mussel meals are counted in the revised first month.
Requirements
Identify the species and source conditions. Assess contamination and possible toxins separately from whether an animal is alive. A shell opening when heated, or a lack of bad smell, does not prove the food safe.
Collection framework
Work only where footing and temperature allow safe inspection. Locate specimens by observation rather than bare-foot sweeping through concealed debris. Keep any collected research specimens separate from ready-to-eat food.
Record labour and edible yield before treating this as a staple. Cooking can control some pathogens; it does not reliably eliminate every environmental toxin.
Research
A species-specific harvest and cooking page is required before narrative consumption. Shell uses for clay temper also require tests; raw shell is not a universally suitable ceramic additive.
This note remains draft with no demonstrated food capability.

04_skills/foraging/basic-foraging.title: Basic Foraging
04_skills/foraging/basic-foraging.content:
Basic Foraging
Purpose
Find food with reliable identification and worthwhile return. Generic categories such as young leaves or colourful flowers are not a safe diet.
Method
Survey a known patch before collection. Identify the whole plant and edible part using several diagnostic features, its habitat and season. Compare potentially dangerous lookalikes. If that cannot be done, leave the plant.
The narrative begins with positively identified hazelnuts, then documented oak acorns processed through Acorn Leaching. These are authored identified resources; this page is not a complete field identification key.
Gather sound material, separate questionable pieces and measure return in edible food after cleaning or shelling. Count collection, carrying and processing time.
Rejected shortcuts
Milky sap, leaf number, flower colour and bitterness do not provide a universal toxicity screen. Do not taste an unidentified plant as an identification experiment. Cooking is not a general detoxification method.
Limits and teaching
Seasonal availability and safe access matter. Local knowledge of a patch can outweigh remembered general botany. Ask or observe when shared communication permits, and distinguish a personal tolerance from a validated food.
R08 demonstrates why apparently familiar edible plants require care. Detailed species keys remain a separate research task.

04_skills/foraging/berry-foraging.title: Berry Foraging
04_skills/foraging/berry-foraging.content:
Berry Foraging
Goal
Collect a positively identified seasonal fruit without treating berries as the principal energy supply.
Procedure
Identify the plant, fruit and edible parts before collecting. Check the relevant lookalikes; names such as berry or rosehip are not identification keys. Select sound ripe material and leave damaged or questionable fruit.
Collect into a clean Bark Container or other appropriate vessel, avoiding compression and contamination from raw meat. Count edible yield and labour. A handful can supplement a nut meal without making its energy budget complete.
Preparation and storage
Preparation depends on species. Some fruits contain irritating hairs, hard seeds or other parts requiring removal. Do not assume every fruit is edible whole, raw or after drying.
Eat small clean lots promptly in the opening sequence. Long-term storage requires a separate drying and packaging procedure. A wet fruit cache is not equivalent to dry kernels.
Limits
The setting permits a small late-season blackberry patch, explicitly as a narrative resource. Do not assert abundant fruit on every day or extrapolate one identified species to all brambles.

04_skills/foraging/edible-plant-identifi.title: Edible Plant Identification
04_skills/foraging/edible-plant-identifi.content:
Edible Plant Identification
Scope
This is a planning and identification framework, not a complete edible-flora key for prehistoric Iberia.
Prioritise resources that are identified, seasonally accessible and capable of supporting useful quantities. For the first month these are Hazelnut Kernels and leached Acorn Meal. Small greens and fruit are supplements.
Working procedure
For a proposed food note species, part, season, preparation, dangerous lookalikes and known contraindications. Check all of those before adding the food to the narrative. Identify the organism rather than using a generic name such as tuber.
Test gathering return by edible output per total labour, including processing and failed searches. Keep a patch record and reserve alternatives for bad weather or disputed access.
Limits
Modern species ranges do not automatically describe 40,000 BP. Scots pine is not interchangeable with stone pine for a high-yield nut supply. Wild garlic’s season and lookalikes need attention; do not introduce spring growth as an autumn staple.
Plant food can be contaminated or spoil. Appearance and taste do not certify safety. Precise identification pages and regional evidence remain unfinished.

04_skills/foraging/mushroom-foraging.title: Mushroom Foraging
04_skills/foraging/mushroom-foraging.content:
Mushroom Foraging
Status and purpose
This page is a draft identification framework. Mushrooms are removed from the revised first month’s meals until species-specific identification and preparation notes are researched. They should not be represented as high-calorie staple foods.
Requirements for a future entry
Supply diagnostic features for the full organism, habitat, maturity, toxic lookalikes and preparation. Inspect each specimen; a familiar group name does not identify every member.
A puffball-like shape, white interior, apricot scent or apparent false gills alone is not a complete identification procedure. Do not promise that chanterelles, wood ears or any other broad group has zero dangerous confusion risk.
Decision rule
Leave uncertain specimens. Cooking does not neutralise all mushroom toxins and tasting is not a safe identification test.
Research and narrative use
Add a verified species note before counting a mushroom lot in the ledger. Record collection and preparation separately from nuts. Local expertise may be useful but should still be represented as knowledge of specific organisms and practices.
This revision intentionally removes the old universal safety claims. No demonstration date is assigned.

04_skills/health/medicinal-plant-assessm.title: Medicinal Plant Assessment
04_skills/health/medicinal-plant-assessm.content:
Medicinal Plant Assessment
Scope
The skill here is assessing proposed plant-treatment claims and recognising what identification, preparation and evidence are missing. This remains an assessment and research framework, not a dosing guide or a substitute for basic hygiene and first aid. The first month does not rely on medicinal plant remedies.
Evidence distinctions
Record species, preparation, dose, intended effect, toxicity, interactions and evidence before including a treatment. Traditional use, a compound’s laboratory activity and a demonstrated clinical benefit are different claims.
Willow contains salicylate-related compounds, but an unspecified bark infusion is not a measured aspirin dose. Plantain, yarrow, St John’s wort, mallow and juniper require their own identification and treatment reviews. Juniper smoke is not demonstrated sterilisation.
Immediate practice
Prioritise Sanitation and Camp Hygiene, clean water, protection from further injury and observation of worsening symptoms. Do not put chewed leaves or contaminated material into an open wound. Ordinary sinew is not sterile suture material.
Research boundary
R08 supports identification caution, not medicinal efficacy. The specific plant-treatment claims need medical and botanical sources before publication. No field-safe recipe or first-month treatment demonstration is claimed.
The traveller can recall potential remedies but may lack the means to identify, prepare and dose them reliably.

04_skills/hunting/atlatl-throwing.title: Atlatl Throwing
04_skills/hunting/atlatl-throwing.content:
Atlatl Throwing
Ability and prior requirements
Coordinate posture, body and arm motion, hook engagement and release with a matched dart. Knowledge of leverage does not supply the timing. Day 30 records first controlled attempts; it establishes neither mastery nor a hunting capability.
Use an inspected Atlatl, Atlatl Dart and Projectile Practice Ground. Projectile Testing supplies observation and stop decisions. A dart is not an arbitrary heavy spear.
Practice and control
Begin with an inspected assembly and a repeatable short position. Rehearse slow seating and the intended movement without promising that slow motion reproduces launch loads. Check the flight space before each attempt.
R22’s coaching account describes coordinated motion and common engagement errors. Early disengagement, an end dragged downwards and sideways release can have different causes. Do not change the nock, shaft stiffness and movement at the same time.
Keep effort modest while diagnosing fit. Higher effort can increase danger and conceal an underlying problem. Stop when repeated inspection shows damage, when footing worsens, when someone enters the area or when fatigue prevents useful comparison.
Feedback
Record actual releases, misses, landings and visible damage. Compare a sequence rather than the best throw. Returning to the same start and target ground matters more than an impressive distance anecdote.
The narrative’s six Day 30 attempts include hand-thrown comparisons with the same blunt dart. That compares the traveller’s two actions, not equal proficiency or a controlled experiment against a local hunter. Later attempts remain erratic.
Operating limits and evidence
A retained flight in one trial does not establish useful killing power, field accuracy, safe joint loading or weather tolerance. Target work omits tracking, approach, a moving animal, recovery and the risks of a wounded quarry.
R22 is modern coaching and observation, not direct evidence for a thrower in this Neanderthal group’s toolkit or a predicted learning curve. Practised local adults can remain markedly better with their own hand-thrown spears while the traveller improves.
Day 37: curiosity and an unequal comparison
Two observers stop north of the west-directed practice line. The traveller lowers equipment, preserves an exit and casts only while they remain outside the flight/retrieval space. One local adult then makes two hand throws with his own stone-pointed spear, recovering and retaining it himself. Greater practical reach, tighter placement and decisive arrival are observations of these users and systems, not a measured species-wide strength relation.
The traveller’s four attempts include two before the observers arrive; only two reach the broad bank patch. Interest in the lever does not mean admiration, teaching, access permission or adoption. R17 supports treating trained hand throwers seriously; R22 supports prioritising coordinated movement and engagement before harder effort or decorative additions.
Repeat before claiming improvement — Day 50
Four private attempts provide a setting to repeat; three broad-bank landings and one miss are all recorded. The head piece, both grass panels and fox strip are removed and recovered so the thrower’s path is clear. No observer appears. A few landings cannot establish that the local expert’s advantage has narrowed; a later watched comparison must earn that result.

04_skills/hunting/hunting-approach.title: Hunting Approach
04_skills/hunting/hunting-approach.content:
Hunting Approach
Ability and scope
Choose, attempt and reassess an approach to an animal while accounting for detection, footing, casting space, retrieval and return. This judgement is distinct from reading sign in Tracking and releasing a projectile into a known bank. A stopped or unsuccessful approach can demonstrate the decision process without demonstrating successful hunting.
The first narrative route is a limited solo approach to observed red deer with an existing ordinary wooden-pointed spear. It is not a universal hunting recipe or a claim that a first-month weapon is adequate for every animal.
Before committing time
Allocate the whole outing, including travel and return, against food work and daylight. Identify a stopping condition before following sign. Keep essential equipment accessible and avoid routes which depend on crossing uncertain water or entering occupied ground. A possible pelt is not stock which can finance today’s clothing.
Use several related signs, substrate and surrounding terrain to choose an observation point. Note a recognisable return route. Watch actual animals before committing to a closer approach when possible; an apparently used trail is not an appointment with its occupant.
Approach and reassessment
Observe air movement locally rather than assuming one breeze persists across a dip or ridge. Keep sight, sound, scent transport, footing and the movement of other animals in view together. Cover which hides the body may also hide the intended cast or recovery route.
Pause after a material change: an animal raises its head, air turns, gravel moves, a second animal leaves cover, or the next step blocks retreat. Record observations without claiming to know the precise cue which caused an animal to react. R35 supports varied vigilance responses to disturbance and cover; it does not specify a guaranteed approach distance or explain the fictional Day 48 response.
Evaluate the intended cast and likely recovery before releasing. Target practice does not answer the consequences of striking a moving animal on screened or dangerous ground. Retaining the weapon and stopping can be the appropriate outcome of an unsuccessful approach.
The solo bottleneck
One person cannot simultaneously maintain observation from several directions, move animals from another opening, recover a difficult strike, carry a whole carcass and watch for competitors. Better reach or a new point addresses only part of that work. The handbook should record processing, carrying and exposure costs when a later catch occurs, rather than ending the chain at impact.
First trial and useful records
Day 48 combines short reconnaissance and an attempted approach. Two red-deer hinds leave through separate cover breaks after a movement/noise and air change; no cast is made. The two-and-a-half-hour outing reduces that day’s gathering, with no meat, hide or new equipment. This is limited judgement practice, not skilled stalking or a successful large-game hunt.
Record the route, observed animals, cover and footing, stopping decision, time and displaced work. Later outings may compare these decisions, but do not turn a single unsuccessful event into a species-wide rule or a catch probability. Local hunters’ environmental experience remains a major advantage.
Evidence and limits
R35 is a field study of modern Scottish red-deer vigilance under different human disturbance and cover. It supports the general need to observe changing responses. The local route, weapon choice, timing, wind and result are authored physical reasoning, not a reproduced 40,000 BP hunt. Weapon performance, injury and recovery require separate evidence before practical publication.

04_skills/hunting/projectile-testing.title: Projectile Testing
04_skills/hunting/projectile-testing.content:
Projectile Testing
Ability and scope
Judge release, flight, retrieval and damage under repeatable conditions. Distinguish material condition, apparatus, movement and observation. A specimen which survives one cast is not a reliable hunting system.
Use Projectile Practice Ground and inspect its flight space before every session. The location must remain suitable for the actual effort and projectile, rather than inheriting safety from an earlier weak trial.
Selecting and maintaining a practice site
Inspect the backstop, flight sides, crest and retrieval route for exposed stone, unstable ground and paths by which a person could enter unseen. Reject obscured landing ground or a site which could carry a miss towards occupied space. The local Projectile Practice Ground is one application of this judgement, not a universal prerequisite site.
Clear modest obstructions for stable footing and retrieval. Ground markers must not create trip hazards. Inspect before each session and stop when weather, entrants or fatigue prevent useful observations. A bank which contains a weak trial does not certify containment at greater effort.
First comparison route
Inspect the Atlatl and Atlatl Dart. Begin with slow fit checks and modest attempts. Record an early disengagement separately from a late dragging release, an inaccurate landing or a damaged shaft. Inspect after each initial cast and stop for spreading damage or uncertain engagement.
Retain the start line, broad target ground, effort intention and specimen identity. Marked Reference Staff can support comparison. Exact speed or impact energy is not supplied by these observations.
Change one significant factor at a time when possible. A drying green shaft is already changing, so repeated results cannot be assigned entirely to improved technique. Keep a second specimen separate until it has passed its own preparation checks.
Feedback and operating limits
Compare whole sequences, including misses. Hand casting the same dart can reveal the traveller’s present handling differences, but unequal proficiency prevents a claim about universal superiority. A neighbour using his own spear introduces other material, body and practice differences.
A successful target cast omits stalking, a moving quarry, wound effects and recovery. Grouping matters independently of distance. There is no hunting range certified by these first trials.
Narrative demonstration and evidence
Day 30 records three hand casts and three erratic atlatl attempts with a green, blunt, unfletched dart. Day 35 records another short sequence, with only half reaching the broad bank patch and early rear-seat compression noted. These are first documented tests, not mastery.
Atlatl Throwing develops motor control; this skill develops judgement about the resulting observations. R22 informs engagement and motion problems through modern coaching. It neither validates the traveller’s specimen nor fixes a learning rate.
Interpreting the Day 37 observation
Separate own casts before and during observation from the local adult’s two casts. Keep user, weapon, start position and target choice recognisable. The neighbour throws a stone-pointed spear; the traveller throws a blunt light dart. Better grouping and practical reach are visible, but penetration, speed and impact energy cannot be equated without comparable measurement. A pointed head is not evidence that the lever is mechanically inferior.
Watching another person can change confidence and task choice without supplying instruction. Retain a private short-line comparison for the next trial. There is still no certified hunting range or clearance test with the Day 40 grass panel.

04_skills/hunting/scavenging.title: Scavenging
04_skills/hunting/scavenging.content:
Scavenging
Goal
Find useful non-food material while avoiding competition at active kills. An old antler shed is a different opportunity from fresh meat defended by a predator.
Method
Use Environmental Observation and Tracking to identify areas worth a limited search. Stop if fresh carnivore sign, poor visibility or a blocked return route raises the risk. Birds circling or resting do not identify a fresh, safe or abandoned carcass.
Inspect detached material for condition before carrying it. Prefer a sound old shed when available. Select dimensions appropriate to the intended tool and leave damaged pieces.
Narrative application
Day 18 recovers an old red-deer antler fragment away from a feeding site. No fresh carcass approach, smell-masking fire or raw meat meal is required to obtain a billet.
Limits and alternatives
A spear is not reliable protection against a large predator. Searching costs daylight and food. An unsuccessful trip does not justify escalating confrontation.
Exchange, wood alternatives or hard-hammer knapping may supply another route. The claim that scavenging is universally safer or more efficient than hunting is removed.

04_skills/hunting/spear-throwing.title: Spear Throwing
04_skills/hunting/spear-throwing.content:
Spear Throwing
Ability and scope
Coordinate a hand-held spear, balanced stance, whole-body movement and release to control flight towards a chosen target. This is a motor skill, distinct from spear construction, thrusting and Atlatl Throwing. Remembered mechanics do not establish practical accuracy.
The base equipment route uses the existing wooden-pointed spear. A separately tested stone-pointed composite weapon is another route with its own shaft, joint and point requirements. A heavier or sharper weapon is not automatically easier to throw or more useful for a given task.
Prior requirements and practice
Inspect the actual spear, grip and target space. Environmental Observation supports checking footing, flight and retrieval approaches, bystanders and changing conditions. The local Projectile Practice Ground is a short experimental site, not permanent containment for every weapon or effort. Reassess its bank and clear space before using a heavier or differently pointed spear.
Begin with controlled, modest attempts at a repeatable position. Keep target choice and equipment consistent while attending to balance, coordinated movement and release. Change one significant factor at a time when possible; do not use maximum effort as a substitute for diagnosis. Keep the field clear during casting and retrieval, and stop when fatigue, uncertainty or damage prevents useful practice.
Feedback and diagnosis
Record all landings, early or late releases, grouping, retrieval and damage. More distance with greater scatter is a different result from repeatable placement. Inspect the shaft and any point joint after impact. Inadequate flight may concern weapon balance, shaft behaviour, grip or timing; an isolated miss does not identify which.
Projectile Testing supplies repeatable comparison judgement. Unlike heads and users cannot establish equal impact energy from penetration. A target hit also omits wind, stalking, moving quarry, an obstructed cast, wounded-animal risk and recovery. Tracking supports different parts of the hunting task; it is not a manufacturing prerequisite for learning a throw.
Observed narrative instance
Day 37 records a local adult’s two hand casts with his own stone-pointed spear into clear bank ground. He selects a target, makes coordinated movements, retrieves and checks his weapon, and repeats from farther away. His practical reach, placement and apparent force are clearly better than the traveller’s unstable blunt-dart casts in that scene. The chosen individual’s robust physique, long practice and prepared equipment contribute; no numerical or species-wide strength rule is inferred.
This page’s own demonstrated_day remains null. The scene is recorded under community_demonstrates, not as the traveller acquiring skill or being taught. Nobody lends a spear, provides a point or performs labour for him. His earlier incidental hand casts with the experimental dart are not evidence of competence with a hunting spear.
Limits and evidence
R17’s experiments with trained modern throwers and replica Schöningen wooden spears show why hand-thrown weapons cannot be assumed ineffective. They do not measure the fictional adult, establish his learning history or predict the traveller’s performance. R21 supports taking both wooden and stone-pointed Neanderthal weapons seriously; neither source reconstructs this particular valley toolkit. The Day 37 result is an authored observation, not a historical test result.
Practise field judgement separately from target movement. Throwing the traveller’s only defensive spear leaves it at the target until retrieved. That loss of immediate access is one reason not to treat a solitary hunting cast as a free opportunity.

04_skills/hunting/tracking.title: Tracking
04_skills/hunting/tracking.content:
Tracking
Purpose
Infer movement from sign while keeping uncertainty explicit. A footprint can be degraded, overlapped or misread.
Procedure
Observe shape, size, stride, orientation and substrate together. Compare more than one print and look for corroborating signs such as feeding damage or droppings. Record freshness as an estimate affected by weather.
Map repeated paths before setting equipment. A trail used by one species may also carry predators or people. Check whether sign persists after rain or frost.
Application
Figure-4 Deadfall Trap, Snare Trap and Scavenging benefit from this knowledge. Track identification improves placement; it does not guarantee a capture or an unoccupied carcass.
Limits
Do not diagnose species from a single adjective such as precise. Local people have accumulated experience of these animals and routes. The traveller’s training supplies a starting vocabulary, but he needs local comparisons.
The first month’s trap records describe authored outcomes, not measured capture probabilities.
Sign becomes an approach question — Day 48
Successive prints and browsing select an observation point, without a precise trail age. Once animals are visible, Hunting Approach considers cover, local air, footing, other animals and recovery. Two hinds leave after the traveller shifts around stony ground; the actual detection cue remains uncertain. No cast, catch, new pelt or neighbour aid follows.

04_skills/measurement/measurement-and-re.title: Measurement and Records
04_skills/measurement/measurement-and-re.content:
Measurement and Records
Ability and first route
Maintain a repeatable local comparison and an external register of inputs, attempts and failures. This cognitive and practical skill combines reference comparison, counting, observation, notation and decisions based on the result. It is not identical to remembering numbers or acquiring a measuring stick.
Day 29 begins a personal system with Marked Reference Staff, a companion scratched bark slip and comparable rough food portions. No community standard, shared notation or exact SI unit has been established.
Inputs and procedure
Keep the reference staff dry and distinguish its starting end. Use the same end-to-end procedure when comparing a ground line; note slope and imperfect placements rather than silently interpreting the count as a surveyed horizontal distance.
Choose a mark for each specimen or configuration. Record attempts in order, including failures, and distinguish groups before changing a method. A counted cast is an event, not automatically an accurate shot. Preserve a way to recognise the target ground and start position on the next visit.
For reserve comparisons, retain the same rough portion procedure. This can expose a trend without producing a calibrated food mass. Food Reserve Management uses that account to change the work plan.
Acceptance and upkeep
A useful first instance lets the traveller return to a chosen comparison, distinguish two specimens and retain failed attempts alongside successful ones. Check worn marks and warping. Copy a reference by comparison rather than substituting a fresh arm-length stick.
The procedure takes work and can be interrupted. A lost register or broken reference needs an explicit replacement decision; memory can recover observations but cannot supply the original physical unit without reconstruction.
Limits and scaling
Author ledger kilograms and hours are modelling estimates. The traveller does not suddenly measure them accurately because he can count stick placements. Writing, timekeeping, balances, calibrated units and surveying remain distinct developments.
Future shared standards require other people to reproduce the comparison, identify disagreement and accept a convention. The first-month cord counts were informal practice; Days 29 onward record a limited personal system, not those later institutions.
Category boundary
Measuring and recording belong to Skills. A measuring rod is equipment; a shared calibration and standards service would be a separate organised system when it needs reproducible references, agreed procedures, responsibilities and independent checks. No such institution has been established here.

04_skills/observation/environmental-obse.title: Environmental Observation
04_skills/observation/environmental-obse.content:
Environmental Observation
Purpose
Build a local map from repeatable observations. Memory of general ecology cannot identify this valley’s safe routes, owners, weather or food yields.
Method
Start with a short circuit around a known base. Mark the relation between shelter, water, escape routes, exposed ground and useful patches. Observe tracks, wind, drainage and signs of previous use without assuming a single cause.
Return by the same route initially. Extend the circuit when food, daylight and condition allow. Distinguish observation from interpretation: smoke is observed; a maintained human hearth is inferred until confirmed.
For useful patches record location, condition, season and return per trip. For unknown people record behaviour and distance, not guessed motives.
Failure and limits
A familiar path is not necessarily a safe or unowned path. Weather, river rise and fresh animal activity can change the risk. Abandon an excursion before fatigue or darkness removes the return margin.
No distant glimpse provides a full species identification, social structure or language. Local people can supply expertise that cannot be reconstructed from a short survey.

04_skills/observation/retreat-planning.title: Retreat Planning
04_skills/observation/retreat-planning.content:
Retreat Planning
Ability and scope
Judge what can be left behind, recognise an exit and inspect an independently reachable fallback site before an emergency. This reduces particular uncertainties; it does not make an occupied camp defensible against several determined people.
Day 33 demonstrates route reconnaissance and a limited return check. It does not demonstrate a supplied refuge, an emergency shelter or success under pursuit.
Planning with actual resources
Use Valley Map and observations of drainage, footing, visibility and access. Choose a route that does not require an untested main-river crossing. Examine the destination for overhead hazards, exposure, fresh animal sign and the practical distance to water.
Revisit at least part of the route in reverse. A journey that works in daylight with empty hands may fail in darkness, rain or with equipment. Do not infer safety because a site is temporarily empty.
Choose a light essential set from existing possessions: cutting edge, maintained ignition provision, drinking vessel, modest food and accessible defensive spear. Test how those items can be carried with existing pouch, basket or sling. A loaded escape pack requires a real load test; a written list supplies no extra carrying capacity.
Feedback and costs
Recognise where the route slows or disappears. Identify the last place at which an alternative is available. Prefer a known detour over a crossing which might trap the traveller after rain.
Count reconnaissance, retracing and any transported stock as work. A cache must subtract food, fuel or implements from the camp inventory; a second fire kit must be made. No duplication is implicit in the word backup.
Limits and further work
An escape plan cannot predict another group’s intention, conceal every movement or protect all possessions. Retreat can cost food access and leave the traveller exposed at night.
The Day 33 fallback bench has natural wind cover and screened ground, but no built shelter, treated-water provision, cache or permanent permission. Construction, supply, route testing under changed weather and a carrying trial remain future tasks. Planning should influence present decisions without becoming imaginary guaranteed protection.
Day 39 carry-order check
After a warning at an occupied nut patch, the traveller tries lifting the existing essentials and walking through the southeast shelter exit. He identifies bulky assets to abandon and clears one snagging twig. This grants no refuge, cached provisions, second ignition set or protection agreement. The fallback bench remains unsupplied through Day 40. Shortening craft work and avoiding one patch are real costs of the incident, without requiring an attack.
A sight gap is not a defence system — Day 47
After the canid visit, clearing a little loose brush improves the view along the southwest approach while preserving the existing exit route. It is not a stockade, alarm or claim of exclusion. The fallback bench is still unsupplied; no rapid flight can depend on an invented cache. Speaking and holding a spear during one distant investigation did not test resistance to an attack.

04_skills/stoneworking/bifacial-knapping.title: Bifacial Knapping
04_skills/stoneworking/bifacial-knapping.content:
Bifacial Knapping
Goal
Develop the practised ability to shape both faces of a stone while retaining useful edge geometry and thickness. Bifacial working is not synonymous with one historical culture or mandatory progression to every later method.
Hard-hammer route
Choose a suitable blank and inspect platforms. Make controlled removals from alternating faces where scar geometry supports the next removal. Preserve a sound gripping area and avoid thinning past the material’s capabilities.
Compare the result with the intended cutting job. A rough serviceable edge can be a successful first result even without perfect symmetry.
Improvement
A Soft Hammer Billet can support selected thinning techniques. It does not replace platform preparation or practical control. Pressure flaking applies pressure rather than striking; it is a distinct technique.
Failure and limits
Crushed edges, steps, hinges and snapped blanks require diagnosis of material and geometry. Stop when fatigue reduces control. One completed biface does not prove mastery or an automatic productivity increase.
Evidence
R04 supports hard-hammer handaxes and use of organic percussors in selected work. Day 19 records a rough tool and practice losses, not instant progression into a new human developmental stage.

04_skills/stoneworking/flint-knapping-ba.title: Flint Knapping Basics
04_skills/stoneworking/flint-knapping-ba.content:
Flint Knapping Basics
Goal and requirements
Produce usable cutting flakes before attempting a finished symmetrical tool. Use a suitable Hammerstone and Knapping Stone. Clear the work area and keep bare feet away from sharp waste.
Procedure

Inspect the core for a sound edge and a platform from which a removal can travel across the surface.
Support it securely so the intended flake path is clear of the hand and leg.
Strike a controlled point near the edge with a consistent swing. Adjust platform geometry, angle and force together; one universal angle does not cover every core.
Inspect the flake and scar. Keep a useful edge even when the removal differs from the intended shape.
Rotate to a new suitable platform. Stop before repeated crushing wastes the core.

Platform preparation and support affect results. A failed removal is evidence for adjustment, not a guaranteed shortcut to mastery.
Test and errors
Test cutting on an appropriate expendable plant sample, not skin. Crushed platforms, hinged flakes and excessive fragmentation indicate problems with geometry, material or technique. Use shorter practice sessions when hands are tired.
Limits
The traveller has practised basic flaking before departure. He still lacks the local makers’ experience with particular stone. Bifacial Knapping adds shape control; acquiring an antler does not automatically teach pressure flaking.

04_skills/stoneworking/stone-selection.title: Stone Selection
04_skills/stoneworking/stone-selection.content:
Stone Selection
Purpose
Select material for the intended job. Hardness alone does not establish knappability. A tough hammerstone and a stone that produces sharp flakes serve different roles.
Method
Inspect cobbles for grain, weathering, cracks and convenient striking surfaces. Choose a sound rounded percussor that can be controlled without excessive strain. For a core, try small removals at an exposed edge and inspect the resulting fracture.
Prefer samples that yield continuous sharp edges and predictable fractures. Discard heavily cracked or crumbly pieces for this task, while noting other possible uses.
Test and limits
Judge the actual sample, not a presumed species of rock. River transport can leave hidden flaws. Conchoidal fracture does not mean every piece is equally easy to work.
Record where useful material occurs and carry only what the work budget permits. The setting supplies accessible knappable cobbles; it does not supply unlimited high-grade flint.
Use Flint Knapping Basics for controlled removal and Hammerstone for percussor choice.
