05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/basic-ba.title: Basic Bark Clothing
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/basic-ba.content:
Basic Bark Clothing
Purpose
Overlapping bark panels provide limited protection against abrasion, sun and wind while better clothing is unavailable. Rough bark panels are not adequate winter insulation or waterproof clothing.
Method
Use a successful material trial from Barkcloth Processing. Overlap small flexible panels where they can be tied without cutting the skin. Use Simple Cordage for adjustable fastenings.
Test sitting, walking and bending. Round harsh edges, loosen chafing ties and add a small pad where available. Dry and repair material without placing it where sparks can ignite it.
Limits
The opening waist covering leaves the torso and limbs exposed. A later rough shoulder screen reduces some wind but is not a warm fitted cape. A few leaves or strips cannot automatically provide every garment in one session.
Keep work near shelter when weather worsens. Fur-On Pelt Clothing adds limited warmth after usable pelts exist, but also requires preservation and sufficient area.
Evidence
Exact material choice and performance require local trials. No historical claim that this was the universal first clothing is retained.

05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/fur-on-p.title: Fur-On Pelt Clothing
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/fur-on-p.content:
Fur-On Pelt Clothing
Scope
A limited temporary insulating panel made from cleaned pelts is protective equipment with a small coverage area. Drying and mechanical softening do not produce the durability or moisture tolerance of well-prepared leather.
Preparation
Flesh Animal Pelt promptly. Work a small sample to compare drying and flexibility. As the skin loses moisture, flex and draw it over a smooth support without tearing thin areas. A greasy surface is not proof of preservation.
A fully dried untreated skin often stiffens. Re-dampening and working can temporarily soften it but does not guarantee it stays soft through rain. Durable clothing requires further preservation, conditioning and repeated work suited to the material.
Assembly
Use Stitching on sound edges, testing holes and seam tension on a scrap first. Place small panels where they provide actual coverage. A rabbit pelt with small patches is a pelvic pad or narrow waist piece, not whole-core insulation.
Test and maintenance
Check walking, crouching and contact with skin. Dry wet panels carefully and inspect deterioration. Rain, sweat and repeated flexing can shorten useful life.
Narrative
A second rabbit pelt provides the waist panel on Days 13–14. Later a damaged fox pelt provides a narrow shoulder piece, not a fitted protective cape proving high status. Both remain marginal equipment supported by bedding and shelter.
Exact preservation and thermal performance need replication before publication.
Days 38–40: prepare before allocating coverage
The new rabbit pelt is a separate incomplete material lot, not an enlargement of the old fox shoulder panel. A small edge-working comparison begins while moisture is leaving: one area bends more readily for now than an adjacent unworked area. Stop for stretching or tearing, adjust damp folds, and reinspect during drying. This does not establish durable leather or a transferable conditioning recipe.
The Day 40 grass back panel develops Plant-Fibre Clothing independently. The new pelt remains unsewn and unallocated at that cutoff. Sewing it later must choose an actual useful coverage area and account for fastening stock; it cannot also furnish another bag or bed.
One rabbit pelt, one crown covering — Day 50
The separate Day 38 pelt is kept protected and worked in brief sessions; by Day 50 its margins bend in gentle inspection while the centre remains firmer. No durable leather is claimed. The entire pelt is allocated to a shallow fur-out crown pad with folded margins, using about 0.2 m reserved sinew for a few folds and 0.8 m inspected nettle line for a loose band around the forehead/back of the head. The band does not run under the chin or around the throat. Face, ears and much of the nape remain exposed.
A short dry walk, head turn and easy-removal check follows pressure-point adjustment. The piece is not a fitted hood or a waterproof cap; wetting can stiffen untreated skin again. The pelt cannot also supply a bag, footwear or enlarged shoulder panel. The older narrow fox strip stays on the anatomical left shoulder. During Day 50 casting the head piece, grass panels and fox strip are all put aside and recovered afterwards. The authored dimensions, seam and fastening quantities need replication before a transferable pattern is published.

05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.title: Plant-Fibre Clothing
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.content:
Plant-Fibre Clothing
Object, function and scope
Wearable plant coverings form an equipment family: hanging grass panels, broader mantles and later wrapped or plaited variants. Their material and fastening requirements differ. Fine spun cloth, footwear and waterproof clothing are not acquired by making the first coarse screen.
The present base route is a flexible twined grass back panel. Its purpose is to reduce direct airflow over part of the back while leaving the arms free. Plant-Fibre Mats covers bedding and other retained sheets; its stiff willow-foundation pad should not simply be worn as a garment.
Materials and construction route
Select long, clean, flexible dry grass from Dry Plant Insulation. Reject fouled, moulding, sharp or rapidly crumbling material. Keep a separate garment lot; do not count the same bundles in bedding, loose stores and worn equipment. Local grass suitability remains a field trial, not a botanical guarantee.
Arrange small overlapping hanging bundles to the chosen coverage. Practise a short top-edge section before committing to the panel. Twining crosses two working elements between neighbouring bundles. Inspect migration, bundle retention and row spacing as the width develops.
In the first instance, paired lengths of the existing single nettle yarn form light retaining rows. Pairing them in twining does not ply them into certified cord. Inspect and rework weak joins; use separately tested Nettle Cordage for the supported top edge and shoulder attachment. Rounded margins and accessible loose fastenings matter more than neat decoration. Avoid a tight loop around the neck or ties that hinder breathing, arm movement or removal.
Account for grass, working yarn, header and fastenings before construction. Stiff splints, wool, imported fibres and unrecorded pelt panels do not belong to this base route. Bark and pelt clothing are alternatives with their own preparation and coverage limits; a mixed covering must allocate each part explicitly.
Construction and performance checks
Lift and bend the panel before wearing it. Inspect creeping rows, slipping bundles, harsh stalks and loose ends. Check walking, crouching and arm raising in a short dry trial. Rework a pressure point and repeat the movement rather than treating first assembly as acceptance.
Observe covered area and actual handling separately from warmth. A reduction in felt airflow is not a measured insulation rating. Wind penetration through gaps, loft, fit and the remaining exposed body all affect the result. Rain can wet and collapse the material; a dry fit check does not establish weather resistance.
Projectile use needs a separate snag and movement check. Do not assume that a panel harmless during walking will clear the thrower’s sweep. Remove it for wet processing or close fire work if it would be exposed to water, heat or sparks; secure it away from the working area.
First narrative specimen and allocation
Day 39 makes a small separate top-edge sample using 0.05 kg grass and 2 m single yarn. Day 40 makes grass-back-panel-a, about 0.5 by 0.6 m, from another 0.55 kg grass, 12 m single yarn in paired rows and 1.2 m tested nettle cord. These are authored consumption estimates, not an experimentally validated bill of materials or a universal yield.
The panel survives short dry walking, crouching and arm-raise checks after one rubbing end is trimmed. It covers part of the back with an open front. The bark waist covering, rabbit pelvic pad and separate fox shoulder panel remain. The new Day 38 rabbit pelt is not yet incorporated. No head covering, footwear, waterproof cape or whole-core winter outfit is established.
Labour, maintenance and further variants
Day 36 gathers and sorts the grass. Day 39 tests the structure at small scale. Day 40 spends three active hours on construction and fitting, in addition to supplies and other inspections. Harvesting and sorting are not removed by the apparent simplicity of twining.
Air under cover and inspect after use. Repair creeping rows; replace crumbling or wet bundles with newly acquired material. Worn ties consume stock. Keep garments away from sparks and the separate firing area. Damp or compressed material cannot be restored to the usable dry inventory merely by renaming it.
A broader core mantle needs additional grass, fastening stock, construction time and front/side fit checks. Added insulation must be retained without blocking movement or encouraging chafing. A second panel cannot be counted until those materials and work exist. Fine textiles depend on a different supply and construction chain.
Evidence and limits
R23 supports the structure of twining. R26 records later museum examples and the disputed cape interpretation of Ötzi’s grass mat. Neither demonstrates this garment at 40,000 BP in Iberia, specifies the local grass or validates thermal performance. The present back-panel design and short-term result are authored physical trials. Replication must test wear, damp recovery, fastening safety and useful coverage before presenting a dependable field design.
Use through Day 45
The back panel is worn briefly on dry gathering/walking portions. Day 41’s brush snag is freed without a counted tear or new allocation. It is taken off for wet bank work, casting and frame construction so the fringe cannot catch. There is still no wet-weather, prolonged-wear or casting-clearance result, no front panel, head covering or footwear. The rabbit pelt D38 remains unassigned.
Separate front panel and use, Days 46–50
Days 46 and 48 each allocate 9 g ready fibre to about 7 m uneven single yarn after rejection within the portion. Day 49 uses 12 m single yarn, 0.5 kg newly gathered long grass and 1.2 m inspected light cord for a roughly 0.45 by 0.6 m front panel. The supported header sits below the collarbones, with loose accessible shoulder/side adjustment and no tight neck loop. The existing back panel remains a separate object. These are author allocation estimates, not experimentally validated yields.
Lift/bend checks and a short dry walk, crouch and reach expose a rubbing stem and migrating row; adjustment precedes repeat fitting. Together the two pieces screen most of the front/back core, leaving side gaps, upper chest and limbs exposed. Day 50’s dry gathering walk reveals header creep which is corrected with the existing tie. There is still no damp-weather, insulation-rating or casting-clearance result. Remove both pieces for water, fire and projectile work and keep them protected when off. The stiff willow bed pad remains bedding. The later pelt crown piece is separately allocated in Fur-On Pelt Clothing.

05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.title: Plant-Fibre Footwear
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.content:
Plant-Fibre Footwear
Design family and intended use
Coarse plant footwear can separate the sole from some dry ground contact and hold a replaceable insulating layer. The first design is a small flexible bast sole with simple forefoot and heel retention, open toes and no tall upper. It is a short dry-ground trial, without waterproofing, a durable tread or established winter protection.
Boots, closed basket-like uppers and plant soles combined with hide are possible later variants. They need separate material allocations and fit tests. Existing pelt clothing is not a supply of unallocated shoe leather.
Inputs and assembly
Select sound flexible Bast Fibre, tested Bark Cordage and clean Dry Plant Insulation. Use simple over-and-under work from Simple Coiling and Weaving to make a small close flat sole. Fold or return the margins so stiff ends face away from the foot; compare it with the wearer’s foot before closing the edge. The material must bend without opening into large unstable gaps.
Bind the edge and use broad enough, adjustable retention at the forefoot and heel. Keep knots out from under the sole. Avoid a tight ankle ring or a tie that becomes constricting as the foot moves. Thin dry grass is a removable liner, distinct from the load-bearing sole. Excess stuffing can worsen fit and slip.
Fit, ground tests and maintenance
Start beside a support on level dry ground. Check walking, turning, crouching, removal and the position of the heel. Inspect feet for rubbing and bindings for creep. Revise one obvious fit issue before extending the trial.
An inclined, wet or loose surface is a new test. Remove the footwear if it rolls under the foot, loses ground grip or obstructs balance. Inspect the underside for thinning and embedded grit; replace damp liner and dry the sole before reuse. A dry-fit success does not justify hunting, river work or a long escape in it.
First narrative instance
Day 52 allocates a new willow-bast lot to two soles and their bindings, plus a separate dry grass lining. After a heel-retention adjustment, the pair stays in place on a brief level dry walk. One sole creeps during a short incline check, so the trial ends. The pair is kept as experimental dry camp footwear. Day 55’s projectile session remains barefoot.
Evidence and alternatives
R37 records much later shoes combining bast mesh, grass padding and leather. The grass’s replaceable role informs a comparison; the traveller does not possess the source specimen’s hide layers, and its reported performance cannot be transferred to these plant soles. Plant suitability, wear, traction and insulation here remain authored trials needing replication. A future independently supplied hide may support another route after its own preparation and tests.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Bark Container
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Bark Container
Purpose
A modest folded bark vessel carries dry material or, after testing, water. This is an equipment specification with its construction method; capacity and leakage are properties of a particular object.
Procedure
Find a sound pliable sheet of suitable bark. Test a small piece before stripping a large one. Fold a shallow vessel with overlapping corners, make supported fastening holes and bind without splitting the material.
Keep sharp stored flakes separate from the vessel. Any lining or sealant for drinking water needs its own suitability assessment; resin is not a default food-safe coating.
Test
Fill with a small volume and observe leakage on dry ground. Mark the successful level. The first-month vessel is tested around 0.6 L, not assumed to hold six to ten litres.
Heat treatment requires Hot-Rock Boiling and repeated inspection. Loss of the vessel ends that route until repaired or replaced.
Limits
Seams can leak and repeated heating can fatigue bark. A basket improves dry carrying; a sound ceramic pot may later improve some cooking operations. Neither is required to make a first bark vessel.
Historical first dates and guaranteed water independence are omitted.
Deliberate second specimen — Day 54
The old vessel supplies a comparison for worn folds and fastenings. A separately collected birch sheet and fresh coarse line make vessel B; a small marked scrap records a rough fold pattern, adjusted for the sheet’s weak areas. One corner is eased and re-bound after a damp trace in the cold test. B then holds two supported boiling charges at an authored working level around 0.5 L. A remains the original 0.6 L specimen. Both stay at the main camp; two short heat tests do not establish B’s lifetime, a ceramic success or a supplied refuge.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Clay Vessel
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Clay Vessel
A ceramic vessel is a product of Pottery. A shaped unfired pot is greenware, and a cracked fired specimen is not automatically a cooking vessel.
Inspect after complete cooling. Check cracks, water stability and leakage before any intended heat cycling. Food suitability and operating strength require additional verification.
The first-month vessel is formed on Day 11, fired on Day 15 and tested on Day 16. It leaks through a crack and is rejected for cooking and storage of drinking water. Its surviving body remains a non-food experimental specimen. Water treatment continues using the tested bark vessel.
A future sound vessel may reduce handling and offer direct heating, but it remains one route among alternatives. It does not become a compulsory predecessor for wooden spindles or every food-processing method.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.filePath: 05_Tools and Equipment/Containers and Carriers/Rawhide Carrying Sling.md
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Rawhide Carrying Sling
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Rawhide Carrying Sling
Purpose and size
A modest carrying cradle consists of one tested hide panel and a separate strap. One juvenile rabbit pelt provides limited area; it does not also supply long shoulder straps and a garment.
Method
Use Rawhide or a cleaned prepared panel, retaining as much sound area as possible. Fold or gather it into a shallow pocket, pierce supported edge holes with Bone Awl, and lace with Simple Cordage. Add a separate cord strap and distribute tension across several attachment points.
Allow the panel to dry in shape away from scorching heat.
Test
Begin with a small load. Increase gradually while inspecting tearing, creep and strap pressure. In the narrative the initial trial stays below a kilogram; later loads remain conservative. Bulk nut harvests use repeated trips and a bark carrier until a basket is made.
Limits
Keep away from hot stones and embers. Damp hide is not a safe high-temperature carrier. It can stretch or weaken when wet and become rigid again when dry.
Repair has a material cost. A bigger hide, woven strap or basket offers an alternative when the carrying requirement grows.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Rawhide Pouch
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Rawhide Pouch
Product and purpose
A small dry-storage case made from available Rawhide protects light implements. The first squirrel pelt yields a tool case, not a food sack.
Procedure
Inspect usable area and choose a fold that preserves it. Damp only what must bend. Use Bone Awl to open holes sufficiently far from edges, then guide a fine tested line by hand or through an eyed needle.
Fold and lace the sides, leaving a simple closure. Do not overtighten so that shrinking skin or thread cuts the holes. Dry around a modest temporary form that can be removed.
Test and maintenance
Load with a light blunt sample before delicate implements. Inspect holes and closure. Wrap sharp flakes separately so their edges do not slice the case.
Keep dry and check damp folds. The first-month case is a small asset made on Day 8, not a permanently unlocked possession.
Alternatives
A tied bark packet or other folded container can protect small objects without sewing. An eyed Bone Needle improves some operations but is not a necessary first route.
No universal lifespan or water-tightness is promised.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.filePath: 05_Tools and Equipment/Containers and Carriers/Woven Foraging Basket.md
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Woven Foraging Basket
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Woven Foraging Basket
Object
A small basket made with tested flexible uprights and woven strands. A stitched coiled basket is another route, not the required same construction.
Manufacture
Use Simple Coiling and Weaving to form a supported crossed base, introduce uprights, weave the walls and secure the rim. Splice material before it becomes too short; avoid sharp ends in the carrying surface.
Test
Load the base lightly, then inspect joining, rim and carrying points. Increase only while it holds shape and strands remain seated. The first-month object receives a conservative load trial rather than an assumed multi-kilogram capacity.
Maintenance and limits
Dry after wet use, repair worn material and protect it from crushing. Ventilation can reduce some moisture accumulation but does not prevent mould in wet food.
Historical first dates, universal recognition and fixed productivity multipliers are omitted pending evidence. Capacity helps collection only when resources, processing and carrying time remain available.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/ach.title: Acheulean Hand Axe
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/ach.content:
Acheulean Hand Axe
Object and role
A bifacially worked stone with a usable edge and a graspable area. The name is historical; the first month’s rough biface does not make the traveller enter a new era.
Manufacture
Use Bifacial Knapping with suitable stone and controlled removals from both faces. A hard hammer can make a rough example. A Soft Hammer Billet is an option for selected thinning work, not an absolute gate.
Preserve sound platform geometry and useful thickness. Do not pursue perfect symmetry at the cost of a broken tool when an adequate edge serves the task.
Test and limits
Test on a modest cutting job and inspect the handhold, edge and fracture. A finished-looking shape does not prove it outperforms a flake. It is not automatically a powerful wood axe, needle drill or precision antler saw.
No game damage statistic or universal butchery improvement is assigned.
Evidence
R04 supports hard-hammer manufacture. Local specialists may already produce more suitable tools; compare their use rather than assuming a design’s modern remembered name establishes superiority.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/haf.title: Hafted Knife
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/haf.content:
Hafted Knife
Object
A cutting flake held in a handle that leaves a useful edge exposed. The handle improves grip in some jobs, but transfers new stresses into the stone and joint.
Assembly
Use Simple Hafting. Choose a blade with a suitable base and a handle seat that supports it without concentrating stress on a thin edge. Bind mechanically; a tested adhesive is optional.
Leave binding away from the cutting path. Allow any adhesive to cool and any wet binding to settle before applying load.
Test
Begin with light controlled cuts in expendable material. Inspect blade movement, binding creep and cracks. Increase the task gradually; do not use shoulder force to pry a delicate flake through seasoned oak.
Maintenance
Clean after use, inspect the joint and renew damaged bindings. Replace the blade if needed. Modularity reduces replacement cost only when replacement parts fit and their performance is tested.
The first-month knife passes modest fibre and thin-wood work, not every imagined high-load task.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.title: Oldowan Knife Flake
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.content:
Oldowan Knife Flake
Object
An unhafted stone flake with a useful cutting edge. The historical name describes a simple form; the traveller is not living through the Oldowan period.
Manufacture and selection
Use Flint Knapping Basics. Select a flake with a sound continuous edge and a surface that can be held securely. Remove or protect an uncomfortable projection only if doing so does not destroy the useful edge.
Use and test
Test on plant material, then use controlled slices for fibre, thin bark or butchery. Support the work so a slip cannot drive the edge into the body. Do not test on a thumb.
Maintenance and limits
Edges chip and dull. Replace or carefully retouch when required. A hand-held flake remains useful alongside Hafted Knife; hafting does not make every cutting task easier.
The ledger treats the working flake cache as replenished consumable tools rather than an exact count of all flakes struck.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.title: Oldowan Scraper
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.content:
Oldowan Scraper
Object
A selected flake with an edge suited to controlled scraping. An edge for thin hide may differ from an edge for wood. Retouch is an option, not proof of a dedicated historical type.
Manufacture and use
Choose a sound blank from Flint Knapping Basics. If needed, make controlled small removals to produce a robust working edge. Support the work and keep the hand clear of a slip.
For hides, begin on a scrap or low-value edge with modest pressure. A sharp cutting edge can damage thin skin; a supported blunt scraping edge may be preferable for fleshing.
Test and maintenance
Inspect the removed material and substrate. Stop if the tool gouges, tears or only polishes the surface. Remove sharp waste and keep food-processing uses separate from dirty hide work.
Limits
One scraper is not ideal for every material. Continuous edge maintenance and user practice matter more than a nominal technological age.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.title: Oldowan Simple Chopper
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.content:
Oldowan Simple Chopper
Object
A core or cobble with a robust worked edge for limited chopping and rough shaping. It is heavier than a flake and can be less efficient for fine cuts.
Manufacture
Use Flint Knapping Basics to remove flakes from selected edges, leaving enough mass and a safe grip. Compare the intended task with a simple unmodified stone or sharp flake before investing more work.
Use and test
Support thin wood on a stable surface, make controlled strikes and inspect the edge. Do not use a brittle chopper as a universal axe for felling large trees or as a fine percussor on another core.
Maintenance and limits
Rework or replace a damaged edge. The tool can provide coarse shaping but does not supply the reach, load path or productivity of a later tested hafted woodworking tool.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.title: Bone Awl
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.content:
Bone Awl
Object and manufacture
A pointed bone implement for opening supported holes. Choose a suitable blank from Bone, score or split conservatively, and scrape and abrade a tapered point with Oldowan Knife Flake and a suitable abrasive surface.
An awl does not require an eye. A failed needle blank can become an awl if the shaft remains sound.
Test and use
Try a scrap panel supported on a safe surface. Rotate or press with control, stopping before the blank bends or splits. Keep the off-hand outside the point’s exit path. Use a thicker point for tougher material and a finer one only where it survives.
Limits
An awl hole still needs suitable spacing and thread. It does not make every rawhide panel strong. The Day 7 awl enables small hand-laced work while the eyed needle remains unfinished.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.title: Bone Needle
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.content:
Bone Needle
Object
A slender worked bone implement with a usable eye. It is a more demanding object than a pointed awl and is not necessary for every early sewn container.
Manufacture
Select a cortical blank with adequate width and thickness for an eye. Score and split carefully where appropriate, then scrape and abrade the shaft. Keep the point suited to the intended material rather than making a fragile needle-thin spike.
Work the eye gradually from opposite sides with a suitable fine stone point and abrasive. Leave enough tissue around it to resist cracking. Polish surfaces that contact thread.
Test and failure
Pass a fine test thread through the eye, inspect abrasion, and sew a scrap with pre-made awl holes. A cracked eye is a failed needle even if the shaft can become an awl.
The first attempt on Day 7 fails at the eye; a usable needle is made on Day 12. No guaranteed first-needle time or rare-breakage claim is retained.
Limits and evidence
A small animal’s bone may not supply a suitable blank. A Bone Awl and threaded hand seam remain an alternative. Exact manufacturing times and durability require replication.
R28 in Research Register compares early eyed needles in Siberia with later preserved European examples and explains sewing with awls. Day 12 is the traveller’s authored experiment, not evidence for an eyed needle in this local group’s kit. See Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/p.title: Plant-Fibre Mats
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/p.content:
Plant-Fibre Mats
Design family and uses
Coarse sheets made from suitable plant foundations and working elements can organise bedding, cover ground or form an outer screen. Twined, plaited and other structures have different controls. The first narrative route is a small twined bedding pad; larger mats and wearable forms are prospective variants.
A mat’s form makes it equipment. Twining supplies one practised technique; Dry Plant Insulation supplies retained loft. A sheet which keeps leaves together is not automatically warm, comfortable, waterproof or suitable clothing.
Base route: small twined bedding pad
Inspect Split Wood Strips for sharp ends and splits. Arrange sound foundations across the chosen size and use paired portions of tested light nettle cord to retain them in spaced rows. Work gradually, checking earlier crossings and the edges against the small sample.
Spread dry grass and leaves into the open structure while keeping a loose layer between the body and stiff foundations. Preserve access for replacing filling. Record strip, line and insulation allocations; the same stock cannot also furnish a cloak or escape bed.
Variants and separate tests
A larger bedding mat requires more material and construction time, along with ground fit and drying checks. A loose covering mat may need different gaps and edges. A wearable panel needs softer materials, mobility, chafing, snagging, wind and damp-weather tests; it is not made by simply calling the bedding pad a mantle.
Plaiting is an alternative with its own material flexibility and edge controls. Fine spun cloth and netting are different constructions, not automatically acquired by twining a sample.
Operation and maintenance
Lay bedding variants on the existing dry resting layer, away from sparks. Try a brief rest before relying on a whole night. Inspect pressure points, sharp protrusions, migrating filling and margins which unravel.
Lift, air and replace wet or flattened material. Remove failed foundations rather than concealing their edges. Loose refreshed bedding is the fallback if the frame becomes uncomfortable.
Current narrative instance
Day 32 makes a small twining sample. Day 35 completes only a roughly 0.4 by 0.5 m pad covering part of the upper-body contact area, with a brief rest and lift trial. Its strip and insulation lots are allocated; it is not a full mattress or a worn garment. The asset bedding-pad-a remains the specific object identifier.
Evidence and limits
R23 supports the twining structure and R24 earlier plant bedding elsewhere. The local willow-strip/nettle-line combination is an authored trial, not an excavated Iberian mat design or an insulation rating. A mat cannot by itself solve a leaking roof, wet ground or incomplete body coverage.
Clothing remains a separate design family
Days 39–40 develop Plant-Fibre Clothing from soft hanging grass foundations, light paired yarn rows and a separately supported upper edge. The bedding pad stays on the bed with its stiff willow foundations and allocated filling. Sharing twining does not make the first pad a ready-made mantle; garment fit and movement require different checks.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/s.title: Spindle Whorl
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/s.content:
Spindle Whorl
Object
A weight fitted securely to a spindle shaft. It helps maintain rotation while prepared fibre is drafted into yarn. The whorl is a component; a shaft alone can also be used with different handling.
First-month wooden route
Cut or select a balanced small wooden disc. Make a central hole by controlled piercing, scraping and abrasion with appropriate stone or bone tools. Fit the shaft without splitting the disc and without an off-centre wobble. Test rotation before attaching fibre.
Wood avoids a ceramic-firing requirement. The traveller makes a working wooden version on Day 21, loses it during the rebuffed approach on Day 25, and makes a replacement on Day 27.
Fibre and testing
Start with clean aligned fibre, attach a leader and draft a small section while controlling twist. Wind the finished yarn. For a strong line, ply appropriate singles rather than treating fine single yarn as finished cordage.
Alternative and limits
A clay disc can be formed, dried and fired through Pottery, then checked for fit and balance. It is not intrinsically the fastest or most reliable first route.
Total output still depends on harvesting, fibre preparation, drafting skill, winding and plying. No tenfold productivity claim or lithic-mode label is assigned.
Replacement spindle and light retaining yarn — Days 46 and 48
The Day 27 wooden replacement is used for two short sessions of turning, drafting, inspecting joins and winding. Each session credits about 7 m uneven single yarn from a separately allocated 9 g prepared-fibre portion, with rejects included. The output retains light grass bundles in twining; it is not certified cord or a measured productivity improvement. The three-dimensional whorl remains securely on its shaft; yarn is wound onto the shaft rather than made by twisting the disc in a flat horizontal circle.

05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/fi.title: Fireboard
05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/fi.content:
Fireboard
Object
A hearth board for friction ignition with a stable spindle socket and dust-collecting notch. Choose dry identified material compatible with the spindle, not merely any wood called softwood.
Manufacture
Use Oldowan Knife Flake to flatten a suitable natural piece and form a shallow initial socket. Establish the socket with controlled rotation. Cut a notch that admits air and allows hot dust to collect on a dry catcher while preserving socket support.
Test and maintenance
Use Bow Drill Fire or a separately tested Hand Drill Fire kit. Inspect socket depth, glazed surfaces, loose dust and scorching. Relocate a worn socket only where enough sound board remains.
Limits
A damp board or unsuitable pairing can fail despite correct posture. A dry-looking exterior is not proof of a dry interior. Keep a reserve kit protected from rain.
Making the board on Day 2 prepares ignition; a sustained ember and usable fire are later demonstrations.
Second board — Day 53
Day 51’s Wooden Splitting Wedge and Wooden Mallet produce a rough willow blank. Day 53 flattens it and adds a sound socket and dust notch; a full new kit then passes one dry ignition trial. Fireboard B belongs to kit B and is not counted as another independent kit. The splitting route is a useful alternative stock preparation method, not a new universal prerequisite for hearth boards.

05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/he.title: Heating Stones
05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/he.content:
Heating Stones
Selected reusable heating stones are heat-transfer equipment. They transfer energy from an outside fire to water in a suitable vessel. Select sound, dry, dense specimens through Stone Selection. Wet river pebbles, porous material and cracked pieces are poor default choices. Even screened stones can fracture on heating or immersion.
Heat away from faces and bystanders. Handle with tested green-wood tongs or another suitable implement, and place rather than drop into the vessel. Replace a cracking specimen and keep fragments out of food.
Camp Fire and fuel supply determine the available heat; stone size, temperature and water quantity determine transfer. Two stones or twenty minutes cannot be a universal boiling recipe.
Use Hot-Rock Boiling for the complete process. Heated material is a temporary state, not an indefinitely stored resource.

05_tools-and-equipment/measuring-equipme.title: Marked Reference Staff
05_tools-and-equipment/measuring-equipme.content:
Marked Reference Staff
Object and scope
A straight, marked stick provides a repeatable local length. It does not realise a metre, measure mass or establish a community standard. Day 29’s staff is an author-chosen first reference for comparing range positions, shafts and small samples.
Making and checking the reference
Select sound dry Wood with a straight edge. Trim protrusions with Oldowan Knife Flake, round the ends and distinguish one end with a notch. Choose the usable length before adding subdivisions. Transfer equal subdivisions by repeated comparison or temporarily folding an existing line; do not assume equal-looking marks are equal. Keep the chosen master when the subdivisions are imperfect.
A companion bark slip can hold simple grouped scratches. Distinguish the reference length from the number of times it is laid along the ground. Label an experiment by a mark the traveller can recognise, rather than treating scratches as a shared writing system.
Check for warping and damaged ends against the original marks. Make a second reference only by comparison with the first. Replacing a staff with an unrelated arm-length stick quietly changes the unit.
Operation, maintenance and limits
Lay the staff end to end along an accessible line, count placements and note gaps or slope. This measures the chosen route or ground line, not an exact horizontal distance. For a target comparison, retain the same start position and procedure.
Store the master dry at the camp’s craft spot. The staff is not the traveller’s spear or a fuel billet. A carried copy would need its own construction and check; none exists on Day 29.
Measurement and Records combines the object, counting procedure and experiment register. Precise equal subdivisions, surveying, weights and independent reproduction remain further work. The author’s kilograms, metres and hours remain modelling estimates rather than quantities this staff suddenly lets the traveller measure.

05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/atlat.title: Atlatl Dart
05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/atlat.content:
Atlatl Dart
Design family and scope
An atlatl dart is a projectile matched to a spear thrower through its shaft, rear engagement, mass distribution and flight behaviour. Blunt practice, fletched and pointed forms are variants on this page. The former Practice Dart and Dart Making pages are incorporated here.
Construction is distinct from Atlatl Throwing and Projectile Testing. A blunt dart can still injure. A hunting point does not compensate for unreliable release.
Base route: blunt unfletched trial
Select a candidate from Dart Shafts and use Oldowan Knife Flake or an appropriate existing edge. Examine grain defects, knots, straightness and changing moisture condition. Compare gentle flex and recovery without inventing a certified strength.
Support and ventilate the blank while monitoring distortion. No number of drying days guarantees suitability. Day 30’s local green hazel candidate is accepted only as an expendable, cautiously tested specimen; it has not become seasoned.
Round the front and shape a conservative rear seat for the real Atlatl hook. Preserve sound end grain, avoid a deep wedging hollow, and remove projecting fragments. Try slow seating and disengagement before a modest launch. Convert the blank into one dart in the asset record; do not retain the consumed shaft as a second object.
Variants and added dependencies






























VariantPurposeAdditional work and acceptanceBlunt unfletchedDiagnose engagement and basic flightRepeated controlled trials; absence of a point does not establish safetyFletchedInvestigate stabilisationSuitable Flight Feathers, alignment, fastening, mass and flight checksIntegral wooden pointA possible field-use routeSound shaping, point durability and whole-system testsSeparate hunting pointDifferent cutting/penetrating formActual point material/component, supported joint via Simple Hafting, binding allocation and dynamic tests
Feathers and an added point are not universal prerequisites. Their presence can change the same dart’s state; fitting them does not automatically manufacture another projectile. A foreshaft or composite shaft is a further variant with its own joints, not an acquired feature of the opening design.
Inspection, performance and labour
Use a cleared and rechecked site; Projectile Practice Ground records the local example. Inspect shaft, rear seat and fittings after early casts, damp weather and storage. Stop for spreading splits, unstable seating or unreliable release. Record failed attempts alongside successful ones.
Compare whole sequences and change one significant factor at a time where possible. A green specimen is changing as it dries, so improvement cannot all be attributed to technique. Gathering, shaping, conditioning, fastening, inspection and retrieval count as work.
Current narrative instance
Day 30 completes one green, blunt, unfletched dart from shaft A and makes three hand casts and three erratic thrower attempts. Day 35 retains it after another short session, noting rear-seat compression and inconsistent landings. Shaft B is still a separate bowed blank. The feather lot is unused; no hunting point or adhesive has been allocated.
The asset key practice-dart-a is retained to identify that specimen. It is not the canonical page title or a promise of a separate hunting-dart article.
Maintenance, alternatives and evidence
Keep the dart supported under ventilated cover. Reinspect before reuse; a second blank needs its own preparation. Loss or damage must reduce inventory. Pointed/fletched variants require new work and relevant stock.
R22 supports examining release and engagement, not a universal recipe for green hazel, a learning rate or reliable hunting range. Tracking, approach, useful field accuracy and recovery remain separate capabilities. The existing plate shows candidate stock and a blunt trial-end detail; it makes no claim that later variants have been built.
Days 36–40: retain one experimental specimen
Day 36 removes only a raised loose projection at the compressed rear seat; slow disengagement improves. It does not deepen the seat, change the hook or fit a point. Day 37’s four modest casts include two broad-bank landings and two misses. The seat survives inspection without a new opening split. A local adult’s own hand-thrown stone-pointed spear visibly outperforms the traveller’s system, but different users, heads and masses prevent a controlled energy comparison.
Through Day 40, practice-dart-a remains blunt, unfletched and changing as it dries. Candidate B is still a bowed blank. Feathers, pitch and sinew are unallocated to projectiles. The new grass back panel has no casting-clearance trial; it must not appear as proven throwing clothing.
Day 42 private trial
Four modest casts include two broad-patch landings and two misses. The rear seat survives inspection without a spreading split. The traveller stops as timing deteriorates with fatigue. There is no new dart, point, fletching, measured range or reliable improvement; specimen A remains green, blunt and unfletched through Day 45.
No hunting configuration is inferred — Days 48–50
Day 48 leaves the green blunt unfletched practice dart at camp and attempts an approach with the existing wooden-pointed hand spear. Day 50 gives that same practice dart four short private casts: three reach the broad bank patch and one misses. The rear seat is intact on inspection. This small unsupervised result is not a local comparison, reliable hunting projectile, second dart or demonstrated accuracy improvement.
Repeat series and observer interest — Day 55
The same blunt unfletched dart survives inspection and eight modest casts from a familiar starting place. The first is low; seven reach the broad chosen bank patch, with closer grouping than the scattered opening trials. These two short series supply a useful own-baseline observation, not a calibrated range, energy, hunting or local-expert comparison. Wood is changing as it dries. Two adults watch and one gestures towards the engagement; no handover, instruction or independent use occurs. Bowed B and the feather lot remain separate unfinished inputs.

05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/index.title: Projectiles
05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/index.content:
Projectiles
Equipment pages are organised by design family. Variants with the same basic mechanism live within the family page.

Atlatl Dart — blunt practice, fletched and pointed configurations, with the current green trial specimen clearly distinguished.
Atlatl — the launcher, including its own construction routes.
Fire-Hardened Spear — a separate spear family that may be thrust or thrown; it remains under Weapons.
Barbed Harpoon Point — a component with its own design and attachment questions.

Dart Shafts describes intermediate stock. Atlatl Throwing and Projectile Testing describe abilities. These are different questions from the finished projectile’s design, rather than competing projectile pages.
Arrow and other families can be added when their distinct requirements matter. No empty hunting-dart or practice-dart capability pages are needed merely to name use variants.

05_tools-and-equipment/stoneworking/hamm.title: Hammerstone
05_tools-and-equipment/stoneworking/hamm.content:
Hammerstone
Object and selection
A hammerstone is a sound stone used as a controlled percussor. Select through Stone Selection, matching mass, grip and surface to the intended core. A very heavy stone is not automatically useful for fine work.
Preparation and use
No shaped cutting tool is required to collect an appropriate cobble. Inspect cracks and sharp projections, then make small controlled trials. Use Flint Knapping Basics with a secure support and a clear flake path.
Test and maintenance
Inspect after impacts for spalling and new sharp edges. Rotate or replace a damaged contact surface. Keep the percussor away from bare feet and stored delicate tools.
Limits
A material suitable as a hammer may be poor as a core. The first-month hammerstone is a chosen natural object, not a technological invention requiring a prior tool to manufacture it.

05_tools-and-equipment/stoneworking/soft.title: Soft Hammer Billet
05_tools-and-equipment/stoneworking/soft.content:
Soft Hammer Billet
Object
A percussor of sound antler, bone or suitable wood for particular knapping removals. The narrative first uses an old red-deer antler section.
Manufacture
Select a section whose existing dimensions can serve. Scrape or abrade sharp damaged ends and inspect cracks. Shape only what is necessary; antler is not easily chopped like a green twig. A grip wrap is optional and belongs around the handhold, not the striking surface.
Use and test
Trial with Bifacial Knapping. Compare platform preparation, flake shape and consistency with hard-hammer work. Contact geometry and technique still govern the removal.
Limits
The billet does not automatically unlock pressure flaking, perfect symmetry or every prepared-core method. Bone, antler and wood are not mechanically identical. Replace unsuitable material or choose another technique rather than declaring technological progress lost.
Evidence
R04 discusses organic percussors alongside hard-hammer work. The traveller’s specific tool and results remain authored trials.

05_tools-and-equipment/toolkits/oldowan-.title: Oldowan Toolkit
05_tools-and-equipment/toolkits/oldowan-.content:
Oldowan Toolkit
Scope
A task-oriented equipment collection combines a selected hammerstone, cutting flakes and optional scraper or robust core edge. The historical label describes simple techniques, not the traveller’s date or intelligence.
Assembly
Use Flint Knapping Basics to produce a small working set. Choose tools for tasks rather than a compulsory quota: a sharp flake for slicing, a supported scraping edge for hide or wood, and a heavier implement only where it helps.
Test and upkeep
Inspect edges, handholds and storage. Replenish expendable flakes and keep sharp waste in a defined place. Food and dirty hide work should use cleanly separated surfaces and implements.
Limits
A toolkit is a combination, not a prerequisite for every component from which it is assembled. Bifacial Knapping and Simple Hafting provide optional routes when the job warrants them.
No claim is made that acquiring this set establishes permanent skill or that every later invention must pass through a formally named era.

05_tools-and-equipment/traps/figure-4-de.title: Figure-4 Deadfall Trap
05_tools-and-equipment/traps/figure-4-de.content:
Figure-4 Deadfall Trap
Mechanism
Three fitted sticks hold a crushing weight under a friction lock. Disturbing the trigger can release the weight. A functioning mechanism is not proof of an appropriate or humane animal trap.
Construction framework
Use Wood and Oldowan Knife Flake to make a supported upright, a diagonal member and a bait member with matching bearing notches. The assembled parts should support a stable weight without hand pressure remaining in the fall path.
Trial the mechanism unloaded, then with a modest test weight and a long remote release. Inspect how it releases and whether the falling weight is guided. Keep hands outside the drop zone; brace during setup.
A construction drawing and experimental replication are still needed before publication as a complete field recipe.
Placement and upkeep
Use Tracking to select a limited trial location. Weather, bait, competing animals and false triggers affect outcomes. Inspect regularly and account for resetting labour.
Limits
The first month’s catches are authored events, not a success probability. A trap that works while unattended still consumes collection, construction, inspection and processing time.
No fixed twenty-minute build, free calories or high-fat yield is assumed.
Day 38 upkeep
One existing trial supplies a small rabbit catch. After collection the bearing surface is inspected and cleaned while the weight is braced. A remote non-animal release check uses a long selected branch with the operator outside the fall path, followed by reset. This is maintenance of deadfall-b, not a fourth installation or a snare replacement. The retained edible meat is cooked and eaten that day; pelt preparation adds its own labour.

05_tools-and-equipment/traps/snare-trap.title: Snare Trap
05_tools-and-equipment/traps/snare-trap.content:
Snare Trap
Scope
A line loop restrains an animal; a spring variant adds a tensioned sapling and a trigger. These are separate mechanisms with separate failure risks. The first-month spring snare is an experimental object, not a guaranteed food engine.
Requirements and trial
Use a sound line from Simple Cordage, an appropriate anchor and selected Wood. Inspect the line in wet and dry condition. The illustrated fixed eye is an overhand loop tied on a bight: double the cord end and tie the doubled section into an overhand knot, leaving a small terminal eye and a visible short tail. It is one continuous cord, not a separate ring. The overhand loop can jam and is not assumed suitable for every fibre or load; test the actual line.
To form the adjustable loop, return the long standing part through that fixed eye. The eye stays fixed while the returned line slides. Neither a fixed bowline nor the illustrated overhand loop is a tightening noose by itself. See Research Register.
Trial loop movement and trigger release separately with expendable loads. Keep the spring and line away from eyes and hands during release. Confirm that the anchor holds and that loading does not cut the cord.
Placement and limits
Tracking improves placement but cannot guarantee species or catch. A spring is not assumed capable of lifting a five-kilogram animal because it resists a hand pull. Suspension does not automatically protect a catch from predators or produce an instant clean kill.
Inspect frequently and record escapes, non-target catches, line damage and contamination. A full construction and operating protocol requires experimental and animal-welfare review before publication.
Narrative
Day 22 installs one trial. Day 23 finds a damaged fox catch, recovers a limited dressed meat lot for immediate cooking and retains a damaged skin for a narrow panel. The gain is real, but dispatch and cleaning cost time, and the broken snare leaves service. Neither the capture nor the plate establishes dependable yield.

05_tools-and-equipment/traps/woven-fishi.title: Woven Fishing Trap
05_tools-and-equipment/traps/woven-fishi.content:
Woven Fishing Trap
Object and status
A small woven cage with an inward-facing funnel and a means to retrieve a catch. An anchored cage and a weir spanning a river are different systems.
Manufacture
Build sound uprights and weave a body with spacing appropriate to the intended catch. Make a separate inward cone, connect it securely and leave an access closure. Inspect for sharp ends and escape gaps.
Test and installation
Test shape and retrieval in shallow safe water, then anchor conservatively where conditions permit. A funnel narrows the exit but does not make escape impossible. Bait, placement and species behaviour affect results.
The narrative begins a trial on Day 20 and finds one small fish on Day 22. That single catch does not prove dependable passive subsistence.
Limits
Inspection, repair, changing flow and retrieval require labour. Floods and trapped animals can damage the cage. No 30,000 BP first date, Mode 0 label or guaranteed respect is retained.
Learning from local fishers and confirming resource access may improve the method more than simply making a larger trap.
Days 36 and 40: closure revision
Day 36 finds a side lift at the rear retrieval cap and a worn tie. The traveller retains the cylinder, inward funnel, anchor and river-margin location. A light collar uses four cumulative metres of newly selected flexible willow withes; 0.8 m of loose nettle cord supplies the new cap tie. Discarded worn binding is not credited as usable stock. Opening, reseating and shallow retrieval checks precede reset.
Day 40 retrieves one small catch through that cap and finds it reseats without the earlier side lift. This confirms a further handling cycle, not the repair’s causal effect on catch rate. Check closure gaps while holding the body in its actual wet shape. Changing funnel, body spacing and location simultaneously would hide what the repair answered. No weir, enlarged trap or dependable fish ration is established.

05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/atlatl.title: Atlatl
05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/atlatl.content:
Atlatl
Object and common design
A spear thrower engages the rear of a matched Atlatl Dart and extends the effective throwing motion. It is a launcher, not an arbitrary heavy-spear attachment or a guarantee of power and accuracy.
This design-family page includes construction, variants, use and maintenance. The former Atlatl Assembly page is incorporated here; making the object and learning Atlatl Throwing remain different achievements.
Base construction: integral wooden hook
Select sound Wood with grain that permits a grip and a supported projecting spur. The first route uses an older fallen branch with a suitable fork. Remove decay and unsuitable pieces before shaping with Oldowan Knife Flake or an appropriate existing edge.
Mark the grain and remove small amounts while retaining enough wood behind the spur. Round the grip without making it slippery. The first object uses a short bark grip wrap, but a wrap is optional handling equipment rather than a cure for a weak hook.
Fit the rear engagement to the actual dart. Try slow seating and disengagement before any launch. Inspect for wedging, sideways loading, cracks and a spur which cuts across fragile grain. Static fit does not certify launch loading.
Variants and additional requirements
An attached antler spur needs a sound shaped component, suitable seating and separately tested fastening through Simple Hafting. It is an alternative route, not a mandatory historical stage. The traveller’s antler billet is not automatically consumed.
Grip shapes and bindings can vary. A balance weight changes inertia and handling and must earn its place in tests; it does not inherently improve performance. Adjusting hook geometry, dart engagement and movement together makes diagnosis harder.
Operation and checks
Use an inspected dart at a selected, rechecked practice site. Projectile Testing defines observation and stop conditions; Atlatl Throwing develops the coordinated movement. Inspect the grip, spur, nock and projectile after early attempts and after storage or wet weather.
Record release, landings and damage separately. A successful target cast does not establish hunting accuracy, penetration or safe recovery of wounded quarry. Experienced local hand throwers may still outperform the traveller.
Narrative instance and maintenance
Day 28 completes the integral-hook object and checks static fit. Days 30 and 35 attempt short launches with one green blunt unfletched dart. Release remains erratic; the hook survives the recorded inspections. The first recorded date is construction, not operational mastery.
Protect the grain and grip under ventilated cover. Recheck a repaired or changing assembly before use. Lost, broken or replaced components need inventory events.
Evidence and limits
R16 places direct European spear-thrower evidence much later than this setting; unfamiliarity here remains an authored possibility, not proven absence. R17 supports taking practised hand throwing seriously. R22 informs engagement and movement problems through modern coaching. None validates this local specimen or makes the device an inevitable route to a bow.
The retained object plate depicts the assembled pre-launch form. The construction plate below is a historical explanatory view, not a second acquired thrower.

05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/barbed-ha.title: Barbed Harpoon Point
05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/barbed-ha.content:
Barbed Harpoon Point
Status and purpose
A planned detachable or attached point with barbs intended to retain an aquatic catch. Its existence in the reference library does not mean the traveller has made one.
Requirements and manufacture framework
Select sound bone or antler of suitable dimensions. Score, scrape and abrade a blank, preserving strength around each barb. Prepare a shaft seat and line attachment appropriate to the design.
Required tests
Check barb strength, joint retention, line security, buoyancy and retrieval on expendable targets before animal use. Record whether the design stays attached or detaches; these are different mechanisms.
Limits
The line, shaft, point, connection and user’s technique form one system. A beautiful barbed point does not establish effective fishing. Species, water depth and entanglement risk matter.
Precise dimensions, local historical evidence and experimental performance remain open. No acquisition or first-month use is assigned.

05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/fire-hard.title: Fire-Hardened Spear
05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/fire-hard.content:
Fire-Hardened Spear
Object and naming
A sharpened wooden spear. The legacy name is retained, but fire treatment is optional and is not assumed to make every point stronger.
Manufacture
Select a sound straight shaft that can be handled safely. Use Oldowan Knife Flake and scraping to shape a gradual point without removing unnecessary supporting wood. Smooth the grip.
The first-month spear is sharpened and dried carefully. No prolonged charring to glass-hard condition is required.
Test and use
Test the point on an expendable plant target and inspect splitting and bending. The tool may aid a controlled shallow-water trial; it does not prove competence at hunting deer or defending against a large predator.
Maintenance and evidence
Inspect after impact or soaking. Repair material loss rather than repeatedly burning the same point. R05 distinguishes hardness from strength and found damaging effects under the treatment tested.
A thrown dart for an Atlatl is a different design. It needs appropriate length, flexibility and a system test.

05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/multi-pro.title: Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear
05_tools-and-equipment/weapons/multi-pro.content:
Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear
Object and status
A draft design with several spread points for shallow-water work. It has not been made in the revised first month.
Base method
Select a sound wooden shaft with enough thickness at the tip. Make controlled longitudinal splits, stopping them with an appropriate binding below the split. Insert small spacers, spread conservatively and shape the points.
This method needs Wood, a cutting edge and Simple Cordage. It does not require an antler billet, handaxe, sinew or microliths. Separate attached bone points are an alternative design.
Test
Inspect for cracks below the binding and for movement of the spacers. Trial against a non-living target in clear shallow water; avoid forcing points into rocks. Points that spread too far can bend and fail.
Limits
Use Basic Spear Fishing for aim and footing. Refraction requires a correction below the apparent position, not a universal behind-the-fish rule.
Historical attestation and operating performance remain research questions; no absolute claim about all early Upper Palaeolithic groups is made.

05_tools-and-equipment/working-tools/dig.title: Digging Stick
05_tools-and-equipment/working-tools/dig.content:
Digging Stick
Object
A sturdy wooden lever or digging implement with a broad bevelled end. A natural sound branch can provide the first version without a dedicated axe.
Manufacture and test
Select a manageable piece with sound grain. Shape the end through controlled cutting and scraping, keeping adequate thickness for the expected load. Smooth the grip and test in loose soil before working harder ground.
Fire treatment is optional and needs testing; slight surface hardness is not equivalent to improved fracture resistance.
Uses and limits
Use to expose an identified food part, sample a stable bank or lift light loose material. Identifying a root remains separate from digging it. Do not undermine riverbanks or lever dangerously large rocks.
Inspect cracks after use. An unproductive digging attempt still costs time and energy. R05 supplies a caution about assuming universal benefit from fire treatment.

05_tools-and-equipment/working-tools/woo.title: Wooden Mallet
05_tools-and-equipment/working-tools/woo.content:
Wooden Mallet
Object and construction
A wooden striker transfers a controlled blow to a wooden wedge. The base route is a small one-piece club: a sound thicker head narrows into a handgrip, with continuous grain through the transition. A separate fitted head is a later variant needing its own joint and retention tests.
Select sound local Wood, rejecting rot, deep checks and a grain-breaking knot at the grip. Start with a naturally convenient form. Use Oldowan Simple Chopper for supported rough reduction and Oldowan Knife Flake for small cuts and scraping; keep the holding hand away from the cut. Round the striking face and abrupt handle transitions. Do not burn away the head or presume fire hardening improves it.
Operation and acceptance
On a low stable workpiece, try modest blows on the intended Wooden Splitting Wedge. Check whether the head sheds fragments, the grip twists, or the transition develops a crack. Increase effort only within the accepted combination. A wedge that needs uncontrolled blows calls for another billet or tool.
Keep hands clear of the striking line. A wooden face is replaceable and can bruise; it does not make impact work harmless. Rest when grip or aim deteriorates. Large log work, a metal froe and sustained heavy duty are outside the first specimen’s scope.
Current specimen and maintenance
Day 51 makes mallet-a from a separately collected short sound hardwood piece and uses it to advance two small wedges in a willow billet. The blank is chosen partly for its natural head-and-grip proportions. This is a limited working trial, without a measured efficiency gain.
Inspect the face and grip between sessions. Trim a small loose surface fragment only while enough sound head remains; retire a cracking head or handle. Store protected from prolonged damp and check drying cracks before reuse.
Alternatives and evidence
A suitable existing percussor may initiate some splits, but a stone face changes wear and fragment hazards. The base route here uses the wooden striker. R36 describes much later wooden mauls and wedges; it supports the functional pairing, not Iberian attestation, the traveller’s local species choice, dimensions or working life. These details require replication.

05_tools-and-equipment/working-tools/woo.title: Wooden Splitting Wedge
05_tools-and-equipment/working-tools/woo.content:
Wooden Splitting Wedge
Function and base route
A tapered wooden wedge opens a split along the grain of a suitable wood billet. Two wedges can alternate: one holds a small opening while the other advances it. The work produces rough split stock; it does not automatically produce straight, dimensioned boards.
Use sound Wood for the wedges and a separately selected workpiece. The first route uses small hardwood wedges, Oldowan Simple Chopper, Oldowan Knife Flake and a Wooden Mallet. No metal axe, saw, froe or hafted adze is required for this limited trial. A naturally split end can avoid forcing a stone edge as a lever.
Form and controlled splitting
Shape a gradual taper with grain running from striking end towards the working tip. Preserve a broad striking surface and remove loose fragments. A needle-sharp tip crushes readily; an abrupt thick taper may jam before the split advances. Exact useful proportions depend on the wood and the workpiece.
Select a small straight-grained billet, examine its end and secure it low against rolling. Keep fingers out of the opening and feet outside the possible falling or slipping path. Start at an existing end check where appropriate. Advance the first wedge with modest blows, then place the second farther along the opening. Release or reposition the first as the crack progresses.
Watch the split ahead of the wedge. Stop if it runs out through the side, reaches a knot, or demands uncontrolled force. Let the stock’s grain govern whether it can serve the intended part. A failed billet can be rejected without treating every wedge as a failure.
Tests, outputs and maintenance
Accept only a split that yields enough sound stock for its particular task after trimming. A rough hearth-board blank still needs flattening, drying assessment, socket work and an ignition trial. Split Wood Strips describes slender stock already used for basketry; large plank production needs additional control and appropriate timber.
Inspect crushed tips, mushroomed heads and spreading cracks. Reface minor damage within sound wood; retire a splitting wedge. Rejects and offcuts do not remain counted as useful blank stock.
Narrative instance and limits
Day 51 makes wedge-a and wedge-b and splits one short dry willow billet. One run-out portion is rejected; one rough board blank is retained for a spare fire kit. No tree is felled, large log divided or measured labour saving claimed.
R36 documents a much later use of wooden wedges and mauls. Local hardness, grain, tool life and labour remain physical-reasoning drafts. The principle can enable repeated wooden parts, but these two specimens have not yet supplied a workshop’s production standard.
