06_structures-and-places/places/fallback.title: Fallback Bench
06_structures-and-places/places/fallback.content:
Fallback Bench
A higher bench southwest of the pine patch, inspected on Day 33 as a possible retreat destination. Natural rock screening offers limited wind cover and a resting surface appears reasonably drained. It is still a candidate, not a supplied refuge.
Route and water
The inspected route follows western ground upstream of the seep’s head, then turns south along higher contour ground. It avoids the larger river and does not require a new bridge. Allow roughly 35–50 minutes one way in ordinary daylight plus inspection and return; load, rain, darkness and vigilance can lengthen it.
There is no established drinking source on the bench. Access towards the known seep remains part of its practical cost. The traveller retraces a difficult portion in daylight, not the whole route under pursuit.
Current state and limits
Through Day 35 there is no constructed shelter, insulated bed, treated-water provision, stored fuel, food cache or second ignition kit here. An empty inspection does not certify absence of animals, other occupants or future danger.
Retreat Planning supplies the judgement. Building and supplying this place later must consume actual work and stock. The map’s dated written addition records it after the Day 28 illustrated state; it must not appear as an already built feature in that picture.

06_structures-and-places/places/meeting-.title: Meeting Ground
06_structures-and-places/places/meeting-.content:
Meeting Ground
Open approach ground south of Neanderthal Clearing, beyond the western flank of the spur. It is outside the neighbours’ hearth/work area and within sight of it. Valley Map fixes the route; no main-river crossing is required.
Dated use
Day 24 plans a cautious approach with room to withdraw. Day 25 attempts a cordage/spindle pitch and retreats after the warning. The original spindle and samples are abandoned, not accepted as gifts. Their loss remains in the daily ledger.
The traveller’s plain wooden spear is concealed at a stopping-place short of and south of this ground, then recovered while retreating. The local man’s weapon is stone-pointed. No equipment ownership transfers merely because objects are present in the same encounter.
Access and uncertainty
The name does not establish neutral ground, consent, agreed diplomacy or permission to return. The neighbours can observe and control the approach. The remembered route is a foot route, not an engineered road or protected corridor.
This location record holds setting relationships. Communication and Exchange describes relevant skills, while the narrative must still earn a shared language and willing interaction. Through Day 35 there is no alliance or community supply.

06_structures-and-places/places/neandert.title: Neanderthal Clearing
06_structures-and-places/places/neandert.content:
Neanderthal Clearing
The neighbouring living/working area lies northwest beyond the rocky spur, on the same western side of the larger river as Traveller’s Camp. Eleven people are observed on Day 21; that is a visit count, not the group’s total population.
What is known
Smoke and distant firelight appear on Day 19 before the occupants are identified. Day 21’s observation from cover shows maintained fire, hides, cordage and practised working. Day 25’s close warning shows a local hafted stone-pointed spear. The group’s broader arrangements, language and resource rights remain unknown.
Do not add permanent houses, pottery, a communal atlatl or a stereotyped technologically helpless population. Their practical skills exceed the traveller’s in several visible tasks.
Approach and limits
The known contact route skirts the spur’s west flank and stops at Meeting Ground south of this living area. It needs no main-river crossing. The traveller has not been admitted to the clearing; observation does not grant entry or ownership.
One rebuffed approach establishes a particular warning, not an intention to kill or a promise of future peace. Different individuals may respond differently. Nothing here supplies gifts, trading resources, instruction or shared provisions.
Use Valley Map for bearings and Setting Specification for the group’s authored technological/anatomical constraints. This is an atlas entry, not a generic model of every Neanderthal camp.

06_structures-and-places/places/projecti.title: Projectile Practice Ground
06_structures-and-places/places/projecti.content:
Projectile Practice Ground
Particular site and status
The traveller’s short-cast site lies west/southwest of camp, above the tributary and short of the western trap circuit. Casts face west into a local earth bank, away from the river and established contact route. See Valley Map and its dated additions.
Day 29 selects and inspects the ground. Day 30 clears modest obstructions and places ground markers; short comparisons begin. Day 35 revisits the same short line. No engineered barrier, target hide, full-force containment or permanent ownership is established.
Access and changing conditions
The approach is a short local detour from the camp terrace. Do not move it to the ridge meeting ground or import the shelter and hearth here. Footing, bank condition, sight lines, possible entrants and retrieval space require inspection on each visit. Clear ground on one day is not a lasting safety guarantee.
The ordinary spear stays reachable outside the casting swing. Markers are small locally collected pieces, not cord stretched across a route or a defensive installation.
What is recorded here
This is an atlas entry, not an invention or generic manufacturing recipe. Projectile Testing contains reusable selection, inspection and comparison guidance. Atlatl Throwing develops movement; Atlatl Dart describes projectile variants.
The earlier site-unit annotation is recorded as dated place preparation rather than a manufactured stock item. Its physical description and the day’s labour remain unchanged. The prepared ground grants no permission over the valley and no ability to stop a visitor.
Day 37 observed use
Two local people stop on open ground north of the short west-directed flight line. After the traveller’s modest casts, one uses a clear part of the same bank for two hand-spear casts, recovering his own equipment. Start positions differ; no expanded full-force range or common ownership is established. The local adult’s presence is temporary, not a new camp landmark. Reinspect the space before later sessions.

06_structures-and-places/places/travelle.title: Traveller's Camp
06_structures-and-places/places/travelle.content:
Traveller’s Camp
The first camp occupies the drained terrace north of the tributary and west of the larger river. It is above the flood level selected for the opening; that judgement is not a promise against every future flood. Ground falls southeast and the fallen-limb shelter entrance faces broadly southeast. Valley Map and its camp inset fix the relationships.
Fixed arrangement
Basic Lean-to is northwest/upslope. The craft spot is south of it and west/upslope of the ordinary outside hearth. Drying and animal processing occupy the southern/southwestern dirty flank; waste lies farther beyond it. Experimental firing uses separate bare ground northeast of the hearth. Drinking collection remains at the upstream seep, away from retting and processing.
The low shelter stays a bark/leaf/branch structure under a thick mossy fallen limb. Repairs do not replace it with a tent or move the fires next to dry bedding. The map’s icons are enlarged, not metre clearances.
Dated state
Day 14 introduces the separate firing place, used on Day 15. Day 34 repairs the northwestern windward covering. Day 35 adds a small bedding-pad variant to the existing resting layer, not a whole mattress or new garment.
Tools and stocks are governed by Survival Ledger. A camp page does not duplicate them into an extra inventory. The practice ground and fallback bench are elsewhere.
Access and exposure
Known gathering and water routes radiate from the terrace. Smoke and visible movement can reveal the area; a shelter is not protection against several determined people. Keep clean/dirty handling separate and the exit usable. Retreat Planning describes the judgement; Fallback Bench remains unsupplied through Day 35.
Days 36–40
Dry grass for clothing is kept under the existing ventilated cover, separately from the bed. Day 38 puts one rabbit pelt into preparation on the existing southern/southwestern dirty frame. Day 39 checks the southeast exit and carrying order without building a barrier or moving supplies. Day 40 makes a removable back panel at the uphill craft spot. No fixed installation, hearth, firing patch or water route moves.
Days 41–45: same site, staged sleeping enclosure
Day 41 inspects the original northwest shelter and runoff. Day 43 brings ten selected light members and a separate cover lot. Day 44 installs two fork braces, a light rail beside the retained limb and three return ribs along the north/east side, keeping the occupied old roof and southeast exit. Day 45 seats four further ribs and partly covers that slope. The upper junction and southeast front remain incomplete. Hearth, craft, dirty frame, waste, firing patch and water routes do not move. This is Framed Debris Shelter work on the existing shelter asset, not a second dwelling. The fallback bench remains unsupplied.
Occupied weather and clothing work — Days 46–50
The northwest sleeping shelter receives upper overlap work, a shower-leak repair and a light movable offset brush bundle beside the southeast mouth. Its footprint, exit direction, retained fallen limb, outside hearth, clean craft spot and dirty flank do not move. Day 47’s large canid investigates the southwest dirty area and leaves; the drying frame remains intact. A narrow sight gap is cleared in loose approach brush, without building a fence or blocking retreat. No neighbour visits or works at camp in this span. The dry garment panels and later small crown pad remain removable items, not camp structures.

06_structures-and-places/structures-and-.title: Structures and Places
06_structures-and-places/structures-and-.content:
Structures and Places
This section separates reusable construction knowledge from the atlas of this particular story. A named place may contain several structures and tools; the place itself is not a technology or a capability unlock. See Category Specification and Page Scope and Organisation.
Structures

Basic Lean-to — the shelter family, including the fallen-limb opening route.
Drying Rack — a camp framework supporting separate drying surfaces.
Kiln — a planned firing enclosure; no kiln has been acquired.

Valley atlas
Use Valley Map for bearings, terrain and route relationships. Its graphic is a Day 28 state; dated written additions govern later locations.

Traveller’s Camp — the existing drained terrace and fixed work areas.
Projectile Practice Ground — the particular west-facing trial site, selected on Day 29 and prepared on Day 30.
Neanderthal Clearing — the observed neighbouring living/working area; access is not granted.
Meeting Ground — the open approach where the first pitch is rebuffed.
Fallback Bench — a Day 33 candidate, still unsupplied.

A place entry records observations and dated changes. It neither duplicates general construction instructions nor silently adds inventory. More atlas entries are added when a location has enough recurring narrative or logistical importance to warrant one.

06_structures-and-places/structures/firi.title: Kiln
06_structures-and-places/structures/firi.content:
Kiln
Status and scope
A planned controlled firing installation. This overview defines dependencies and design decisions; it is not a construction-ready kiln blueprint.
Requirements
A kiln needs a chamber suited to the intended temperature, fuel and air admission, an exhaust path, stable supports, safe access and a way to evaluate the firing. Pottery experience helps identify what the clay load needs. Pre-Kiln Firing is a useful development route rather than a universal physical necessity.
Design work
Choose the target material and firing range before choosing a geometry. Assess refractory quality, wall thickness, expansion, loading and airflow. Design a small trial that can fail without collapsing onto workers. Separate fuel supply, chamber maintenance and load cooling.
A named banked or updraft kiln is not enough: future instructions must specify dimensions, materials, draft, operating sequence and observable limits, backed by a relevant tested design.
Tests and scaling
Measure or otherwise calibrate temperature where possible; compare multiple firings and sacrificial samples. Inspect cracking and support movement. Plan repairs, fuel storage and ventilation.
Limits
An enclosure does not guarantee fuel economy or a hotter load. Do not infer wall temperature by touching hot walls. This note remains planned with no first-month construction or demonstration.
Structure and operation
This page describes the constructed site enclosure. Its location, access and maintenance are distinct from the operation performed there. A named local place and movable objects used within it keep their own roles; classification creates no new construction or operating success.

06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.title: Basic Lean-to
06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.content:
Basic Lean-to
Purpose and base route
A low debris lean-to provides a sheltered resting space with wind protection, drainage and ground insulation. A debris shelter can be assembled from natural fallen branches without cordage; a lashed frame is an improvement.
Construction
Select stable ground above runoff and flood level, away from dead overhead limbs and active animal paths. Place a sound ridge support and lean smaller pieces into a stable frame. Cover to reduce wind and rain using appropriate layered material.
Build a substantial insulating bed separate from the outside hearth. Make the resting cavity small enough to reduce exposure without trapping smoke or eliminating ventilation.
Test
Inspect joints and covering before occupying. During rain, identify leaks and drainage. Replace compressed or damp bedding. In cold conditions assess whether you can remain warm at rest; a roof alone does not establish protection.
Limits and scaling
Collection takes time and may fail in wet conditions. A lashed lean-to using Simple Cordage and Basic Thatching can last longer but still needs repairs. No universal two-hour completion or guaranteed thermal performance is assigned.
The first month’s camp remains marginal during rain. Improved shelter reduces risk; it is not proof of winter readiness.
Structure and operation
This page describes the constructed site enclosure. Its location, access and maintenance are distinct from the operation performed there. A named local place and movable objects used within it keep their own roles; classification creates no new construction or operating success.
Staged rebuilding from Day 41
Day 41 inspects the support, drainage and exit without dismantling the occupied roof. Days 44–45 add the first framed-debris return-side variant in the same footprint. The daily asset remains shelter-a. That upgrade has its own incomplete cover and test history; it does not rewrite the opening lean-to or create another camp.

06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.title: Framed Debris Shelter
06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.content:
Framed Debris Shelter
Structure, function and scope
A compact sleeping enclosure with a selected load-bearing frame, retained overlapping plant cover and a separately insulated resting layer. This family includes small fork-supported and ribbed variants; it is not a log house, animal-hide tent or certified winter dwelling. The base route uses suitable sound wood and stable bearing geometry. Cordage and more elaborate joints are optional routes with separate requirements.
Site and frame
Use Shelter Construction to select drained ground, inspect overhead support, keep an exit and stage the build. Arrange the resting space for the whole body, allowing movement and ventilation rather than treating a sealed cavity as inherently warmer or safer. A small span can reduce material and loading, but dimensions must fit the occupant and actual pieces.
For a fork-supported light rail, seat sound forked pieces on stable ground and verify resistance to rocking and rolling from outside the fall space. Fit ribs with secure upper bearing and non-creeping feet. The whole assembly must carry its intended covering in wet as well as dry conditions. Do not jack up a heavy retained fallen limb with improvised light props.
Natural bearing joints can reduce line demand. A selected lashing requires suitable cord, geometry and load checks; short ties used to retain a light cover do not establish structural rope capacity. No numerical universal load or span is assigned.
Cover, bed and operation
Sort Plant Covering Stock by retention and weather-facing role. Fit lower layers first where overlapping construction requires it, then direct upper runoff outside. Cover junctions and the entrance deliberately; a visually closed roof may still leak at its meeting line. Basic Thatching provides related layering judgement, but different plant materials need different treatment.
Keep Dry Plant Insulation as a separate clean sleeping layer. Check compression, cold ground contact and morning damp. Preserve ventilation and an accessible opening. Keep the present fire and hot stones outside this combustible enclosure; adding combustion inside requires a different proven exhaust and clearance design. R32 supports the exposure and combustion concerns, not the frame’s engineering.
Inspection and maintenance
Check supports, bearing contacts, rail rotation, rib feet, cover retention, runoff, entrance and bed. Inspect after weather and before occupation. Unload or withdraw if supports shift or cracks develop. Dry stock needs replenishment, and wet cover can both add load and lose insulation. Record the labour and materials required by repairs.
First local instance: Days 44–45
The existing northwest camp shelter, asset shelter-a, is rebuilt in stages in the same footprint. Its southeast entrance, craft spot, outside hearth and water routes remain fixed. Two light fork braces, a slender rail and seven return ribs are the ten newly selected members. The rail sits beside the retained limb; the limb’s original bearing is not dismantled or lifted.
Day 44 installs the braces, rail and three ribs, using 0.4 m short roll-restraint ties while preserving the old covered side. This is the first limited framework demonstration, not a weatherproof chamber. Day 45 installs four further ribs and allocates 6 kg mixed cover, with 0.8 m light retaining ties. The return slope is partly covered; the upper junction and southeast front remain unfinished. A breeze and short resting trial show limited improvement. Four kilograms of cover stock remain for further work. No rain or winter test has occurred.
The upgraded instance is one existing shelter, not a second building or supplied Fallback Bench. Its first-month Basic Lean-to state remains in the dated record and map. A successful completion still needs observed weather performance, maintained bedding, clothing, food and fuel; shelter alone cannot establish winter readiness.
First shower repair and entrance trial — Days 46–50
Day 46 allocates 3 kg existing coarse cover and 0.2 m light retaining line to connect the return cover at the upper junction without changing the heavy limb’s support. Day 47 showers reveal one inward path at a curled lap; it is unloaded locally, adjusted and extended with 0.5 kg protected cover. No further drip appears there during later watched showers, and no support movement is visible during inspection. This is a narrow weather result, not a wet-load or storm rating.
Day 49 collects 2.5 kg coarse cover and uses 2 kg as a movable offset brush wind baffle at one edge of the southeast mouth. Its support is the existing outer rib margin and ground; no new post, door, hinge or second structure appears. The clear passage and ventilation remain. One kilogram cover stays loose at Day 50. Separate clean bedding is renewed after the local wet edge and again on Day 50. The fire remains outdoors and the same northwest footprint is occupied. Clothing and supply still constrain winter readiness.

06_structures-and-places/structures/work.title: Drying Rack
06_structures-and-places/structures/work.content:
Drying Rack
Structure and scope
A supported rack holds material above ground for controlled drying trials. The frame and a validated meat-preservation process are separate capabilities.
Construction
Use sound poles and Tripod Lashing or another stable support. Secure crosspieces, test the load and keep the structure away from sparks and strong heat. Provide a clean surface appropriate to the material.
Keep raw hides, fibre and food on separate surfaces; a used hide-drying frame is not automatically clean cooking equipment.
Operation and limits
Observe airflow, damp folds and heat exposure. Smoke can add flavour and alter surfaces but does not prove that pathogens are destroyed or that food is shelf-stable. Pine bough smoke and creosote are not a universal food-preserving recipe.
R07 explains why low-temperature drying can leave pathogens alive. A future preservation method needs specific heat, drying, storage and verification controls.
First-month role
Day 6 installs a small drying frame for the pelt and tendon. Meat is cooked and eaten that day. No stored smoked-meat output is entered into the ledger.
Structure and operation
This page describes the constructed site framework. Its location, access and maintenance are distinct from the operation performed there. A named local place and movable objects used within it keep their own roles; classification creates no new construction or operating success.

07_technologies/adhesives/pine-pitch-man.title: Pine Pitch Manufacture
07_technologies/adhesives/pine-pitch-man.content:
Pine Pitch Manufacture
Goal
Compare small resin-adhesive batches for one defined non-food joint. Do not manufacture an untested large batch or claim a universal chemical recipe.
Method
Collect Pine Resin into a dedicated tray. Heat a small amount indirectly near, not in, flame. Provide a clear working area, ventilation and a means to withdraw from ignition.
Compare cooled unfilled resin with a small selected addition of clean finely crushed Charcoal. Add incrementally and keep an approximate record. Avoid smoke-generating overheating. Other fillers or plasticisers require separate tests and cannot be substituted blindly.
Apply a small sample to expendable wood and stone, allow it to cool, then inspect adhesion, brittleness and heat softening. Repeat a relevant wet trial if the joint may be exposed.
Output and limits
A successful small trial yields Pine Pitch Adhesive for a modest Simple Hafting test. Increasing filler can reduce performance. Binding and geometry remain important.
Do not use the formulation as a wound treatment or drinking-vessel seal without specific evidence. R03 documents ancient adhesives but does not validate this pine-resin mixture.

07_technologies/ceramics/clay-vessel-mak.title: Clay Vessel Making
07_technologies/ceramics/clay-vessel-mak.content:
Clay Vessel Making
Goal
Form and dry experimental greenware. Making a shape is not yet making pottery or a usable cooking pot.
Method
Collect a small Clay batch and remove coarse debris. Compare test pieces at the intended moisture with and without a conservative selected temper addition. A coil that cracks does not tell you to add more sand by default.
Keep stored clay damp. Form a small pinch vessel with approximately even walls and a smooth transition between base and side. A modest 6–8 mm wall is the narrative trial target, not a universal optimum.
Dry slowly in shelter with airflow. Check the base and walls repeatedly. Time alone is not proof of dryness; thickness and weather matter. Repairing a dry crack with wet clay can introduce a new weak join.
Test and failure
Set aside a cracked test vessel rather than treating it as ready for cooking. Use small sacrificial samples to study drying and firing. The first narrative pot is formed on Day 11, fired on Day 15, then cooled overnight and rejected as a cooking vessel on Day 16.
Next process and limits
Pit Fire provides the first firing route. Pottery combines forming, firing and performance tests. A clay whorl is an optional separate object; it does not require a successful cooking vessel.
R10 supports later Palaeolithic ceramics elsewhere, not Neanderthal figurines or this exact early pot.
Comparison pair through Day 40
The two Day 34 samples from one body remain unfired. Thickness is the intended comparison variable; their external dryness does not establish dry centres. A cooler thicker sample on Day 39 supports waiting, not measuring internal moisture or declaring the thin sample accepted. Neither is broken or converted to a vessel by Day 40. A later sacrificial check or small firing must identify which pieces remain, record fuel and allow cooling before water-contact testing.

07_technologies/ceramics/pottery.title: Pottery
07_technologies/ceramics/pottery.content:
Pottery
Capability
Pottery is a repeatable process of producing suitably fired ceramic objects. A formed vessel or one surviving firing is insufficient to establish reliable cooking-pot production.
Workflow

Select and characterise a Clay body.
Form and dry pieces through Clay Vessel Making.
Apply a tested firing route, initially Pit Fire.
Cool without thermal shock and inspect the load.
Test water stability, leakage, abrasion and the intended operating heat cycles.
Record failures and repeat with controlled changes.

The first-month vessel is rejected for cooking after a crack and leakage appear. Its fragments and intact portion can serve as non-food experimental samples.
Alternative roles
Small fired weights can be tested independently of cooking pots. A Spindle Whorl can also be wooden, so ceramics need not become the bottleneck for spinning.
Evidence and limits
R10 documents later Upper Palaeolithic ceramic objects elsewhere. It does not demonstrate cooking pots at the narrative’s date or substantiate the old Neanderthal figurine claim.
Water-tightness, thermal resistance and food-contact suitability need separate tests. No permanent unlock or first-month production mastery is recorded.

07_technologies/container-making/coiled-.title: Coiled Basket Making
07_technologies/container-making/coiled-.content:
Coiled Basket Making
Purpose
Produce and test a stitched coiled container from a flexible foundation and separate binding fibre. This page organises the manufacturing route; Simple Coiling and Weaving develops the coiling and tension-control skills used within it. This is an alternative to a willow stake basket.
Method
Select a foundation that bends to the initial radius without splitting. Start a small loop and secure it with a tested line. Add successive coils and stitch through suitable gaps or use Bone Awl to open a controlled path.
Raise the wall gradually, maintain consistent tension and stagger added material. Taper the final foundation and secure the finish so ends cannot pull free.
Test
Load lightly and inspect base, seams and rim. Avoid forcing a delicate eyed needle through thick wooden rods. A hand-sized trial can establish the motion without consuming enough fine cord for a whole basket.
Limits
Coiling, rod weaving and knotting a net are different operations. The narrative’s Day 19 coiled trial does not establish net production or a universal basket predecessor.
Preparation, fine binding line and stitch labour can make a coiled design expensive for the current camp. Compare Woven Foraging Basket before assuming the historical-looking route is optimal.

07_technologies/fire/camp-fire-managemen.title: Camp Fire Management
07_technologies/fire/camp-fire-managemen.content:
Camp Fire Management
Purpose
Maintain an outside fire for warmth, cooking and material work after ignition. The first route uses Bow Drill Fire; another validated ignition method can replace it.
Procedure
Clear a small site on stable ground away from debris bedding, roots, overhanging material and stored fuel. Prepare Tinder Bundle, kindling and a supply of Dry Fuel before ignition.
Transfer a successful flame into small dry pieces, then increase fuel gradually while preserving airflow. Match fire size to the task. A large fire wastes fuel and can still heat an exposed sleeper unevenly.
Keep a means to control spread. Protect an ember bed only where conditions permit, inspect it before leaving and treat restart as necessary if no live ember remains.
Test and maintenance
Record fuel collected and burned. At night, insulated bedding supplies the base protection; the narrative does not assume hourly feeding compatible with eight hours of uninterrupted sleep.
Limits
Smoke can discourage some animals or insects but does not guarantee safety. Carbon monoxide can accumulate even with little visible smoke. Do not enclose a fire in a debris shelter.
R14 supports evidence for ancient fire-making knowledge. The local group does not need the traveller to introduce fire.

07_technologies/fire/pit-firing.title: Pit Firing
07_technologies/fire/pit-firing.content:
Pit Firing
Purpose
A small open or shallow-pit firing trial for dry clay pieces. It is one route to ceramic manufacture, not a unique sequence through which all future firing must pass.
Preparation
Use dry sheltered ground, clear surroundings and Dry Fuel. Greenware from Clay Vessel Making must be dry through its section. Preheat gradually outside the main heat before increasing exposure.
Support the pieces so fuel collapse will not strike them. Arrange small dry fuel to admit air rather than burying everything under damp earth at ignition.
Firing and cooling
Raise heat gradually, then maintain sufficient heat for the tested body. The exact temperature-time schedule requires clay-specific replication. Fire colour and blackened surfaces are imperfect indicators, not a precise pyrometer.
Allow the fuel to burn down and the load to cool in place. Do not pour water over it or remove hot pieces. The narrative waits overnight.
Test and limits
Use sacrificial pieces for water stability, abrasion and fracture checks. A pot surviving the fire does not prove adequate firing, food suitability or thermal-shock resistance.
No fixed success percentage, guaranteed vitrification or automatic waterproofing is assigned. Fuel and supervision must be budgeted. Improvements are in Pre-Kiln Firing; a kiln is not a prerequisite.

07_technologies/fire/pre-kiln-firing.title: Pre-Kiln Firing
07_technologies/fire/pre-kiln-firing.content:
Pre-Kiln Firing
Purpose
Improve repeatability of an open firing site through support, wind control, airflow and controlled cooling. This page describes an improvement framework; it does not supply a validated firing schedule.
Method
Start from a documented Pit Fire trial. Record fuel, loading, weather and failures. Change one major variable at a time: a low wind screen, spacing between pieces, dry support material or fuel arrangement.
Keep an air path for combustion. An earth covering can retain heat but can also starve the fire or introduce moisture. Reduced oxygen is not automatically hotter or better.
Tests
Use comparable sacrificial pieces to check water stability and strength. Compare fuel cost and repeatability over more than one firing. Do not call a black ringing fragment fully vitrified solely from sound or colour.
Limits
Temperature and time both matter. Duration cannot compensate indefinitely for inadequate temperature. Enclosing the site also increases structural and ventilation requirements.
Kiln is a later controlled-chamber route. A surviving single piece establishes a result, not a dependable production process.

07_technologies/food-processing/acorn-le.title: Acorn Leaching
07_technologies/food-processing/acorn-le.content:
Acorn Leaching
Goal and preparation
Remove enough tannin from an identified acorn batch for the intended food use. Tannin concentration and processing behaviour vary by species, particle size and method.
Collect sound acorns, shell and reject damaged kernels. Record shelled edible mass. Crush to an appropriate size using clean stones.
First-month warm-water route
Use a tested Bark Container and Hot-Rock Boiling. Process a small batch so water can be changed without losing the meal. Cycle fresh hot water over the material, keep it separated from dirty handling equipment, and compare progress.
A reduction in bitterness is a useful process observation, not universal chemical validation. The number of cycles and completion criteria need species-specific evidence. Do not promise four cycles or ninety minutes for every batch.
Alternatives
Cold soaking or flowing-water leaching can avoid heating, with different time, containment and contamination requirements. A permeable basket or bag helps retain particles, but must itself be suitable for food.
Output and limits
Wet Acorn Meal is recorded separately and consumed promptly. Drying a thick cake near a fire is not sufficient proof of a durable travel ration.
The first narrative trial begins on Day 17 and yields a small wet batch on Day 18. The expedition uses dry nuts instead of an instantly manufactured large acorn brick.
Repeated small charges: Days 42–44
The Day 41 harvest is 0.8 kg sound shelled untreated input. A 0.6 L vessel cannot take that whole mass plus water and hot stones. Day 42 processes half in four roughly 0.1 kg charges; Days 43 and 44 each process 0.2 kg in two charges. Fresh-water/reheating estimates are 6 L and 2 kg extra fuel on Day 42, then 3 L and 1 kg each following day. Drinking water and ordinary fuel remain separately counted. Outputs of 0.65, 0.35 and 0.35 kg cooked wet meal include water and are entirely eaten on their production days. No wet food store or drying process is demonstrated.
R33 in Research Register provides an ethnobotanical comparison, not a validation of these local rates or the acceptance decision. Shelling, crushing, vessel capacity, fresh water, heat and repeated handling constrain throughput. The same remembered process does not guarantee the same completion time for another oak lot.
Repeat in small charges — Days 47–49
The 0.6 kg own shelled input collected on Day 46 is processed in three 0.2 kg portions, two charges per day. Each day models roughly 3 litres extra processing water and 1 kg extra heating fuel beyond ordinary cold-weather use. Reduced astringency and the already trialled local route remain limited authored acceptance observations, not a universal chemical test. The new output is about 0.35 kg wet meal each day, cooked and eaten with no retained wet food. R33 does not validate these yields.

07_technologies/material-processing/bark.title: Barkcloth Processing
07_technologies/material-processing/bark.content:
Barkcloth Processing
Scope
Prepare local bark fibres or panels for modest protective use. Beaten barkcloth and a stiff bark wrap are different products. The narrative initially has ties and overlapping rough panels, not a finished broad cloth.
Procedure
Select an identified locally available material. Test a small strip for separation, flexibility and skin irritation without assuming all inner bark behaves alike. Harvest modest amounts from suitable fallen or damaged material; dead bark may have degraded fibres.
Separate useful inner material with Oldowan Knife Flake. Try scraping, soaking or controlled beating on a supported surface as the material allows. Compare the result dry and damp before allocating the whole batch.
Test and limits
Check coverage, edge abrasion and durability during movement. A narrow strip that becomes flexible is not evidence of a full shoulder cape. Mark unsuccessful material and choose another route.
The older tropical options are removed. A universal one-to-three-hour barkcloth recipe is not validated for this Iberian setting.
Use
Basic Bark Clothing uses the successful limited panels. Bedding and shelter still supply much of the early thermal protection.

07_technologies/material-processing/nett.title: Nettle Fibre Processing
07_technologies/material-processing/nett.content:
Nettle Fibre Processing
Goal
Recover useful bast fibre, then prepare it for the intended line or yarn. Retting, extraction, cleaning, drying and spinning are distinct operations.
Water-retted route
Take a tested batch from Nettle Retting. Rinse downstream of clean-water collection, then drain. Break the woody core without crushing fibres, and peel off long bundles.
Scrape or rub gently to remove adhering debris. Compare a small clean sample before processing the remainder. Excessive abrasion shortens fibres. Dry protected with airflow, then split and align to the intended diameter.
Test
Flex and pull sample bundles. Reject weak or decomposed fibre. Record approximately how much usable dry output remains after cleaning. A heap of wet stems cannot be counted as the same mass of ready-to-spin fibre.
Alternative and limits
Direct mechanical extraction may avoid retting at greater labour or different quality. R11 supports multiple routes; exact local performance remains unmeasured.
The narrative begins extraction on Day 16 and keeps the remaining material states distinct. A Spindle Whorl does not remove this preparation bottleneck. A group must reproduce the complete chain before community capability is claimed.
Batch B: first accepted portion
Day 43 cleans and checks a selected dried portion, crediting 18 g usable dry fibre after rejection of weak/woody sections. Remaining coarse material is still in process. The stem bundle was unweighed, so no extraction efficiency is inferred. Day 45 allocates 10 g from the combined prepared stock to hand-made line; the output is not also credited as yarn.

07_technologies/material-processing/nett.title: Nettle Retting
07_technologies/material-processing/nett.content:
Nettle Retting
Purpose
Manage a batch through controlled biological breakdown to loosen bast fibre. This process includes placement, changing conditions, sample checks and the decision to stop; it is distinct from the hand skills used to strip and twist the output. Water retting is one option; dry or fresh mechanical extraction can provide other routes with different labour and quality.
Procedure
Identify and select mature suitable stems. Protect hands from stings, remove leaves and bind a modest labelled batch. Place it in a secured downstream processing pool, separate from drinking-water collection and food preparation.
Inspect samples regularly. Peel and flex a stem: fibres should separate while retaining useful strength. Smell alone does not define readiness. Remove a batch before fibres become weak or fragment.
Rinse and proceed to Nettle Fibre Processing. Do not promise readiness on a fixed day. Temperature, stem maturity, microbes and water conditions matter.
Alternative and limits
Dew retting uses field exposure and repeated turning but has different weather and contamination constraints. Mechanical stripping avoids waiting but can be labour-intensive and give rough output.
The narrative’s batch starts on Day 4 and passes its test on Day 16. Earlier status estimates are not a second chronology.
Evidence
R11 supports multiple extraction routes. It does not establish an exact wild-Iberian schedule, a universal strength increase or instant community adoption.
Second narrative batch
Day 31 starts a separately harvested small stem bundle B in the established downstream pool, secured with a short allocated bark tie and weighted retaining branch. It is not prepared fibre. Checks through Day 35 do not yet find useful separation, so the batch stays in process with no assigned output. The first batch’s twelve days do not determine this colder batch’s readiness or yield.
Checks through Day 40
Batch B stays secured in the established downstream pool. Day 39 begins to find some outer-bundle release; Day 40 still finds uneven separation across the bundle. Neither event creates prepared fibre. Continue sampling for useful separation and retained fibre integrity, rather than declaring readiness from elapsed days. Later removal, rinsing, extraction, protected drying and accepted usable yield must each be recorded.
Batch B: condition-led stop on Day 42
After distributed sample checks, the bundle begun on Day 31 is lifted and rinsed on Day 42. That ends its immersion, not the complete production chain. Selected strips dry under existing ventilated cover; the coarse remainder stays a separate unfinished portion. The old immersed tie is not returned as ready loose cord. R11 does not establish this elapsed time as a recipe.

07_technologies/material-processing/rawh.title: Rawhide Processing
07_technologies/material-processing/rawh.content:
Rawhide Processing
Goal
Dry a cleaned hide into untanned material for rigid cases and bindings. Fur may remain, but drying does not create durable soft leather.
Method
Flesh Animal Pelt promptly with a supported edge that does not tear it. Spread or support it under moderate even tension; do not pull a thin rabbit skin to extreme tension merely because a frame is strong.
Dry in protected moving air, away from scorching heat. Inspect frequently for damp folds, insects, tearing and deterioration. Adjust supports as the material changes.
Test
The dried skin should hold the intended shape without decomposition or weak holes. A rigid panel can be dampened locally for shaping, but repeated wetting changes dimensions and strength.
Limits
Dry rawhide is not a waterproof bottle. It softens and can deteriorate in damp conditions. Smoke is not a universal preservative and should not be used to certify cleanliness.
A Smoking Rack is optional equipment for a separated drying task. A clean supported frame can work without it.
Fur-On Pelt Clothing adds a temporary softening workflow; a tannery is a later process with different requirements.

07_technologies/systems/food-reserve-man.title: Food Reserve Management
07_technologies/systems/food-reserve-man.content:
Food Reserve Management
Continuing service
Keep an explicit account of edible input, meals, losses and an accessible remaining reserve, then use it to limit optional work. The first route handles previously identified hazelnuts with the existing small basket and local comparison marks. It does not establish a preservation technology or certify food safety.
Day 29 introduces a repeatable rough portion comparison and scratch register. The traveller estimates the reserve in comparable portions. Kilograms in the author ledger are a separate model.
Routine and controls
Separate today’s intended food from the working reserve before becoming absorbed in an experiment. Inspect storage for dampness, pests and obvious damage. Keep food away from raw-animal work and waste. A basket provides containment, not a sealed pest-proof or rainproof store.
Record what actually enters as edible prepared food. Unopened shells and unprocessed acorns are not ready meals; wet acorn output is not counted as new energy because water made it heavier. Catch-specific fresh food remains separately accounted for.
After meals, update the portion account and note discarded food separately. Measurement and Records retains the comparison procedure so changing a handful does not quietly enlarge the reserve. Imperfect marks still reveal a persistent deficit.
Acceptance and ongoing supply
Useful operation means that a missing meal or loss changes the record, a depleted reserve changes tomorrow’s work, and no stock is counted twice. It is an accounting improvement, not proof of adequate nutrition, real kilogram accuracy or predictable gathering rates.
Compare ordinary days with days spent travelling or experimenting. When collection falls below consumption, optional work draws on a finite buffer. Increasing that buffer requires actual independent gathering or another established supply route.
Failures and fallback
Wet storage, a lost basket, contested patches and diminishing harvest can interrupt the system. Records do not rescue spoiled food or replace an absent food source. Smell and appearance cannot certify safety.
Day 35’s reserve is smaller than Day 28’s despite one small fish catch. The immediate fallback is to shorten optional practice and assign time to gathering, not assume a future deer kill, gift or trade. Drying fish, durable acorn storage and winter ration sufficiency remain unestablished processes.
Shelter work and the short reserve, Days 41–45
The new acorn route processes 0.8 kg shelled untreated input across Days 42–44, in vessel-sized charges. Wet output is cooked and consumed on each processing day; no reserve of dried meal is created. The kernel reserve declines from 1.31 kg at Day 40 to 0.93 kg at Day 45 despite these meals and one small fish. The next work must give food collection priority alongside the unfinished roof, rather than treating new structures as proof of seasonal surplus.
Short buffer after construction and scouting — Days 46–50
Longer independent gathering on Day 46 adds 0.75 kg edible kernels and 0.6 kg untreated acorn input. The acorns are processed as three 0.2 kg portions on Days 47–49, with two small charges each day. All wet meal is cooked/eaten; no dry travel cake or shelf-stable store appears. The Day 48 outing reduces gathering to 0.25 kg. Day 50’s small fish is consumed immediately. Kernels end at 0.94 kg, still around two recent daily portions, despite better clothing and shelter. The approved 7–10-day target remains unmet.

07_technologies/systems/sanitation-and-c.title: Sanitation and Camp Hygiene
07_technologies/systems/sanitation-and-c.content:
Sanitation and Camp Hygiene
Goal
Reduce contamination using available separation, clean water and handling practices. The absence of germ theory among a fictional group cannot be inferred from a dirty-looking camp.
Camp arrangement
Keep drinking-water collection upstream and separate from waste, butchery and fibre retting. Choose a waste area away from water and routine foot traffic without assuming one fixed distance fits all ground.
Separate dirty raw-animal work from cooked food and delicate clean tools. Clean hands and implements after processing. Once Hot-Rock Boiling is available, reserve treated water and a clean vessel for appropriate uses.
Limits
This reduces some exposure without providing modern sterile facilities. A clear spring, clean-looking surface or absence of symptoms does not establish freedom from pathogens. Smoke is not sterilisation.
Teaching and scaling
Explain and demonstrate a specific separation, compare it with existing practice and check whether it remains workable. Larger camps need water supply, waste removal, food handling, drainage and responsibility for maintenance.
R06 and R07 establish important modern constraints; they do not validate every improvised camp practice.
Accessible remnants and animal investigation — Day 47
A large canid investigates the dirty flank while the traveller stays on the clean side. Its departure without damage does not establish deterrence. A trapped old scrap prompts removal of animal remnants, cleaning, protected pelt handling and inspection of the established separated waste route. Waste is not shifted into the watercourse or left as a bait pile just outside the shelter. Modern attractant management in R34 informs the reasoning, not a guaranteed prehistoric outcome. The animal replaces planned yarn work with watch and cleanup.

07_technologies/systems/teaching-and-kno.title: Teaching and Knowledge Preservation
07_technologies/systems/teaching-and-kno.content:
Teaching and Knowledge Preservation
Goal
Build capabilities that survive the traveller’s absence. Knowing an instruction, copying a motion and independently producing a useful result are different milestones.
First teaching method
Use Communication and Exchange to establish the problem and the learner’s existing technique. Show a small operation with prepared inputs, then allow a willing learner to try without continual correction.
Compare output and failure signs. Repeat with a new input or changed condition to check transfer. When a process has several stages, demonstrate or explain each stage, including preparation and maintenance.
Verification and scaling
Record who has reproduced what, with which tools and materials. One spun short sample is evidence of that action; it does not establish fibre harvesting, retting, plying, net making or a community textile industry.
Later develop Measurement and Records, redundant teaching, shared tool specifications and arrangements for maintaining knowledge. Respect learners’ priorities and consent; novelty is not an entitlement to their labour.
The first month contains a failed approach, not a shared teaching trial. No willing learner has reproduced a method under the traveller’s instruction by Day 28. This system remains planned, with no demonstration date.

07_technologies/water/hot-rock-boiling.title: Hot-Rock Boiling
07_technologies/water/hot-rock-boiling.content:
Hot-Rock Boiling
Goal
Heat water to an observable rolling boil in a tested non-metal vessel. This is an alternative to a sound ceramic pot, not a method that requires pottery.
Method
Use a tested Bark Container, suitable Heating Stones and Water from the least visibly contaminated appropriate source. Prepare a stable vessel support and tested handling sticks.
Heat screened stones outside the shelter with faces clear of possible fragments. Transfer carefully, avoiding a sharp impact on the vessel. Stir or move the water safely so local hot spots do not masquerade as bulk boiling. Add enough heat for a sustained observable boil; steam alone is not the endpoint.
Follow the relevant time at boil: R06 gives one minute at ordinary elevation, and longer at high elevations. The fictional camp is low elevation. Count from the rolling boil, not from the first steam.
Test and limits
Watch seams and supports throughout. Stop on significant leakage, cracking stone or vessel damage. Keep cooling treated water apart from dirty collection implements. Boiling does not remove chemical toxins.
The Day 4 heat trial is stopped for leakage; Day 5 reaches the first observable boil. Wear interrupts treatment on Day 9, and Day 10 repairs restore it. The method is still a draft requiring practical validation of the exact bark-and-stone system.

08_eras/01_lower-paleolithic.title: Lower Paleolithic
08_eras/01_lower-paleolithic.content:
Lower Paleolithic
Orientation
A broad archaeological label for early stone-tool traditions, with boundaries that vary by region and research convention. It is not a skill level a society must finish before entering another era. Earlier toolmaking can coexist with later methods when it remains useful.
Connection to the handbook
Oldowan Toolkit describes a practical flake-and-core route; Acheulean Hand Axe describes a bifacial tool. Their labels identify historical traditions, not a universal progression or a guarantee that one tool outperforms another at every task.
A traveller at the chosen date can make a simple flake without recreating the entire history associated with it. What matters here is the raw material, striking skill, edge performance and work required.
Limit
The traveller’s first month is situated much later than this broad period. The era note provides historical orientation rather than the setting’s date or a hard prerequisite.

08_eras/02_middle-paleolithic.title: Middle Paleolithic
08_eras/02_middle-paleolithic.content:
Middle Paleolithic
Orientation
A regional archaeological framework associated with several prepared-core traditions and, in Europe, much Neanderthal material culture. It is not synonymous with one species, a fixed toolkit or limited cognitive ability.
Connection to the setting
At roughly 40,000 calibrated BP, the handbook is set near a complicated regional transition and overlap. World distinguishes the fictional valley from the regional evidence in Research Register.
The local people already work stone, hides, wood and fibres. The traveller’s first flakes are a response to his equipment shortage, not an improvement on their knapping. Cordage evidence (R01), manufactured adhesive research (R03) and inferred fire-making (R14) help constrain the portrayal.
Limit
Do not assign the group every technology found at every Neanderthal site. Describe what he observes and leave unseen practices open.

08_eras/03_upper-paleolithic.title: Upper Paleolithic
08_eras/03_upper-paleolithic.content:
Upper Paleolithic
Orientation
An archaeological framework used for later Pleistocene assemblages in parts of Eurasia. Tool traditions, ornaments and symbolic objects vary widely; the term does not mark a uniform biological or intellectual threshold.
Connection to the handbook
Bone Needle, Atlatl and ceramic experiments deserve their own local, chronological evidence when used as historical claims. The traveller can deliberately attempt a device outside its regional archaeological record, but the page must label that as a fictional intervention and state its manufacturing requirements.
R10 describes ceramic objects from a later Upper Palaeolithic context. That evidence cannot make the first-month Iberian pot or cooking ceramics historically routine.
Limit
A long list of later technologies is a set of research possibilities, not proof of inevitable adoption. Environmental opportunity, labour, materials and social transmission still determine whether a device is useful.

08_eras/04_mesolithic.title: Mesolithic
08_eras/04_mesolithic.content:
Mesolithic
Orientation
A regional term commonly used for some postglacial hunter-gatherer societies, with differing dates, definitions and material traditions. Other regions use different frameworks. It does not describe a universal intermediate stage between mobile foraging and farming.
Connection to the handbook
Broadening food sources, storage, transport and seasonal planning can make a community more resilient without requiring immediate agriculture. Small composite tools or fishing equipment are useful only where their resources and maintenance costs fit.
The Civilisation Roadmap treats such capabilities as possible parallel routes. A community can intensify selected resources while continuing to move seasonally.
Limit
Do not turn this label into a compulsory list of inventions, or assume that increasing sedentism, population and cultivation always occur together. Those relationships require local evidence and explicit narrative choices.

08_eras/05_neolithic.title: Neolithic
08_eras/05_neolithic.content:
Neolithic
Orientation
A regional archaeological term often associated with cultivation, domesticated animals and changing settlement patterns. These features develop on different schedules and do not form one package everywhere.
Connection to the handbook
Farming requires more than remembering how to sow seeds. The setting needs suitable wild populations, land access, seasonal knowledge, selection across generations, storage and a reason to accept labour and risk. Domestication is a sustained biological and social process.
Pottery, weaving, polished stone and permanent buildings should each have independent requirements. A sound pot can be useful to mobile people; a cultivated crop does not automatically create surplus or free specialists.
Limit
The mission roadmap must justify the transition with food budgets and labour, including failed harvests and competing options. Treat agriculture as a capability to evaluate rather than the predetermined end of every foraging society.

Acquired
Demonstration and development state
The traveller begins with remembered knowledge, but his practical capability must be demonstrated under local conditions. The tables below show the first documented instance, which may be a limited construction or trial. Read the linked page and daily scene for its test and limits. A demonstration date is not a claim of mastery, permanent reliability or community ownership.
Current objects, consumables, repairs and gifts are separate in Survival Ledger. Observed community practices are recorded separately below. Planned pages have no demonstration date and are excluded from the demonstrated tables.
The five capability categories describe the page’s subject, independently of its state. Category Specification defines stocks, abilities, equipment, organised processes and structures. Local places are atlas records, outside the capability graph. Topic Index browses related subjects together. A first recorded construction or process start does not certify every variant, useful performance or sustained supply.

09_reference/capability-dependency-map.title: Capability Dependency Map
09_reference/capability-dependency-map.content:
Capability Dependency Map
Default routes, alternatives and tests
The handbook follows capabilities rather than an archaeological technology ladder. Remembering an advanced design does not supply the material, precision, labour or test needed to rely on it. The categories follow Category Specification: materials are stocks, skills are practised abilities, equipment supplies object functions, structures arrange built sites, and processes organise inputs into an outcome. Local atlas places are outside this graph. Categories do not prescribe an invention order.
The graph below is an overview of the revised first month; Dependency Register is the complete generated table.
An arrow means an input or prerequisite in this selected route, not a claim about universal invention order. Wood, labour, water and other shared inputs are omitted from this small diagram for legibility; read the reference requirements.

Where remembered knowledge can shorten a route
