R04 supports the distinction between rough hard-hammer bifaces and later refinement. A research-supported historical alternative is not automatically a tested manufacturing procedure here.
What the graph cannot show alone
A construction can be complete while operational performance is unknown. The Day 28 thrower is an example. A successful isolated test may still fail as a routine supply method; the single Day 22 fish is another.
The neighbouring people have their own demonstrated practices. Their skills are not unlocked by the traveller’s demonstration date. Communication, consent, teaching, repair capacity and food surplus govern whether a technique spreads. The graph must eventually include these capacities alongside physical inputs.
The Civilisation Roadmap extends this approach through measurement, agriculture, chemistry, machine tools, power, institutions and space systems. Later entries should expose critical paths and competing routes rather than mark an era as completed.

09_reference/civilisation-roadmap.title: Civilisation Roadmap
09_reference/civilisation-roadmap.content:
Civilisation Roadmap
The dependency problem
The endpoint is a society capable of building, operating and replacing space systems, then designing a defence mission appropriate to the threatening object. One remembered design is insufficient: industry needs reproducible materials, energy, measurement, supply chains, institutions and skilled people.
This is a research roadmap, not a claim that every listed historical step is necessary. Routes should be compared by time, labour, material access, failure cost and long-term maintenance.
Capability stages




























































StageRequired capabilitiesWhat must be demonstrated before advancingIndividual stabilityShelter, repeatable ignition, food access, water treatment, useful edges and containersSeveral days of maintenance without consuming the last reserve; fallback for failed fire or weatherCooperative productionShared communication, reciprocal exchange, local resource access, distributed skillsOthers reproduce useful processes and consent to continued workSustained surplusSeasonal food management, storage, sanitation, transport, durable shelterA group can feed specialists and tolerate bad harvests or interrupted routesMeasurement and recordsShared units, counting, geometry, durable marks, comparison standardsIndependent workers make compatible parts and diagnose failuresThermal and chemical industryControlled firing, fuel supply, refractory materials, extraction and separationRepeated batches meet known material and performance criteriaMechanical industryStructural metals, joining, bearings, seals, precision tools and power sourcesMachines can be built, serviced and reproduced by several workshopsElectrical and scientific industryConductors, insulation, magnets, generation, instruments, chemical purityStable power, calibrated measurements and reliable component manufactureTransport and communicationsRoads or waterways, vehicles, navigation, signalling and supply managementGoods, people and information move reliably beyond one settlementSpace systemsPropulsion, guidance, structures, testing, tracking, launch facilities and operationsUncrewed systems achieve defined flight goals with independently verified telemetryPlanetary defenceSurvey, orbit determination, target characterisation, mission design and coordinationThe actual threat and proposed intervention are analysed and tested at the necessary scale
Food production does not have to mean immediate agriculture. Productive fisheries, managed wild resources and storage may support some specialisation first. Domestication needs suitable organisms, generations and incentives; the protagonist cannot summon modern crops.
Shortcuts worth investigating
Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit reviews the current assemblage against archaeological parallels. The immediate bottleneck is seasonal resilience: an enclosed dry sleeping space, useful insulation, food reserves and protected fuel take precedence over adding experimental devices. Month Two Outline carries that priority into the next recorded work.

Measurement and experimental records before metallurgy: cheap concepts can prevent expensive trial-and-error.
Wooden spindles before ceramic whorls: an alternative material removes a firing dependency.
Water treatment before pottery: bark vessels and heated stones offer a tested alternative route.
Mechanical hafting before glue: geometry and binding can secure some tools; adhesive improves particular joints.
Community instruction before complex machines: parallel expertise may outperform one exceptional maker.
Starting with the most useful local metal route rather than compulsory bronze-first progression.
Delaying technologies that are physically possible but have poor returns at the current population or mobility.

For each proposed shortcut, write its actual requirements and a counterexample where it would fail. Avoid labelling an entire historical development a wrong turn without assessing the constraints faced by its inventors.
Later technical paths to expand
Each row is a research programme. Turn it into reference pages only after selecting a feasible route and defining a measurable acceptance test. These branches overlap; they are not compulsory historical eras.







































































ObjectiveBase inputs and supporting capabilitiesRoute decisionsAcceptance testReliable food storageIdentified foods, sound containers, pest control, seasonal records and clean handlingDry storage, tested drying, or another validated preservation process suited to the food and climateLoss and illness rates, edible reserve through a defined lean intervalRepeatable hot-work materialsClay and other candidate minerals, prepared fuel, controlled airflow and temperature assessmentFiring bodies, refractories and furnace lining must be tested separatelySeveral batches survive their intended heat, load and moisture conditionsUseful extracted metalSuitable ore, extraction chemistry, fuel or reductant, refractory vessel, separation and workability testsChoose by local ore and application; a copper-first or iron-first route has different costsReproducible material with measured properties sufficient for its actual jobReproducible mechanismsShared length standards, geometry, abrasives, cutting tools, suitable structural materials, joining and lubricationWooden machines can do selected jobs before a metal workshop; different loads require different bearings and wear surfacesIndependently made replacement parts fit and survive a specified dutyImproved precisionStable reference surfaces, alignment methods, cutting-edge materials, feed control and inspectionA workshop can improve its own tools incrementally; the first generation must be achievable with existing meansMeasured error and repeatability improve across independently built partsScaled mechanical powerA site-specific energy source, transmission, structure, maintenance and operatorsWater, wind, animal effort and other sources have different site and labour constraints; steam adds pressure-vessel and sealing demandsUseful output, uptime and maintenance cost under a recorded loadElectrical supply and instrumentsConductors, insulation, magnets, mechanical drive, calibrated comparisons and safe test methodsDemonstration current, reliable generation and an industrial distribution system are separate achievementsStable specified output, repeatable readings and repair by other workersControlled chemical supplyFeedstocks, separation and reaction methods, resistant vessels, mass records and contamination controlRequired purity depends on the next use; laboratory success is not bulk productionBatch consistency at the scale and purity needed by the consuming processSpaceflightProven structures, propulsion, guidance, power, tracking, computing, test facilities and trained operationsComponent tests, uncrewed flight trials and payload goals should expose separate dependenciesDefined flight outcome and independently checked telemetry, with failures analysedDefence missionSurvey instruments, long observation records, orbit models, target characterisation, space systems and coordinationChoose intervention against the specified object, timing and uncertainty; no single remembered device guarantees successQuantified mission effect and remaining uncertainty against the actual threat
The space branch cannot be made concrete until the asteroid specification is settled. R12 in Research Register supplies a real deflection demonstration, not the requirements for this fictional threat. First specify what departure humanity could already build and why that capacity was inadequate; otherwise the mission’s endpoint may contradict its opening.
How to assess an earlier innovation
Use a short comparison record: the problem, two routes, every input, required precision, available labour, time to a first useful result, maintenance, likely failure and who benefits. Then explain what remembered knowledge changes.
Knowledge can suggest a material substitution, remove an unnecessary intermediate step, guide an experiment or avoid a known failure. It cannot create a missing organism, local ore, energy source or cooperative workforce. Earlier feasibility and worthwhile adoption are different questions.
For example, the wooden spindle removes successful firing from one route. It may still be a poor investment if fibre preparation is the bottleneck or if a mobile group needs little fine yarn. A machine becomes a shortcut only when its entire process improves the relevant task.
A claimed historical wrong turn needs the same comparison under the resources, institutions and incentives of the people who chose it. The protagonist’s hindsight alone is not evidence that their choice was irrational.
Institutional dependencies
Communication and Exchange, Teaching and Knowledge Preservation, Measurement and Records and Sanitation and Camp Hygiene begin early. Larger production later needs resource agreements, dispute resolution, responsibility for shared equipment and succession.
The traveller’s mission succeeds only when capabilities survive his absence. Community production is verified separately from his own demonstrations.
Narrative scale
Days 1–28 cover immediate survival and first contact. The approved second-month outline follows independent seasonal preparation, practical testing and limited contact. Cooperation can develop later when repeated willing interaction and useful results justify it. Later parts should follow projects, migrations, generations and industrial programmes. Detail follows the dependency being tested, not a fixed calendar format.
Next chapter after revision
Month Two Outline covers Days 29–56 and was approved by the author on 3 October 2026. It keeps the traveller independent, prioritises cold-weather clothing and defence, and develops the atlatl through a disappointing early comparison followed by growing late interest. No trade, group provisioning or immediate recruitment supports his progress.
Day 29 begins from the actual Day 28 stock: inspect the green shaft candidates, prepare a compatible practice projectile only if suitable, and maintain food, water and fuel. A calendar date does not force a launch or large-game kill. Draft the daily work and introduce new capability pages from the approved outline, using Valley Map to maintain terrain, travel and camp continuity.
Opening week of Month 2 drafted
Days 29–35 now follow the approved outline in text. Use Survival Ledger for continuing stocks, First Month Ledger for the fixed Day 28 starting state, and Valley Map including its dated additions for locations. First launches remain erratic; the small bedding pad, comparison record and inspected retreat route do not solve winter clothing or food supply. Day 36 begins with the actual reduced reserve and unfinished batches rather than a fresh inventory.
Page scale and reflective rhythm
Page Scope and Organisation keeps equipment at the design-family level, with variants rather than one article per use. Structures and Places distinguishes construction knowledge from the local atlas. Measurement and Records is a skill; shared standards/calibration remain future systems.
Reflections appraises completed-day states at the approximate new/full moon milestones in Lunar Calendar. These reviews connect surviving capabilities, supply, danger and intention without advancing the event ledger.
Continuing from Day 40
Month Two Outline now records Days 36–40 (Moon 2 Days 7–11). The first observed atlatl comparison disappoints without closing off later interest. A repaired fish closure, one rabbit catch and a limited grass back panel are the new practical developments. Spear Throwing records local competence separately from the traveller’s atlatl practice; no community supply or shared production is gained.
The next work must confront the 1.31 kg kernel reserve, scarce loose binding and unfinished retting, pelt and clay trials. Food and fibre condition govern Days 41–42; scouting and lone-hunter failures belong to the following phase. A more consistent projectile, wider core coverage and a supplied refuge must still be earned before the Day 56 appraisal. The full-moon reflection remains scheduled for Day 44, not written from future outcomes.
Continuing from Day 45
Month Two Outline records Days 41–45. Shelter assessment has led to a limited return frame and partial covering, while acorn processing exposes the small vessel’s throughput cost. A selected 18 g fibre output is useful without completing the whole batch. The full-moon Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15 uses only Day 44 state.
The next bottlenecks are food collection, the roof’s upper junction and weather performance, whole-body insulation, redundant fire/water and a supplied retreat. The current 0.93 kg kernel reserve cannot finance prolonged hunting or simultaneous workshops. Short practice can continue when those needs allow; no observer’s interest supplies shared production.
Continuing from Day 50
Month Two Outline now includes earned shower repair, an aborted deer approach, two-sided coarse core coverage and a limited crown pad. These improve particular tasks while leaving the food buffer short. Atlatl consistency, proper foot protection, spare ignition, a second water vessel and a supplied retreat remain dependent work. No alliance or reliable ceramic production is established. Subsequent industry still needs surplus and resilience, not a longer catalogue of prototypes.
Workshop foundations — Days 51–55
The next five entries put reproducible stock, ground contact, duplicate ignition, repeated vessel manufacture and an observable projectile trial ahead of extended routine narration. Wooden Mallet and Wooden Splitting Wedge begin a limited route to useful wooden blanks; Plant-Fibre Footwear has a narrow test rather than a solved winter outfit. Two independently made ignition kits and two tested bark vessels reduce particular interruptions while remaining at the same camp.
Day 55’s observer interest is an opening for future learning, with no cooperation yet demonstrated. The next scale change should follow a technical project and its adoption, keeping Teaching and Knowledge Preservation central. Remembered knowledge becomes a civilisation’s capability only when other people can choose, reproduce, maintain and extend useful work.

09_reference/day-40-technology-and-winte.title: Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit
09_reference/day-40-technology-and-winte.content:
Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit
Finding
At Moon 2 Day 11 - A Covering That Can Be Worn, the traveller has a Palaeolithic subsistence toolkit with a few later or geographically distant experiments. A Middle Palaeolithic comparison best describes much of his everyday working equipment; the eyed needle and trial spear-thrower bring Upper Palaeolithic comparisons. No single archaeological era possessed precisely this assemblage. He is not at a Neolithic level: there is no farming, stockkeeping, reliable pottery production or settled food surplus.
His knowledge exceeds his production capacity. A leaking pot, an erratic dart and a dry-fit grass panel are genuine experiments, but they do not establish dependable cooking ceramics, hunting or cold-weather clothing. His seasonal resilience is well below what we should give an experienced local group in the narrative. This is an inference from his recorded limitations, not a measured ranking of cultures.
The greatest omission is a credible cold-season living system. Better shelter must become an immediate work programme, alongside insulation, food and protected fuel. Another attractive implement will not solve that gap.
Historical comparison
Dates below are examples of evidence, not invention dates or compulsory technological stages. Organic objects preserve unevenly; absence at a site cannot prove that its inhabitants lacked a technique. BP dates are approximate years before present, normally 1950. Global parallels do not establish presence in this fictional Iberian valley.


















































Capability actually recordedArchaeological comparisonConsequence for the handbookSimple flakes, scraper, chopper and rough bifaceThese belong to technological traditions much older than the setting. An object can resemble an Oldowan or Acheulean form without making its maker a member of that archaeological culture; see R04The existing page names should describe forms or teaching routes, not a sequence of eras he has personally completedWooden spear and elementary woodworkingPreserved Pleistocene weapons and worked wood substantially predate 40,000 BP. Schöningen has an unusually varied assemblage (R31); its dating has been revised and remains a research issueWoodworking is a major practical branch. A wooden point is credible, and local composite stone-pointed spears are also defensible (R21)Managed fire, hafting, adhesive and cordageNeanderthal fire-making evidence and manufactured adhesives already appear in the register. The Abri du Maras three-ply cord is associated with roughly 52,000–41,000-year-old deposits (Hardy et al., 2020)He cannot credibly astonish competent neighbours merely by displaying a cord or haft. His local material judgement can still be inferiorPlant bedding, coiling and twining trialsPlant bedding is documented at Sibudu around 77,000 BP and Border Cave at least 200,000 years ago (R24, R29). The latter is grass bedding, not proof of woven matsInsulation is an ancient foundation, not an optional modern comfort. A basket or fish cage does not by itself establish a Mesolithic package; the exact mechanisms remain authored trialsBone awl, usable eyed needle and limited sewingA 2024 synthesis places early eyed needles around 40,000 cal BP in Siberia and later in Europe; it also explains why awls can support fitted clothing without needle eyes (R28)The Day 12 needle is a plausible knowledgeable traveller’s experiment, not an established local Neanderthal possession. Its manufacturing success merits more scrutiny than its simple appearance suggestsAtlatl with one green, blunt, unfletched practice dartDirect European thrower evidence in R16 is later than the setting. A 2023 impact-fracture study argues for thrower use at Maisières-Canal around 31,000 BP (R27); this is indirect inference from stone armaturesPotential novelty remains plausible, earlier absence unproven. Current performance earns no hunting advantage; experienced hand throwing matters (R17)Clay vessels: one failed pot and two unfired samplesXianrendong pottery was made by foragers around 20,000–19,000 cal BP, long before agriculture (Wu et al., 2012)Pottery need not wait for farming. Here it remains an attempted anticipatory innovation; a useful water-holding vessel and a thermally reliable cooking pot are separate achievementsSmall traps, intermittent fishing and a predominantly gathered dietPerishable gear is particularly hard to date. Neither cordage nor a woven impression establishes this exact rear-cap fish cage, figure-4 mechanism or spring snareKeep those designs labelled as physical trials. Judge yield, maintenance and seasonal access rather than assigning a confident earliest date to every modern named mechanism
Neanderthal hide-working also deserves more weight. Specialized rib smoothers from French Neanderthal contexts were interpreted through comparison and experiments as hide-working tools (Soressi et al., 2013). This supports portraying skilled material workers, while leaving their precise garments and treatments uncertain. No borrowed tool, skin or instruction is credited to the traveller.
Winter: what the current camp does not supply
An open lean-to can be useful temporary cover. The label alone cannot determine whether a particular winter stay is possible. In this story, the combination of exposed sleeping space, modest bedding, bare front torso/head/feet and a very short food buffer makes it an inadequate planned winter home. Rain and wind are dangerous even before severe frost: wet exposure can cause hypothermia at cool temperatures (CDC). Local minimum temperatures, rain, wind and snow still require a narrower setting decision; there is no defensible universal wall thickness or survival temperature for the current shelter.
At Day 40 there are 1.31 kg of edible kernels, about 2.6 recent half-kilogram rations, and 24 kg usable dry wood. These are author-model stocks, not independently validated energetic margins. The grass garment covers only the back, the new rabbit pelt is unfinished, the second fibre batch is still processing and the fallback bench has no shelter or cache. See Survival Ledger.
The next structure should be a compact, substantially enclosed sleeping shelter with a stable frame, overlapping weather cover, wind protection, a controllable entrance and a whole-body bed that stays dry after compression. Choose between rebuilding at the present terrace and a separately inspected better site; a convenient cave must not appear by assumption. Survey drainage, overhead hazards, access and escape before committing scarce labour. Thick debris is labour and bulk, not a free substitute for sound framing or waterproofing.
A low framed/debris sleeping chamber is a better near-term candidate than a log house, masonry room or animal-hide tent. Sound fallen pieces, natural forks and supported joints may reduce the need for long structural lashings; they still need inspection and stability checks. The present fallen limb can be retained only if sound. Thin cross-cover, overlapping roof material and bulky bed fill are separate jobs and separate allocations. Do not make a short supply of fine nettle line carry an entire new building by assumption.
Keep combustion outside the proposed small combustible sleeping enclosure. Bringing the hearth inside is a different engineering problem involving exhaust, air supply, sparks and clearances; a smoke hole does not certify it. Wood combustion can accumulate carbon monoxide in enclosed or partly enclosed spaces (CDC). Rebuilding cannot silently move existing installations on Valley Map.
Missing foundations and priority order

Dry sleep and usable insulation. Collect sufficient cover and bedding in separate lots; assess compressed bedding, leaks, draughts and morning damp. Extend practical core protection and make modest head/foot trials. Dry rawhide is not supple, wet-resilient leather. Hide conditioning needs materials, work and tests, with a plant-based fallback if captures fail.
Seasonal calories and storage. The recurring productive hazel circuit is the largest unverified resource assumption. Research its plausibility at this place/date and model reduced access and diminishing returns. Expand only positively identified, locally available foods; refine the already introduced acorn processing and record its water/fuel costs. Protected nut storage needs drying, pest checks and loss records. Unvalidated smoked meat cannot become winter rations (R07).
Protected fuel, tinder and redundancy. Cover and inspect fuel; colder nights and wet weather change consumption. Protect an independently usable ignition provision and build a second tested water vessel. A prototype does not provide a spare. Shelter materials, cord, ordinary fuel and experimental firing compete for the same labour and stock.
Woodworking and repair capacity. Controlled splitting, wedges, wooden striking tools, abrasion and tested frame joints could give better returns than another weapon. Introduce only techniques and equipment actually needed for the chosen build, with wood selection and load checks. A handaxe is not automatically a convenient felling axe.
A supplied retreat and clean camp. The fallback site needs its own earned minimal cover, tinder and provisions before it offers much security. Keep processing waste and attractants away from sleep and reserve food. Escape and observation are feasible goals; a few brush obstacles cannot defend him against several determined people.

Not currently glaring omissions: metallurgy, agriculture, domestication, a bow, a large kiln or a loom. Each demands inputs and maintenance he lacks. A grinding/pounding setup, food carriers and cord production are worth improving when they relieve a measured bottleneck. Measurement is already a skill; his personal comparison staff can improve repeatability without pretending he has calibrated units.
Recommended adjustment to the remaining month
Read this alongside Month Two Outline. Preserve independent acquisition, cautious contact and the eventual narrowing atlatl gap, but make cold-season preparation the main work allocation.

Days 41–42: maintain food supply; appraise the existing shelter and possible construction site; check material availability and plan a staged build. Care for the pelt and inspect retting. Short projectile practice proceeds only within the actual budget.
Days 43–49: devote multiple recorded work sessions to framing, weather cover, bedding and clothing, then repairs under ordinary weather. Hunting attempts can be brief or aborted; they must not crowd out the build. Defer firing if it consumes the ordinary fuel reserve or dry-work space.
Days 50–56: improve observed failures, protected stores, spare fire/water provisions and the refuge. Let steadier casts attract interest during short practice. No deer kill or guaranteed food surplus is required.

The Day 44 reflection should assess shelter work, diminishing food access and labour choices against the actual completed ledger. By Day 56 the intended outcome is a materially better, inspected cold-weather camp, not a declared winter solution. If food, materials or weather prevent that result, the next strategic choice must explicitly include further relocation research rather than relying on narrative optimism.
Longer horizon
Remaining alone is a valid month-two constraint. Eventually, rebuilding civilisation needs distributed labour, shared standards, seasonal support and knowledge reproduced by other people. The bottleneck will move from remembering designs to supporting workshops and recovering from failure. Archaeological societies were not solitary inventors equipped with one specimen of each named object. Track the ability to maintain a working system alongside the growing topic index.

09_reference/first-month-ledger.title: First Month Ledger
09_reference/first-month-ledger.content:
First Month Ledger
Scope and assumptions
This is a generated author continuity model, not measured survival performance. Daily frontmatter is the source of truth. Regenerate with python tools/update_views.py after editing events, then run python tools/validate_vault.py. The original prose is preserved in the pre-revision archive.
The fictional valley has productive hazel patches within a manageable daily circuit in early autumn. Kernel weights are edible mass after shelling; shells are excluded. Gathering and processing take daily labour. Recorded collection is a setting assumption requiring palaeoecological and field review, not a demonstrated regional yield. No imported seed, store or unexplained food subsidy is counted.
The energy column uses explicit rough working assumptions: 6 kcal/g hazelnut kernels, 1.5 kcal/g dressed game or fish, and 2 kcal/g wet acorn meal. These are not extracted food-composition values (see R13 in Research Register). Wet meal composition is especially uncertain. Against an illustrative 2,500–3,500 kcal/day activity requirement, early days can be deficient and later entries are not all assured adequate. Cold, body size, illness, digestibility and work could change the balance. Internal conservation cannot prove long-term health or a realistic gathering rate.
Fuel is dry usable wood mass, excluding wet collected material. Collection and burn estimates are authored, without calorimeter or weather validation. Water columns count completed treatment and untreated drinking separately; evaporation and other water uses are not modelled. Initial untreated drinking is a survival risk, not a recommended procedure. Zero untreated intake means treatment was recorded, not independently certified.
Daily food continuity
Kernel use includes an explicitly recorded damp loss on Day 13. All retained fresh game is cooked and consumed on its catch day, including the limited 0.90 kg fox lot on Day 23. Discarded trimming is excluded from edible inputs. Acorns enter as 0.40 kg unprocessed input on Day 17, convert to 0.65 kg wet meal on Day 18 (water adds mass), and are eaten over Days 18–19. The input lot contributes no calories before processing.

Work and sleep allowances leave other time for meals, pauses and unavoidable interruptions. They are estimates, not proof of physical feasibility. Important events and limits

Day 3: first ignition; the fire kit needs continued maintenance. Stored heat is not permanent access to fire.
Days 4–5: first vessel heat trial fails, then repair permits recorded boiling. Day 9 wear interrupts treatment; Day 10 repairs restore it.
Day 7: the awl works. A needle attempt fails; a usable eyed needle follows on Day 12.
Days 9–10: the first rabbit pelt becomes a small carrying sling; the load test is under one kilogram.
Days 11–16: a small pot is shaped, dried, fired, cooled and rejected for leakage. It remains a non-food sample; no ceramic cooking asset is counted.
Days 4–20: the nettle batch is retted, processed in two halves, and partly made into cord. The first processing date is Day 16; elapsed time is twelve days, not a universal recipe.
Days 13–14 and 24: small hides become a pelvic pad and narrow shoulder panel. They do not amount to a winter coat.
Day 21: a wooden spindle bypasses ceramic success. A few metres of single yarn do not demonstrate a sustained productivity improvement.
Day 23: the damaged snare is removed. A limited fox meat lot is cooked and eaten, with additional work and fuel; its damaged pelt becomes a limited panel on Day 24.
Day 25: the first approach is rebuffed. Samples and the first spindle are abandoned during retreat, not accepted gifts. Day 26 records self-repair and planning, with no fibre exchange or shared teaching. No communal provisions or adoption are established.
Days 27–28: a replacement spindle is made. Two green dart candidates, a feather lot and an untested wooden atlatl remain distinct assets.

The earliest practical review should test food yield, bark-vessel reliability, heating-stone selection, fibre throughput and rawhide performance. Research Register records the evidence gaps; Civilisation Roadmap keeps later development tied to surplus and verified capabilities.

09_reference/illustration-continuity.title: Illustration Continuity
09_reference/illustration-continuity.content:
Illustration Continuity
Approved character and style
The user selected the watercolour-and-ink Day 1 image on 1 October 2026 and approved the protagonist’s appearance. Use _Artwork/survival/day-01.png as the primary visual reference in every later Survival scene. Do not redesign him from a text description alone.

Preserve his recognisable facial profile, nose and brow, dark wavy ear-length hair, short dark beard/stubble, skin tone and lean sinewy build. His apparent age in this reference is about thirty; the ageless premise does not mean an artificial young face. Retain ordinary human proportions. Use smooth transparent watercolour for skin and selective fine ink around contours; avoid dense hatching, repeated dots or etched grooves that can read as scars or patterned skin.
The approved style combines fine brown ink with luminous watercolour, warm paper texture, restrained earth colours and softly dissolved margins. Keep a wide approximately 16:9 composition and a readable action. Facial views, light and viewpoint can vary; identity remains stable. Avoid switching to photography, oil painting, engraving or fantasy effects.
Match a specific moment in the day
Read the entire day’s narrative and its frontmatter, then check the preceding day’s First Month Ledger state. Select one actual action. Do not illustrate every outcome as a montage or equip the morning traveller with objects he only makes that afternoon.
Define the moment, allowed objects, forbidden future objects, clothing, unfinished processes and weather before generation. A construction can be shown in progress without claiming a functioning capability. Scenes should distinguish a failed test from a successful one.
Use the original approved Day 1 image for character and style in new scenes. A separate established equipment plate may additionally supply object geometry only when needed; record that limited role and do not import its layout, lettering or cutaway into the narrative. Describe the current camp and objects in the day-specific brief, using the ledger and narrative to establish their state. Do not pass the preceding day’s illustration forward as a reference. Keep object descriptions concrete about material, scale, unfinished work and permitted use.
First ten scenes




























































DayOpening sceneContinuity constraints1Building the provisional debris shelterRough bark waist panels, simple flakes, hazelnuts; no fire2Cutting the fireboard notchUnhafted flake and prepared bow-drill parts; no ember, vessel or spear3Transferring the first tiny flame from tinderBow drill set aside; fire outside the dry shelter; no water vessel or animal products4Inspecting and emptying the leaking bark vesselSmall folded birch-bark tray, plain wooden spear, limited bark shoulder screen; no boil5Checking a later batch after the vessel repairSmall reinforced tray and hot stones, surface-wide boiling; wooden handling sticks and digging stick6Adjusting the first squirrel pelt on the frameOne small pelt, tiny cleaned bones and unprocessed tendon; no needle, awl, made sinew thread, bags or stored meat7Testing a tiny bone awl on supported scrap hideA short sinew lot and broken eye attempt; no usable eyed needle or case8Adjusting the first small tool-case seamSquirrel rawhide folded into a palm-sized case, pre-pierced holes and hand-guided bark line; no usable needle9Adjusting supports on the juvenile-rabbit panelSmall clean panel reserved for tomorrow’s carrier; no finished sling or skin garment10Testing the carrying cradle with a modest blunt loadRabbit rawhide cradle, separate plant-cord strap and a few small stones; load below one kilogram, no skin garment
The hearth is outside the illustrated framing on Days 5–10. Their absence from the picture does not remove them from the narrative. A scene need not show the whole camp’s inventory.
Scenes for Days 11–15



































DaySelected momentContinuity constraints11Forming the small pinch vessel at the uphill work spotDamp clay and comparison strips; no fired vessel or new fur clothing12Inspecting the polished intact needle eye before threadingSmall bone needle and pre-pierced scrap; no thread connection or oversized awl13The brief unsuccessful spear-fishing trial in river shallowsStable ankle-deep footing, continuous wooden point, no catch; unfinished fur pad remains at camp14Spreading fresh dry litter over the shelter bedLow interior viewpoint, small fitted pelvic pad over remaining bark coverage; no indoor fire15Watching the supervised firing trial burn down at duskSame broad open pinch cup on a visible stone support in the separate cleared outside firing place; pot stays hot, untested and in place
Weather follows the current entries: cool autumn conditions, a light frost on the upper slope on Day 13, and damp sheltered ground. Do not infer heavy snow or river ice from the older filenames. Scene descriptions follow the revised page bodies and ledger, including no crayfish meal on Day 11 and no fish catch on Day 13.
Scenes for Days 16–20



































DaySelected momentContinuity constraints16Extracting nettle-fibre ribbons at the downstream rinsing placeModest fibre yield and separate woody cores; camp furniture remains above the river, cracked pot is not cookware17Twisting a measured fibre portion into light lineFine hand-made cord with remaining fibre separate; no heavy rope, basket, billet or finished biface18Inspecting the old antler fragment on the upstream excursionWeathered red-deer fragment away from an active kill; no fresh carcass, hunt or prepared billet yet19Inspecting the retained rough biface beside an ordinary flakeAsymmetrical unhafted tool and broken trial blank; unused percussors and unfinished basket outside the crop20Testing the small completed willow basket with a blunt loadModest handmade carrier with two small rounded stones; later cage and adhesive work outside this moment
Days 16–20 retain the small fitted pelvic fur pad over bark waist coverage and the limited single-shoulder bark screen. They do not acquire a large hide or full fur garment. Day 16 uses the downstream rinsing place; Day 18 shows the upstream route. Neither moves the shelter or hearths from the drained camp terrace. Close craft views omit fixed features that are outside the frame.
The first pot remains a rejected, leaking non-food specimen after Day 16. The Day 20 fishing cage is an unfinished land-based prototype in the text, and is not shown before its construction. Cord, basket, antler and biface states follow the selected moment rather than all end-of-day possessions.
Scenes for Days 21–28


















































DaySelected momentContinuity constraints21Checking the first wooden whorl’s fit and balanceOne small wooden disk and shaft; unthreaded before the fibre trial, no ceramic success inferred22Removing the single small fish through the opened rear access of the willow cageIntact cylinder and inward entrance funnel match the equipment plate; untied rear cap beside it, one small catch23Inspecting the repaired little squirrel-hide pouchTiny mouse-skin edge patch; the fox pelt is still drying elsewhere, not worn24Adjusting the narrow fox shoulder panel’s tiesLimited coverage over one shoulder; no whole hide, coat or replacement of the older waist coverage25Backing away from a hafted stone-pointed spear after the failed spinning pitchLocal Neanderthal has a knapped stone point and close natural bindings; traveller’s spear remains plain wood and is cached outside frame. Spindle and samples abandoned; no accepted gift26Rebinding the knife alone at the traveller’s own campExisting cord reused, plain wooden spear accessible; no shared spindle lesson or new thrower yet27Placing the two green shaft candidates under coverPlain blunt unfletched rods; no completed darts, dry seasoned shafts or new drying rack28Inspecting grain around the integral wooden hookOne-piece wooden thrower, short bark grip binding, no launch or hunting success
The Day 24 fox panel is narrow and remains so through Day 28. The fitted rabbit pelvic pad, bark waist panels and limited bark screen continue to supply their separate coverage. Do not enlarge the fox skin into a poncho or whole torso garment.
Day 25 shows open ground outside the neighbouring living area. The traveller withdraws when warned; no shelter, work spot or hearth moves to this location. Day 26 returns to his own camp. Local cordage and material handling remain skilled, and the failed pitch does not establish acceptance or a shared trial.
Local hair, skin, gender, individual features and plain hide wraps are casting choices, not documented biographies. Use R18 for actual Neanderthal craniofacial and bodily features: low receding forehead, prominent brow ridge, projecting midface, substantial nose, weak chin and compact robust build with relatively short distal limbs. Draw capable hands and ordinary upright posture, with individual expressions. Neither sapiens faces in fur nor stooped ape-like caricatures are suitable. Threat belongs to the situation, not their anatomy or species.
Day 27 replaces the spindle abandoned during retreat on Day 25. The two green shaft candidates, feather lot and partly shaped thrower are separate inputs. Day 28’s assembled thrower has an integral wooden hook, not an added antler spur; only static seating is tested in the narrative. The selected illustration precedes that seating test and shows grain inspection, with no projectile in frame.
Setting and material scale
Use World and Setting Specification. The same terrace sits above the river, with a low fallen-limb debris shelter and interrupted woodland among open rocky slopes. The season is early autumn; do not add winter snow, modern agriculture, a village or dense uniform forest.
R15 in Research Register supports a general mosaic of open ground and scattered woods. Exact trees, local hazel productivity, the terrace and weather remain fictional choices; these pictures are not archaeological reconstructions of an identified site.
Important materials should be readable: bark is a folded or overlapping plant sheet, not cloth; a plain wooden spear has a point continuous with its shaft; an unhafted flake has no fitted handle. The first water vessel is about 0.6 litres and should be shown at a modest hand-relative scale. One squirrel cannot supply a large-mammal hide, a pile of long bones or a coil of finished thread.
Images are narrative illustrations rather than dimensioned manufacturing drawings. Consult reference pages for the method, test and remaining practical evidence gaps.
Camera and camp geography for Days 11–15
Change the viewpoint to suit the day’s action. Day 13’s fishing trial takes place at stable river shallows below the terrace; camp furniture does not follow the traveller there. Day 14 is viewed from low inside the shelter looking outward. These are views of the same setting, not new camps.
Retain the relationships established in the text and original illustration: the fallen-limb shelter is on drained ground above the river; the craft spot is uphill of the ordinary hearth; the ordinary hearth is outside the shelter; drying and animal processing occupy their separate dirty-material side. The original outward camp view places the shelter toward the left and the valley downhill toward the right. That screen arrangement applies to that viewpoint, not to every camera position. Compass bearings are now fixed by Valley Map: the camp slope and shelter entrance face broadly southeast, with the larger river to the east. The original screen arrangement belongs to an east/southeast-facing view. Exact metre distances remain unspecified; enlarged map icons do not provide them.
Day 14 introduces a separate outside experimental firing place, used on Day 15. Keep its load and fuel distinct from the ordinary food-and-water hearth. Do not place either fire beside the leaf bedding. Unneeded fixed features can remain outside the image instead of being moved to fit the composition.
The clothing changes only when recorded. Days 11–13 retain the bark waist panels and limited bark shoulder screen; Day 13’s small fur pad is unfinished. Days 14–15 may show the fitted small pelvic pad with limited extensions and adjustable ties, with bark still supplying the remaining waist coverage. It does not become a fur skirt, torso garment or large-animal hide.
Avoiding accumulated artifacts
Repeated edits can change fine details or retain defects from a reference. They are a plausible contributor to the artifacts observed in Days 5–6, although the images alone do not establish the cause.
Generate each day independently from the original Day 1 reference. The reference fixes identity and style; the text supplies the new action and current equipment. Ask for softly washed skin, subtle paper grain and selective ink, without pervasive hatch patterns. Keep one principal action and omit unused equipment from the frame to reduce opportunities for invented or oversized props.
If a generated scene has a defect, revise the brief and generate a fresh scene from Day 1. Do not feed the defective scene back through successive corrections. This reduces the chance of carrying an error forward while preserving the approved appearance. Review each result before selecting it.
Save the selected PNG directly, without recompressing or repeatedly resaving it. File copying preserves the output bytes; fresh generation addresses changes introduced by rendering, a separate issue from file compression.
Review and embedding workflow

Generate a fresh scene with the original Day 1 character/style reference and the day-specific brief.
Inspect the face, hands, action, material scale, tool ends, clothing, setting and unwanted texture. If necessary, revise the brief and regenerate from Day 1; do not chain edits.
Save the selected image inside _Artwork/survival with a day-specific filename. Preserve previous versions if a selected image is later replaced.
Set illustration, illustration_scene and illustration_checked_on in the day’s metadata. Embed the local image at the beginning of the body with standard Markdown. Illustration-only work preserves prose; an authorised narrative revision must first establish the new text and resource events, then recheck any retained artwork.
Record prompts, input roles, fresh retries, any corrections and selected outputs in _Artwork/survival/generation-prompts.json.
Run the vault validator and rebuild exports. It checks local image existence and agreement with metadata; visual accuracy still needs human inspection.

These first six images were generated with the built-in image-generation tool. Day 1 reuses the approved image; Days 2–6 are new scenes. Days 5–6 received a correction for material scale and plain wooden tool ends. The reviewed status here means editorial continuity review, not validation of a reconstructed environment or a field method.
Days 7–10 were generated with the built-in image-generation tool using only the original Day 1 image as their reference. Days 8 and 9 each required a fresh replacement to remove distracting or incorrectly scaled props; neither replacement used the rejected image. All four selected outputs have zero edit passes. Their scenes are embedded in the daily pages and collected in _Artwork/survival/days-07-10.md.
Days 11–15 follow the same independent-generation workflow, with views chosen around the day’s action. Two needle close-ups were rejected for scale or thread-connection errors; the selected Day 12 scene shows the polished eye being inspected before threading. A firing view was replaced to retain the Day 11 pinch cup’s broad open shape and show its stone support clearly. No rejected image was passed forward as a reference. All five selected PNGs have zero edit passes and unchanged source-copy hashes; they are embedded in the daily pages and collected in _Artwork/survival/days-11-15.md. Failed network requests and visual rejections are recorded separately in the prompt manifest.
Days 16–20 were generated afresh with the built-in image tool and only the original Day 1 reference. Seven rendered outputs were discarded after visual review; one network failure was recorded separately. Revised briefs were regenerated from Day 1 rather than edited from rejected scenes. All five selected PNGs have zero edit passes and verified unchanged source-copy hashes. Their scenes are embedded in the daily pages and collected in _Artwork/survival/days-16-20.md.
Days 21–28 were generated independently with the built-in image tool and only the original Day 1 reference. The prompt manifest records 2 discarded rendered outputs, 0 service failures and any interrupted requests separately. The original eight PNGs had zero edit passes and verified source-copy hashes. This is historical generation provenance: the 3 October contact revision supersedes Days 22, 25 and 26, while retaining the other scenes after checking them against the revised text. The current selection is in _Artwork/survival/days-21-28.md.
Equipment, skills and process compositions
Follow Category Specification when choosing a plate’s subject. Equipment illustrations show the apparatus and useful form, joint or construction details; skill illustrations show a practised operation or controlled comparison; process and system illustrations show stages, operating relationships and tests. An equipment page can still use a construction sequence, and changing its category does not require discarding an accurate approved image.
The current manual plate index and its equipment, skill and process galleries use the current categories. Original PNGs and generation prompts stay in their batch folders to preserve provenance. Their page links follow the migrated notes. The same image does not become a second piece of equipment merely because it appears in two galleries.
Original tools illustration batch
The original batch provided 19 isolated tool plates, now linked to equipment pages in 05_Tools and Equipment. The style is a mid-century practical manual: fine navy ink, warm ivory paper, clear uppercase labels and restrained material hatching. Small detail views explain an eye, tip, socket or whorl component where helpful. The first seven generated plates are monochrome; following the user’s update, the remaining twelve have pastel material washes. Use the pastel treatment as the default for future equipment plates: pale honey or ochre for wood, cool grey-blue and lavender for stone, and straw or sage for woven plant material.
The bone-awl plate is the fixed style reference where an image input is used. Its role is typography, paper, linework and layout; each new brief supplies the different object’s shape. Some plates were generated from text alone. Never use the immediately preceding plate as the next reference or repeatedly edit a flawed output.
Read the full equipment page before choosing a design. The wooden spindle whorl is stored under Fibre Equipment, alongside its functional role rather than a presumed clay material. The clay vessel is the cracked rejected specimen described in the first month. The wooden spear has a point continuous with its shaft; its legacy title does not require a blackened tip. The harpoon point and multi-pronged fishing spear remain illustrative planned designs, and the thrower remains untested. An illustration does not change demonstration or acquisition status.
Feature callouts should identify visible parts and have readable leaders to those parts. Do not invent dimensions, operating capacities or historical dates. These plates communicate form and material; the text supplies the manufacturing framework and required tests. Woven patterns and proposed designs remain illustrative rather than validated fabrication specifications.
The selected plates are in _Artwork/tools. The gallery collects the complete set; _Artwork/tools/generation-prompts.json records prompts, references, fresh retries and source-copy hashes. All selected outputs were rendered afresh and have zero edit passes.
Original technology illustration batch
The original technology batch provided 27 illustrations in the approved manual style: navy ink, warm ivory paper and restrained pastel material washes. Following the category revision, 11 illustrate equipment, two illustrate skills and 14 illustrate processes or systems. The artwork remains attached to its subject. The digging-stick plate was the fixed style reference where an image input was used. Every selected plate was a fresh generation; none used a preceding generated scene as its reference.
Choose the composition around the operation. Use a short sequence for forming, drying, firing, cooling or material preparation; an enlarged detail for folds, seams and joints; a cutaway for a conceptual firing chamber; and a component study when the complete design remains unresolved. Keep the focal arrangement clear and labels concise. The text retains the full method, tests and limitations.
Development status must remain legible. Pottery ends in a leakage test reflecting the rejected first-month specimen. The kiln is labelled as a concept. The thrower remains assembled but untested, and the dart-making plate shows shaft candidates and a planned blunt trial. Drying equipment shows its pelt-processing role. Images do not change acquisitions or demonstrations.
The two trap plates have deliberately limited scope. The deadfall plate shows candidate members and a separate test stone; the snare plate studies the running-loop component. Neither supplies a verified complete construction drawing or establishes operating performance. The pages’ existing experimental requirements still apply.
Review supports, heat paths, material states, feature leaders and relationships between parts, in addition to lettering and style. Fresh replacements clarified non-combustible supports in the open-firing plates. An assembled deadfall overview was discarded because its support relationship was misleading. If an image service rejects a detailed plate, narrow it to a faithful useful material or component study and record that scope. Do not replace a rejected design with an inaccurate functioning-looking mechanism.
The complete original batch is in its gallery, with current page categories and links. _Artwork/technologies/generation-prompts.json records selected outputs, full prompts, earlier attempts, fixed references and PNG copy hashes. Images explain the authored framework; they are not dimensioned manufacturing drawings or archaeological identification plates.
Contact revision — 3 October 2026
The approved Day 1 remains the traveller’s identity and style source. New Day 22 uses the fishing-cage equipment plate solely for object geometry: retrieve through the rear access, not the entrance funnel, with intact side walls. Day 25 replaces the overly friendly contact picture with a warning and withdrawal, with anatomical Neanderthal features. Day 26’s former spindle-handling scene is shelved because the shared trial no longer occurs; its replacement shows self-repair and defensive awareness at his own camp. The narrow fox panel remains on his left shoulder from Day 24 onward.
The snare component plate is replaced with a tied fixed terminal eye, visible knot and tail, and a separately traceable running strand through that eye. The source is an overhand loop on a bight (R20), not a free-standing toroidal ring. This remains a component study, not certification of the full spring mechanism.
Original selections and prompt records are preserved in the shelved-art gallery. The revision gallery and complete prompts record new selections and review limits. Fresh replacements use the original references, never a rejected output.
Day 25 spear selection — later update on 3 October 2026
The user selected the earlier stone-pointed version after an evidence check (R21). Its original rendering is restored without edits, as _Artwork/survival/day-25-v3-stone-point.png. The prior wooden-pointed selection is shelved. Distinguish ownership in every future scene: the local man has a hafted stone point; the traveller retains the plain integral wooden point until he actually makes or acquires something else. The warning, retreat and resource losses are unchanged. The original prompt requested wood, so the restored output’s stone point is recorded as a user-approved variation supported by revised text, not a newly generated image.
Area map — 3 October 2026
Use Valley Map as the written spatial authority and Day 28 graphical overview. North is up; the stream runs east to a south-flowing larger river. Retting is downstream of drinking collection, and the fish cage is at the western river margin below the confluence. Both camps are west of the larger river; the contact route passes west around the rocky spur. A scene from another camera changes screen positions, not these terrain relationships. The camp inset keeps the craft spot upslope of the outside hearth, the dirty flank separate and experimental firing on its own bare patch. Future fixed constructions require dated additions and updated state maps.
Days 29–35: selected scenes — 4 October 2026
The text-only commission is superseded by seven independent images for continuous Days 29–35, now titled Moon 1 Day 29 and Moon 2 Days 1–6. Each uses the original Day 1 protagonist/style reference; Day 35 additionally uses the new mat plate for flat structure only. No preceding daily scene or rejected image is used as input.













































Continuous daySelected momentLimits retained29Making the bark comparison register beside the reference staffEdible kernels; intact staff, no calibrated units30Inspecting the green dart’s rear seat between first erratic castsUnfletched experiment; front and thrower outside crop31Stopping with the spear low while two distant figures watchNo approach, alliance or attack32Making the small twining sampleNo full mat or wearable covering yet33Inspecting the fallback benchNo shelter, supply cache or water provision; continuous wooden spear34Repairing the windward shelter covering in rainSame shelter, separate outside hearth; no new coat35Lifting the first small flat bedding padLimited partial-bed size; no mattress, folded trough or cloak
The current selections, all complete prompts, nine rejected outputs, input roles and exact PNG source-copy hashes are in _Artwork/2026-10-04. The twelve new manual/place plates use the fixed digging-stick reference for style only. Atlas plates have enlarged illustrative features, not surveyed distances or extra possessions. The camp plate shows area relationships without inventing a large hide; the sanitation plate is a separation principle, not a second geographical authority. The subsequently commissioned Reflection frontispieces are recorded below; see Reflection Artwork Proposals.
Page families and moon lighting — 4 October 2026
The same physical dart can pass between practice, fletched and pointed configurations within Atlatl Dart; only daily state permits a configuration in a scene. At Day 35 the specimen remains green, blunt and unfletched. Plant-Fibre Mats contains the small pad as one variant; no larger mat or garment appears through that day.
Use Lunar Calendar and daily model phase fields for future night scenes. Full-moon light depends on weather and sight lines; a new-moon reflection cannot justify a full lunar disk. Reflection snapshots refer to their milestone cutoff, not the current latest day. This revision reuses all existing artwork without generating or editing PNGs.
Reflection frontispieces — 4 October 2026
The approved section style is translucent watercolour, matte gouache and sparse graphite/fine brown contour ink on toned paper. Deeper tonal masses, generous negative space and an introspective composition distinguish these frontispieces from daily action scenes. Each selected picture was rendered independently from the original Day 1 identity reference; Reflection 02 additionally uses Day 15 solely for cup/support geometry, and Reflection 03 uses the fixed atlatl plate solely for launcher geometry. Four earlier outputs were rejected for an overly literal daily-illustration treatment, geographical/state problems or an invented cup handle. No selected or rejected Reflection is passed forward as an input.
Arrival has no fire, moon disk, food reserve, vessel, spear or animal products. The first full-moon review keeps the cup cooling, untouched and untested on the separate firing support; it shows no crack or prepared nettle fibre. The next new-moon review has the blunt unfletched green dart, unused feathers, rejected pot and limited fox shoulder panel, but no Day 31 observers, new batch, bedding mat, clay comparison pair or supplied fallback bench. New-moon darkness is not lit by a full moon.
The selected series links all three pages. Full prompts, limited reference roles, retries and unchanged PNG source-copy hashes are in _Artwork/reflections/generation-prompts.json. Embedding preserves the authored reflections, snapshot tables and resource history. A frontispiece interprets the recorded state; it grants no extra demonstration or possession.
Reflection 03 anatomy correction — 4 October 2026
The original selection was shelved after an apparent third leg was identified. Its replacement was rendered independently from the original identity and launcher references, with a simple seated pose on a low natural rock. Both thighs, knees, shins and feet were visually traced before selection. The final practice dart remains blunt and unfletched. The two correction attempts and superseded selection are recorded in the prompt manifest; no rejected output was passed forward. Reflection text and inventories are unchanged.
Skill plates — 5 October 2026
The new skill series uses navy ink, restrained pastel washes, ivory paper and sparse labels, with the original digging-stick plate as the style reference. Existing Simple Hafting and Bifacial Knapping images are retained. Skill illustrations explain a technique or judgement; generic clothed demonstration figures are not the traveller’s dated wardrobe, a local group’s exact dress or proof of skill mastery. Plant and mushroom plates are observation studies, not identification keys or medical prescriptions. Terrain diagrams explain principles, not surveyed changes to the valley atlas.
All prompts, reference roles, rejected renders, selection records and unchanged PNG copy hashes are in the commission gallery. The original Day 1 reference anchors every new daily scene. No prior daily output is cumulatively edited. Mechanical mistakes or unwanted possessions trigger fresh compositions from the original inputs.
Commissioned scenes for Days 36–40 — 5 October 2026
The subsequent artwork commission uses independently rendered Day 1 identity and style references. Selected moments are rear-cap repair at the river-margin cage (36), the local adult’s hand-spear comparison with the traveller standing back (37), fleshing the rabbit pelt at the dirty frame (38), twining the grass sample (39), and dry fit checking the back panel near camp (40). Retried compositions use the original references again; rejected scenes are not passed forward.
The grass sample first appears on Day 39. The wearable roughly 0.5 by 0.6 m grass back panel appears only after Day 40 construction; it has soft hanging grass foundations, two paired-yarn retaining rows and modest cord fastenings, with an open front. It is distinct from the stiff willow bedding pad. The original fox panel remains on the anatomical left shoulder; the new rabbit pelt is not worn through Day 40. Bare feet, no head covering, existing bark waist panels and small pelvic pad remain.
The trial dart is always blunt and unfletched through Day 40. No second dart, jointed point or fletching appears. The local adult retains his own stone-pointed hand spear. Keep watchers north of the west-directed practice line, clear of the cast and retrieval space. Neanderthal anatomy must retain the R18 cranial and compact robust-body distinctions without caricature. No new camp building, moved hearth, supplied fallback bench, bright full moon or neighbour provisions is introduced by art.
Days 41–45: staged shelter work — 5 October 2026
Each daily picture uses the original Day 1 identity/style reference independently. The selected moments show inspection (41), lifting the condition-checked retting bundle (42), selecting light forked members (43), seating the first bare return frame (44), and beginning partial cover (45). The grass back panel is removed for these work moments; the narrow fox panel stays on the anatomical left shoulder. No completed coat, hunting point or fletching is introduced.
The existing northwest shelter footprint, covered side and heavy fallen-limb bearing remain. The light rail stands beside the retained limb on two small forks; it does not raise the heavy wood. Day 44 has three bare ribs and four stock ribs. Day 45 has all seven ribs and only partial lower/middle return cover; the upper junction and southeast front remain unfinished. The outdoor hearth is outside the pictures, never moved inside. These views are cropped scenes, not replacement maps.
The three reference plates describe material sorting, a general construction skill and the shelter design family. The more complete cutaway is a general concept, not a claim that Day 45 achieves it. Reflection 04 uses the Day 44 bare-frame cutoff, modest food, one blunt unfletched dart and the deferred lever ambition. Its first render was rejected for an invented skin mark and missing fox panel; the replacement again uses the original identity reference. No rejected output becomes an input.
The commission gallery records selections, full prompts, limited reference roles and exact PNG source-copy hashes.
Days 46–50: exposure, approach and wearable coverage — 5 October 2026
The five scenes use the original Day 1 identity/style reference independently: nut selection in the accessible circuit (46), a distant canid investigation from the clean side (47), an aborted ordinary-spear approach to two red-deer hinds (48), a lift check of the separate grass front panel before fitting (49), and dry walking adjustment with paired core panels and the limited rabbit crown piece (50). No prior or rejected daily rendering is used as input.
Clothing follows the moment: the old back panel is worn for Day 46 dry gathering, put aside during Day 47 rain/dirty-flank work and Day 48 hunting approach, and removed for Day 49 construction. The new front panel appears only as the Day 49 workpiece, then worn with the old back panel on Day 50. Both are flexible hanging grass with light paired retaining rows and separate cord support, not stiff willow bedding or fine cloth. The Day 50 crown pad is one allocated rabbit pelt, with a loose forehead/back band, exposed ears/face and much nape. The separate narrow fox piece stays on the anatomical left shoulder. Feet remain bare.
The Day 47 animal is separated from the upright traveller by open ground, not attacking or forced away by a depicted strike. Day 48 carries the plain integral wooden point, with no atlatl, hunting dart, stone point or acquired deer hide. The shelter visible in later scenes retains its footprint, heavy limb and old side, plus the covered/repaired return slope. The entrance baffle appears only after its Day 49 work and remains a small movable offset bundle beside a clear southeast passage. No indoor hearth, new map landmark, log house or winter guarantee is introduced.
The Hunting Approach manual plate explains observation and reassessment in generic terrain, not a surveyed map or numerical hunting recipe. Its clothed teaching figure does not extend the traveller’s wardrobe. Selected images, any retries and exact PNG source-copy hashes are in the commission gallery.

09_reference/lunar-calendar.title: Lunar Calendar
09_reference/lunar-calendar.content:
Lunar Calendar
Fictional epoch and practical rhythm
Arrival is near a new moon. For author bookkeeping, set the model’s new-moon epoch to Day 0, immediately before the first numbered day. This is a new setting choice, not an astronomical reconstruction of a dated 40,000 BP sky.
Use a mean phase cycle of approximately 29.53 days and schedule alternating full/new reviews at the nearest narrative day to each half-cycle. Research Register supplies the astronomical context. The period is a bookkeeping approximation, not a local ephemeris.













































Half-cycleApproximate milestoneReflection0Arrival · Day 1 near new moonReflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 11Day 15 · full moonReflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 152Day 30 · new moonReflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 13Day 44 · full moonScheduled; text not yet written4Day 59 · new moonScheduled; text not yet written5Day 74 · full moonScheduled6Day 89 · new moonScheduled
Narrative and illustrations
A full moon can contribute light when weather and terrain permit; it does not make night travel safe or eliminate cloud. At new moon there is no bright lunar disk lighting the camp. Do not insert a visible full moon into a scene because the art would look attractive.
Daily moon fields are modelled, not claims that the traveller observes the sky every day. Check them and the weather when drafting a night scene. No existing image is edited solely because these metadata fields are added.
Survival titles use Moon N Day M, with the original subtitle retained. Continuous day metadata preserves chronology, demonstrations and inventory replay. Moon 1 begins on continuous Day 1; the next labelled moons begin on the rounded mean new-moon days: Day 30 starts Moon 2 Day 1, Day 59 starts Moon 3 Day 1. Thus successive labelled moons can have 29 or 30 days. The daily moon_day and moon_cycle_model fields are derived, not independent counters. The small phase-rounding window is deliberate bookkeeping, not a precise observed new-moon instant.
The arrival reflection is at the end of Day 1 near the epoch, not another astronomical new moon. Later reflections occur at the rounded half-cycle milestones;
Continuous day numbers preserve chronology. A moon-cycle count supplements them; the original four-week “Month” outline labels are planning blocks, not physical lunar periods.
Reflection cutoffs and bookkeeping
A reflection belongs to the end of its milestone day and uses only that snapshot. Day 15’s vessel is still cooling and untested; Day 30 has first erratic casts but no second nettle batch, twining sample or fallback-site reconnaissance.
The helper tools/lunar_calendar.py supplies the deterministic author model. tools/update_views.py updates daily phase fields and reflection snapshot tables; the validator checks milestone days and snapshots. Narrative prose remains authored and must be revised deliberately if a source day changes. Reflection pages never enter stock replay as additional Survival days.

09_reference/month-two-outline.title: Month Two Outline
09_reference/month-two-outline.content:
Month Two Outline
The author approved this outline on 3 October 2026. It is a planning framework, not an extension of the event ledger. Month 2 means the next four narrative weeks, Days 29–56, following the first twenty-eight-day block. Daily entries, acquisition dates and new capability pages will be built from this approved framework after establishing the area map. Dates below identify broad phases; they do not force a successful experiment on a particular day.
Where we want to be on Day 56
The traveller is still alone, but his camp, clothing and working routines have begun to support a colder season. He has made the atlatl into a useful practice system through his own work. It has not made him a skilled hunter or erased the advantage of experienced local spear users. The neighbours have noticed his improvement and sometimes choose to watch. They have not joined him, supplied him or agreed to protect him.
The month’s main question is: can one person turn a precarious camp into a more resilient way of living before cold and diminishing harvest access outrun his labour? The answer is a qualified improvement. Winter survival remains the next pressure; he has not accumulated enough food or clothing to declare that problem solved.























































AreaProposed end statePractical limitShelterA compact, substantially enclosed sleeping space with stable framing, improved weather cover, a controllable entrance, whole-body dry bedding and an unobstructed way out, earned through several work sessionsCold-weather performance needs inspection and repair; combustion remains outside this combustible enclosure, and winter readiness is not assumedClothingFirst useful covering across most of the core, combining a coarse plant-fibre outer wrap, insulation and individually acquired small pelt panels; rudimentary head and foot protectionIt needs maintenance and drying; it is not a full fur coat, waterproof suit or dependable severe-winter outfitFoodGathering still supplies most energy; traps and fishing make intermittent contributions. Aim for roughly 7–10 days of edible reserve at the current rationThis is a target to test against actual yield, not a guaranteed delivery of nuts every day or a winter storeFire and waterBetter protected dry fuel and tinder, a maintained spare ignition provision and a second tested bark-vessel routeRepairs and renewed ignition still cost time; pottery is not the only means of treating waterProjectilesA functioning thrower, two serviceable practice darts and a repair/spare provision, with noticeably better release and groupingSuitable shafts, attachments and practice must be earned; no automatic numerical range, accuracy or killing powerHuntingSeveral deliberate attempts have exposed approach, wind, terrain, retrieval and lone-hunter limitationsA large animal is not a required kill; target proficiency is not field proficiencyPotteryPreferred modest result: a small unglazed vessel survives firing and repeated water-holding checksCooking and thermal-cycle performance remain separate tests; repeatable production is not establishedDefenceBetter awareness, accessible equipment, an alternative retreat route and a small independently supplied emergency shelter/cacheWarning and escape improve; he cannot defend property or hold off several determined peopleContactDifferent individuals show avoidance, warning, indifference or curiosity; late observers see the projectile gap narrowingNo alliance, recruitment, shared instruction, trading or communal provisions
The starting constraints
Read Survival Ledger before drafting each day; First Month Ledger preserves the opening inventory. The Day 28 state includes:

2.59 kg of edible hazelnut kernels, roughly five days at the recent half-kilogram daily use. This excludes shells and does not represent a month of food.
16 kg of usable dry fuel, roughly three days at recent ordinary consumption, before extra firing or colder-weather demand.
2.6 m of loose nettle cord and 0.8 m of bark cord, plus 16 m of uneven single yarn. Yarn is not a substitute for tested load-bearing line.
44 g of prepared nettle fibre, a replacement wooden spindle and 0.7 m of reserved sinew thread. Significant new clothing, bindings and traps need further collection and processing.
One experimental fish cage, three deadfall trials, a damaged snare already removed from service, a repaired bark vessel and a leaking pot retained only as a specimen.
An assembled but untested atlatl, two green shaft candidates and a small feather lot. There are no finished darts.
Very limited clothing: bark panels, a small pelvic pad and the narrow fox shoulder panel. The first-month fox skin has already been allocated; it cannot become another garment.

The second month cannot repeat first-month hazel yields indefinitely. Falling availability, weather and territorial boundaries should begin to affect the gathering circuit. Cooler weather can also slow drying and fibre processing. A material’s elapsed calendar time is never its acceptance test.
Four phases
Days 29–35 — Make room for the next month
The first priority is continued food, water, fuel and warmth. Atlatl work proceeds alongside those needs, rather than filling the whole day.
Technical work: inspect the shaft candidates, make an expendable practice projectile only when its condition permits, and establish a clear range with an earth backstop away from occupied routes. Short controlled attempts reveal release or fit problems. Introduce a marked wooden reference staff and simple comparison records. Start a further independently collected fibre batch early, while using current fibre carefully. Repair the windward shelter cover and make a small mat or insulating bed layer before attempting a large garment.
Defence: identify an alternative site and route before needing them. Protect spare tinder and usable fuel. Keep the spear reachable during vulnerable work and ensure clothing and essential implements can be taken quickly. Spread brush for a windbreak or to make one approach more visible, not as an impregnable wall. Maintain the separation of food, dirty processing, waste and bedding.
Narrative movement: he sees local people overlooking his part of the valley or passing within sight of his camp. They do not attack, but their attention removes any comforting assumption that he is hidden. He decides what he would abandon to get away. This does not create a theft or injury that the ledger must silently absorb.
End of phase: preliminary casts and small practical camp improvements; new fibre and ceramic trials started but unfinished. A clothing problem is already being worked on, rather than postponed until a hunt supplies a hide.
Days 36–42 — Curiosity without admiration
Technical work: continued short practice sessions; diagnose shaft straightness, engagement, release and attachments one change at a time. Improve the existing fish cage’s closure, weave gaps, anchoring or location after inspection, with catch and empty checks recorded. Test a revised small-game mechanism on non-animal loads before putting scarce cord back into service. Process newly acquired pelts while they are useful; stitch patches and trial softening/conditioning on small pieces. Prepare small ceramic comparison samples and let drying proceed while other work continues.
The first observed atlatl use: a few neighbours notice practice on open ground, outside both camps. One watches the lever and the dart’s flight with clear interest. The curiosity is about its operation; it does not mean they have been impressed by the result. A strong, practised adult makes a few hand-thrown casts with his own spear. His throws are visibly more forceful and much more accurate than the traveller’s unstable attempts. The traveller loses the comparison despite the device’s potential.
Keep this encounter brief and wary. People recover their own equipment; nobody lends a spear, gives a lesson or supplies a point. Individual robust physique, long practice, good equipment and the traveller’s poor form explain this result. It is not a species-wide law about strength. A different local person may warn him away from a route or gathering patch later in the week. Curious observers do not speak for the whole group.
End of phase: the traveller has learned what his proposed advantage actually needs. He returns to material and technique work, without being accepted as a teacher. Clothing and camp repairs continue to matter more than proving himself to an audience.
Days 43–49 — The hunting problem is larger than the weapon
