Hunting work: one scouting outing maps tracks, wind, approaches and safe exits. A later approach to red deer, already present in the setting, fails when terrain or an alert animal exposes him. Another attempt may end without a cast because the shot or retrieval would be poor. He can experiment with his ordinary spear and later a tested dart; he does not have companions to move animals, cover another exit, help with recovery or defend him during processing.
The narrative should show why a stronger throw would not solve those problems. A promising opportunity can consume half a day and leave him hungry with no new hide. Failed outings must reduce work elsewhere or draw on a finite reserve. Do not provide several simultaneous workshops while he is away.
Technical work: use the failures to decide which improvement is worth making. Continue target practice, shaft repair and tracking observations. If sound material, adequate binding and joint trials permit, a separately made stone-pointed spear becomes an optional upgrade; the knife’s light-work hafting success does not certify it. Fishing and small-game capture remain more accessible supplements than ambitious deer hunts.
The first worthwhile small ceramic firing occurs only when samples are dry and extra fuel has been collected. A wet spell or repeated ground frost exposes gaps in bedding, covering and drying arrangements. Some craft work is delayed so he can maintain warmth and ordinary supply.
Defence incident: an animal investigates the dirty-material flank or food-handling area. He notices in time and withdraws or guards his distance; the outcome is neither a heroic predator kill nor proof that fire deters everything. Improve waste handling and the warning arrangement afterwards. A serious bite or spear wound is not needed to communicate the risk.
End of phase: hunting is now an observed labour and coordination problem. The first substantial core covering is in use, and experimental items have either passed limited checks or been kept out of service.
Days 50–56 — Progress that someone else can see
Technical work: repeat the useful settings instead of starting another invention for its own sake. Improve dart consistency, release and grouping. Maintain the fish cage and the small number of active traps he can inspect. Test the ceramic survivor through repeated water holding; retain the bark treatment route. Repair clothing after actual walking, damp weather and work. Evaluate the food and fuel buffers against the colder routine.
Hunting: a modest opportunistic success is possible if the preceding entries earn it, but the recommended outline does not require a deer kill. Small catches can supply useful meat and pelt patches without ending the food problem. Missing the right opportunity remains a valid outcome, even as target performance improves.
Renewed interest: a familiar observer returns or deliberately waits near the practice place. The traveller’s casts are now recognisably steadier and more useful. At a distance he can repeatedly control, the gap has narrowed enough to sustain attention. The strongest local thrower remains better overall. A longer look, a gesture towards the hook or a cautious request to see another cast provides the ending; no one joins his camp or becomes an apprentice.
End-of-month decision: he must choose how much of the remaining autumn to allocate to food and clothing, how much to projectile practice, and whether staying at this exposed camp is still wise. Interest is a possibility for later contact, not protection against a change of mood.
Technology priorities and overlooked foundations
The lowest barriers are processes he can attempt with his current edges, fire, cordage and natural objects. They still cost suitable material, labour and trials. The month should develop a few connected lines rather than catalogue everything possible.













































































PriorityLineWhy it matters nowPlausible work and dependenciesEssentialFibre and strong cordNearly every useful upgrade competes for the same small stockCollect and process new batches; compare hand-made cord with plied yarn for the intended load. Cold retting and joins need inspection, not a fixed deadlineEssentialInsulation, clothing and shelterCold and wet threaten every other projectCoarse twined mats, a wind-resistant outer wrap, replaceable dry insulation, small pelt panels and fit tests. Allocate hides and binding explicitlyEssentialFood reserve and protectionExperiments and hunting outings need a bufferBetter basket closures, dry raised/protected storage where achievable, separated portions and loss checks. Extend acorn processing cautiously; wet meal is not a durable rationEssentialAtlatl and hunting practiceMain technical and social story, with no automatic advantageCompatible darts, stable release, maintenance, tracking, approach and recovery. Matched trials precede hunting relianceEssentialDefence, warning and retreatPossessions and fire cannot make a lone man secureSight lines, accessible spear, predictable exit, secondary shelter and a small cache supplied from his own inventorySupportingPersonal measurement and recordsImprove comparisons before precision tools or cooperationMarked reference staff, retained clay samples, counted batches and repeatable targets. His perfect memory retains observations; physical standards make dimensions and comparisons repeatableSupportingSplitting and simple woodworkingEfficiently produce splints, handles and stakesA wooden mallet and wedges, selected straight grain and controlled splitting, using existing cutting tools. No large-log cabin or sawmillSupportingWater and ignition redundancyOne failed vessel or damp kit should not force an immediate crisisSecond modest bark container after testing; spare dry tinder and a maintained ignition provision. Every cord allocation countsLimited experimentImproved ceramicsLearn why the first vessel failed, with modest fuel exposureSmall comparable bodies, thickness/drying/firing changes, one controlled factor at a time, then a small vessel. No assumed kiln or cooking-pot productionConditionalPelt conditioningDry rawhide alone is poor long-lived clothingCompare repeated working and a species-appropriate dressing/conditioning route on scraps. Fresh animal inputs must come from his own catches; no old unrecorded brain or fat storeStretchA crude equal-arm balanceCompare small material batches if volume comparisons prove inadequateOwn wooden beam, cord, containers and reference objects. It provides relative mass, not accurately realised grams; defer if it displaces warmth or food
A simple pounding/grinding surface for acorns is another useful low-barrier refinement of work already started. It earns attention if shelling and size reduction are actual bottlenecks. A fish net, stone lamp, large tanning vat, bow, kiln or substantial perimeter fence each has more material or labour costs than the bare idea suggests; none is needed as a Month 2 milestone. Metallurgy, agriculture and domestication remain later branches.
Clothing without a convenient large hide
Start with a plant-based solution to wind and exposed core, while captures supply additions. A coarse wrap or mantle is a different proposition from spinning and weaving metres of fine cloth. Matting, stuffing and replacement of dry insulation can use much coarser locally tested material. Wet or compacted stuffing may perform poorly; mobility, drying and chafing have to be observed.
Independently caught rabbits and other already established small quarry supply individual skins, meat and occasional sewing inputs. Each skin is small. Several may improve chest, back, head or foot protection; they cannot simultaneously furnish a coat, bag, boots and bedding. Aim for useful core coverage assembled from mixed materials. Provide sufficient plant-based covering even if pelt returns disappoint, rather than making survival depend on a fixed number of captures.
Make early foot protection a modest field trial. Wrapped coverings or a coarse sole with replaceable insulation can relieve cold and rough-ground exposure but can also slip, stay wet or abrade. They do not instantly become fitted waterproof boots. A head covering and better bedding may offer more benefit per unit of scarce material than another decorative fur strip.
The recommended ending uses no required large-mammal pelt. A successful self-hunt would open another branch, but its hide still needs processing and its meat creates urgent preservation or disposal work. It must not become a solved winter outfit the same afternoon.
Defence as a continuing constraint
The local people have generally warned or watched, not attempted to kill him. He has no grounds to assume their intentions are permanently benign, and no realistic ability to defeat several skilled adults. Their knowledge of his camp’s area is itself consequential.
Defence therefore concerns noticing, avoiding, leaving and surviving exposure after leaving. Shelter improvements should allow him to leave quickly. Keep a ready bundle of essentials instead of imagining he can carry the whole workshop. The alternative site needs its own surveyed water access, shelter work and a small dry provision; moving supplies there reduces what remains at the main camp. An escape cache is not a second full inventory.
A simple non-injuring noise warning is worth a small trial if it is made without consuming necessary trap or shelter cord. False alarms, weather and exhaustion limit it. No injurious perimeter traps, underground gauntlet or palisade appears as a substitute for people. Fire stays outside the debris shelter; a larger blaze can consume the fuel reserve and advertise his location.
Allow the fear to alter decisions: shorten a practice session when watched, leave a contested patch, inspect an approach before concentrating on stitching, or keep a valuable object at camp rather than taking it to another uncertain meeting. Show costs and restraint, not an attack every few days.
Rules for the atlatl comparison and contact
The atlatl launches a matched dart, not an arbitrary heavy spear. Local adults throw their own spears by hand. Compare the two users and complete weapon systems honestly; do not turn unlike heads, masses and target conditions into a numerical energy test. The early local casts should visibly outperform his in practical reach, control and useful impact. Later progress is clearest in repeated grouping and stable flight rather than a single lucky longest throw.
Different adults can have different responses. Larger robust build and stronger practiced movements may contribute to the selected local expert’s advantage, along with decades of experience and better prepared equipment. Do not claim that every Neanderthal is larger or stronger than every sapiens. The traveller may improve equipment faster than bodily technique. Hunger, cold, clothing interference and arm fatigue can also affect sessions.
The first curious encounter arises from people seeing practice; he does not immediately make another persuasive visit to their camp. He keeps the flight path away from them, lowers the equipment before anyone approaches and ends the session if the distance becomes uncomfortable. We can show curiosity in actions without translating a precise sentence or inferring agreement.
All materials, tools, food, clothing and improvements come from his own work. No trading, gifts, loans, communal meals, collected cast-off equipment, scavenged group kills or recovery of the abandoned spindle enters this month. He can see what others do and recognise their competence, but no instruction or labour from them subsidises his output. Their spear demonstrations use and retain their own equipment. Acknowledging their skill and limited gestures do not become shared production.
Labour, seasonal pressure and branches
Protect ordinary supply first. A typical day might require 4–6 hours for food, water, fuel, checks and camp work, leaving 1–3 hours for one principal project and a brief practice session when conditions permit. These are draft planning allowances; later daily events must show real collection, processing, travel and repair costs. Rest and sleep remain necessary. Long hunts, firings and bad-weather repairs replace craft work, not accumulate on top of it.
Use repeated routines in the ledger without retelling identical scenes. Select different narrative problems: a rope join, a cold morning, a contested route, a failed approach to prey, a promising clay specimen or a watcher waiting for another cast. A successful incremental improvement can stand without an obligatory failure immediately beforehand.





































If this constraint dominatesConsequence for the outlineNut returns or access worsenMore gathering, cautious acorn work and use of the finite reserve; postpone a firing or demonstration. Reaching the preferred food buffer is no longer guaranteedNew fibre is still unsuitableContinue coarser tested binding/material routes and reduce project scale; no finished textile or repaired snare appears from an unfinished retPelts are scarcePlant-based core covering, bedding and exposure limits carry more of the thermal burden. Large hunting remains a choice, not a convenient delivery mechanismThe ceramic trials fail againRecord the improved diagnosis and keep bark boiling; the preferred vessel outcome can slip without blocking the month’s essential workA hunting opportunity failsNo carcass, skin, sinew or calories are credited. Target skill may still improveLocal pressure increasesEnd meetings or leave a route; use the retreat provision if necessary. No violent victory or new social arrangement is forcedThe projectile gap narrows slowlyPreserve clear improvement over his own baseline and modest observer interest; no need to surpass the best local hunter on Day 56
Pages to add when the days establish them
Existing pages such as Atlatl Dart, Projectile Testing, Measurement and Records, Simple Cordage, Acorn Leaching, Pottery and Fur-On Pelt Clothing can develop as demonstrated work warrants it. Their current metadata stays unchanged until an authored event establishes the relevant milestone.
Candidate new subjects include dry insulating plant material, prepared dressing stock, a marked measuring staff, wooden wedges and mallet, a coarse mat or mantle, foot coverings, a non-injuring warning device and a distinct pelt-conditioning process. These are prospective titles, not newly acquired capabilities. Apply Category Specification to the actual subject: stocks are materials, practiced control is a skill, the object is equipment, and a distinct production route or continuing arrangement is a process/system. Extend existing pages when that avoids duplicating the same method.
Evidence informing the proposal
R17 and R21 in Research Register support taking hand-thrown weapons and local expertise seriously; neither predicts a particular fictional adult’s result. John Whittaker’s coaching account explains why release, engagement and technique require practice. It informs the learning problems, not a guaranteed one-month performance curve.
Harrison’s experimental pottery firing report supports examining local bodies, preparation and firing as an experimental sequence; it is not evidence for this valley’s clay or fuel yield. Smithsonian Museum Conservation Institute’s bibliographic record on buckskin preparation identifies conditioning and working as distinct from simply drying a hide. It does not establish a fur-on recipe for these small animals or transfer a whole tanning operation into an afternoon.
The exact new methods, local plant suitability, hunting performance and storage losses need targeted evidence checks when the daily work is drafted. The outline establishes desired questions and modest outcomes, not validated field instructions.
Approved direction
The author approved the four-phase arc: independent survival and cold-weather preparation lead the month, with a disappointing early atlatl comparison and growing late interest; mixed-material clothing requires no deer kill, and pottery remains conditional. Days 29–50 are now drafted. Continue day by day from the latest Survival Ledger, introducing capabilities only when the work and its tests occur.
Geographic reference
Use Valley Map for the Day 28 terrain, camp layout, contact route and provisional travel allowances. Month 2 facilities appear only after their sites are selected and their construction and supply are recorded.
Drafted opening week
Days 29–35 record the first phase; their daily illustrations were subsequently added on 4 October 2026. The personal measurement/food account, experimental casts, new retting batch, bedding trial, weather repair and fallback-site reconnaissance are completed in text; reliable dart performance, fibre output, fired ceramics, clothing coverage and a supplied refuge remain unfinished.

Moon 1 Day 29 - A Margin Before an Experiment
Moon 2 Day 1 - Six Attempts and No Advantage
Moon 2 Day 2 - They Know Where to Look
Moon 2 Day 3 - A Small Pattern for the Cold
Moon 2 Day 4 - A Way Out Is Not a Refuge
Moon 2 Day 5 - Rain Finds the Weak Places
Moon 2 Day 6 - A Pad, a Short Trial, and a Smaller Reserve

Moon-cycle reviews
Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1 appraises the opening constraint after first trials, before Days 31–35. The next full-moon review is scheduled for Day 44, with another new-moon review on Day 59. Use the actual completed-day state then; scheduled reflections force no catch, cooperation or success. “Month Two” remains the approved Days 29–56 planning block rather than an exact lunar month.
Drafted continuation: Days 36–40 / Moon 2 Days 7–11
The opening of the second phase now exists in text. The first observed comparison occurs on Day 37: operation draws attention, but the practised local adult’s own hand-thrown spear clearly outperforms the traveller’s erratic dart. Day 39’s warning at an occupied nut patch prevents that curiosity becoming implied permission or protection. No supplies, tools, instruction, trading or cooperation are gained.



































DayRecorded developmentRemaining limit36Repair the cage’s rear cap, screen long grass, remove a loose rear-seat projectionRetention and slow-fit checks only; no new catch or garment37First watched atlatl use and two superior local hand-spear castsUnequal qualitative comparison; four erratic own casts, no lesson38Own deadfall catch, prompt food and pelt care, non-animal mechanism checkMeat eaten; pelt remains unfinished, no dressing stock39Withdraw from occupied patch, check carry order, test a flexible grass edgeSmaller harvest; no refuge, no full covering40First dry-fit-tested grass back panel and another small fishFront core, head and feet remain exposed; no rain/casting test
At Day 40 the author model has 1.31 kg of kernels and 24 kg of usable dry fuel. The food buffer remains below even the Day 28 starting stock; do not fund a long hunt or firing from an invented surplus. Loose line and yarn have also tightened: 0.6 m nettle cord, 2 m single yarn, 24 g prepared nettle fibre and 0.7 m sinew remain. The new retting batch, rabbit pelt and two clay samples are still incomplete. Projectile A is still green, blunt and unfletched; B is a bowed blank.
Next priorities, Days 41–42: accessible gathering and, if needed, cautious extension of the established acorn route; appraisal of the shelter and available construction materials; condition-led fibre extraction when samples justify it; and care of the new pelt. A short private projectile trial fits only within that survival budget. A second dart needs separately accepted stock. A broader covering needs new material. Supplying the fallback site remains a missing defence task. Ceramic sample readiness may be checked, but firing requires extra fuel, drying and time.
Adjusted Days 43–49 work allocation: several recorded construction sessions for a compact enclosed sleeping shelter, weather cover, whole-body bedding and better clothing take priority. Short scouting and unsuccessful or aborted hunting approaches retain the wind, terrain and lone-hunter lessons, without displacing the build. Weather and an animal investigation put costs on work and waste handling. Refuge provision and a ceramic survivor remain conditional; defer firing if ordinary fuel, dry workspace or labour is inadequate. No catch or progress is forced to occur on a particular date.
Retained Days 50–56 ending: more consistent casts and grouping can draw renewed interest while the local expert remains better overall. Compare with his own baseline; there is no sudden adoption or alliance. The 7–10-day food buffer is still a target, not an assured result. The next reflection remains scheduled for continuous Day 44 (Moon 2 Day 15), using that completed day’s state.
Day 40 audit: immediate cold-season priority
The user’s winter concern prompted Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit. This adds an explicit shelter programme to the remaining outline; it creates no construction, stock or event before Day 41. The earlier phase descriptions remain the approved narrative arc, subject to the survival-first work allocation above. An open lean-to, modest bed and exposed front/head/feet cannot serve as the planned winter solution. Select a sound site and frame, record the cover and insulation inputs, inspect ordinary weather failures and repair them. Keep combustion outside the proposed small combustible sleeping enclosure. Day 44’s reflection should appraise this work and its food cost; Day 56 should show substantial improvement without declaring winter solved. Acquisition remains independent and contact cautious.
Drafted Days 41–45 / Moon 2 Days 12–16
The audit’s shelter priority now has earned work: assessment on Day 41, condition-led retting stop and small acorn charges on Day 42, independently collected frame stock and partial fibre output on Day 43, a limited return framework on Day 44, and extra ribs with partial covering on Day 45. The old occupied side is retained, the southeast exit stays usable and combustion remains outside. Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15 appraises Day 44 before the Day 45 cover and new line.
Day 42’s four private casts remain erratic. Day 43 declines to follow deer tracks because building and food own the day; no hunt, kill or neighbour aid is forced. All new acquisitions are independent. Remaining Days 46–49 can include a deliberate but budget-limited scouting/hunting lesson, the planned animal investigation and further core protection, conditional on food and weather. Ceramic firing may be deferred.
At Day 45 the model retains 0.93 kg edible kernels, 24 kg dry fuel, 32 g prepared fibre, 1.4 m loose cord and 4 kg coarse cover. The Day 41 acorns are all processed and eaten. Food collection, the upper roof junction, weather checks and better front/head/foot insulation now govern the next decisions. There is still no supplied refuge, second vessel, spare ignition kit, second dart, reliable winter coat or alliance. Later atlatl interest remains an intended arc, not an accomplished result.
Drafted Days 46–50 / Moon 2 Days 17–21
The roof meets its first showers: Day 46 completes the upper overlap, Day 47 finds and repairs an inward leak, and Day 49 adds a movable offset entrance baffle with a clear exit. Clean bed renewal is separately allocated. A large canid investigation on Day 47 replaces yarn work with vigilance and cleanup; no attack, theft, injury or predator kill is forced.
Day 48 combines short scouting with an aborted ordinary-spear deer approach. Wind/footing, alert animals, screened recovery and solo observation matter more than nominal reach. It produces no cast or hide and reduces gathering. The green blunt dart stays at camp. New yarn sessions and hand cord earn a separate grass front panel on Day 49. Day 50 allocates the entire existing rabbit pelt to a limited dry-use crown pad. Most front/back core now has a coarse screen, but sides, limbs, face, ears, much nape and feet remain poorly protected.
Day 50’s four private casts do not establish a narrowing local gap; renewed interest belongs to the remaining Days 51–56, after repeated work. The model retains 0.94 kg kernels and 26 kg dry fuel, 4 g ready fibre, 4 m single yarn, 1.2 m nettle line and 0.5 m sinew. No stored meat/acorn meal, second dart, firing survivor, spare ignition, second vessel or supplied refuge exists.
Next allocation: prioritise attainable food yield and drying, a limited foot-protection trial, redundant ignition/water and independent retreat provision. Keep hunting short and conditional; another attempt need not succeed. Shelter and garment weather maintenance remain ongoing. Defer pottery or a second projectile if food, stock or labour cannot support them. The 7–10-day food target remains a goal, not an end-of-month guarantee. The next phase reflection is continuous Day 59.
Technology-led Days 51–55 / Moon 2 Days 22–26
The author’s 7 October course correction brings routine survival into the background while keeping constraints credible. The new sequence develops a small workshop and a useful demonstration:



































DayTechnical questionRecorded result and next dependency51Can wedges produce useful stock with existing stone edges?One mallet, two wedges and a rough willow board blank; ignition preparation follows52Can local plant stock stay beneath the foot?Experimental pair holds after heel adjustment on level dry ground; incline creep limits use. New coarse line supports later work53Can ignition be reproduced with independent parts?Complete kit B produces ember and flame after tension/alignment checks in a dry camp test54Can a second vessel incorporate the first one’s lessons?Cold hold and two supported heat trials; pattern retained, ceramic comparison still ahead55Can a repeatable release earn attention?Better own-baseline grouping and limited observer curiosity; no exchange, lesson or alliance
Exact routine yields and stocks stay in Survival Ledger, without repeated narrative recitation. The food reserve is still short. Both ignition kits and both vessels remain at main camp; retreat provision remains an open task. No large hide, stored meat, new ceramic survivor or hunting dart is introduced.
Day 56 can appraise the month’s independent improvements and choose the next project without forcing an acquisition. Revisit foot retention; select a genuinely suitable second shaft before added projectile fittings; plan ceramic comparison pieces with protected drying and sufficient fuel; and decide how to provision a retreat without merely moving the only service from camp. Growing contact must remain voluntary and materially unsubsidised through the approved Month Two arc. Later passage lengths should follow projects rather than every supply round. The next lunar reflection remains Day 59.

09_reference/research-register.title: Research Register
09_reference/research-register.content:
Research Register
How to use this register
Sources support specific claims, not entire pages. Notes list identifiers in sources and explain their scope in the body. All links below were checked during the October 2026 editorial review. Abstract-level access is identified where full text was unavailable. The author summaries are paraphrases.
Historical evidence elsewhere does not establish presence in the fictional valley. Modern safety guidance identifies constraints; it does not certify an improvised prehistoric process. Uncited manufacturing specifications remain physical-reasoning drafts requiring experimental review.
R01 — Neanderthal cordage
Hardy et al. (2020), Direct evidence of Neanderthal fibre technology and its cognitive and behavioral implications, Scientific Reports. Direct evidence includes a three-ply inner-bark cord fragment from Abri du Maras. This supports fibre-working ability, not a known spindle inventory for every group. Abstract/search access; publication identity also checked through PubMed.
R02 — Regional coexistence
Djakovic, Key and Soressi (2022), Optimal linear estimation models predict 1400–2900 years of overlap between Homo sapiens and Neandertals prior to their disappearance from France and northern Spain. Full article inspected. The overlap is modelled at regional scale; direct local interaction remains unresolved. Do not translate it into a dated occupation of this fictional valley.
R03 — Manufactured adhesives
Identifying Palaeolithic birch tar production techniques: challenges from an experimental biomolecular approach (2023), Scientific Reports. Supports ancient manufactured adhesives and the difficulty of distinguishing production methods. It does not establish the traveller’s pine-resin recipe or its strength.
R04 — Hard-hammer handaxes
Taphonomic and technological analyses of Lower Palaeolithic bone tools from Clacton-on-Sea, UK (2022). Includes discussion of rough handaxes manufactured with hard-hammer removals and later refined work with organic percussors. Supports making antler an improvement or method option, rather than an absolute gate for every biface.
R05 — Fire treatment and wood strength
“Fire hardening” spear wood does slightly harden it, but makes it much weaker and more brittle (2016). Abstract inspected. The experiment found increased hardness alongside reduced strength and fracture performance. Effects depend on treatment and wood; do not represent charring as a universal durability upgrade.
R06 — Drinking water treatment
CDC: About Water Treatment Options When Hiking, Camping, or Traveling. Full page inspected. Clear water can carry pathogens; observable boiling is a practical endpoint. Boiling does not remove chemical contamination. Temperature-time claims need an actual means of verification.
R07 — Meat drying and pathogen control
USDA FSIS: Jerky and Food Safety. Guidance inspected. Low-temperature drying can leave pathogens alive. Its modern validated procedures use controlled heat and measurements absent from the initial camp. The revised narrative consumes game on the catch day and does not count unvalidated smoked meat as stored rations.
R08 — Plant identification
BfR: Odour test with pitfalls — what to look out for when collecting wild garlic. Supports the danger of confusing edible plants with poisonous lookalikes. Neither smell alone nor broad rules about colour, leaf count or bitterness are a reliable general identification procedure.
R09 — Giant hogweed
National Park Service: Species Spotlight — Giant Hogweed. Describes sap-associated phytophotodermatitis. This plant is removed from the setting’s friction-fire materials. Other plant candidates still need species-specific review.
R10 — Palaeolithic ceramics
Smithsonian Museum Conservation Institute record: Dolni Vestonice ceramics and Smithsonian Human Origins artifact scan. Supports Upper Palaeolithic ceramic objects at this later site. It does not support the old claim that Neanderthals made ceramic figurines, or demonstrate cooking pottery in Iberia at 40,000 BP.
R11 — Nettle extraction
Bacci et al. (2011), Effect of different extraction methods on fiber quality of nettle, Textile Research Journal. Abstract inspected. Compares several extraction routes. Cultivar, temperature and processing conditions limit transfer to wild prehistoric plants. The narrative’s twelve-day ret is an authored successful batch, not a universal duration.
R12 — Planetary defence
NASA: Planetary Defense — DART. Supports kinetic-impact deflection as one demonstrated modern technique. It does not imply that this fictional massive object can be diverted by a DART-sized mission or that the protagonist can skip space-industry dependencies.
R13 — Food composition reference
UK Government: Composition of foods integrated dataset (CoFID). Dataset landing page inspected; no specific cell was extracted for the first-month ledger. The ledger uses a declared approximate energy model rather than presenting a database-derived value. Wild plants, edible yield and activity requirements need separate research.
R14 — Neanderthal fire-making
Sorensen et al. (2018), Neandertal fire-making technology inferred from microwear analysis. Supports an interpretation of flint-and-pyrite fire-making evidence. It does not prove that every group relied on the same method or needed the traveller to supply ignition knowledge.
R15 — Cantabrian environmental mosaics
Fernández-García et al. (2023), Reassessing palaeoenvironmental conditions during the Middle to Upper Palaeolithic transition in the Cantabrian region, Quaternary Science Reviews 301, 107928. Publisher abstract and highlights inspected during the illustration pass. The synthesis describes variable conditions and open meadows with scattered forested areas during MIS 3. It supports the general landscape mosaic, not the exact fictional terrace, a reconstructed day’s weather, productive hazel patches at this date or the species of every illustrated plant. The valley’s local resource abundance remains an author assumption.
R16 — European spear-thrower evidence
Lombard (2022), Re-considering the origins of Old World spearthrower-and-dart hunting, Quaternary Science Reviews. Publisher abstract/search material inspected; full text not accessed. Direct European examples discussed include Le Placard around 25,852–25,432 and Combe Saunière 1 around 24,619–23,934 calibrated BP. These later finds do not establish the absence of earlier perishable devices, or any particular Neanderthal group’s toolkit. The narrative treats unfamiliarity at 40,000 BP as possible, not proven.
R17 — Hand-thrown wooden spears
Milks et al. (2019), External ballistics of Pleistocene hand-thrown spears: experimental performance data and implications for human evolution, Scientific Reports 9, 820; author-hosted paper. Publication abstract/search material inspected. Experienced throwers using replica Schöningen wooden spears demonstrate why such weapons should not automatically be described as short-range ineffective tools. This is an experimental comparison involving much older artefacts, not direct measurement of late Neanderthal performance. It does not predict an inexperienced traveller’s advantage.
R18 — Neanderthal anatomy for illustration
Smithsonian Human Origins: Homo neanderthalensis and How do we know these are different species?. Pages inspected. Use low foreheads, prominent brow ridges, projecting midfaces, large noses and compact robust builds with relatively short distal limbs. The intended contrast is anatomical, not a sapiens face in fur. Ordinary upright posture and capable hands preserve their humanity; individual hair, skin, clothing and expressions remain casting choices.
R19 — Wild-game meat and parasites
CDC: About Trichinellosis and CDC DPDx: Trichinellosis. Pages inspected. Foxes and other wild carnivores can carry Trichinella. Cooking and avoiding raw-to-cooked contamination matter; drying, smoking or freezing wild game are not reliable substitutes. Modern temperature verification requires a thermometer. This supports explicit uncertainty in Day 23’s immediate cooked-food decision, not an unsupported claim that the whole catch was contaminated or that visual doneness certifies safety.
R20 — Fixed overhand loop
NetKnots: Overhand Loop Knot. Instructions inspected. The terminal eye is formed by tying an overhand knot in a doubled bight of the same cord. It is a fixed loop and can jam; it is not the same as a single-strand stopper knot. Returning the long line through this eye forms a separate adjustable-loop arrangement. The source supports the fixed knot’s structure, not prehistoric attestation, natural-fibre strength or a validated spring-snare installation.
R21 — Neanderthal wooden and stone-pointed spears
Rots et al. (2021), A Leaf Point Documents Hunting with Spears in the Middle Paleolithic at Hohle Fels, Germany, Mitteilungen der Gesellschaft für Urgeschichte 30, DOI 10.51315/mgfu.2021.30004. Publisher-indexed text inspected; the full page was blocked by verification. Functional analysis supports stone weapon tips and hafting in European Middle Palaeolithic contexts. A pointed stone alone does not establish spear use.
Russo et al. (2023), First direct evidence of lion hunting and the early use of a lion pelt by Neanderthals, Scientific Reports 13, 16405. Full relevant sections inspected. The Siegsdorf lesion is interpreted as a wooden thrusting-spear wound; the discussion notes continuing wooden weapons alongside likely stone-tipped weaponry. Both choices are therefore defensible. This supports the fictional group’s composite spear, not an exact reconstruction of a northern Iberian specimen, a claim about relative prevalence at 40,000 BP, or automatic superiority in every task.
R22 — Atlatl engagement and coached practice
John Whittaker, How to throw with an atlatl, World Atlatl Association, revised 20 April 2023. Relevant coaching text inspected. It describes coordinated motion and engagement/release errors through modern observation and teaching. This supports distinguishing early disengagement, dragging and movement problems. It does not certify a particular green hazel specimen, predict a one-month learning curve or establish prehistoric regional presence.
R23 — Twining structure
Western Australian Museum: Twined Stitch and UCL Digital Egypt: Basketry techniques. Relevant text inspected. These museum/university descriptions distinguish paired crossing working elements around foundations from coiling and simple interlacing. They support the structure described in Twining, not its attestation in the fictional valley. The willow-strip, nettle-line bedding pad is an authored trial.
R24 — Palaeolithic plant bedding
Wadley et al. (2011), Middle Stone Age bedding construction and settlement patterns at Sibudu, South Africa, Science 334, 1388–1391, DOI 10.1126/science.1213317. Indexed abstract material consulted. It reports plant bedding around 77,000 years ago. This establishes plant bedding as more than a modern imagined comfort, but does not demonstrate woven mats, Iberian plant species, the traveller’s insulation performance or a transferable insect-repellent treatment. The present dry-grass/leaf choice remains a setting assumption and physical trial.
R25 — Lunar phases and reflection rhythm
NASA Science: Moon Phases. Relevant phase-cycle material inspected. A new-to-new phase cycle averages about 29.5 days; new and full moon alternate approximately halfway through it. This supports a roughly fortnightly rhythm, not a perfectly repeating fifteen-day half-cycle. The Day 0 epoch, rounded review days and sky/weather choices are fictional author bookkeeping, not a reconstructed ancient calendar. No dated 40,000 BP ephemeris is asserted.
R26 — Plant coverings and the limits of analogy
South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology: Clothing, relevant clothing and grass-mat sections inspected on 5 October 2026. The museum describes grass and other plant material in the much later Iceman equipment, and explicitly treats the former grass-cape interpretation as disputed. It does not establish a cape at the traveller’s date. The handbook therefore does not invoke an “Ötzi cape” as proof for its authored back panel.
Textile Museum of Canada: Rain Cape, collection record, search-indexed material inspected; direct retrieval failed. The record identifies grass/bark and twined/knotted construction. British Museum: palm-leaf rain cape, search-indexed object description inspected. These later ethnographic objects show that plant coverings can be wearable equipment. Their plants, structures, climate and treatment do not supply the local grass recipe, waterproof performance or prehistoric attestation. Days 39–40 remain small fictional physical trials supported structurally by R23.
R17’s hand-spear experiment and R22’s coaching account were rechecked for the Day 37 comparison. They inform the role of experience and movement, not that particular adult’s exact force, a species-wide strength rule or the traveller’s rate of improvement.
R27 — Earlier indirect spear-thrower evidence
Coppe, Taipale and Rots (2023), Terminal ballistic analysis of impact fractures reveals the use of spearthrower 31 ky ago at Maisières-Canal, Belgium, Scientific Reports 13, 18305. Abstract and relevant introduction/results inspected on 5 October 2026. Experimental fracture comparisons support the authors’ inference of spear-thrower delivery around 31,000 BP. This is trace-based evidence from stone armatures, not a preserved thrower. It supplements R16 without establishing a device in the fictional valley or proving absence at 40,000 BP.
R28 — Sewing and clothing chronology
Gilligan et al. (2024), Paleolithic eyed needles and the evolution of dress, Science Advances 10, eadp2887. Abstract and thermal-origins material inspected. The synthesis reports early eyed needles around 40,000 cal BP in Siberia, around 38,000 in the Caucasus and by about 26,000 in Europe, while discussing fitted clothing made with other sewing tools. These are preserved examples, not universal invention dates. The traveller’s Day 12 needle is a knowledgeable experiment, not established local kit. The source does not validate his blank, labour estimate or winter garments.
R29 — Very early plant bedding
Wadley et al. (2020), Fire and grass-bedding construction 200 thousand years ago at Border Cave, South Africa, Science 369, 863–866, DOI 10.1126/science.abc7239. Indexed abstract inspected. Reports grass bedding at least 200,000 years ago. This extends R24 without establishing woven mats, Iberian materials, insulating thickness or a transferable pest-control recipe.
R30 — Neanderthal specialized hide-working tools
Soressi et al. (2013), Neandertals made the first specialized bone tools in Europe, PNAS 110, 14186–14190, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1302730110. Indexed abstract and experimental-description material inspected; full-page retrieval returned verification. Rib lissoirs are interpreted as specialized hide-working tools using form, wear and replication. This supports sophisticated material work, not a complete reconstruction of clothes or a tanning recipe for the traveller.
R31 — Pleistocene woodworking and revised dating
Leder et al. (2024), The wooden artifacts from Schöningen’s Spear Horizon and their place in human evolution, PNAS, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2320484121. Indexed abstract inspected. The rich assemblage makes woodworking visible beyond a single spear. Revised age for Schöningen hunting spears indicates intensification of Neanderthal cooperative behavior around 200,000 years ago (2025), Science Advances, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.adv0752, indexed abstract inspected. This proposes a younger age than the roughly 300,000 BP estimate in older literature. Do not present the earlier estimate as settled or the revision as a universal starting date for wooden weapons.
R32 — Cold exposure and enclosed combustion
CDC: Preventing Hypothermia and CDC Yellow Book: Heat and Cold Illness in Travelers, relevant prevention and heat-loss material inspected on 5 October 2026. Wet exposure, wind, inadequate insulation and depleted energy matter even without extreme subzero weather. This supports a joint shelter/clothing/food assessment, not a calculated survival limit for the authored lean-to.
CDC: Carbon monoxide poisoning — questions and answers, indexed institutional summary inspected. Wood combustion can accumulate CO in enclosed or partially enclosed spaces. The proposed small combustible sleeping enclosure keeps its hearth outside; a smoke opening alone is not a certified exhaust design.
R33 — Acorn processing and storage analogy
National Park Service: Tools and Trade and Plant Use, relevant ethnobotanical material inspected on 5 October 2026. These institutional accounts describe stored acorns, pounding and water leaching in Californian Indigenous practice. They support treating untreated acorns, processed meal and storage as separate stages. They do not supply the Iberian oak species, local yield, a validated hot-stone/bark-vessel procedure or the traveller’s labour and edible-output estimates. The Day 42–44 small-charge results remain authored trials; reduced astringency is not a universal chemical acceptance test.
R34 — Wildlife attractants and the limits of deterrence
National Park Service: Wolf Ecology, safety and ecology material inspected on 5 October 2026. The institutional account describes wolves associating accessible food with human-use places and advises avoiding approach and unattended food remnants. It supports cleanup and distance as parts of risk management. Yellowstone animals, habituation history and visitor equipment are not a reconstruction of prehistoric Iberian wolf behaviour. The Day 47 canid visit, departure and lack of loss are authored events; speech, a spear and an outside fire are not guaranteed deterrents. Cleanup does not make the camp predator-proof.
R35 — Red-deer vigilance and cover
Jayakody, Sibbald, Gordon and Lambin (2008), Red deer Cervus elaphus vigilance behaviour differs with habitat and type of human disturbance, Wildlife Biology 14, 81–91. Abstract and study methods inspected on 5 October 2026. The field study records differing vigilance with cover and human disturbance in the modern Scottish Highlands. It supports treating animals as responsive participants rather than fixed targets. It does not establish the fictional animals’ detection cue, a universally safe distance, weapon efficacy, cooperative-hunting requirements or an ancient Iberian behaviour schedule. The solo logistical analysis and Day 48 choices remain authored physical reasoning.
R36 — Wooden splitting tools
National Park Service: Mountain Life field-trip guide, historical-tools section inspected on 7 October 2026. Describes wooden gluts driven with a maul in much later Appalachian woodworking. This supports the wedge/striker pairing, not Palaeolithic Iberian attestation, local wood suitability, exact geometry or measured labour savings. Its unrelated historical claims are not adopted. Day 51’s small-billet result remains authored physical reasoning requiring replication.
R37 — Footwear layers and replaceable plant lining
South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology: Clothing — Shoes, shoes section inspected on 7 October 2026. Describes the much later Iceman’s bast mesh, grass padding and leather layers, with a need to renew wet padding. This supports separating retention, lining and outer sole functions. Day 52 has no comparable leather: its plant soles, fit, traction and comfort are authored experiments, not the source design’s reported performance or prehistoric regional attestation.
Next evidence work

Specific local palaeoecology and species availability, including hazel productivity.
Experiments for bark containers, fire-kit woods, fibre yields, bone needles and thin rawhide loads.
Clay-body and firing trials with known temperatures and measured porosity.
Spindle throughput measured over harvesting, preparation, spinning and plying.
Projectile construction, shaft moisture, flexural behaviour and practice requirements.
Practical sanitation and first aid under the setting’s material constraints.

Record new evidence before marking a consequential procedure publication-ready.

09_reference/revision-record.title: Revision Record
09_reference/revision-record.content:
Revision Record
5 October 2026 — skill artwork and Day 40 audit
The artwork commission covers five daily scenes for continuous Days 36–40, Plant-Fibre Clothing and the 29 previously unillustrated skills. The two existing skill plates are retained. Daily scenes use the original Day 1 identity/style reference; manual plates use the original digging-stick style. Geometry references have limited roles. Selected PNGs are copied unchanged, with prompts, rejections and hashes retained in _Artwork/2026-10-05. Mechanical, anatomical or inventory errors are replaced by fresh renders, not cumulative edits. The pre-art notes are archived in _RevisionArchive/2026-10-05-before-skills-and-days-art.zip.
Added Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit and evidence records R27–R32. The comparison separates Palaeolithic working tools from later experiments and dependable seasonal capacity. Month Two Outline now prioritises an enclosed dry sleeping shelter, insulation, food and protected fuel across the remaining work; hunting and firing compete for the same budget. The chronology and limits of the Day 12 eyed needle are clarified. Civilisation Roadmap links the audit. These planning/reference changes add no construction, stock, contact benefit or completed daily event.
This is a dated work record. Counts, folders and descriptions in earlier sections reflect the state at that revision. Category Specification, Topic Index and Dependency Register describe the current organisation.
1 October 2026
The user authorised revision of the setting, style guide, templates, first month, reference dependencies and civilisation roadmap. The original dependency-focused purpose remains central, with narrative used to expose implementation difficulties and local expertise.
A pre-revision archive preserves all 118 original Markdown notes, the old combined context and the two export scripts: _RevisionArchive/2026-10-01-before-revision.zip. This includes the user’s uncommitted note contents; Git history was not used as a substitute for this archive. Obsidian settings were not changed.
Main editorial choices

Retain approximately 40,000 BP and northern Iberia; label the exact valley, weather and encounters as authored choices.
Clarify transit as living-body-only, and provide prior practical training without granting mastery.
Make hazelnuts the explicitly accounted first-month staple; game remains supplemental.
Replace unsupported water pasteurisation, raw-organ meals and preserved-meat stock with observable boiling and same-day game consumption.
Retain a ceramic pot trial but remove it from the indispensable route. A wooden whorl provides the first spindle demonstration.
Separate successful construction from operational performance and community adoption.
Replace deterministic status displays with cautious, reciprocal first contact.
Track state through daily events and verify conservation automatically.
Expand the mission roadmap through measurement, surplus, institutions, industry and space systems.

Remaining limits
Reference notes have been edited for factual claims, dependency logic and practical scope. They remain drafts where detailed experimental verification or identification evidence is absent. The resource ledger is an internally consistent author model, not a demonstrated survival plan. Open setting decisions remain in Setting Specification.
The archive contains the removed prose and historical claims. Existing daily filenames are retained so external links do not silently break; displayed titles may describe the revised emphasis.
Completed revision and checks
The working vault now contains 145 Markdown notes: 28 daily entries, 99 capability notes, five era notes, and the setting, authoring and reference material. All 28 days and the pre-existing material, skill, tool and technology notes were revised. Unsupported claims were replaced with bounded methods or explicit research gaps; the archive preserves the earlier text.
The first month ends with an assembled but untested wooden thrower, green shaft candidates, a replacement spindle, a modest nut reserve and tentative reciprocal contact. Successful pottery, dependable fishing, large-game hunting and community-wide adoption are not claimed.
The default graph contains 141 prerequisite edges. Validation checks all wiki-links and linked headings, metadata and duplicate YAML keys, acyclic dependencies, demonstration order, asset and food quantities, fuel, and work-hour sums. In-memory defect checks confirm that it detects cyclic tool requirements, gifting the same spindle twice and reusing consumed rabbit meat. Archive integrity was checked against all 121 stored files, including the 118 original notes.
Generated acquisition views exclude undemonstrated pages and separate local observations from the traveller’s capability dates. Food disposition is explicit, so calorie estimates do not depend on prose wording. The export tools use only numbered content folders, sort days naturally, validate before writing and produce text parts outside the content graph.
These are editorial, structural and model-continuity checks. Dataview rendering has not been tested inside Obsidian, and the improvised techniques and assumed local resource yields have not been experimentally validated. No website was built or published in this revision.
Next substantive work
Develop reciprocal learning and seasonal preparation before asserting a stable specialist economy. Priorities are protection for feet and exposed skin, dependable shelter and water equipment, food yield and storage evidence, shared communication, and repeated independent production. Projectile trials are one bounded experiment within that work.
Later chapters should change scale to weeks, seasons and projects as appropriate. The expanded roadmap restores the original technical mission, with explicit route comparisons and acceptance tests through industrial production and spaceflight.

09_reference/survival-ledger.title: Survival Ledger
09_reference/survival-ledger.content:
Survival Ledger
Scope and assumptions
This is a generated author continuity model, not measured survival performance. Daily frontmatter is the source of truth. Regenerate with python tools/update_views.py after editing events, then run python tools/validate_vault.py. The original prose is preserved in the pre-revision archive.
The fictional valley has productive hazel patches within a manageable daily circuit in early autumn. Kernel weights are edible mass after shelling; shells are excluded. Gathering and processing take daily labour. Recorded collection is a setting assumption requiring palaeoecological and field review, not a demonstrated regional yield. No imported seed, store or unexplained food subsidy is counted.
The energy column uses explicit rough working assumptions: 6 kcal/g hazelnut kernels, 1.5 kcal/g dressed game or fish, and 2 kcal/g wet acorn meal. These are not extracted food-composition values (see R13 in Research Register). Wet meal composition is especially uncertain. Against an illustrative 2,500–3,500 kcal/day activity requirement, early days can be deficient and later entries are not all assured adequate. Cold, body size, illness, digestibility and work could change the balance. Internal conservation cannot prove long-term health or a realistic gathering rate.
Fuel is dry usable wood mass, excluding wet collected material. Collection and burn estimates are authored, without calorimeter or weather validation. Water columns count completed treatment and untreated drinking separately; evaporation and most other water uses are not modelled. Explicit additional processing-water estimates appear below and are not drinking intake. Initial untreated drinking is a survival risk, not a recommended procedure. Zero untreated intake means treatment was recorded, not independently certified.
Daily food continuity
Kernel use includes an explicitly recorded damp loss on Day 13. All retained fresh game is cooked and consumed on its catch day, including the limited 0.90 kg fox lot on Day 23. Discarded trimming is excluded from edible inputs. Acorns enter as 0.40 kg unprocessed input on Day 17, convert to 0.65 kg wet meal on Day 18 (water adds mass), and are eaten over Days 18–19. The input lot contributes no calories before processing.

Fuel, drinking water and time

Important events and limits

Day 3: first ignition; the fire kit needs continued maintenance. Stored heat is not permanent access to fire.
Days 4–5: first vessel heat trial fails, then repair permits recorded boiling. Day 9 wear interrupts treatment; Day 10 repairs restore it.
Day 7: the awl works. A needle attempt fails; a usable eyed needle follows on Day 12.
Days 9–10: the first rabbit pelt becomes a small carrying sling; the load test is under one kilogram.
Days 11–16: a small pot is shaped, dried, fired, cooled and rejected for leakage. It remains a non-food sample; no ceramic cooking asset is counted.
Days 4–20: the nettle batch is retted, processed in two halves, and partly made into cord. The first processing date is Day 16; elapsed time is twelve days, not a universal recipe.
Days 13–14 and 24: small hides become a pelvic pad and narrow shoulder panel. They do not amount to a winter coat.
Day 21: a wooden spindle bypasses ceramic success. A few metres of single yarn do not demonstrate a sustained productivity improvement.
Day 23: the damaged snare is removed. A limited fox meat lot is cooked and eaten, with additional work and fuel; its damaged pelt becomes a limited panel on Day 24.
Day 25: the first approach is rebuffed. Samples and the first spindle are abandoned during retreat, not accepted gifts. Day 26 records self-repair and planning, with no fibre exchange or shared teaching. No communal provisions or adoption are established.
Days 27–28: a replacement spindle is made. Two green dart candidates, a feather lot and an untested wooden atlatl remain distinct assets.

The earliest practical review should test food yield, bark-vessel reliability, heating-stone selection, fibre throughput and rawhide performance. Research Register records the evidence gaps; Civilisation Roadmap keeps later development tied to surplus and verified capabilities.
Current period and unfinished work
This ledger continues through Day 55. First Month Ledger preserves Days 1–28 and their ending inventory; it is not the current stock view.
Days 29–35 establish a personal comparison record, an experimental green blunt dart, a small practice ground, a separately allocated bedding pad and retreat reconnaissance. At that week’s end, the new nettle batch and clay samples remain unfinished. No community supplies, hunting point, second completed dart, escape cache or supplied refuge are acquired in the opening week. The kernel reserve changes from 2.59 kg on Day 28 to 1.71 kg on Day 35; the dry-fuel stock ends that week at 19 kg.
Latest recorded ongoing states:

Eight casts in two modest repeat series show improved grouping against opening own trials; broad patch and changing wood limit inference.
Two adults watch; one approaches a little and gestures at engagement. No handover, coaching, supplies, independent replica or alliance.
Dart A is blunt unfletched and unseasoned by proof; B remains a bowed blank, unused feathers remain separate.
Two ignition kits and two bark vessels stay at main camp; fallback bench still needs provision.
Plant footwear has only a limited level-dry result; shelter, coverings, clay samples and unfinished fibre retain their recorded limits. Food buffer remains short.

09_reference/valley-map.title: Valley Map
09_reference/valley-map.content:
Valley Map

This is the author’s spatial reference for the fictional valley in World, showing the camp and known landmarks at the end of Day 28. It is not a map the traveller has drawn, a real archaeological site, or a surveyed plan. Compass bearings, the arrangement of resource patches and the walking allowances below are new setting choices made on 3 October 2026. They consolidate the earlier descriptions without adding possessions or events.
The illustration provides the visual overview. The written relationships below govern continuity when an enlarged icon or decorative label is ambiguous. Terrain and ownership beyond the explored area remain unknown. R15 supports the broad regional landscape mosaic, not these particular locations.
Orientation and water
North is up. The larger river runs generally north to south through the eastern part of the map. The smaller stream runs west to east and joins it below the camp terrace. Both the traveller’s camp and the Neanderthal clearing are on the western side of the larger river. The established contact route requires no main-river crossing, boat, bridge or wading invention.
The camp sits north of the small stream, on a sheltered, drained terrace west of the main river. Ground around the shelter falls towards the southeast. Its entrance faces broadly southeast. The familiar Day 1 view looks out towards the east/southeast: the shelter is on the left and the valley drops away to the right. Other cameras can reverse screen positions while retaining these bearings.
The drinking-water seep is uphill and west/southwest of camp, at the upstream end of the small-stream route. The retting/rinsing pool is farther east and downstream of that collection point. Retting, clay work and dirty animal processing never move upstream of drinking collection. Appearance is not a water-safety test; Hot-Rock Boiling still applies.
The fish cage is at the accessible western margin of the larger river, just downstream of the tributary confluence. It is anchored in a shallow, locally sheltered margin and can be retrieved from stable footing. Its cylinder, inward entrance funnel and removable rear cap remain the design in Woven Fishing Trap. Neither an illustration nor this map creates a weir across the river. Day 22’s opposite-bank wolf is a transient sighting, not a permanent predator landmark.
Landmarks and travel allowances
These are provisional one-way allowances for a cautious, lightly loaded traveller from camp in ordinary daylight. They are author budgeting assumptions, not timings measured in the narrative. A loaded return, gathering, a trap check, a concealment pause or watching people adds time; poor weather and vigilance can lengthen every trip. Do not derive metres from the graphic.











































































LandmarkFixed relationshipOne-way allowance / useWater seepWest/southwest, upstream on the small-stream route5–10 minutes; collection and treatment are additional workRetting poolSouth/southwest, downstream of seep, before the confluence5–10 minutes; fibre work and rinsing remain separate from campFish trapSoutheast, western river margin below confluence10–15 minutes; checking does not guarantee a fishWillow and nettleAlong selected downstream tributary margins10–15 minutes to nearer stands; new harvesting needs inspectionClay bankTributary exposure southeast of camp, upstream of river confluence10–15 minutes; usable clay still requires testsGravel barEast/northeast, west bank of main river above confluence15–25 minutes; carrying stone back is slowerHazel and oakProtected patches west/northwest of camp10–25 minutes to nearer patches; the label denotes an area, not inexhaustible foodPine patchSouthwest, beyond the nearer stream margins15–25 minutes; fuel/resin gathering and transport add labourTrap circuitWestern terrestrial gathering area, near the nut patches10–20 minutes to the nearer trial sites, plus the circuit itselfRidge lookoutNorth of camp on the near/southern end of the rocky spur20–30 minutes; distant smoke can be seen beyond the ridgeMeeting groundNorthwest, beyond the spur’s western flank, short of the neighbouring living area40–60 minutes by the contact route; waiting and withdrawal are additionalNeanderthal clearingNorthwest of the ridge; same west-bank territory as the travellerBeyond the meeting ground; no permission to enter is assumedUpstream bendNorth/northeast along the west-bank river route35–50 minutes; Day 18’s old-antler excursion and carnivore-sign area
The trap-circuit label is deliberately an area marker. The three small deadfall trials have not acquired surveyed positions, and the damaged Day 23 snare is out of service. Do not read an active snare into the map. The upstream-bend label groups an excursion locality; it does not put the old antler at an active kill or establish a predator’s territory.
Resource icons show observed patches, not inventories, guaranteed seasonal yields or uncontested access. First Month Ledger governs what has actually been collected and retained.
Camp inset: fixed areas
The inset enlarges the camp and is not to scale with the main map. North remains up. It shows six areas already established by Day 28:

Shelter: northwest and upslope; a low leaf/bark/branch shelter under a thick fallen mossy limb. Preserve this structure rather than replacing it with a tent, hut or rock cave.
Craft spot: south of the shelter and west/upslope of the ordinary hearth. Its abrasion stone is a manageable ground-level stone, not a raised worktable.
Fire pit: southeast/downhill of the craft spot, outdoors and clear of the dry shelter. Leave an open access gap; no fire is brought beside the bedding for visual convenience.
Drying and processing: on the southern/southwestern dirty-material flank. The small drying frame and processing surface are separate from clean food and drinking-water handling.
Waste: farther southwest beyond that flank, on dry ground away from water collection and outside the stream bed. Future prose must account for removal and runoff, rather than treating a waste symbol as automatic sanitation.
Firing clearing: northeast of the ordinary hearth, separate bare ground well clear of shelter, drying frame and food work. It is the experimental outside firing place introduced on Day 14, not a kiln.

The inset’s miniature hearth and shelter symbols are exaggerated. They do not establish safe metre clearances. Future construction scenes must show an appropriate cleared buffer for their actual fuel, sparks and materials.
Contact route and retreat
Day 19’s smoke/firelight is observed beyond the ridge. Day 21’s cautious route follows the near slope to cover rather than entering the clearing. The main contact route leaves camp to the northwest, skirts the western flank of the spur, and reaches open meeting ground south of the Neanderthal clearing. It does not cut through their hearth/work area.
The concealed stopping-place for the traveller’s spear lies on that approach, south of and short of the meeting ground. He retrieves it on the retreat in Day 25. The map’s dotted line marks a remembered walking route, not an engineered road or safe corridor. The clearing’s occupants can see open ground and may control access to nearby resources. Nothing here guarantees neutral land.
No secondary shelter, supplied emergency cache or atlatl practice range has yet been built. The approved Month Two Outline will require choosing those sites through observation and work. A future range must have a clear flight/retrieval area and backstop, directed away from the river, contact route and occupied camps. A retreat site must be independently reachable and supplied; the map cannot grant it for free.
Use in later writing and illustration
For each new scene, name its location, compass view, slope/water direction and objects actually present at that moment. Check travel and return allowances before assigning the day’s work. At the camp, retain the inset relationships even when some features are outside the frame. At other locations, do not import camp furniture to make the scene recognisable.
Keep the landscape a mosaic of sheltered woods, open ground and rocky relief. Map ornament does not imply continuous forest, modern cultivation or a medieval settlement. The neighbouring clearing icon represents a maintained hearth and working ground; it specifies no permanent architecture or full group population.
Add a dated update when a fixed object or route changes. Keep the Day 28 map as a historical state; do not quietly draw completed Month 2 facilities into it. The machine-readable layout and full generation prompt are stored in _Artwork/maps/location-layout.json and the full original and correction prompts, _Artwork/maps/valley-day-28-v1-prompt.txt and _Artwork/maps/valley-day-28-v2-prompt.txt. Their normalised anchors express relative placement, not ground measurements. See Illustration Continuity for scene and character rules.
Dated additions after the illustrated state
The main picture remains a Day 28 map. Separate later Survival scenes and place plates illustrate the dated additions without changing that historical overview. The written bearings remain authoritative.

Day 29 selection / Day 30 preparation: the small practice ground lies west/southwest of camp, above the tributary and short of the western trap circuit. Casts face west into a local earth bank, with the river and contact route outside the intended flight line. The site requires reinspection; markers do not establish permanent safe access.
Day 33 reconnaissance: an alternative bench southwest of the pine patch has natural rock screening. The route follows western ground upstream of the seep’s head, then turns south along higher ground, avoiding a main-river crossing. Allow roughly 35–50 minutes one way in ordinary daylight, plus the return and inspection. Water is not established at the bench; it remains an unsupplied candidate, with no constructed shelter or cache.

These additions are new authored locations and time allowances, not points which were secretly explored on Day 28. Preserve the camp inset’s fixed arrangement while repairing the roof or adding a small pad to its existing bed.
Days 36–40: observed use without a new installation
The fish cage receives a rear-closure repair at its existing western river margin below the confluence. Day 37’s watchers stand north of the west-directed short practice line, and one local adult casts his own spear into the bank after the traveller stands clear. This is a temporary event, not a second practice range or new camp.
Day 39 finds people gathering at the western edge of the familiar nut circuit, short of the spur contact route. Their warning leads to withdrawal; it does not define a surveyed territorial boundary or move the neighbouring clearing. All craft and pelt work retain the camp inset’s clean/dirty arrangement. No refuge or cache exists at the fallback bench through Day 40. The Day 28 graphic remains a historical overview.
Dated shelter work: Days 41–45
The Day 28 artwork remains the early-state overview. Day 41 assesses the existing northwest camp shelter. Ten selected light members are gathered on Day 43. The Day 44–45 north/east return framework and partial cover rebuild the same footprint, preserving the southeast entrance, the retained limb and the old occupied side. No fire, craft, processing, firing or water feature moves. See Traveller’s Camp and Framed Debris Shelter for the dated construction state; this addition does not redraw the original map into a completed winter camp.
Dated observations and work: Days 46–50
The original map remains the Day 28 overview. The later shelter overlap and offset entrance bundle stay in the northwest camp footprint with a clear southeast mouth. The Day 47 canid visit is transient on the southwest dirty flank; the cleared sight gap is not a permanent predator territory or new road. Day 48 follows deer sign within the western gathering terrain, short of the occupied nut patch/contact route. It adds no new named site, camp, river crossing, surveyed deer trail or supplied fallback bench.

09_reference/vault-maintenance.title: Vault Maintenance
09_reference/vault-maintenance.content:
Vault Maintenance
Edit the source, then derive the views
Daily frontmatter contains demonstrated capabilities, assets, food lots, fuel, drinking-water quantities and work estimates. Reference frontmatter contains default requirements, alternatives and improvements. Do not edit the generated tables to change history.
Use these commands from the vault folder, in order:
python tools/update_views.py
python tools/validate_vault.py
python tools/export_context.py
The tools require Python 3 and PyYAML. Both were available during this revision. The root combine_files_full.bat performs the same update-and-export workflow when double-clicked; combine_files_parts.bat also creates text parts. Export validates the vault before replacing the previous full context.
update_views.py writes first-recorded demonstration dates into capability pages and derives First Month Ledger, Survival Ledger, Acquired, Dependency Register and Topic Index. The first ledger remains a fixed Days 1–28 view; Survival Ledger replays all days and shows the latest inventory. Preserve their logic in the generator if changing their prose. validate_vault.py reads without editing. It checks category folders, subtypes, domains, primary tags, metadata, duplicate YAML keys, links and heading targets, local illustrations, prerequisite cycles, demonstration order, food and asset conservation, fuel balances and work-hour sums.
After selecting a plate or moving an illustrated page, run python tools/update_artwork_galleries.py to refresh the original generation-batch galleries and the current equipment, skill, process and structure galleries. Original PNGs and full prompts stay in their generation folders; current page links follow the category organisation.
These checks do not certify species identification, material performance, the realism of labour estimates or historical presence. Read Research Register and the note’s evidence limits before treating a procedure as publishable.
Lunar reviews and page moves
Use Page Scope and Organisation when combining variants and object-specific assembly. Preserve stable canonical IDs, old name/path aliases, real image assets and exact historical prompts. The 4 October migration manifest records merged IDs and paths; original galleries use their actual recorded image rather than substituting a merged page’s primary image.
tools/lunar_calendar.py defines an approximate fictional epoch and milestone rhythm. update_views.py fills daily model phase fields and cutoff-specific reflection snapshots. validate_vault.py checks phases, reflection cutoffs/snapshots and place references as well as capabilities. Write/refine reflection prose deliberately after source-day changes; the table’s regeneration does not rewrite the judgement. No review creates another ledger day.
Exports and recovery
The full context includes Markdown only from numbered vault folders, in natural order. It excludes tools, Obsidian settings, archives and old exports. Split outputs are .txt files in _ContextExports, outside the content graph. INDEX.txt identifies the current set; old extra parts may remain and should not be included unless listed. A single unusually long note can exceed the approximate part size.
The initial prose archive is _RevisionArchive/2026-10-01-before-revision.zip. The category revision snapshot is _RevisionArchive/2026-10-02-before-category-revision.zip; it includes notes, helper scripts, artwork records, workspace settings and PNG fingerprints. The PNG files themselves remain unchanged in the vault. Inspect individual files to recover earlier prose; do not extract an archive over the working vault unless deliberately restoring that state. Revision Record describes the scope and choices, and the category migration map records former and current paths.
Adding a day or a capability
Use Category Specification and Page Templates. Give each note a unique stable id, one primary type/tag, a valid subtype and at least one recognised domain. Classify the subject rather than its complexity, history or development state. The category definitions and domain vocabulary are in tools/category_model.py. Use real filenames or aliases in wiki-links. Keep survival days consecutive, and use stable lot and asset keys. Positive events introduce stock; negative events use, lose or gift it. Zero-change asset events record condition of an existing object.
When moving or renaming a page, preserve the stable ID and useful old names/path aliases, update ordinary Markdown and gallery links, and rebase its relative image path. Regenerate views and exports. A category change does not create a new physical asset, demonstrate a missing skill or validate a process.
Food disposition is collected, consumed, processed or lost. Consumption reduces stock and contributes to the explicit energy model. Converting acorns adds a processed wet output separately; water gain is not additional food energy. Fresh game lots use catch-specific names such as rabbit-day29 and are consumed the same day in the first-month model.
demonstrates refers to the traveller’s own limited capability instance. Structures join that graph; places use locations_used, locations_observed and dated location_events rather than demonstration or stock events. community_demonstrates records observations or shared trials separately. If a listed default prerequisite has not been demonstrated, either provide the missing work or describe and encode the actual alternative route. Do not invent an acquisition date to silence the check.
A later period needs its own accounting scope. Change the same-day game rule only alongside a researched preservation method and storage model; change the daily narrative scale when seasons and projects become the useful unit.

Mission Coordination
The mission depends on people being able and willing to reproduce, maintain and extend capabilities. These social subjects follow the same categories as the physical handbook: a person’s ability is a skill, while coordinated arrangements are systems.






























SubjectPrimary categoryRole in the missionCommunication and ExchangeSkillEstablish shared meaning, observe responses and negotiate cooperationTeaching and Knowledge PreservationTechnology — systemDevelop learning and preservation that can survive the traveller’s absenceMeasurement and RecordsTechnology — systemMaintain shared references and observations that support comparison and replicationSanitation and Camp HygieneTechnology — systemCoordinate water, waste, handling and maintenance across the camp
These are linked capabilities, rather than duplicate copies in the Mission folder. Their pages describe limited demonstrations, unresolved questions and later requirements. Category Specification explains the conceptual split, Topic Index groups the related pages, and Civilisation Roadmap carries the mission through surplus, institutions, industry and space systems.
